Chapter 01 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 538, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal. The Periya Puranam has a total of two Kanda (sections) and thirteen Sarukkams (chapters). The first Kanda has five Sarukkams, and the second Kanda has eight Sarukkams. We have completed the first Kanda and its five Sarukkams. Now we will begin and contemplate the second Kanda.

The first Sarukkam in this second Kanda is Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam. In chronological order, among the thirteen Sarukkams in the Periya Puranam, this Sarukkam is the sixth. The Periya Puranam is a recorded work authored by Sekkizhar Peruman, based on the Thirutthondathogai, a holy hymn composed by Sundaramoorthy Swamigal, and structured to suit that form. There are eleven Thiru-verses in the Thirutthondathogai. In these eleven Thiru-verses, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal has praised various devotees and Nayanmars.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman composes these eleven Thiru-verses as eleven Sarukkams. He has structured the stories of the Nayanmars praised in each of those verses within their respective Sarukkams.

Thus, there are eleven Sarukkams for eleven verses, plus an introductory Sarukkam called Thirumalai Sarukkam. As an introduction, and with the thirteenth as the concluding Sarukkam called Vellanai Sarukkam, Sekkizhar Peruman has extensively composed the Periya Puranam into a total of thirteen Sarukkams.

In this manner, we have contemplated the first five Sarukkams, starting with the Thirumalai Sarukkam, which is the first Sarukkam of the Periya Puranam, followed by the four Sarukkams corresponding to the first four verses of the Thirutthondathogai.

Now, we move to the fifth verse in the Thirutthondathogai. Sekkizhar Peruman has named each Sarukkam based on the words found in the first line of each corresponding verse from the Thirutthondathogai.

Therefore, the fifth verse in the Thirutthondathogai begins with “Vambara Varivandu.” Accordingly, Sekkizhar Peruman has named this Sarukkam as Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam. The fifth verse of the Thirutthondathogai is as follows: Vambara varivandu manam naara malarum madhumalar narkondraiyaan adiyalaal penaa Embirann Sambandhan adiyaarkkum adiyen Eyarkon Kalikkaman adiyaarkkum adiyen Nambiran Thirumoolan adiyaarkkum adiyen Naattamigu Thandikkum Moorkikkum adiyen Ambaran Somasi Maaranukkum adiyen Aarooran Aaruril Ammanukku aale. This is the fifth verse of the Thirutthondathogai. In this holy verse, Sundaramoorthy Swamigal has praised six Nayanmars.

The devotees are as follows: Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar, Eyarkon Kalikkama Nayanar, Thirumoola Nayanar, Thandiyadigal Nayanar, Murka Nayanar, Somasi Mara Nayanar.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal sang about these six Nayanmars in the fifth verse of the Thirutthondathogai.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman, who named this Sarukkam Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, has arranged and sung these six stories within this Sarukkam. The first story arranged therein is the story of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar, which narrates his holy history. The fifth verse of the Thirutthondathogai begins with “Vambara varivandu manam naara malarum madhu malar narkondraiyaan adiyalaal penaa.” Embirann Sambandhan adiyaarkkum adiyen, thus Sundaramoorthy Swamy first praised Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Therefore, in this Sarukkam, the story of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar is the first Puranam. In chronological order, the story of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar is the twenty-eighth Puranam in the Periya Puranam. We are contemplating the holy lives of the Nayanmars according to the order of Thirutthondathogai, which is a collection, then Thirutthondar Thiruvandhadhi, which is a type of work, and then Periya Puranam, which is an elaborate work. In that sense, here too, we should contemplate in the same order. Before that, we should briefly contemplate the holy life of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar and then extensively, if we contemplate it as shown by Sekkizhar Peruman, it will pave the way for a good understanding of this holy Puranam. Based on this idea, let’s begin by briefly contemplating the Puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar.

The Puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar is a very extensive Periya Puranam.

Therefore, even the summary of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar’s Puranam is quite elaborate for us.

Now, let’s first contemplate Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. The Chozha kingdom, ruled by Chozha kings who steadfastly followed the ancient Shaivism and came from a lineage that never deviated from it, is the Chozha-land. The Kaveri river flows and enriches that land. The adornment and ornament of that land is the ancient town known as Kazhumalam. It is a very prosperous and excellent holy place where ancient families of Brahmins flourish. The beautiful streets in that town are.

This town is a holy place that floated above the floods that came during the twelve ages, without being submerged.

Therefore, this holy place has twelve names. These twelve names are Brahmapuram, Venupuram, Pugali, Venguru, Thonipuram, Poontharai, Sirapuram, Puravam, Sanbai, Kaali, Kochchayavam, Kazhumalam. These are the twelve names for that holy place. That holy place is currently known by the famous name of Sirkazhi. In that holy town of Sirkazhi, in the Brahmin lineage, in the Kauniya Gotra, lived a great man named Sivapada Hrudayar. Sivapada Hrudayar was a great person whose nature it was to perform austerities for the well-being of this world.

His wife, who also came from this unique Shaivite tradition, was a person of immense and rare glory, known as Bagavathiyar. Due to the excellence of her chastity, she understood her husband’s wishes and lived her domestic life accordingly, excelling in it. The lineages of both of them had traditionally followed the Shaivite path. They conducted their married life, knowing nothing else as a support other than the sacred feet of Lord Shiva.

In those days, the false religions of Jains and Buddhists were widespread in this world. Because of this, the sacred ash, which was the light of the primeval Shaivite path, was not honored here. Seeing this, Sivapada Hrudayar was deeply distressed. He also desired to have a child who would bring joy to his domestic life.

Therefore, Sivapada Hrudayar thought that the child he desired should be capable of refuting other religions and promoting the sacred ash. To have such a child, he worshipped at the sacred feet of Periyanayagi Ammaiyar and Thoniyappar, who reside in Thonipuram. and received a boon. By the grace of God, Bagavathiyamaiyar conceived. For the salvation of this world, they performed all the appropriate scriptural rituals and ceremonies for ten months with great care, and Sivapada Hrudayar rejoiced with his relatives in immense joy.

At this time, with the sun and other planets in their auspicious and powerful positions, with a good hora rising, on the day of Thiruvathirai, which was full of prosperity, the child who would cause the annihilation of other religions, allow the primordial Vaidika Shaivism to flourish, make the path of sacred ash uniquely excellent everywhere, fill Tamil Shaivism, make the glory of all directions overcome by the south, and make this earthly world prevail over the upper and lower worlds, so that current and future faults might be removed, and the heterodox paths of Jains and others would perish, the divine child, Shiva-bearing Pillaiyar, made his holy advent in Sirkazhi.

At that time, all the residents of Sirkazhi experienced immense joy. Without their knowing it, happiness abounded. Auspicious omens and good signs occurred everywhere. They beautifully adorned the holy mansion of Pillaiyar with auspicious decorations and performed good deeds. They performed many ceremonies according to the birth chart for ten days. They performed the naming ceremony on the auspicious day.

They placed the Lord, who resembled the rising sun, in a cradle, like a unique child on a lotus. They fed him milk and adorned him with sacred ash.

Thus, with praises of childhood stages like Thal, Sengkeerai, and Sappani, Pillaiyar grew for one year and reached the stage of toddling. When he was three years old, a special event occurred. The Lord, remembering His ancient state of never forgetting His feet, mercifully incarnated as Pillaiyar, yielding to the penance of Sivapada Hrudayar.

Therefore, Pillaiyar, who had no personal desires, incarnated here solely to reveal the nature of holy service to this world. In earlier times, Pillaiyar had remained in constant attendance upon the Lord.

Now, the awareness of being separated from the Lord and having come to this world would occasionally arise in Pillaiyar’s holy heart. Whenever this happened, he would weep with the indication of being separated from the Lord. In this state, when Pillaiyar, who is Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, reaches three years of age, a miraculous event is about to happen.

We will continue to contemplate the brief history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 02 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 539, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal. We are contemplating the brief summary of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar’s Puranam. In Shaivism, ‘Pillaiyar’ refers to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Therefore, wherever ‘Pillaiyar’ appears in the Periya Puranam, we must remember Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Generally, in common usage, there is a custom of calling Vinayagar as Pillaiyar. It is a Shaivite tradition to refer to Vinayagar as Mootha Pillaiyar (Elder Pillaiyar) and to honor Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as Pillaiyar or Aazhudaya Pillaiyar.

Thus, when Pillaiyar was in his third year, a special event occurred at that moment. On one auspicious day, Sivapada Hrudayar went to bathe, to complete his duties as prescribed by the Vedic rituals.

At that time, by the grace of Lord Shiva, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman also cried and followed his father. His father went behind him. Seeing this, as if in anger, his father forbade Thirugnanasambandha Peruman to come. Nevertheless, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stamped his small feet adorned with anklets and followed his father.

Therefore, his father took Thirugnanasambandha Peruman with him that day. Reaching the bank of Brahma Theertham, one of the sacred ponds in Sirkazhi, Sivapada Hrudayar made Pillaiyar sit on the bank.

Then, he entered the Brahma Theertham, bathed, and performed various rituals. To perform Agamarshanam, Sivapada Hrudayar immersed himself in the water. Even then, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman began to cry, citing his inability to remain there.

However, this was not the real reason for Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s weeping; he began to cry for the salvation of the world. As his previous consciousness of constantly remembering the Lord’s feet by rule surged, Pillaiyar, standing on the bank, wept for the salvation of the world, with tears overflowing, rubbing his eyes with his hands, and his lips trembling. With tears flowing from his eyes, without looking elsewhere, as if he recognized his higher connection, Aaludaiya Pillaiyar looked at the Thonipuram peak of the Lord, called out “Amme Appa” (Mother, Father), and cried out.

At that moment, Lord Thoniyappar, remembering his past devotion and to bestow his grace, appeared with the Goddess on the bull, coming to the bank of the pond. Recalling the great boon He had granted to Sivapada Hrudayar and Bagavathy Ammaiyar, or to bestow divine wisdom that would solely cherish His sacred feet, Lord Shiva instructed the Goddess to milk divine wisdom into a golden cup and feed it to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Accordingly, the Goddess came near Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, wiped his tears, and then, holding the golden bowl full of divine wisdom-infused milk, gave it to him, saying “eat this food,” and thus ended the child’s crying. Because he was nourished with this milk of wisdom by the one who is father and mother to all, this child became Aaludaiya Pillaiyar. Along with that, he became Thirugnanasambandhar, the unique embodiment of divine wisdom, unknowable even to all devas and sages. Pillaiyar, the foremost among ascetics, understood at that moment the two types of complete knowledge: the incomparable artistic knowledge of Apara and Para Gnanam, and the true knowledge that transcends understanding. He asserted that God and His devotees are the ultimate reality, and that the doctrines of other religions, which do not grasp this truth, are destined to perish. Sivapada Hrudayar, who had immersed himself in the water, completed all his rituals in a short time and came to the shore.

He saw Pillaiyar, who was overflowing with supreme wisdom. He angrily asked, “Who gave you this milk food?” and, fearing contamination, brandished a small stick, saying, “Show me who gave you this.” The little great one, Pillaiyar, with tears of joy overflowing, pointed with a finger of his raised hand towards the sky, where Lord Shiva stood with the Goddess on the bull, radiant with full divine wisdom and compassion. He then, with the exalted words of profound wisdom that filled and overflowed from within him, began to sing the holy hymn “Thodudaiya Seviyan,” a truthful and divine verse, identifying Lord Thoniyappar by his attributes and saying, “Is it not this Lord who did this to us?” In that hymn, he revealed the grace that Lord Shiva bestowed upon Ravana, demonstrating that even if people err, if they surrender, the Lord will graciously help them. He explains that Brahma and Vishnu worshipped and were saved, showing that Lord Shiva grants grace only to those who humbly worship, not to those consumed by ego. In that holy hymn, he also preaches that the paths of Jains and Buddhists are inferior paths that lead to blame.

Thus, Pillaiyar completed the holy hymn and concluded with the Thirkkaidaikkaappu (final blessing). Seeing the grace of the Lord, the Devas showered flowers from the sky. Celestial drums resounded. The Gananathas roared with joyous cries. The Lord, along with the Goddess, who is the boat for devotees to cross the ocean of birth, appeared in the sky and ascended to Thiruthoni. Seeing the Lord ascend, Pillaiyar followed Him and went to Thiruthoni.

His father, with clasped hands, rejoiced and danced. He understood the meaning of the hymn’s Tamil. Though he, the father, did not see the Lord uniquely as the child who followed Him did, he realized from the events that this was indeed the grace of Lord Shiva of Thonipuram.

So, he followed Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and entered the Thiruthonipuram temple. Witnessing and hearing this miraculous event, Brahmins and devotees gathered at the temple entrance. Pillaiyar saw the Lord and Goddess at Thiruthoni, sang a hymn saying “My Lord was here with Uma,” worshipped, and then departed from there.

The devotees and those gathered at the temple tower entrance took the sacred feet of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman upon their heads, worshipped him, and praised him in various ways, rejoicing. His father, Sivapada Hrudayar, carried Pillaiyar on his shoulder, and with everyone surrounding them, he returned to his holy mansion in a procession around the town.

At that time, auspicious instruments like conch and drum resounded.

That day, after residing in the holy mansion, he went to the Thiruthoni temple at night, worshipped the Lord and Goddess, and on the next day, after worshipping similarly, Pillaiyar went to Thirukolakka to worship Lord Shiva. We will continue to contemplate the brief story of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 03 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 540, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, after visiting the holy place of Thirukolakka and worshipping the Lord, began the hymn “Madayil Vazhai Paaya” and sang it, keeping rhythm with his hands. Pillaiyar, with his tender hands, kept time and composed this holy hymn.

At that moment, by the grace of the Lord, golden cymbals inscribed with the sacred five-syllable mantra, Sri Panchaksharam, appeared in his hands. Seeing them, Pillaiyar placed those sacred cymbals on his head, worshipped, rejoiced, and completed the hymn. Tumburu, Narada, and others also praised the excellence of the sound emanating from those sacred cymbals. As Pillaiyar walked with the sacred cymbals in his hand, his father carried him on his shoulder. He then went to Sirkazhi, worshipped Thoniyappar, and sang the hymn beginning with “Poovaarkkondrai,” set to the Takkaraga melody he had previously composed, accompanied by the sacred cymbals. He then returned to his holy mansion and, after giving darshan to the residents of that town, resided there.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s journey to Thirukolakka was his first holy pilgrimage.

Now, for the second pilgrimage, the holy birthplace of Pillaiyar’s mother, Bagavathy Ammaiyar, is the holy place called Thirunanipalli. Brahmins from Thirunanipalli came to Sirkazhi and worshipped Pillaiyar. Hearing the great news that Pillaiyar had received divine wisdom, Brahmins and others from other holy places came and worshipped Pillaiyar, rejoicing.

At that time, the Thirunanipalli Brahmins requested Pillaiyar to visit their region and worship the Lord in their holy place. Agreeing to this, Pillaiyar worshipped Thoniyappar, then sat down and set off towards Thirunanipalli. As the holy place Thirunanipalli appeared before him, Pillaiyar asked his father what that place was. His father said it was Thirunanipalli. Hearing that, while still on his father’s shoulder, Pillaiyar sang a hymn beginning with “Kaaraigal Koogai Mullai,” stating “Emdhai Mevum Nanipalli idhuthey, Idhanai ninaippavar vinaigal keduvatharkku aanai namathey” (This is Nanipalli where my Lord dwells; those who remember this, their sins shall be destroyed, this is our decree). In that hymn, he gracefully mentioned the words indicating lotus, palm, and groves.

The land of that village, which was previously arid, transformed into a coastal and forested region.

The Brahmins of that village bowed at Pillaiyar’s feet and worshipped him.

Thus, Pillaiyar resided in Thirunanipalli. On that day, Brahmins and devotees from Thiruthalaichangadu also came, bowed at his feet, and requested Pillaiyar to visit their village. Pillaiyar went to Thiruthalaichangadu, worshipped the Lord there, and sang a hymn. From there, he entered and worshipped Thiruvazhamburam, then went to the holy place Thiruchaikkadu and praised the Lord.

There, he worshipped by singing the hymn “Manpugar.” From there, he reached the holy place Thiruvenckadu, praised the three ponds, sang a hymn, and then, after worshipping Thenthirumullaivaayil, he reached Sirkazhi and praised the Lord. This was Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s second holy pilgrimage.

Now, for the third holy pilgrimage, after visiting Thirukuruhaavoor and praising the Lord by singing a holy hymn, he returned to Sirkazhi.

At that time, Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar and his musician wife, Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar, arrived in Sirkazhi. Pillaiyar went to meet them. They bowed to Pillaiyar, rose, and praised him. Pillaiyar spoke sweet words to them, saying, “Oh sir, we are blessed that you have come here.” He invited them to the temple and asked them to play the Yazh (lute) for their Lord there. Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar and his wife played the Yazh, spreading music that was praised by Vidyadharas and Gandharvas. Pillaiyar arranged accommodation for them and provided a splendid feast.

Yazhpanar bowed to Pillaiyar and requested, “Your Grace’s holy hymns, I shall play them on the Yazh. Please grant me the grace to always be with Your Grace and serve you.” Pillaiyar agreed to this request.

From that day onwards, Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar and his wife remained constantly with Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with unwavering love and friendship.

Now, for the fourth holy pilgrimage undertaken by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the divine intention arose in Pillaiyar’s holy heart to go to Thillai and worship the Lord of Dance. He conveyed this to his father, who also desired to accompany him. They worshipped Lord Thoniyappar, who resides in Sirkazhi, received his gracious permission, and set off towards Thillai. Along the way, they praised all the holy places they encountered, crossed fertile lands and marshes, and reached the bank of the Kollidam river. As the Kollidam river, scattering precious gems and corals, bowed and welcomed Pillaiyar, they crossed it. and arrived at the sacred boundaries surrounding Thillai. Along the path, ponds offered their lotus faces, and groves blossomed with fragrant flowers.

The sky, filled with sacrificial smoke, resembled a canopy of delicate blue silk.

Thus, he passed through the cultivated fields, worshipped the gardens, and arrived at the southern entrance. The Thillai வாழ் Andhanars (Brahmins of Thillai) and holy devotees came forward to welcome him into the holy city. Entering through the southern gate, he bowed to the sacred street, worshipped the gopuram, rose, and praised. He circumambulated the holy mansion, worshipped the Perambalam (great hall), and reached the Thiruvannukkan doorway. With hands clasped above his head, his heart melted with devotion as he entered, and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who was bestowed with true wisdom, saw the hall, and the unique dance of joy arising from the complete wisdom within. He worshipped it and praised the Lord of Dance, saying, “You have easily bestowed the Shiva-bliss that comes directly into my consciousness, even within the reach of the five senses in a physical form.” Due to the excellence of Lord Shiva’s rightful act, he placed the Thillai வாழ் Andhanars first and sang the hymn “Katraangkeriyompi,” worshipping.

After worshipping for a long time, he came out of the temple and went to reside in one of the four sacred streets that bestow great austerities. From there, he worshipped the Thiruvambalam.

Later, he went to the holy place Thirukalippaalai, worshipped, and sang a hymn. The Thillai வாழ் Andhanars, amazed at the fortune of being servants to the Lord of Dance, one day saw Thiruvetkaalam. appeared to Pillaiyar. Pillaiyar showed it to Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar. Pillaiyar worshipped the Thillai Vaazh Andhanars before they could worship him. He went with them, worshipped the Thiruvambalam, and sang the hymn “Aadinai Naaru Neyyodu Paal Thayir,” expressing the state he had witnessed in that hymn.

Then, he took leave and departed.

At that time, Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar requested Pillaiyar to visit his native place, Thiru Erukkathampuliyur, and other holy places along the bank of the Nivva river. Agreeing to this, he, along with his father, attendants, Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar, and Mathanga Choolamani Ammaiyar, proceeded along the Nivva river bank and reached Thiru Erukkathampuliyur.

At that time, Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar bowed to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and said, “This is the village of your servant.” Pillaiyar replied, “Oh sir, this place has performed immeasurable austerities in the past for you to be born here.” Then, after worshipping the Lord of Thiru Erukkathampuliyur and singing a holy hymn there, they proceeded to Thirumudhukundram, also known as Virudhachalam. He sang the hymn “Mudhukundrai adaivom” and circumambulated that hill. He sang the Thiruvirukku Kural hymn and went before the Lord, where he sang the hymn “Murasu adhirndhu” and worshipped. He then resided in that holy place.

Afterwards, he went to Thiruppennagadam, worshipped the Lord there, and sang the hymn “Theengu Neenguvee Thuunganai Maadam Thozhil”. MinkaLe“ (Worship the Sleeping Elephant Temple to remove evil) and reached Thiru Arathurai. Whenever he undertook such pilgrimages, Pillaiyar would be on his father’s shoulders, and sometimes he would walk. As Pillaiyar walked during his pilgrimage, his lotus feet slowly grew sore. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman had no attachments, so he did not undertake pilgrimages in the same way others did. That is, others would undertake them for the removal of impurities and the purification of karma.

But Thirugnanasambandha Peruman undertakes pilgrimages for Lord Shiva. As this was happening, when they came to a place called Maranpadi, Pillaiyar saw that those accompanying him were weary from the journey.

Therefore, in Thiruvainthil, he sang the hymns and stayed there.

That night, Pillaiyar stayed in that village with his attendants. That village is praised as Thiru Arathurai.

The Lord of Thiru Arathurai, intending to relieve Pillaiyar’s fatigue from the journey, appeared in a dream that very night to all the Brahmins, devotees, temple attendants, and all the residents of that place, saying, “Thirugnanasambandhan is coming to us. Go and give him the pearl palanquin, pearl cymbals, and pearl umbrella that I have kept.” When everyone in that village gathered at the temple and the temple doors were opened in the morning, they saw all those items – the pearl palanquin, pearl cymbals, and pearl umbrella – there at the temple entrance. They rejoiced at seeing the divine grace, worshipped, and with great fanfare, carried them forth to welcome Pillaiyar.

Here, the Lord also graciously appeared in a dream to Pillaiyar, instructing him to accept and utilize them. Realizing this, Pillaiyar rose and informed his father and the devotees.

Then, as the darkness faded and morning dawned, he applied sacred ash and chanted the holy five-syllable mantra. At that moment, the devotees of Thiru Arathurai arrived, bearing all those divine items, with cries of “Hara Hara,” welcomed him, bowed, and praised him. They explained that these were all gifts bestowed by the Lord. Seeing this, Pillaiyar’s heart melted with thoughts of the Lord’s immense grace. He began to sing the holy hymn “Enthai Easan” and praised, then circumambulated the effulgent pearl palanquin, bowed down to the ground, and standing in the radiant light of the sacred ash, he honored its brilliance. Realizing this was the Lord’s grace, he ascended the pearl palanquin while chanting the holy five-syllable mantra.

The devotees cheered and rejoiced with cries of “Hara Hara.” The Vedas resonated, and flowers rained from the sky. Seeing Pillaiyar shining on the pearl palanquin like the moon rising from the ocean of milk, all the devotees shed tears of joy. The time, the conch, the cymbals, and other instruments bestowed by the Lord proclaimed many glories of Pillaiyar, saying, “Thirugnanasambandhan has come! The master of three kinds of Tamil has come!

The child who speaks divine words has come!” Thus, Pillaiyar reached Thiru Arathurai. Long before the entrance, he dismounted from the palanquin, entered the temple, came before the Lord, clasped his hands, prostrated himself, and immersed in devotion, praised the Lord’s great grace. He resided in that holy place for some days. During those days, he also visited and worshipped holy places like Thirunelvennai and then returned to Thiru Arathurai to reside.

We will continue to contemplate the brief history of Pillaiyar.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 04 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 541, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal. While Pillaiyar was staying in the holy place of Thiru Arathurai, the Lord Thoniyappar, with Periyanayaki, residing in his native Sirkazhi, appeared in Pillaiyar’s consciousness. Pillaiyar’s heart melted, and with the intention of going to Sirkazhi, he worshipped the Lord of Thiru Arathurai, received his gracious permission, and departed by ascending the palanquin.

The Brahmins and devotees rejoiced. The sacred cymbals sounded. As he proceeded, people from each village, having adorned their villages with arches and other decorations, came to welcome and worship Pillaiyar. He visited and worshipped Thiruppazhuvoor, where the Brahmins, the Malayalis, praised and sang praises for the gift, then worshipped Thiruvijayamangai, Thiruppurambayam, and other holy places, arriving at Thiruchengaloor. The people of that village adorned the town and came to welcome him. As Pillaiyar arrived at Thiruchengaloor, he understood that this holy place was where Chandeepa Pillaiyar had made his divine advent.

Therefore, instead of riding in the palanquin, he dismounted, worshipped, and along with the people of that village, entered the holy town. He worshipped the Lord in the temple according to custom, and there he sang a holy hymn. In that hymn, he praised and glorified Chandeepa Pillaiyar, Chandeswara Nayanar, and resided in that holy place for some days. From there, he worshipped Thiruppanandal, Thiruppanandanallur, Thiru Omapuliyur, Thiruvalkozhithur, Thirukkadambur, Thiru Thirunaraiyur, Thirukaruupariyalur, and other holy places, then reached Sirkazhi. Hearing that Pillaiyar had arrived in Sirkazhi, the Brahmins and devotees of Sirkazhi adorned the town, carried full golden pots, and came to welcome him. They saw Pillaiyar in the magnificent pearl palanquin, surrounded him, cheered, and praised him.

Pillaiyar also dismounted from the palanquin, went forward to greet them, worshipped, rejoiced with them, and went to the temple. He worshipped Thoniyappar, sang praises, and came out.

At that time, Thiruneelakanta Yazhpanar followed Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. He granted him leave to stay in his mansion and returned to his own holy mansion. As the Brahmin women, carrying lamps, full pots, and other auspicious items, came to greet Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, his mother, Bagavathy Ammaiyar, first applied sacred ash to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and worshipped him. He bestowed his grace upon her, then duly entered his holy मठ (Matham) and resided there, worshipping Thoniyappar daily and singing hymns. As these days passed, the age for Pillaiyar’s Upanayanam (sacred thread ceremony) arrived. Pillaiyar, who had attained divine wisdom transcending the world, donned the deer skin and sacred thread, with all the Brahmins performing the ancient Vedic rituals.

Pillaiyar, who was never subject to birth, participated in these Vedic rituals according to worldly custom, as if he were a ‘twice-born.’ The Brahmins there, demonstrating these Vedic rituals, taught him the mantras, saying, “We have given you the four Vedas.” Before them, Pillaiyar himself chanted countless sacred Vedas. Seeing this, all the Brahmins were amazed. They regarded Pillaiyar as if a thousand crores of suns had risen simultaneously, and considered him a meditative object standing before their eyes. They sought clarification from Thirugnanasambandha Peruman on all the doubts they had in the Vedas and attained prosperity. Pillaiyar graciously taught all the mantras to those Brahmins and also enlightened them, dispelling the confusion that arose from their Vedic ritualistic texts.

Pillaiyar then composed the Sri Panchakshara hymn, proclaiming that the primordial source of all mantras is the Lord’s holy five-syllable mantra. Everyone who heard it attained great prosperity and rejoiced. Pillaiyar worshipped Thoniyappar daily. and resided there. During these days, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman arrived in Sirkazhi to see and worship Pillaiyar. Pillaiyar, rejoicing that it was a blessing of good deeds done, went with a group of devotees to welcome Thirunavukkarasu Peruman. When Pillaiyar saw the Lord of endless holy attire approaching, he worshipped, recognizing him as the holy attire of a devotee appearing directly.

Thirunavukkarasu also bowed in return. Pillaiyar spoke sweet words to him, took him to the temple, and together they worshipped at Thiruthoni. They returned to his holy mansion, where they served holy food to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, who was a holy devotee. Both resided there in joy, filled with overflowing love and friendship, worshipping the Lord together. After some days, Pillaiyar expressed his desire to visit and worship other holy places. Having obtained the consent of Pillaiyar, ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān took his leave and departed.

Pillaiyar, having bid him farewell, returned to worship Thōṇiyappar and remained in Sīrkāzhi. During these days, ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān composed devotional hymns (Thirumozhi Māṭṭu Mālai, Māṭṭu Vazhimozhi, Thiruviyamakam, Ēkapātham, Thiru Irukku Kural, Thiru Ezhukūṟṟirukkai, Īraḍi Īraḍimēl Vaippu, Nāḷaḍimēl Vaippu, Thiruvirākam, ThiruchchakkaraMāṭṭu) with various metrical variations. He sang all the poetic structures about the Lord of Sīrkāzhi, the fundamental literary source, through his hymns. ThiruNīlakaṇṭa Yāzhppāṇa Nāyanār and Mathaṅkachūḷāmaṇi Ammaiyār sang these hymns, both playing the seven-stringed Yazh and vocally.

Thus, after praising Thōṇiyappar and singing many hymns, Pillaiyar stayed in Sīrkāzhi. During those days, Pillaiyar conceived a desire to visit and worship all the holy places throughout Tamil Nadu. He conveyed this desire to his father. His father, unable to bear separation from ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān and also needing funds for a Yaga, said, “I will accompany you for a few days.” With the holy devotees and Brahmins accompanying them, Pillaiyar took leave of ThiruThōṇiyappar and set off with his father and ThiruNīlakaṇṭa Yāzhppāṇar. Devotees in various towns decorated their cities and welcomed him. ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān visited holy places in every town.

Now embarking on the fifth pilgrimage, Pillaiyar worshipped ThiruKaṇṇannār Temple and continued his journey northwest along the northern bank of the Kaveri. He went to ThiruPuḷḷirukku Vēlūr, known as Vaitheeswaran Koil, and sang hymns describing its glory, as it was worshipped by the two bird-kings, Sampathi and Saḍāyu. From there, he worshipped other shrines such as ThiruNinṟiyūr and ThiruPuṅkūr.

Afterward, he reverently worshipped ThiruPazha Maṇippaḍikkarai, ThiruKuṟukkai, Thiru Anniyūr, ThiruPanthanaiNallūr, ThiruMaṇañjēri, and Thiru Ethirkoḷpāḍi. On the bank of the Kaveri, at ThiruVēḷvikoḍi, he sang hymns in the daytime about the wedding festivities and at night about staying at ThiruThurutthi.

Later, he visited ThiruKōḍikkā, ThiruKaṇjanūr. He worshipped all the holy places like ThiruMānthurai, ThiruMaṅgalakkuḍi, and ThiruVisalūr, and arrived at Thiruṉthēvaṉkuḍi.

There, he sang and worshipped the Lord, proclaiming Him as the cure, the mantra, and all that is needful.

After that, he worshipped the nearby shrines and reached Thiru Innambar, where he sang a hymn called “IḍaMaḍakkāṉa ThiruMukkāl.” Then he proceeded to the shrine of Vaḍa Kuraṅkāḍu Thuṟai. This is the place where Vāli, from the Ramayana, worshipped Lord Shiva, and ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān sang about it in his hymn. After worshipping several other holy places, he arrived at ThiruPazhanam, where he worshipped reverently. He then reached ThiruAiyāṟu.

The devotees of ThiruAiyāṟu beautifully decorated the town and gave him a grand welcome. Descending from his palanquin, he worshipped the town of ThiruAiyāṟu. When his five senses were overwhelmed, he sang a hymn with the theme of “fear not” about ThiruAiyāṟu. He entered the temple, worshipped, and then sang and praised with the hymn “Kōḍal Koṅkam.” He stayed there for some days. From there, he visited and worshipped shrines like ThiruPerumPuliyūr. Again, during his stay at ThiruAiyāṟu, he decided to travel westward.

After seeking auspicious leave, he worshipped ThiruNeythāṉam and ThiruMizhappāḍi, staying there for a few days.

After that, he worshipped shrines like ThiruKāṉūr, Thiru Anpil Ālandurai, and Vaḍakarai ThiruMānthurai, singing hymns and offering worship.

Then, Pillaiyar set off to worship the holy place of ThiruPāchchilāchiramam. We will continue to contemplate the brief history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 05 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam Part 542, Vambara Varivaṇḍuch Chaṟukkam, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, recounts the history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nāyanār. ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān arrived at the holy place of ThiruPāchchilāchiramam. In that town, Koḷḷimazhavan had a daughter afflicted with Muyalakan disease, which seemed incurable. Koḷḷimazhavan was a Shiva devotee, coming from a lineage of those devoted to Shiva’s feet.

Therefore, he brought his daughter and placed her before the Lord in the temple. At that moment, Pillaiyar arrived. The sound of holy instruments was heard there. Immediately, Koḷḷimazhavan left his daughter in the temple and rushed off to decorate the town. He adorned the town to welcome ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān. He went forth to receive Pillaiyar.

He prostrated himself before Pillaiyar’s palanquin. Pillaiyar blessed him to rise. Koḷḷimazhavan rose and brought Pillaiyar to the temple. Pillaiyar circumambulated the temple according to custom and, upon reaching the Lord’s presence, saw Koḷḷimazhavan’s daughter lying unconscious there. He asked what had happened. Koḷḷimazhavan recounted the history of his daughter’s Muyalakan disease and how all efforts to cure it had failed.

Hearing this, Pillaiyar, out of compassion, from that very spot, worshipped the Supreme Lord and began the hymn “Thuṇivaḷar Thiṅgaḷ” (The growing crescent moon), singing “Maṇivaḷar Kaṇṭarō Maṅgaiyai Vāḍa” (Does the jewel-necked Lord let the maiden wither). He sang that hymn to remove the disease. As he concluded the hymn, the Muyalakan disease left the girl. She rose completely cured and stood by her father. Koḷḷimalavan, with his daughter, prostrated at Pillaiyar’s feet. Pillaiyar worshipped the Lord.

After staying there for a few days, Pillaiyar worshipped other shrines, including ThiruPaiṅgīli and Thiru Īṅkōymalai, and then journeyed westward to Koṅgu Nāḍu. On the southern bank of the Kaveri in Koṅgu Nāḍu, at ThiruKoḍimāḍa Cheṅkūṉṟu, devotees welcomed Pillaiyar. He worshipped the Lord, sang hymns, praised Him. Pillaiyar remained in that town.

Later, he departed from there, worshipped all the Shiva shrines in the western direction, went to ThiruNāṉā (Bhavani Temple), worshipped the Lord, and then returned to ThiruKoḍimāḍa Cheṅkuṉṟūr where he had stayed before.

During that time, the cold season arrived, and a chilling wind blew intensely. As Pillaiyar’s attendants had stayed in that region for many days, they developed a fever due to the cold, affecting all the devotees as if to afflict them. They informed Pillaiyar and worshipped him. He prayed for the Lord’s grace and, with the sentiment, “Though this is the nature of this land, it should not befall us,” He sang a hymn to the Lord, beginning with “Avviṉaikku Ivviṉai” (For that deed, this deed) and praising with “Seiviṉai Vanthu Emai Thīṇḍap PeṟāthiruNīlakaṇḍam” (No deed can touch us, O Blue-throated Lord), issuing a divine command. By this command, the disease was removed not only from the people living in that area but also throughout the entire country.

After staying there for some days, he worshipped many other shrines and went to ThiruPāṇḍik Koḍumuḍi, where he worshipped and sang the hymn “Pāṇḍik Koḍumuḍiyārē.” Then he journeyed eastward, worshipped at the holy temple of Selva Karuvūr Thiru Āṇilai, then revered ThiruVeñjamā Kūḍal, worshipped many shrines, and departed from Koṅgu Nāḍu. He arrived at ThiruVāṭpōkki, a shrine on the southern bank of the Kaveri, and worshipped there. He delighted in worshipping many hills and holy places, then worshipped ThiruParāyththuṟai, Thiruchchi. He worshipped shrines such as Senthuṟaidi and Thiruchchirāppaḷḷi, and then arrived at ThiruĀṉaikkā.

There, he worshipped the Lord, who emerged beneath a white Naval tree, and praised Him in his hymn by mentioning the services rendered by Airāvatham and Kōchcheṅgaṇ Chōzhar. He also sang the hymn called “Kūḍa Sathukkam,” which praises ThiruĀṉaikkā, Mahendram, Kailai, and ThiruVārūr, and stayed there for some days.

Afterward, he worshipped ThiruThavaththuṟai, ThiruPāṟṟuṟai, ThiruVerumpiyūr Malai, and then worshipped ThiruNeḍuṅkaḷam. He sang a hymn with the theme of “remove the troubles that prevent devotees from expressing their love.” After worshipping ThiruKāṭṭuppaḷḷi, devotees grandly welcomed him. He went to ThiruPūnthurutthi, worshipped PoiYili Appar, then worshipped ThiruKaṇḍiyūr Veerattam.

There, among the devotees. He sang a devotional hymn inquiring about the Lord’s grace.

After that, he worshipped ThiruSoṟṟuththuṟai, ThiruVēthikuḍi, ThiruVeṇṇi, ThiruChakkaraPpaḷḷi, Thiru Ālandurai, and ThiruPālaisthuṟai, then reached and worshipped ThiruNallūr, where he resided. From there, he worshipped ThiruKarukāvūr, ThiruAvazhivanaḷḷūr, ThiruParuthiniyamam, and ThiruĀvūr Pasupathīchcharam, and then returned to ThiruNallūr. From there, he was welcomed by devotees and affectionately worshipped ThiruValañchozhi. He resided in that holy place, praising daily with great love.

At that time, summer arrived. Due to the sun entering Mithuna hora, its scorching rays caused even the oceans to shrink. The summer intensified, becoming a severely hot season. It transformed into a time of intense heat.

At that time, Pillaiyar, walking from ThiruValañchozhi to reach Pazhaiyāṟai, joined and worshipped at ThiruĀrai Mēṯṟazhi, and then proceeded to worship ThiruPattīchcharam. To alleviate the heat of the sun, Shiva Bhoothas erected a cool pearl canopy over his head and proclaimed, “Pattīsar has blessed us and sent us.” Immediately, his attendants held the jeweled shaft of the canopy. As the Devas showered flowers, those very flowers formed a flower canopy. Pillaiyar, as if under the shade of the Lord’s feet, resided beneath that canopy. He reached ThiruPattīchcharam, where, with great love, he worshipped and praised the Lord. From there, he went to worship Thiru Irumpūzhaí, and sang a hymn that expounded the meaning of the sacred Vedas.

From there, Thiru. He worshipped shrines such as Aṟathai Perumpāzhi, ThiruChērai, ThiruNāḷūr, ThiruKuḍavāyil, ThiruNaṟaiyūr, Thenthiruppūththūr, and ThiruSivapuram, and then arrived at ThiruKuḍamūkku, also known as Kumbakonam. Devotees welcomed him. He worshipped the Lord at ThiruKuḍamūkku, ThiruKīzhkōṭṭam, and ThiruKuḍanthai Kārōṇam, and also reverently worshipped the Mahamaham sacred tank.

Afterward, he worshipped ThiruNāgēswaram and delightedly resided there. Subsequently, seeing ThiruViḍai Maruthūr appear before him, he sang “Iḍaimaruthu Īthō” (Here is ThiruViḍai Maruthūr) and went to worship and immerse himself in song. During his stay there, he journeyed along the Kaveri bank, worshipped ThiruKuṟaṅkāḍu Thuṟai, and reached ThiruĀvuḍuthuṟai. He worshipped the Lord at ThiruĀvuḍuthuṟai and resided there.

At that time, the period for performing the Yaga. Upon its arrival, ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān’s father came to ThiruĀvaḍuthuṟai and informed Pillaiyar, who was residing there. Pillaiyar, firmly believing that “Are not the Lord’s feet the ultimate wealth?”, went to the temple and stood before the Lord. He sang a hymn with the sentiment, “I have nothing else to give to those who ask for wealth; I know nothing but Your feet,” stating, “Is this how You rule us? We have nothing. Is this Your sweet grace?” As he sang this hymn, by the grace of the Lord, Shiva Bhoothas placed a purse containing one thousand gold coins on the pedestal, saying, “This purse of gold will never diminish; the Lord has granted it to you,” to Pillaiyar.

That Bhootha. Pillaiyar, hearing this, worshipped, took the purse, and gave it to his father, saying, “With this, you and the other Brahmins in Sīrkāzhi should perform many good Yagas to worship the Lord.” He further blessed, saying, “This purse of gold will increase without diminishing.” Afterward, ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān’s father went to Sīrkāzhi and conducted good Yagas there.

Then, Pillaiyar worshipped the Lord at ThiruĀvaḍuthuṟai.

Following this, he worshipped ThiruKōzhambam, Vaikal Māḍakkōyil, ThiruNallam, ThiruAzhunthūr Māḍakkōyil, ThiruThurutthi, and Mūvalūr. He then entered ThiruMayilāḍuthuṟai, welcomed by devotees, worshipped, rejoiced, and resided there.

After that, he worshipped ThiruChempanpaḷḷi, ThiruVizhanagar, and ThiruPaṟiyal Vīraṭṭam, and then proceeded towards the seashore, worshipping ThiruVēṭṭa. Pillaiyar worshipped Kuḍi and reached ThiruTharumapuram. This place was the birthplace of ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar’s holy mother.

Therefore, ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar’s relatives welcomed and worshipped both Pillaiyar and ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar. There, ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar informed all his relatives that he had served Pillaiyar by playing and singing his hymns on the Yazh. ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar blessed his relatives. Hearing this, they praised ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar, saying, “The sound of those hymns, arranged and performed by you on the Yazh, has caused that music to resonate and flourish throughout the world.” They praised ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar, stating that the hymns were set to music because of his skill. Hearing this, ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar trembled.

He worshipped Pillaiyar and requested, “You must bless me with a boundless hymn, a hymn whose greatness cannot be confined by musical scales. To let not only these people but everyone in the world know your greatness, please sing a hymn that transcends musical limitations.” Pillaiyar then sang a hymn. He sang it in a way that could not be contained by the vocal chords or instruments of people, nor by the efforts described in musical treatises. He sang the hymn beginning with “Māthar Maḍappiḍi” and worshipped the Lord. He graciously sang that hymn. The minstrel, as before, tried to play that hymn on the Yazh, but he found that the hymn could not be contained within the scope of the Yazh.

Then he prostrated at Pillaiyar’s feet and said, “I began by saying I would play the music of this great one’s hymns on the Yazh, I would set it to the Yazh. Is it not because I have this instrument in my hand?” And he raised it to break it. Seeing this, Pillaiyar stopped him, took the Yazh, and said, “Sir, why are you breaking this Yazh? Can the grace of Ammaiyappar be contained within this instrument? It is customary to play within the limits of the instrument, as much as is suitable for our nature, so that the world may know. Can the greatness of that music, which cannot be measured by thought, be contained in action?

“You shall continue to play this Yazh.” He spoke thus and handed over the Yazh. ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar took it, held it in his hand, and, along with his relatives, worshipped Pillaiyar’s feet. After staying there for some days, Pillaiyar worshipped other shrines and proceeded to the holy place of ThiruNallāṟu. Devotees welcomed him, worshipped him, and surrounded him as he entered the temple. He worshipped according to custom and sang the hymn “Pōgamārtha Pūṇmulaiyāḷ” (She with adorned breasts, full of pleasure), praising the Lord.

“Pillaiyar then graciously asked ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar to play that hymn on the Yazh. ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇar played it on the Yazh as requested, and everyone rejoiced.

“We will continue to contemplate the brief history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 06 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam Part 543, Vambara Varivaṇḍuch Chaṟukkam, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, recounts the history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nāyanār. Departing from the holy place of ThiruNallāṟu and worshipping other shrines, ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān arrived at the holy place of ThiruChāththamaṅgai. ThiruNīlanakka Nāyanār decorated the town and, with auspicious signs, welcomed Pillaiyar. Pillaiyar entered the Ayavanthi Temple, worshipped, and then graced ThiruNīlanakka’s home. He sat there with the devotees as ThiruNīlanakka Nāyanār offered a feast.

That night, according to Pillaiyar’s instructions, ThiruNīlakaṇḍa Yāzhppāṇa Nāyanār and his wife, Mathaṅkachūḷāmaṇi Ammaiyār, were given a place to rest beside the sacrificial fire altar where ThiruNīlanakka Nāyanār maintained his ritual fire in the middle of his house. They slept there. The sacrificial fire blazed brightly.

Afterward, he sang a hymn praising the unique qualities of ThiruNīlanakka Nāyanār, granted him leave, cherished his friendship, and proceeded to worship other shrines. Subsequently, Pillaiyar worshipped holy places such as ThiruNāgai Kārōṇam and Thiru Kīzhvēlūr. Hearing of Pillaiyar’s arrival, Siruthoṇḍa Nāyanār rushed to worship him and requested him to come to his hometown, ThiruCheṅkāṭṭaṅkuḍi. Pillaiyar, delighted, worshipped the Lord at Gaṇapathīchcharam there, sang a hymn praising the greatness of Siruthoṇḍa’s holy service, and then resided in his home.

Later, he went to ThiruMarugal and worshipped. During those days, a merchant, accompanied by a woman, spent the night in a monastery in ThiruMarugal.

At that moment, a snake bit him. The poison spread, and life was about to depart. The woman, weakened and distraught, wept and cried beside him, unable to touch him. Even with all the treatments given by powerful sorcerers skilled in Garuḍa Vidya and Iḍibhāvaṉa, the poison did not recede. As the long night approached dawn, the woman, utterly exhausted, wept bitterly. “I left my parents and came here with you as my refuge.

“If you leave me, what will I do? Is there no one here to relieve this suffering?” she cried out in deep sorrow. She stretched out her hands towards the entrance of the Lord’s temple and worshipped. All the devotees cried out, “May all beings thrive! O Lord Who consumed poison! O Lord Who, at the request of Kama’s consort, revived him after being consumed by fire!

“O Lord Who kicked Yama for Mārkaṇḍeya, who sought refuge in You! Please grant Your grace so that this venom may subside and I may overcome this ocean of suffering.” She cried out, praising the Lord. That sound, at dawn, reached the ears of Pillaiyar, who had risen to worship the temple. Pillaiyar, with compassion in his heart, went with the devotees to where she was. He saw her crying out, praising Lord Shiva’s grace. He asked her, “Do not be afraid.

“Tell me your suffering and worry.” She fell at Pillaiyar’s feet, worshipped, rose, and spoke. He asked her, “Do not be afraid. Tell me your suffering and worry.” She fell at Pillaiyar’s feet, worshipped, rose, and spoke. “In the village of Vaippūr, near this town, lives a merchant named Thāman. He is my father. The man lying here, bitten by a snake, is my father’s son-in-law.

“My father has seven daughters. He promised to give his eldest daughter in marriage to this man, but he did not fulfill that promise. He took a large sum of money and married his eldest daughter to someone else. My father continued to promise each of us to this man, but he married each of us off to others. I was the only one remaining.

“So, with great concern for him, I left my parents and came here with him. As soon as we arrived, he was bitten by a snake. He died from a snakebite. I stand here like a ship capsized in the middle of the ocean. If you would show mercy to relieve my sorrow,” he said, Pillaiyar, to bestow grace upon her, pleaded with the Lord of ThiruMarugal to remove the poison and sang the hymn “Uḍaiyāṉai Ivaḷ Ivvāṟu Uṉ Mezhithal Uṉakku Thakumō” (Is it proper for You, O Lord, to allow her to suffer thus?), which includes the phrase “Saḍaiyāy Eṉumāḷ” (The one who says, “O Lord with matted locks”). Immediately, the merchant revived, free from the poison.

“The crowd of devotees shouted the Lord’s name in jubilation. The woman and the merchant clasped their hands above their heads and prostrated at Pillaiyar’s feet. Pillaiyar blessed them with a good life by arranging their marriage and, granting them leave, departed from there. On that day, Siruthoṇḍa Nāyanār came and requested him to stay. As he was taking leave, the Lord revealed His form at ThiruCheṅkāṭṭaṅkuḍi there.

“Therefore, he sang the hymn “Aṅgamum Vēthamum” (Both the limbs and the Vedas), combining two hymns, and resided with Siruthoṇḍanār in ThiruCheṅkāṭṭaṅkuḍi for some days. Afterward, he returned to ThiruMarugal and, after some days, went to ThiruPukalūr and worshipped. He resided in the monastery of ThiruMuruga Nāyanār.

“At that time, ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān, after worshipping the Lord in ThiruVārūr, arrived there, intending to worship ThiruPukalūr. Upon hearing this good news, Pillaiyar, with great love, along with his devotees, came to the border of ThiruPukalūr to welcome ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān. As Arasu also arrived, both, out of their mutual affection, bowed down and expressed their joy, each offering and receiving good wishes. Since Arasu had come after worshipping ThiruVārūr, Pillaiyar asked him, “How many times have you worshipped ThiruVārūr and been saved?” He asked how many times he had worshipped ThiruVārūr and been saved. He replied by describing the opulent festivities of the ThiruĀthirai festival in the hymn “Muththuvithāṉam.” Hearing this description, Pillaiyar immediately, out of love, said to Arasu, “I will go to ThiruVārūr, worship, and then return to join you.” He obtained Arasu’s consent and immediately proceeded to ThiruVārūr.

“Arasu, with his love following Pillaiyar, went to worship ThiruPukalūr and resided there, praising the Lord. Pillaiyar worshipped at ThiruVīrakkuḍi Veerattam.

“Then, singing “Ārūr Aḍaivōmē” (Let us reach Ārūr), he approached the outskirts of ThiruVārūr. There, the town of ThiruVārūr appeared like a golden world, with abundant groves, tall mansions, and banners touching the solar orb. He sang a hymn proclaiming, “This is Ārūr.” He reached the border of the holy city. The flood of love overflowed boundlessly. He descended from his palanquin, worshipped by showering abundant flowers from his hands, and prostrated, singing “Thiru Irukku Kural.” At that moment, Ārūr shone with great splendor. By the grace of Thyāgathyāgēsa Perumān, devotees and attendants came to the city’s border to welcome Pillaiyar.

“Before them, Pillaiyar sang the hymn “Anthamāy Ulakāthi” (The end and beginning of the world), with the line “ThiruVārūr Enthaithāṉ Eṉa Ēṉṟu Koḷluṅkaḷō” (Will my Father of ThiruVārūr accept me?). He then reached the temple, worshipped at the Thēvāsirya Maṇḍapam, circumambulated the holy precinct, entered, and before the Lord, prostrated many times with great love, rose, sang hymns, immersed himself in devotion, came out, and reached the monastery. He worshipped the path of righteousness of ThiruVārūr and resided there, worshipping the Lord who resides in the anthill at all times. During that time. He remembered having been told to stay in ThiruVārūr. Worshipping ThiruVārūr, he set off towards ThiruPukalūr, with the thought, “O mind, fear not!

“Worship Shiva’s Ārūr. Worship without fail to be saved. It is difficult.” He sang the hymn “Pavaṉamāychchōḍaiyāy” and, worshipping ThiruVārūr, departed from there. Along the way, he worshipped shrines like ThiruPaṉaiyūr and arrived at ThiruPukalūr.

“There, ThiruNāvukkarasu Swamigal, ThiruMuruga Nāyanār, and other devotees came, bowed, and welcomed him. Pillaiyar went with them to the temple, worshipped, and then stayed for some days in ThiruMuruga Nāyanār’s monastery.

“During that time, ThiruNīlanakka Nāyanār and Siruthoṇḍa Nāyanār also arrived there. Pillaiyar, along with the virtuous devotees, stood in worship of the Lord, intently discerning the true essence of noble devotion, and resided there with them as days passed. He resided there, intently discerning the true essence of noble devotion, as days passed. On that day, he sang a hymn of ‘harmonious music’ and praised the greatness of that holy place. From there, he desired to worship other shrines. Siruthoṇḍa Nāyanār and ThiruNīlanakka Nāyanār returned to their respective holy places.

“Muruga Nāyanār remained in ThiruPukalūr. Pillaiyar, after worshipping Pukalūr, began to proceed further. ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān and Pillaiyar journeyed together on their pilgrimage.

“At that time, as Pillaiyar walked close to ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān, ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān said to Pillaiyar, “You should ride in the pearl palanquin that the Lord has given you.” Pillaiyar said to ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān, “If this is the Lord’s grace, then you, with your devotees, go ahead. “I will follow you,” he said. Arasu agreed to do so, and from that day on, their entire pilgrimage together proceeded in this manner.

“Thus, Pillaiyar and ThiruNāvukkarasu Swamigal reached the holy place of ThiruAmpar. ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān sang the hymn “Pulku Poṉṉiṟam” (Embrace the golden hue) and extolled the holy work done by Kōchcheṅgaṇ Chōzhar there. From there, ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān and ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān went to worship ThiruKaḍavūr.

“There, Kuṅkiliya Kalaya Nāyanār welcomed these two great individuals. Upon reaching ThiruKaḍavūr, Pillaiyar sang the hymn “Saḍaiyuḍaiyāṉ” (He with matted locks), praising the Lord who heroically kicked Yama in that holy place, and then resided in the monastery of Kuṅkiliya Kalaya Nāyanār with ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān. Pillaiyar accepted the feast arranged by Kuṅkiliya Kalaya Nāyanār with great pleasure. He gladly accepted the feast and stayed there.

“Afterward, he worshipped shrines like ThiruĀkkūr and ThiruPāmbaram, and then approached ThiruVēḷimizhalaí. ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān went first, followed by Pillaiyar.

“The Brahmins in that town welcomed both of them and decorated the town. They sang the hymn “Arayār Virikōṇa Vāḍai” (The fragrance of broad, conical garments), and after both great persons worshipped the Lord, ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān and the devotees stayed in a monastery outside the temple wall, while Pillaiyar resided in a monastery on the northern side, near the gopuram. During those days, Brahmins from Sīrkāzhi came to ThiruVēḷiMizhalai, desiring to see Pillaiyar, and visited ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān.

“There, they worshipped the Lord and then. They worshipped the feet of ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān and requested him to come to Thōṇipuram (Sīrkāzhi) with them. Pillaiyar replied that they could stay there tonight and, after receiving the grace of the Lord of ThiruVēḷiMizhalai, depart for Sīrkāzhi.

“That night, ThiruThōṇiyappar himself appeared in Pillaiyar’s dream and revealed, “I will show you the celestial vimana of ThiruVēḷiMizhalai as I am in Thōṇi; I will show you the sight from Thōṇipuram. You shall know it.” Pillaiyar, realizing this, arose in wonder and went to the temple. He saw ThiruThōṇiyappar himself in the celestial vimana of the ThiruVēḷiMizhalai temple and began the hymn “Maimaru Pūṅkuzhal” (Dark, fragrant tresses), singing about Pukali and ThiruVēḷiMizhalai. He rejoiced, singing the hymn with the sentiment, “What is this wonder that the form residing in Thōṇi is manifest in the celestial temple of Vēḷi?” He rejoiced, singing and praising. He also conveyed this to the Brahmins who had come from Sīrkāzhi and permitted them to return to Sīrkāzhi.

“Those Brahmins returned to Sīrkāzhi. There, Pillaiyar resided at ThiruVizhimizhalai, worshipping the Lord with ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān.

“We will continue to contemplate the brief history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nāyanār.””
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 07 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam Part 544, Vambara Varivaṇḍuch Chaṟukkam, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, recounts the history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nāyanār. ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān and ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān were residing in ThiruVīḷimizhalai.

At that time, there was a prolonged drought in the world. Rivers dried up, and creatures suffered from lack of food. Even the worship of the Devas was disrupted. A great famine arose in the world. Seeing this, both great individuals wondered if Shiva’s devotees would face sorrow. They worshipped the Lord and retired for the night.

That night, the Lord of ThiruVīḷimizhalai appeared in their dreams. He said, “The hunger and illness caused by these worldly events will not afflict you, yet to alleviate the suffering of those who follow Shiva’s path, you two will be given a coin each at the eastern and western pedestals of the ThiruVīḷimizhalai temple.

“We will continue to provide this until this suffering ends.” He appeared in their dream and stated that the hunger and disease afflicting the world would not reach them, but to alleviate the suffering of those who stand in the path of Shiva, he would provide one coin each at the eastern and western pedestals of the ThiruVīḷimizhalai temple, and this would continue until the suffering ended. Both great individuals, realizing this, praised the Lord’s grace and circumambulated the temple. Pillaiyar found a coin granted by the Lord on the eastern pedestal. He bowed, took it, and revered it.

“Similarly, the Lord gave ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān a coin at the western pedestal.

“The Lord ordered that the devotees be fed daily, and made arrangements for them to have delicious meals twice a day.

“Thus, the feeding of devotees regularly took place at ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān’s monastery and ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān’s monastery. However, at ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān’s monastery, there was a delay in preparing food for the devotees. When Pillaiyar asked why, they explained that the coin ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān received was of lesser value, and it took time to exchange it and purchase food items. They also mentioned that ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān’s coin was of full value.

“Therefore, ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān praised and worshipped the Lord, singing the hymn “Vāsi Thīravē” (May the defect be removed). From that day onwards, the Lord bestowed a full-value coin upon ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān.

“Later, rain fell, the world recovered from its distress, and prosperity returned. After praising the Lord for many days, both great individuals sought permission from the Lord and departed from there to worship other shrines. They visited and worshipped holy places such as ThiruVāñchiyam, ThiruThalaiyālaṅkāḍu, ThiruPeruvēlūr, ThiruChāththaṅkuḍi, ThiruKaravīram, ThiruViḷamar, ThiruVārūr, ThiruKārāyil, ThiruThēvūr, ThiruNellikka, ThiruKaichchinnam, ThiruThēṅkūr, ThiruKoḷḷikkāḍu, ThiruKōṭṭūr, ThiruVeṉthuṟai, ThiruThaṇḍalai Nīzhneṟi, and ThiruKaḷar. They then arrived at the holy place of ThiruMaṟaikkāḍu.

“The devotees of ThiruMaṟaikkāḍu welcomed both of them, worshipped, went to the temple, worshipped according to custom, and entered. In earlier days, the Vedas had worshipped there and sealed the temple doors, making it impossible to open them until today. The temple doors, sealed by the Vedas, remained closed because the devotees, who possessed the ability to chant those Vedas, had not removed the seal. Both great individuals arrived before that holy entrance.

“At that moment, Pillaiyar turned to ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān and said, “Whatever may happen, we must open this main entrance, enter, and worship the Lord. For that, you must sing a hymn.” He replied, “If this is your grace, I shall sing as you wish.” He sang the hymn “Paṉṉiṉēr Mozhiyāḷ” (She of fragrant words), but even after completing all ten verses, the door did not open. ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān, with great sorrow, pleaded with the Lord in the concluding verse of his hymn, and the holy door opened.

“The devotees shouted “Hara Hara” and rejoiced. Both great individuals entered through that path, worshipped the Lord, praised His grace, immersed themselves in the flood of joy, sang hymns, and then came out.

“At that moment, ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān asked Pillaiyar to sing a hymn to close the holy doors. As Pillaiyar began to sing the hymn “Chathuram Maṟaithāṉ” (The Four Vedas), the door immediately became sealed and closed. Seeing this, the devotees rejoiced and praised both the Lord’s grace and the two great individuals.

“From that day on, the custom of devotees entering and worshipping through that holy entrance came into being.

“Thus, contemplating the immense grace bestowed by the Lord, the rarity of his own hymn that opened the door, and the ease with which Pillaiyar closed it, ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān. As ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān was resting in a part of the monastery, the Lord appeared in his dream in the guise of a Shaiva ascetic and said, “I am in Vāymūr; follow me.” Realizing this, he immediately prostrated himself, rose, and followed that ascetic.

“At that moment, ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān asked, “Where has Appar gone?” Learning of Appar Swamigal’s departure, he immediately followed him. Both reached ThiruVāymūr.

“The Lord revealed a wondrous golden temple, entered it, and disappeared.

“At the same time, Pillaiyar arrived beside ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān.

“The Lord then granted Pillaiyar a vision of His Rishabha form in the sky. Pillaiyar sang the hymn “Thaḷirizha Vaḷar” (The tender-leafed growth). He also showed that divine vision to ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān.

“Afterward, both went to ThiruVāymūr, worshipped, and then returned to ThiruMaṟaikkāḍu and resided there.

“At this time, the Samaṇa religion was flourishing in Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu, and the influence of Shaivism had diminished somewhat.

“The King of Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu had also converted to the Samaṇa faith. The good path of Shaivism had deviated and changed there. All the towns of Tamil Nadu were filled with Samaṇa pāḷi and schools. Everywhere, the Samaṇas proliferated. Only two individuals, the Pāṇḍiya Queen Maṅgaiyarkkarasiyār and the Minister Kulachchiraiyār, upheld the Shaiva faith there. They, too, were distressed by the harm that had come to their country and continued to follow the Shaiva tenets without the Pāṇḍiya King knowing of their adherence.

“They practiced Shaivism without the Pāṇḍiya King knowing.

“At that time, they heard the news that Pillaiyar was residing in ThiruMaṟaikkāḍu. They sent their attendants as messengers to Pillaiyar, requesting him to come to Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu to spread the glory of Shaivism.

“Therefore, the messengers of Pāṇḍiya Queen and Kulachchirai Nāyanār arrived at Pillaiyar’s monastery in ThiruMaṟaikkāḍu, approached Pillaiyar, and made their request. Pillaiyar graciously granted them audience and then, accompanied by ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān, went to worship the Lord. From inside the gopuram, he recounted all these events to ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān. Pillaiyar informed ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān of his intention to go to Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu.

“At that moment, Vāgīsa Perumān said, “Child, those Samaṇas are wicked and deceitful. “The planets are not in a favorable position right now, so I do not approve of you going to Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu,” ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān refused. To this, ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān replied, “If we worship the Lord, the planets will not be evil; they will bestow only good. The Lord’s sacred ash will defeat the Buddhists and Samaṇas in argument; this is certain.” With these words, he sang the hymn “Vēyuṟu Thōḻi Paṅkaṉ” (He whose consort has bamboo-like shoulders), which is a hymn to dispel planetary evils. Hearing this, ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān agreed and prepared to accompany him. Pillaiyar stopped ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān, asked him to stay there, worshipped the Lord, took his leave, and departed.

“ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān also took his leave and remained there. Pillaiyar, having bid farewell to ThiruNāvukkarasu Perumān, chanted the five-letter mantra, meditated on the Lord’s feet. He adorned himself with the sacred ash and rode in the palanquin. All the devotees chanted the names of Shiva. As people from all four directions praised and devotees welcomed him everywhere with auspicious signs, ThiruGnanaSambandha Perumān traveled towards Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu, worshipping the shrines along the way. Pillaiyar continued, worshipping and singing hymns at holy places such as ThiruAgaththiāṉpaḷḷi, ThiruKōḍikkuḷakar, ThiruKaḍikkuḷam, ThiruIḍumpāvaṉam, and ThiruUsāththāṉam.

“He passed through fertile Marutham lands, rich with ponds and flowerbeds, and passed through towns where Brahmins and good devotees resided. Leaving the Chōzha Nāḍu, he crossed the Mullai land and then the land inhabited by warriors, and arrived in the glorious southern Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu. Having crossed the land inhabited by forest dwellers, he arrived in the southern Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu.

“There, he worshipped ThiruKoḍuṅkuṉṟam, also known as Pirāṉmalai, and traversed hills and forests to reach the holy city of Madurai. As Pillaiyar arrived in Madurai, ominous signs appeared for the Samaṇas in Pāṇḍiya Nāḍu. Owls and other ill-omened birds fought above the Samaṇa pāzhi, schools, and refectories, foretelling the impending calamities for them. Their peacock feathers, staffs, and mats fell down. The Samaṇas stumbled, and their left eyes twitched. The Samaṇas abandoned virtues like patience, and evil traits predominated.

“Additionally, the Samaṇas experienced bad dreams. Saying these things to each other, all the Jains surrounding Madurai gathered in Madurai and shared the bad omens that had befallen them. An Ashoka tree fell to its roots on top of the Arhat, and then that Arhat deity – the Jains shared all these bad dreams and evil dreams with each other.

“Therefore, they grieved, lamenting that harm was about to befall the Jains, and this was indeed true, so they did not eat and wailed. As the Jains reached this state there, auspicious omens appeared for Queen Mangaiyarkarasi and the wise minister Kulachiraiyar. Seeing this, both rejoiced. The good news of Pillaiyar’s arrival The arrivals convey to both of them, and great joy arises. Queen Mangaiyarkarasi instructs the minister, “Go before Pillaiyar, welcome him well, and bring him here.” Minister Kulachirai Nayanaar, believing this action will reassure the king, travels a long distance outside Madurai and welcomes Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan at the border of Madurai. He tells the king that he must worship the Lord enshrined in Aalavaai and goes with his retinue to Aalavaaiyudaiyar’s temple to stand there and welcome him himself.

“As the pearl palanquin proceeds like a full moon, the pearl umbrella provides shade, the crowd of ash-clad devotees swells, the Brahmins’ Vedic chants resound, and the sweet Tamil breezes serve from all sides, Jainism like an army of virtue advancing as the great army of sin breaks and flees, like the Ganga coming to wash away the defilement of Jainism, like the lamp of knowledge rising to dispel the darkness of Jainism, showing many good things that foster Saivism, with all the auspicious symbols announcing, “The one who knows the other religions has come!” Pillaiyar proceeds.

“Now, let us reflect on the condensed sacred history of Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan, who continuously came to Madurai, the capital of the Pandya country. Thiru Thiruchitrambalam.””
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 08 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part Five Hundred Forty-Five, Vampara Varivanda Charukkam, authored by Sekkilar Swamigal. The sacred history of Thiru Gnanasambandha Nayanaar. Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan arrives in Madurai, the capital of the Pandya kingdom. Kulachirai Nayanaar lies prostrate on the ground, bowing towards the crowd of devotees accompanying Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan. Seeing his prostrate state, the attendants inform Pillaiyar, who is in the palanquin.

Hearing this, Pillaiyar descends from the palanquin, approaches Kulachirai Nayanaar, and raises him from his prostrate position. Kulachirai Nayanaar then stands with folded hands. Pillaiyar speaks in a sweet voice, asking, “Are the divine blessings of the Lord abundantly bestowed upon Mangaiyarkarasi, the daughter of the Chola king, and upon you, who possess a rectified mind?” To this, the minister replies, “We suffered no harm in the past, and we shall receive special blessings in the future. This is because of the great fortune of Your Holiness’s arrival today. We are always blessed by His grace.

“This country, steeped in an unrighteous path, and its righteous Tamil king have obtained salvation and achieved the glory of shining in the light of the sacred ash.” He further states, “Our lives have been uplifted by the great news of Your Holiness’s arrival.” Kulachirai Nayanaar then adds, “Queen Mangaiyarkarasi ordered me to go forth and prostrate myself before Your Holiness.” Having said this, he bows again. As Pillaiyar blesses him and proceeds, the city surrounded by walls Madurai appears before them. Pillaiyar asks the devotees, “Where is the Lord’s sacred Aalavaai?” They point with their hands, indicating the towering gopuram reaching the sky is Thiruaalavaai. At that very spot, Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan prostrates himself on the ground and begins singing a Thiru Pathigam (devotional hymn) starting with “Mangaiyarkarasi.” In that hymn, he praises the services of both Queen Mangaiyarkarasi and Kulachirai Nayanaar. Proceeding further with the minister, he approaches Thiruaalavaai, bows at the side of the gopuram, circumambulates the mansion, and enters the sacred temple. He beheld the Lord of Aalavaai, fulfilling the purpose of his eyes, prostrated himself countless times, and sang the Thiru Pathigam “Neelama Midatru” (The Long-Throated One) in praise, then reached the outer court.

“Pillaiyar, upon entering, When he entered, Mangaiyarkarasi, who had stood aside without coming forward, now approached with tears welling up, bowed down, and stood with folded hands. When the minister announced her as the Chola princess, Pillaiyar, filled with great joy, went to meet her. The Queen prostrated herself at Pillaiyar’s feet. Pillaiyar, with great compassion, raised her, and the Queen, overjoyed that her desire was fulfilled, spoke with trembling voice and tearful eyes, saying, “What great penance have I and my land performed!” Pillaiyar then blessed her, saying, “We have come to see you, who live righteously amidst the rival religions.” The minister narrates all the events. Pillaiyar blesses the Queen, bids her farewell, and proceeds with the true devotees.

“The devotees serving at Thiru Aalavaai come forward and say to Pillaiyar, “We have performed immeasurable penance for Your Holiness to come here to dispel the darkness of Jainism.” They prostrate themselves. After bestowing his gracious glance upon them all, Pillaiyar takes a seat with the devotees in the sacred monastery shown by Kulachirai. Kulachirai provides a feast, by the grace of Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, for Pillaiyar who is residing there. As Pillaiyar and his devotees were seen arriving during the day, the Jains, upon hearing the music played in the darkness of the night, became agitated and envious. They decided to plot against the king. They went to the palace, informed the gatekeepers, and then nervously presented themselves before the king.

“When the king asked why they had come, they replied that it was very painful to tell. The king asked, “What trouble has befallen you?” They replied, “Oh King, a Saivite Brahmin has arrived in your Madurai, and because of this, we have been defiled by his presence.” Hearing this, the king said, “I too have been defiled just by hearing this!” He then asked, “Who is this Shiva devotee, and why have they come here?” The Jains replied, “A young Brahmin from Seerkazhi in the Chola country, who has received the grace of Sulapani, has come here with a group of devotees, riding in a pearl palanquin. He has come to defeat us in debate.” When Pillaiyar’s sacred name reached his ears, the king became angry and asked, “If that youth has come here, what should we do?” The Jains replied, We must cause trouble for that Brahmin.

“Therefore, we will use our mantras to create fire in the monastery where he is staying, so he will leave this city without spending the night. If this is what must be done, then do it immediately, the king commands. The king, full of anxiety, goes to sleep.

“At that moment, Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, seeing the king silent and troubled, asks, “My lord, you are not happy. What has happened to you?” The king replies, “Someone from Seerkazhi in the Chola country, who has received the grace of Shiva, has come here to defeat the Jains in debate. Because of this, the Jains feel defiled by sight, and I feel defiled by hearing.” Queen Mangaiyarkarasi says, “Given your situation, it would be appropriate for you to side with those who win the debate, considering their profound divine nature. Do not grieve.” She then rejoices over Pillaiyar’s gracious arrival to claim her and shares this news with the minister. The minister bows and says, “We have been blessed with the arrival of Pillaiyar, so what harm can the deceit of the Jains inflict now?” Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, greatly afraid, replies, “These treacherous wretches will only do evil. If they cause any harm to Thiru Gnanasambandar, then it is our duty to protect him.” She then asks about the Jains’ situation.

“The Jains, having taken leave from the king, proceed to cause fire in Pillaiyar’s monastery through their incantations. The primordial mantra, the sacred five-syllable mantra, will be recited. Will the rules of other mantras operate in the direction they look, or will they not?

“Thus, the Jains realize that their magical incantations have no effect on Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan.

“Therefore, unable to create fire through mantras, they resolve to go directly and set fire themselves. They approach the sacred monastery where Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan is residing and carry out their intended action. Seeing the fire breaking out there, the attendants, panicking, extinguish it and inform Pillaiyar. Pillaiyar, with compassion, says, “Should these sinners commit such harm in this sacred monastery where great ascetics sleep?” Then, he reflects, “Even though this harm was done for my sake, can it truly affect Shiva’s devotees?” Angered, he realized that the king’s justice had weakened here, and that was the reason. He commanded the Thiru Pathigam “Seyyane” (O Red One) and instructed the fire set by the Jains in the monastery where Saivites resided to gently go and affect the Pandya king.

“With the intention of protecting Mangaiyarkarasi’s sacred necklace and anointing the king with sacred ash to save him, he commanded the fire to gently go and affect him. That fire then went and afflicted the Pandya king, manifesting as a fever.

“Let us continue to reflect on the condensed sacred history of Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 09 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part Five Hundred Forty-Six, Vampara Varivandu Charukkam, authored by Sekkilar Swamigal. The sacred history of Thiru Gnanasambandha Nayanaar. The fire set by the Jains in the monastery where Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan was staying slowly transformed into a burning fever for the Madurai king. In accordance with Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan’s command, that night passed and dawn broke. Hearing about the evil deed committed by the Jains during the night, Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, the queen of that land, and the great minister were deeply distressed, regretting that they had invited Pillaiyar to a country where such evil people lived.

Later, learning that no harm had befallen the monastery where Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan was staying, they were somewhat comforted.

At the same time, the king’s bodyguards arrived and announced that the king had contracted a fever. Queen Mangaiyarkarasi and Kulachirai Nayanaar quickly went to the king’s chambers. The king’s fever burned throughout his body like fire. Even those standing outside the king’s chambers were scorched by the heat.

Therefore, those who came near the king could not approach him and stood at a distance. Even banana plantains and banana leaves brought near the king withered and blackened. Such was the heat in the king’s body. Although doctors applied treatments according to the medical texts, they could not even slightly reduce the fever.
