The great minister Kulachirai Nayanaar tells the king that the cause of all this is the evil deed committed by the Jains, and its consequence.

Therefore, if one tries to cure this fever, it will not be cured, but will only increase. If a solution is desired for this, then the grace of Pillaiyar is needed. If Thiru Gnanasambandha Moorthy Nayanaar, who has attained divine knowledge, directs his gracious gaze, this fever will be cured, and the suffering of rebirth will also be dispelled.

Thus, the great minister Kulachirai Nayanaar informs the king. For the first time, Kulachirai Nayanaar whispers the name Thiru Gnanasambandar into the king’s ear. As soon as the king heard that sacred name, his suffering slightly diminished. The king looked at the great minister and said, “It would be very good if the Saivite Brahmin youth came here and cured this illness of mine. I will join the side of those who cure this disease and win. If you agree to this, then summon him.” Hearing this, Queen Mangaiyarkarasi and the great minister Kulachirai Nayanaar immediately went to Pillaiyar’s sacred monastery.

There, they informed the guards at the monastery gate. They ask the guards to convey their arrival to Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan. The guards then go to Pillaiyar and relay the message. Pillaiyar instructs the guards to bring Queen Mangaiyarkarasi and Minister Kulachirai Nayanaar inside. Queen Mangaiyarkarasi and Kulachirai Nayanaar enter the sacred monastery.

There, they see his divine form. They behold Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan. They see the support of the Vedas. They see the crescent moon growing on earth, not in the sky. They joyfully behold the seven births of the song that praises Shiva’s glory. They behold the divine form of knowledge, the unique support of the four Vedas, Sekkilar Peruman composes this verse here: ‘The crescent moon that grows on earth, not in the sky, a unique support of the four Vedas, the seven births of the song that praises the glory of the Lord with honey-laden Konrai flowers in his red matted locks, they joyfully beheld.’ As soon as they saw Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan, remembering the cruel deeds committed by the Jains against him, tears streamed down their faces.

With folded hands, they sighed deeply, their voices trembled, their bodies shook, and they fell to the ground, as if knowing nothing. They clasped Pillaiyar’s lotus feet, like someone lost in the sea of worries finding a raft, or someone who finds a boat clinging to it, they clung to Pillaiyar’s lotus feet. Out of love, you relentlessly lay prostrate there. Pillaiyar lovingly lifted and comforted both of them with his sacred hand. He asked them, “O virtuous ones, is there any harm upon you?” They recounted everything that had happened. They pleaded, “If you cure the king’s fever and defeat the Jains, then the king’s life and our lives will be saved.” Pillaiyar reassures them, saying, “All creation and destruction are His deeds.

“I understand the Lord’s will to dispel the evil that may befall the sinful Jains and to defeat them.” The Lord Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan sets out to understand the divine will and enters the Thiru Aalavaai temple in Madurai. Facing Sokkanatha Perumaan, he sings the Thiru Pathigam “Kaattuma” (Will you show?), addressing the Lord who is a form of fire, saying, “I have come seeking your divine will to debate with the Amaras, who have no prescribed path.” He then focuses on the Lord’s grace.

“Following this, with the intention of defeating them in debate, he sings the Thiru Pathigam beginning with “Vedavai Velviyai” (Vedic sacrifice). He supplicates the Lord at Thiru Aalavaai, saying, “O Primordial One, I earnestly desire only your glory, which is knowledge.” Having received the Lord’s grace, he joyfully ascends the palanquin and proceeds. The shouts of “Hara Hara” raised by the devotees The roaring echoes filled everywhere. Like the radiance of the sacred ash, Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan’s pearl umbrella and insignia resounded, and this sacred sight shone in the streets of Madurai city. The people of Madurai city were then followers of other religions, Jains. Nevertheless, they pondered, “What penance have we performed for this holy figure, Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan, to come and enter Madurai for the sake of the Pandya king?” Queen Mangaiyarkarasi’s palanquin followed behind Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan’s palanquin.

“Minister Kulachirai Nayanaar, the great lord, walked among the crowd of holy devotees in front of Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan’s palanquin.

“Thus, Pillaiyar arrives at the palace. The minister goes ahead and informs the king of Pillaiyar’s arrival. Hearing this, the king’s distress further lessens. The king instructs that a jeweled seat be placed beside his head for Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan.

“Thus, the ability to speak also comes to the king as soon as he hears the news of Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan’s arrival. He then orders the minister to bring Pillaiyar. The Jains ask the king, “Is this how you preserve our religion? Why did you invite him?” They further tell the king, “We Jains and Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan will attempt to cure your disease at the same time. Even if the disease is cured by the grace of Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan, you must say that it was cured by us,” the Jains tell the king.

“At that time, it was the period when the fruits of the king’s past penance were coming to fruition.

“Therefore, the king, not agreeing to the evil words of the Jains, tells them, inspired by divinity, “You two should cure it separately.” At the same time, Pillaiyar descends from the palace courtyard and enters the palace. The king sees Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan like the moon descending from the sky to dispel the darkness on earth. Upon seeing him, the king The king salutes with folded hands and indicates the jeweled seat beside his head. Pillaiyar then ascends that jeweled seat. As soon as he beheld Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan’s divine form, the king’s fever further subsided. The king then asks Pillaiyar, with great eagerness, “Which village are you from?” Pillaiyar replies, “Seerkazhi, also known as Thiru Kazhumalam, is our village.” He then recites the Thiru Pathigam called “Thiruchakkaramaatru,” listing the twelve names of Seerkazhi.

“At that moment, the Jains surround Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan, shouting and bickering. Pillaiyar tells them, “Speak the truth of your teachings, expound upon its reality.” Hearing this, many Jains again gather around Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan, agitated and wailing. Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, unable to bear it, her heart trembling, addresses the king, “Pillaiyar is a young boy, while the Jains are innumerable and have surrounded Pillaiyar. Pillaiyar will cure your illness; let these Jains speak afterward.” The king replies, “Do not worry,” and tells the Jains, “You Arhats and this devotee of Shiva, please reveal your clear divine essence to me.” Pillaiyar then addresses Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, He sings the Thiru Pathigam, “Maani Neerveli.” In that hymn, he reassures her, “Do not fear me as a child. With the Lord of Aalavaai standing, I am not weak before these ignoble ones.” Furthermore, addressing the persistently wailing Jains and Pillaiyar, who sat calmly, the king says, “You should individually attempt to cure my fever. Whoever cures my fever most quickly will be considered victorious in the debate.” Immediately, the Jains choose the king’s left side and attempt to cure his fever according to their customs, chanting mantras.

“They chant mantras and stroke him with peacock feathers. However, the king’s fever intensified. The king then looks at Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan, wishing him to make an effort to cure the disease on the king’s right side.

“At that moment, Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan sings the Thiru Neetru Pathigam (Hymn of Sacred Ash), beginning with “Manthiramavathu Neeru” (The mantra is sacred ash), declaring that the sacred ash of Thiru Aalavayaan will dispel the fever on the king’s right side, acting as both mantra and medicine. Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan then takes the sacred ash with his own sacred hands and anoints the king’s right side with it. The fever immediately subsided, and the king’s right side cooled down like a pond. The heat from the right side gathered on the left side, and the disease intensified like fire. On the left side, the Jains trembled. The fever on the king’s left side, which was their chosen side, increased and scorched the Jains themselves.

“Therefore, they moved away from the king and left. The Jains, unable to bear the fever, then heard the king declare, “At the same time, on one side, I feel as if I am in a cruel hell; on the left side, where the Jains claimed to cure, I feel a terrible hell.

“At the same time, on the right side, where Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan applied the sacred ash with his divine hands, I feel heavenly bliss. In my present form, I feel the nature of both sides.” Amazed, he tells the Jains, “You have lost. Leave me and go.” He then pleads with Pillaiyar, “Please bless me so that this disease is completely cured.” Pillaiyar completes the hymn and anoints the king’s left side with sacred ash, and the fever on the left side also completely disappears. The Pandya king is fully saved. Queen Mangaiyarkarasi and the great minister Kulachirai Nayanaar bow at Pillaiyar’s feet, saying that the king has attained a state beyond rebirth.

“The king, with folded hands above his head, states, “I have been saved by seeking the feet of Gnanasambandar, before the shameless Jains, and my disease is cured.” Let us continue to reflect on the condensed sacred history of Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan. Let us contemplate Thiruchitrambalam.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 10 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part Five Hundred Forty-Seven, Vampara Varivandu Charukkam, authored by Sekkilar Swamigal. The sacred history of Thiru Gnanasambandha Nayanaar. The Jains realize that all their magical arts have been defeated by Pillaiyar’s words. Pillaiyar tells the Jains, “Speak the truth of your scriptures.” Fearing defeat in a logical debate, the Jains tell Pillaiyar, “Let us not engage in logical debate. Let us engage in debates that can be seen with the eyes, that are evident.” Hearing this, the king asks derisively, “Do you not know that my disease was cured by Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan?

“What debate do you need now? What debate are you going to do?” To this, the Jains say, they say, “Let’s have a fire debate.” The Jains state, “We and Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan will write the truths of our respective scriptures on palm-leaf manuscripts and place them in fire. Whoever’s manuscript does not burn or char in the fire will be the winner.” Immediately, Pillaiyar says, “If this is a debate, it must be conducted before the king.” The king then sets up the fire. Pillaiyar, with his sacred hands, takes a manuscript from his collection of sacred texts, which he preaches as the true nature of Shiva, along with sacred ash. The hymn on that particular manuscript was the Thiru Pathigam of Thirunallaaru, beginning with “Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyaal.” He takes that manuscript, declaring, “This is the sacred name of the Lord. Even if it is put into fire, nothing will happen to it.” He then sings the Thiru Pathigam, “Thalirilav Valaruli,” in praise, and places the manuscript into the fire for the kings and the assembly to witness.

“Pillaiyar offered the leaf into the fire, making the Lord, who holds Uma on His left side and is an Eight-Formed One, the subject. Because of this, the leaf remained fresh and green; the fire could do nothing to it.

“After this, the Jains, doubting whether their leaf containing the tenets of their religion would survive or burn, placed it into the fire. The Jains’ leaf burned like cotton in the fire. To everyone’s astonishment, Pillaiyar retrieved the leaf he had placed. It was fresher and greener than before. He showed it to the king and the assembly.

“Then he re-inserted the leaf into the sacred texts. The king looked at it with wonder.

“Then he told the Jains, “Show me the leaf you put in the fire.” The Jains searched for the leaf they had put in the fire.

“At that time, the heat was intense, so the king poured water to extinguish the fire. Only charcoal remained. The king, laughing, said, “You were unable to cure my disease then and lost.

“Now, you have also lost in this fire debate.” The Jains say, “Let’s have another debate.” The Jains say, “Let’s have another debate.” The king asks, “What other debate is there?” They say, “We will write the doctrines of our respective religions on palm leaves and cast them into a flowing river. If the leaf remains there without being carried away by the current, that leaf is the winner.” They challenge him to a water debate. Pillaiyar accepts it and says, “So be it.” At this point, the great minister Kulachirai Nayanaar comes forward and says, “Let us decide now what those who lose this debate should do.” The Jains, angered and envious of the minister, declare through their own mouths, “If we lose this debate, then the king will impale us on a stake.” Hearing this, the king forgot all their actions and, in anger, said, “You have spoken thus; now, come, let’s put the leaves in the water.” Pillaiyar descends from his jeweled seat and proceeds in his palanquin. The king rides on his horse. The Jains also come.

“As Pillaiyar proceeded through the streets of Madurai city, all the people of Madurai praised him. They discussed among themselves in many ways about the past events and what would follow from them, praising Pillaiyar and the glory of Saivism. The people of Madurai and the sacred emblems proclaimed Pillaiyar’s glories in various ways. With the king and queen following behind and the Jains coming as a separate group, Pillaiyar arrived at the banks of the Vaigai river.

“There, the river water flowed very swiftly. He tells them to cast their leaves concerning their religions. The Jains, who are empty like chaff in grain, write down their religious tenets, “Asti Nasti” (Existence-Nonexistence), and despite seeing the swiftness of the water, out of eagerness, they cast their leaf into the Vaigai River. The river quickly carried the leaf away. Seeing their leaf being swiftly carried away and disappearing, the Jains scattered in dismay and trembled, realizing their end had come. Nevertheless, hiding their fear, they say, “Let’s see what happens if you also cast your leaf into this water.” The king then looks towards Pillaiyar’s divine indication.

“He sang the Thiru Paasuram for the destruction of other religions. The king of the Pandya country, blessed with the sacred ash applied by Pillaiyar’s divine hand, had his past evil karmas removed, attained equanimity in karma, and achieved the ability to know the Lord.

“Therefore, for the king to understand this, Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan sang the Thiru Paasuram Pathigam, beginning with “Vaazhgaanthanar” (He who lives as a lord). In this Thiru Pathigam, he illustrates the universal truths of the Vedas, Sivagamas, Puranas, and Itihasas, teaching the world that the worldly Vedic rules and righteous path are indeed the Saivite path. Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan wrote on the leaf, If the leaf goes against the current, then knowledge is love for the Lord, and pronouncing this command, he finished writing on the leaf. He then casts the leaf into the Vaigai River with his sacred hands. Just as the minds of great ascetics go against the current of rebirth, the leaf cut through the waters of the Vaigai River and went against the direction of the river’s flow, showing that this is the true essence. In that hymn, he prayed for the king’s prosperity, and just as Anapayan Chola’s righteous scepter was exalted, the hunch of the Pandya king, the ruler of the south, straightened at that very moment.

“Seeing the leaf travel against the current of the Vaigai River, the celestials showered flowers, and all the Jains stood in fear. To retrieve that leaf, Kuthir Kulachirai Nayanaar, goes riding a horse. Pillaiyar sings for the leaf to stay at a place called Thiru Edagam. The leaf stays at the site of Thiru Edagam. The great minister Kulachirai Nayanaar takes the leaf, places it on his head, comes to the king, bows to Pillaiyar, and shows it to everyone. A shout of “Hara Hara” arose there.

“Immediately, the king said, “The Jains have now lost.

“Moreover, they previously offended Pillaiyar, and they set fire to the sacred monastery where Pillaiyar was staying.

“Therefore, it is righteous to impale them on the stake,” and the king commanded the minister. Pillaiyar also heard this. The king’s command to punish them for committing the terrible act of setting fire to the monastery where Saivites resided is Pillaiyar’s view was that it was appropriate.

“Therefore, Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan did not overturn the king’s order. According to the king’s command, the eight thousand Jain gurus of the eight great hills who had set fire to Pillaiyar’s monastery were impaled on the stake. Those stakes shone as pillars of victory, proclaiming the glory of Saivism and the fame of Pillaiyar.

“After that, Pillaiyar gave sacred ash to the king. The king also humbly accepted and completely applied the sacred ash. Seeing this, the people of Madurai also adorned themselves with the pure sacred ash. Everywhere, Vedic justice prevailed. The expanded radiance of the sacred white ash purified all directions. At that very moment, the darkness of Jainism vanished.

“Thus, giving life to the king Giving life to the king, showing him the true path, and removing Jainism, Pillaiyar’s truth, which he used to uplift the world, spread and flourished. The sacred path of Saivism prevailed, Vedic sacrifices and rains occurred without fail. By chanting Shiva’s name, this world was freed from the suffering of rebirth. With the king, queen, and minister accompanying him, Pillaiyar proceeded to praise the Lord of Thiru Aalavaai. The people of Pandya Nadu, who are of the Kanniya country, attained the fruit of having eyes to witness this. Entering the temple, with tears streaming down their faces and hands clasped, Pillaiyar prayed to the Lord, singing the Thiru Pathigam “Veedaal Aalavaai” (O Lord of Aalavaai, who granted salvation), saying, “O True One, who can bestow fearlessness upon this humble servant!” The king also praised the Lord, saying, “O Lord, you have bestowed this gracious Pillaiyar upon me to redeem me from the illusion of the Jains and take me into your grace.”

“After praising and worshipping, he sent the king and queen back to the palace, and Pillaiyar, after praising the Lord, resided in the monastery. The Pandya king, Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, and Minister Kulachirai Nayanaar worshipped and praised Pillaiyar’s feet daily. Pillaiyar, with deep devotion, sang hymns in praise of the Lord enshrined in Aalavaai, his heart melting with love. During this period, Sivapatha Hrudayar in Seerkazhi thought of Pillaiyar, whom he had received through his penance. Memories of Pillaiyar overwhelmed Sivapatha Hrudayar. He worshipped Thoni Appar and set off towards the Pandya country, worshipping the Lord in all the holy places along the way, and arrived in Madurai.

“Sivapatha Hrudayar went to Thiru Aalavaai, worshipped the Lord, and then went to the monastery where Pillaiyar was staying, which was nearby.

“The devotees inform Pillaiyar of Sivapatha Hrudayar’s arrival.

“Then, Pillaiyar, going before his father and bowing, as his father, who had followed the path of penance, came forward to bow to him, thinks of the lotus feet of the Divine Couple who, through his (Pillaiyar’s) connection, had cut off the bonds of rebirth when he appeared in Thoni at Seerkazhi. With folded hands and tears streaming down his eyes, he says, “O great ascetic, it was when I was in my unknowing childhood that the great Lord and my Divine Mother took me into their grace.” With this thought, he sings the Thiru Pathigam, “Mannil Nalla Vannam Vaazhalaam” (We can live well on earth). After feasting his father during those days, he also goes with the devotees to worship the Lord of Aalavaai and then departs from Madurai, intending to worship other holy places.

“At that moment, the king and queen their bodies softened, their hearts melted, and tears flowed down their faces, they fell at Pillaiyar’s feet and worshipped him. At that moment, Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan blessed them, saying, “Come with me to worship other holy places in this country, so that you may not suffer separation from me.” After that, he worshipped the holy places of Thirupparankundram and Thiru Aappanur, then went to Thiruputtur and worshipped there, staying for a few days.

“Afterwards, he visited and worshipped all the Pandya country’s holy places, including Thiru Poovanam, Thiru Kaanapper (Kalaiyar Kovil), Thiru Chuzhiyal (Thiru Chuzhi), Thiru Kutralam, Thiru Kurumbala, and Thirunelveli. Pillaiyar then reached Thiru Rameswaram and worshipped the Lord in the temple established and worshipped by Lord Vishnu. The king, Queen Mangaiyarkarasi, and the minister accompanied him and worshipped there. Standing on that seashore, Thiru Gnanasambandha Perumaan praises and worships the holy places in Lanka, the island nation, where the Lord is enshrined: Thirukonamalai and Thirukketheeswaram.

“Then, from there, he bows and proceeds north, worshipping many holy places, including Thiru Aadaanai and Thiru Punavaayil, which are holy sites in the Pandya country. He praises and worships them, bestowing grace so that people may live well, experiencing the clarity of the Vedic path and the glory of the sacred ash everywhere. He then arrives at Manamelkudi, the capital of Minister Kulachirai Nayanaar, and stays there, honored by the king, queen, and Kulachirai, visiting and worshipping other holy places.

“Let us continue to reflect on the condensed sacred history of Thiru Gnanasambandha Nayanaar.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 11 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam Part 548, “Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam,” by Sekkizhar Swamigal, the history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. While staying in Manamelkudi, the hometown of Kulachirai Nayanar in the Pandya kingdom, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman decided to journey to the Chozha kingdom. The King, the Queen, and the Minister, unable to bear separation from ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, declared their intention to accompany him. To them, the Child Saint said, “Listen to me; remain here and foster the path of Shiva.” He spoke comforting words to alleviate their distress. Unable to refuse, they respectfully took their leave with unwavering friendship.

The Child Saint then departed from the Pandya kingdom, journeyed to the Chozha kingdom, and there, wherever his devotees received him, he visited various sacred places in the Chozha kingdom. He worshipped at shrines such as Thirukkalar and Thiru Pathalicharam, and then reached Mullivaikkarai. A massive flood raged in the river, preventing boatmen from operating their vessels; they had tied their boats at the landing and departed. The Child Saint, having arrived at that bank, beheld the shrine of Thirukollampoodhoor on the opposite bank. Desiring to visit and worship there, he untied all the bound boats and, with his devotees, boarded one. He then sang the devotional hymn “Kottame Kamizhum” and miraculously propelled the boats across the river to the other bank without any boatmen.

There, he worshipped the Lord at Thirukollampoodhoor. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman praised the Lord. Desiring to worship the Lord of Thirunallar, who had been instrumental in his victory in the Anarvadam at Madurai, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman visited all the shrines along the way. He reached the Thirunallar temple, circumambulated it according to custom, and prayed to the Lord. With tears streaming down, he extolled the Lord with the hymn “Kannarivi Payanendru Padagamelladi.” He sang of the unique nature of the Lord who, in the debate with the Jains before the Pandya king’s assembly, had caused the leaf thrown into the fire to remain green, thus abiding as his inner support in Thiru Alavai. Such is the meaning of the Thirunallar hymn.

Afterwards, he stayed there for some time, then took leave and proceeded to worship at Thiruthelicheri. On the way, he arrived at Bodhimangai, a city of the Buddhists. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, known as Parasamaya Kolarivan, the slayer of other religions, was heralded by the blowing of trumpets as he entered the town. Hearing this, the Buddhists, unable to tolerate it, gathered under the leadership of Buddhanandhi. They confronted the group of devotees and angrily declared, “You may boast of these symbols of victory only after you have defeated us.” The devotees informed the Child Saint, who was approaching in his palanquin. The Child Saint graciously replied, “Let us engage in debate directly, without delay; we shall expose their false doctrines.” Meanwhile, a devotee among the sacred assembly, who was writing the Thirumurai, unable to bear the unrighteous actions of the Buddhists, uttered, “May the head of this Buddhist fall, for the five letters (Namasivaya) are the weapon against the enemies of karma, adorning the Lord with water.” Immediately, a thunderbolt struck Buddhanandhi’s head.

His body and head fell apart. The Buddhists fled in fear.

The devotees informed the Child Saint of this incident. He declared, “This is an act of Shiva’s grace; everyone, chant the name of Haran!” The chanting of Shiva’s name resounded to the heavens. The fearful Buddhists who had fled reassembled, bewildered, wondering if it was a trick or their Shaivite truth. They returned, led by a Buddhist named Sariputhan from among them. They requested a philosophical debate rather than one involving sorcery. The Child Saint agreed, dismounted from his palanquin, and ascended to the debate hall.

He invited the Buddhists to debate. They arrived with Sariputhan. The devotee who had cursed Buddhanandhi bowed before the Child Saint. He engaged in a scriptural debate with them. The debate revolved around their leader, the principles he upheld, and their definition of liberation. In this debate, the devotee demonstrated that the Buddhist doctrines were baseless, making them realize it.

He asserted that Shaivism alone is the true reality, and there is no other true reality, citing Vedic pronouncements and the conclusions of the Agamas, thus defeating the Buddhists in the debate. As the Child Saint’s compassionate gaze fell upon them, the Buddhists bowed and worshipped him. After explaining to them that all moving and unmoving beings are Shaivite, the Child Saint departed from there and journeyed to Thirukkadavoor to worship. He inquired where ThiruNavukkarasar Swamigal was staying.

The devotees replied that ThiruNavukkarasar Peruman was residing in Thirupoonduruthi, engaged in sacred service. Hearing this, he departed with a great desire to meet ThiruNavukkarasar Peruman. He worshipped at all the shrines along the way and arrived near Thirupoonduruthi. Hearing the news that ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman was coming to Thirupoonduruthi, Vakeesar came forth. He was overjoyed, considering it a fruit of his past good deeds to go and worship the Child Saint. He worshipped the Lord and then entered the throng of devotees in the Child Saint’s procession.

Without being seen by the Child Saint, he worshipped him and joined those carrying the palanquin, helping to bear it, his heart overflowing with joy. No one there recognized ThiruNavukkarasar Peruman.

At that moment, a divine intuition arose in the Child Saint’s mind, and he inquired, “Where is Appar now?” Hearing this, ThiruNavukkarasar Peruman replied, “Having performed unparalleled penance in the past, I am now blessed to carry your sacred feet.” Filled with awe, the Child Saint immediately descended from the palanquin and prostrated before him, asking why he had performed such an act. Vakeesar prostrated in return, asking, “How else should one serve ThiruGnanaSambandhar?” The Child Saint embraced him with great affection, and all the devotees cheered. The two great saints proceeded together to the temple, entered, and worshipped the Lord Poiyili Appar enshrined in the Thirupoonduruthi temple. They came before the sacred entrance.

Then, Vakeesa Peruman inquired about the Child Saint’s journeys and returns. He recounted all those events.

The King worshipped him and declared, “You have been a great fence for the flourishing crop of sacred service.” Vakeesa Peruman rejoiced upon hearing of how he had revived the Pandya king with sacred ash, bestowed affection upon the Queen and the Minister, and re-established the Vedic path. Vakeesar then spoke of his own journeys, having visited Thiru Ekambaram in the great Thondai kingdom. Hearing this, the Child Saint also resolved to visit and worship in the Thondai kingdom. Appar Peruman, hearing the news from ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar, resolved to go and worship the Lord at Thiru Alavai. Seerkazhi Peruman, GnanaSambandha Peruman, decided to go to Seerkazhi. He worshipped the Lord, took leave of Vakeesar, and departed.

He worshipped at Thiru Naitthanam and Thirupazhanam on the northern bank of the Cauvery, then arrived at Seerkazhi. Hearing the news that the Child Saint, having dispelled the darkness of Jainism and reinstated the sacred ash in the Pandya kingdom, was arriving, the Brahmins of Seerkazhi, chanting Vedas, came to receive him. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman descended from his palanquin and, seeing the temple, folded his hands in worship. He respectfully entered the Seerkazhi temple, worshipped, and ascended to worship Ammai Appar at Thiru Thoni. With goosebumps all over his body, tears streaming, and his heart overflowing with joy, he bowed and sang the Thiruyamaga Thirupathigam in praise.

Afterwards, he came out, worshipped the temple, and on the way, with women offering praises, he bestowed gracious leave upon Thiru Neelakanda Panar, allowing him to reside within his sacred form, and then returned to his sacred abode, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman.

At that time, Bhagavati Ammaiyar, the mother of the Brahmin lineage, came and bowed at his feet. He also mentally worshipped the Mother’s feet in Thiru Thoni.

Then, he worshipped Thoniyappar, sang a hymn in praise, and departed. The Child Saint resolved to go to the auspicious Thondai kingdom to see and worship Kambar, who had been embraced by the Mother.

Now, ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar’s sixth pilgrimage is about to begin. This will be a pilgrimage to the Thondai country.

We will continue to contemplate the brief history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 12 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam Part 549, “Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam,” by Sekkizhar Swamigal, the history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman begins his sixth pilgrimage from Seerkazhi. This sixth pilgrimage is to the Thondai kingdom. He informed the devotees of Seerkazhi of his intention, worshipped Thoniyappar, and took leave to depart.

At that time, the Peruman’s father also prepared to accompany him. The Child Saint then bade farewell to his father and the devotees from Seerkazhi who had started with him, asking them to stay there, perform sacrifices, and worship Thoniyappar. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, worshipping at all the shrines along the way, arrived at Thillai. He worshipped Thirupuliyur and was blessed to witness the Lord’s ecstatic dance. Continuing, he worshipped at Thiru Thinnainagar, Thiru Manikuli, Thirupathiripuliyur, Thiru Vadugoor, Thiru Vakkara, Thiru Irumbaimakazham, and other shrines, finally reaching Thiru Athikai Veerattanam. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman was graced with a vision of the Lord dancing, surrounded by bhoota ganas.

He sang the hymn “Kundai Kuralbhoodham” there. He then worshipped at Thiru Amathur, and visited Thiru Kovaloor and Thiru Arayaninallur. While circumambulating, he saw Thiruvannamalai in the distance, pointed out by his devotees, and went to worship it with great fervor, chanting “Poovar Malara,” He stayed at Thiruvannamalai for several days, worshipping the Lord.

Afterwards, he journeyed north, visiting many of the Lord’s shrines, crossing great mountains and forests, and arrived at the blessed Thondai kingdom. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman reached the sacred site of Thiru Oothur, worshipped and praised the Lord, and settled there.

One day, a devotee came before the Child Saint, weeping, and informed ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, “I cultivated palm trees for the service of the Lord, but all these palm trees grew to be male trees.

“Therefore, they did not bear fruit. Seeing this, the Jains mockingly say, ‘The palm trees you cultivate for your deity do not bear fruit!’ O Lord, only you can bless me,” he pleaded. Hearing the devotee’s plea to ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, the Child Saint, filled with compassion, went to the temple and sang a hymn to the Lord. In the concluding verse of that hymn, in the Thirukkadaikappu, he sang of the truth, “Kurumbai aan panaiyin kulaivoothur” (male palm trees bearing clusters at Oothur). In accordance with that truth, all the male palm trees bore abundant clusters of unripe female palm fruit. All who witnessed this were astonished.

“Thus, having fulfilled the devotee’s wish, the Child Saint remained happily in that town. Seeing this, the Jains were perplexed and left that country. The Child Saint then asked what happened to those female palm trees that bore fruit in clusters. Due to the Child Saint’s divine words, those palm trees, released from their former attachment, were purified and, in time, attained Shivam.

“Afterwards, he worshipped and departed, visiting many shrines where the Lord resided, including Thiru Makaral and Thiru Kuranganilmuttam. The Child Saint then arrived near Thiru Kanchi. Learning of his arrival, the devotees of Kanchi, overjoyed, decorated the city and, with auspicious offerings, came to receive the Child Saint. As everyone rejoiced, he journeyed among them and reached Thiru Ekambaram.

“There, he worshipped the Lord with devotion, sang the hymn “Maraiyanai” in praise, and then came out and stayed in the monastery. He approached the great charitable Kamakottam and worshipped there. He consistently worshipped Thiru Ekambanar without fail. He sang hymns such as Thiruyamagam and Thiruvirakkural, and then worshipped at Thiru Kachi Nerikkarai, Thiru Kachi Anekathangavatham, Thiru Kachi Metrali, and other sacred places before departing. He then went to the southern bank of the Palar river, worshipped at Thiru Marperu and Thiru Vallam. From there, he worshipped Thiru Ilambaiyangottoor on the northern bank, visited Thiru Virkolam, Thiru Ooral, and other shrines, and then arrived near Thiruvalangadu.

“This sacred place is where my mother, Karaikkal Ammaiyar, worshipped by walking on her head, for all the world to see.

“Therefore, the Child Saint, hesitant to step on Thiruvalangadu, stayed in a side building outside Thiruvalangadu for that night. In the middle of the night, Thiruvalangadu Appar appeared in his dream and asked, “Have you forgotten to sing of me?” Immediately, he arose, having understood and worshipped. He praised the Lord’s compassion, his body trembling, and sang the hymn “Thuncha Varuvarum Thozhuvipparum,” composed in the Pazhapanjarappann tune, extolling the Lord. In that hymn, he glorified the story of Pazhayanoorar, who valued his word more than his life. In the morning, he related this incident to the devotees who had gathered, and with heartfelt devotion, he sang praises. From there, he worshipped and sang of Thiruppasur and Thiruvenpakkam, and then, remembering Thiru Kannappa Nayanar, he resolved to visit Thiru Kalatthi mountain.

“Therefore, he departed from there, crossing fertile lands and entering the dry forests. He worshipped at Thiru Karikkarai, where clouds gathered, and then journeyed through the mountainous terrain. As the throngs of devotees, like a sea, surrounded him, animals, hearing the loud trumpeting announcing the arrival of Thiru GnanaSambandhan, were unified in thought and gathered around. Journeying thus, he passed by the hunting grounds where Thiru Kannappa Nayanar’s sacred footwear had trodden, and other places revered by even the Devas, and approached Thiru Kalatthi.

“There, throngs of devotees, matted-haired sages, Kapalis, and various Shaivite ascetics gathered to welcome the Child Saint. The Child Saint descended from his palanquin, bowed, and inquired which of the mountains was Thiru Kalatthi mountain. When they pointed it out, he was overjoyed. He worshipped and sang the Thiruviragappan hymn, extolling Kannappar’s service, recounting how ‘celestials and asuras’ (Vaanavargal Thaanavargal). He reached the foothills of the mountain, worshipped the mountain as he ascended, circled the temple, and approached the sacred presence. He prostrated himself fully, joining his hands, and arose, as if seeing the fruit of worshipping the Lord, and there he saw Kannappa Nayanar.

“Then, with a joyful heart, he experienced the true form and the Lord who was established within that love, all at once. He arose, worshipped many times, was immersed in devotion, and then departed to stay there. He stayed for many days, worshipping the Lord at every appointed time, and was delighted to reside there. Since the custom of refined Tamil was not prevalent in the northern and western directions, he worshipped various shrines such as Thirukayilai, Thiru Kedaram, Thiru Gokarnam, Thiruparuppatham (Srisailam), and Thiru Indra Neela Paruppatham from his abode in Thiru Kalatthi. He sang hymns about them.

“Afterwards, he resolved to visit and worship Thiruvottiyur. With the Lord’s grace, he departed from that sacred city and set out towards Thiruvottiyur, singing the hymn “Enthaiyar Inaiyadi En Manathullave” and worshipping as he proceeded. He traveled along the northern bank of the Palar river, worshipping all the shrines he had previously visited, including Thiruverkadu and Thiruvalithayam, and then arrived at Thiruvottiyur.

“The devotees of that city prostrated and came to receive him. He, too, descended from his palanquin, prostrated, and sang the hymn “Vidayavan.” He entered the Thiruvottiyur temple, worshipped and praised in the customary way, and then joyfully resided in that city with the devotees.

“We will continue to contemplate the brief history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 13 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam Part 550, “Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam,” by Sekkizhar Swamigal, the history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. In Mylapore, also known as Thiru Mylapuri in Chennai, lived a merchant named Sivanesar. He was extremely wealthy, deeply devoted to Shiva’s devotees, and highly virtuous.

At that time, he heard about the Child Saint’s incarnation in Seerkazhi, his attainment of divine wisdom, and his actions in destroying other religions. Hearing all this, Sivanesar developed an unceasing love for the sacred feet of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar and greatly rejoiced in hearing about the miraculous deeds performed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. Although Sivanesar was a great wealthy man, he had no children. Due to his devoted worship, delighting and pleasing the devotees of Lord Shiva, a rare daughter was born to him. As the girl child was like a flower, he named her Poombavai and lovingly raised her. When the girl child turned seven, Sivanesar proclaimed that the man who would marry her would be the sole heir to all his wealth.

During those days, the Child Saint traveled to the Pandya kingdom, cured the Pandya king’s fever, debated and defeated the Jains in fire and water, destroyed them, bestowed sacred ash upon the Pandya king, And heard all about the divine acts that spread Shaivism in the Pandya kingdom. Sivanesar prostrated and worshipped in the direction where the Child Saint was. Hearing all these divine acts of the Child Saint, Sivanesar joyfully announced to all his relatives and kin that he had given his daughter Poombavai, all his wealth, and himself to the Child Saint, the ruler of the Kali country.

One day, while Poombavai was plucking jasmine flowers, a snake bit her finger, leaving four teeth marks. The poison ascended to her head, and the girl fell unconscious. Physicians, astrologers, and experts in various arts like Garudan Vidhya All those skilled in their respective fields tried to save her, but the girl’s life departed. Sivanesar and his relatives were distressed.

However, since they had dedicated the girl child to the Child Saint, they resolved not to grieve. They cremated her body and collected the remaining ashes and bones in a pot. This pot was placed in a maiden’s chamber, and her companions were instructed to offer lamps, garlands, and other services daily. Sivanesar and his family maintained this practice. During these days, Sivanesar received the good news that the Child Saint was currently residing in Thiru Ottriyur. Sivanesar was overjoyed.

He gave gold and garments to those who brought the news. He arranged for a flowery canopy, a “Nadaikavanam,” from Thiru Mylapore to Thiru Ottriyur. He planted plantain and betel nut trees, and adorned the path with banners and garlands, decorating it like a divine realm. He, along with his devotees, set out to worship the Child Saint.

At the same time, the Child Saint, having worshipped in Thiruvottiyur, was approaching Thirumylapuri with a throng of devotees. Sivanesar, overjoyed, prostrated on the ground. The Child Saint descended from his palanquin, worshipped before the assembly of devotees, and arose. Hearing the accounts of Sivanesar the wealthy merchant, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman arrived at Thirumylapuri. Bearing in his heart the events that had befallen the merchant, and filled with compassion, he worshipped the sacred Kapaleeswaram of the Lord. ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar circumambulated the temple.

He went before the Lord, worshipped the God of Gods, Kapaleeswaram. He praised and immersed himself in devotion to the ambrosia of Kapaleeswaram, then came out of the temple. Stepping outside, he addressed Sivanesar the wealthy merchant, saying, “Bring the pot filled with your daughter’s bones from outside the temple walls.” Sivanesar then took the pot from the maiden’s chamber. Placed in a covered palanquin, surrounded by her companions, he brought it to the outer entrance of the temple. He then took the pot from the palanquin, placed it directly before him, and bowed. When ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar asked for the pot containing the bones, and Sivanesar, the wealthy merchant, brought it, the people of Mylapore gathered to see what would happen.

The Child Saint, contemplating the greatness of the Lord’s compassion, thought that in this world, by merely using the bones of the deceased, that life could be restored to a good path through the continuation of those bones. He then, calling out the girl’s name, Poombavai, declared that if the greatest benefit of those born into this world is to offer food to the devotees of Lord Shiva and to witness the Lord’s festivals with one’s own eyes, then, before all the people of this world, “Come forth!” He announced this, worshipped the Lord, and began to sing the hymn “Mattitta.” Within that hymn, the divine words “Podhiyo” (Arise!) acted like ambrosia, entering the bones in the pot, causing a form to coalesce within. The air that passed through the verses caused a body, growth, and radiance to fill and be contained within the pot. Before she arose, the Child Saint sang the tenth verse.

At that moment, a hand appeared outside the pot, the pot broke, and Poombavai arose like a lotus bud unfurling. That is, Poombavai, the girl, gained her form with the first verse sung by ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. In the following eight verses, she grew to the same extent, appearing as she would have at twelve years of age. At the time of Poombavai’s demise, she was seven years old; now, five years had passed, making her twelve.

Thus, she emerged from the pot, fully grown as she would have been at twelve years. Seeing this, the Child Saint concluded the hymn with the “Thirukkadaikappu” (concluding verse), thus completing the hymn. Those who witnessed this miracle, the true devotees, chanted “Hara Hara!” The celestial beings showered flowers. The kings They joined their hands and prostrated themselves. Those of other religions were confused in mind and body, falling into disarray, wondering how this could happen. The beautiful form that had risen, from head to toe, with every limb perfectly adorned with the highest marks of beauty, shone.

Poombavai appeared, astonishing both heaven and earth, an embodiment of beauty. Brahma, who has an immeasurable lifespan, and who, at such an advanced age, had succumbed to lust and lost his good sense upon seeing the illusory beauty of Tilottama, whom he himself had created with his four faces, sank into desire.

However, here, the Child Saint, having completed sixteen years of age, When Poombavai, even more beautiful than Tilottama, came back to life, our Child Saint saw in her only the overflowing compassion of the Lord. The Child Saint did not see Poombavai; he saw only the overflowing compassion of the Lord. Seeing this, Sivanesar prostrated himself at the sacred feet of the Child Saint. Poombavai bowed to the Lord and then to the Child Saint. The Child Saint then addressed Sivanesar, saying, “Take our daughter and go to your home.” Sivanesar bowed to the Child Saint and requested, “Please marry my daughter, Poombavai.” The Child Saint refused, saying, “The daughter you had fell due to poison. This girl, however, has been reborn through the Lord’s compassion.

“Therefore, what you ask is not appropriate.” The Child Saint comforted the grieving merchant and his relatives, explaining the truth of the Vedas to clarify their minds. They, too, abandoned their desire. The Child Saint entered the temple, compassionately worshipped the Lord of Kapaleeswaram, who had bestowed his grace. Sivanesar, unwilling to give Poombavai’s heart to anyone else, brought her back to the maiden’s chamber. Poombavai also attained Shivam.

“The Child Saint stayed in that sacred city for some days. Taking leave from the inhabitants of that city, and assuaging Sivanesar’s sorrow with sweet words, he departed and reached Thiruvanmiyur.

“There, he worshipped the Lord, the medicine for birth and death, He praised Him with a hymn composed in question and answer format, and resided there happily for some days. From there, he proceeded to Thiru Idaichuram, worshipped the Lord, marveled at the color of His sacred form, and sang a hymn praising, “Ivar Vanamenna.” He then arrived at Thirukazhukunram, circumambulated the mountain, worshipped the Lord, and sang a hymn in praise, “Kadhal Seyya Kovil Kazhukunre.” Afterwards, he reached Thiru Achirupakkam, worshipped there, sang the hymn “Aatchi Kondaar,” and resided there happily.

“Then, his devotees welcomed him as he journeyed to other shrines, worshipping at Thiru Varishili, Thiruppuravarpankattoor, and other sacred places, finally arriving at Thillainagar.

“The Brahmins of Thillai and the sacred devotees welcomed him. He descended from his palanquin, and with great love and folded hands, he went and worshipped Thillai. He bowed at the northern entrance and worshipped the sacred streets. He proceeded, worshipped the Perambalam, bowed at the sacred Anukkathiruvayil, and reached the Ponnambalam. He worshipped the divine dance of the great dancer who transcends qualities, bowed at the Thirukazhitrupadi, and was immersed in boundless bliss, reaching a state beyond the shores of supreme joy. When it was not the appointed time, he went outside and worshipped at every auspicious hour, staying there.

“Hearing the news of the Child Saint’s arrival, Sivapathakirudhaiyar, Brahmins, and devotees from Seerkazhi arrived at Thillai. The Thillai Brahmins honored them. They joined the Child Saint, worshipped the Lord of Ambalam, and were joyful. The Child Saint took leave of Koothaperuman and set out towards Seerkazhi, worshipping at many shrines along the way. Seeing the city of Seerkazhi from a distance, he descended from his palanquin, worshipped, and began to sing the hymn “Vandar Kuzhal Arivai,” extolling the Lord, as if the palace was supported by the sky. He continued to sing the hymn “Vezhupuram.” As he approached the city and reached the outer shrine, he offered flowers, incense, and lamps, then sang the concluding hymn “Kalinaagar Sermin,” urging them to enter the city of Kali.

“He entered the sacred city, his love overflowing, and systematically circumambulated the temple, worshipped, and ascended to Thiru Thoni. He joined his hands before Ammai Appar, fell in prostration, and was immersed in devotion, experiencing great bliss. He sang many hymns in praise, received divine leave, and then returned to his sacred abode and resided there.

“We will continue to contemplate the brief history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 14 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam Part 561, “Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam,” by Sekkizhar Swamigal, the history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar. Sekkizhar Peruman sings of the Child Saint’s crying. The verse is: “His lotus eyes filled with tears, he rubbed them with his lotus hands, his beautiful, red, cherry-like mouth and coral lips trembled, and as the endless sound of the Vedas surged, all beings rejoiced, and the holy calf-like one cried.” Generally, when children cry, tears first well up in their eyes, then they rub their eyes with their hands, after which their lips tremble, and then they cry out with sound. These are the stages observed when a child cries. The same method Sekkizhar Peruman employs here in his song: “His lotus eyes filled with tears, he rubbed them with his lotus hands, his beautiful, red, cherry-like mouth and coral lips trembled.” The terms “lotus eyes,” “lotus hands,” and “flower-red-cherry-mouth” indicate that the Child Saint’s eyes, hands, and mouth were all beautiful like lotus flowers.

Why did he cry? The Child Saint cried so that the sound of the Vedas would surge and all beings would rejoice. This crying is the means; the surging of Vedic sound and the rejoicing of all beings are the benefits. The benefit here means enabling these beings to attain the qualification for Shivam. That is why it is indicated here as “all beings rejoicing.” This means that just as a Guru purifies a disciple through his gaze, by placing his sacred hands on the disciple’s head, and by imparting instruction, these references to “lotus eyes,” “lotus hands,” and “lotus mouth” even in song, refer to the lotus flower.

This is like the “Thiruvalar Thamarai” (sacred blooming lotus) mentioned in Thirukovaiyar.

Therefore, because the Child Saint cried, the sound of the Vedas surged, and because of this, beings rejoiced.

Thus, the Child Saint’s crying was the means, and the surging of Vedic sound and the rejoicing of beings was the benefit. “Surging of Vedic sound” means the spread of Thevarams, which are the essence of the Vedas, In this world. Mahadheva Sivagnana Munivar Peruman further explains this by saying, “Tamil Vedas spread throughout the lands, causing all to sing.” Such a Child Saint is like the calf of righteousness. He is in the youthful form of righteousness. The righteousness referred to here is the good fortune of experiencing Shiva without forgetting Him. The Child Saint appeared as if that goodness itself had taken a form.

Why did the Child Saint cry thus? He cried looking at the Thonipuram peak in Seerkazhi. Sekkizhar Peruman sings, “His body trembled, tears fell, he cried looking elsewhere; did he cry remembering his past association (with Shiva), or was it the state of childhood? He cried looking at the Thiru Thoni peak of the red-bodied, white-ash-smeared Lord, calling out ‘Amme Appa!’” The Child Saint cried, with tears falling upon his sacred body, looking at the surrounding areas. Sekkizhar Peruman sings, “We do not know if the Child Saint cried remembering his former state, his past association, or if it was due to his current state of childhood.” There could be two reasons why the Child Saint cried, calling out “Amme Appa!” One is that the Child Saint realized his past association; the other is the state of childhood he was currently in.

We cannot know which of these two reasons caused him to cry, says Sekkizhar Peruman. He implies that we should infer and understand it through our own estimation. This is an excellent tradition of the Guru. When it is said that he cried because he realized his past association, “past association” refers to the Lord, Shiva. Realizing it means experiencing that realization outwardly.

Here, the Child Saint has two associations: that of Shiva and that of Sivapathakiruthaiyar at present. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that perhaps the Child Saint cried because he contained within himself that divine association, his past association with Shiva. His father having descended into the sacred waters, the Child Saint, instead of crying at the sight of his father, cried looking at the peak.

Therefore, it was his past association, realizing the Lord Shiva. He cried looking at the Thiru Thoni peak. In the Seerkazhi temple, the Brahmmapureeswarar temple, the peak that stands like a mountain, which is in the shape of a Thoni, that unique grand temple, he cried looking at the peak of the sanctum sanctorum, the Vimana. From the bank of the Brahmatheertham, he cried looking at the Thiru Thonipuram peak. “Peak” can mean Vimana.

At the same time, “peak” can refer to the letter “Si” (சி). The letter “Si” in the sacred Panchaksharam refers to Lord Shiva. The Child Saint cried, looking inwards at the sacred essence, Shiva, who resides in Thiru Thoni as the peak. The Agamas state that in the Sri Panchaksharam, the letter “Si” signifies Shiva, the letter “Va” signifies divine grace, and the letter “Ya” signifies the soul.

Therefore, the Child Saint cried, calling out “Amme Appa,” to the sacred essence, Lord Shiva, who resides in the Thiru Thoni temple as the peak. He places the Mother first, “Amme,” and the Father next, “Appa,” because the Mother is the one who introduces the child to the Father and unites the child with the Father. The Mother.

Therefore, he first sings of the Mother. Even in the scriptures, it is stated that it is divine grace that purifies souls and unites them with Lord Shiva. Even in Thiruvachagam, Manikkavasagar Peruman sang, “Ammaiye Appa Oppila Maniye,” placing the Mother first.

Therefore, although the great saint, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, wished to see the Father, he cried, placing the Mother first, “Amme.” In the words “Amme Appa,” the first letter is ‘A’ (அ), and the second letters are ‘M’ (ம்) in “Amme” and ‘Pa’ (ப்ப) in “Appa.” The letter ‘A’ (அ), being the first letter, naturally emerges when we open our mouths. This letter ‘A’ (அ) and then the letters ‘P’ (ப்) and ‘M’ (ம்), which are formed when the lips close after opening the mouth, are the letters ‘Pa’ and ‘Ma’.

Therefore, these words “Amme Appa” are naturally the first words uttered by children. Gnana Shastras state that the Lord, mingled with the primordial pure Maya, creates this world with the support of Shakti.

Thus, Shakti and Shiva are the Mother and Father of the world, according to Shaiva Siddhanta. This is from Thiru Kayappakkam. Sivachettiyar’s commentary notes that since he called out and wept looking at the peak, both of them come. The peak is where the Lord resides. Sivagnana Siddhiyar states that the Mother and Father who create knowledge in all souls, and the Father with the Mother, come and bestow knowledge upon them. This knowledge will be beneficial to all souls.

Now we speak of how the Mother, who is divine grace, nurtures and prepares souls by providing them with bodies, instruments, worlds, and experiences. The Mother, being divine grace, prepares these souls and unites them with the Lord.

Thus, to those souls who have been united with the Lord, that is, those who have been granted moksha. To those souls who have attained the sixfold liberation, the Lord bestows His wealth, His property, which is Sivananda.

Therefore, He is the Father, and She is the Mother.

Thus, when Pillaiyar called out “Mother, Father” and wept, would the Lord remain silent?

The Lord manifests Himself. We shall reflect on this further.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 15 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 562, ‘Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam’, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, recounts the history of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Nayanar. Pillaiyar, looking towards the peak of Thonipuram, weeps.

At that moment, Lord Shiva, who was enshrined in Thiru Thoni, emerges to bestow His grace upon Pillaiyar. The verse states: “Thiruthoni veetrirundharul nokkal munnilamai thiruthondu munniyavarkku arul purivan pon malai valliyum thamum porudaimeel ezhundharuli chenniyilam pirai thikazha sezhumpoykai marunganaindhaar.” This means that to bestow grace upon Pillaiyar, who remembered his former state of sacred service, the Lord manifested Himself with His divine gaze, along with the golden mountain goddess, Uma, seated on His bull, with the young crescent moon shining on His head, near the rich pond.

The Lord manifests Himself to fulfill His divine gaze.

The Lord manifests Himself to fulfill His divine gaze. Pillaiyar called out, “Mother, Father!” Accordingly, the Lord, along with Uma, the mountain goddess, adorned with the crescent moon, appears on His bull, in that divine form. He manifests near the Brahma Tirtha pond. The next verse states: “Thirumarai nool vedhiyarkkum theviyarkkum thaam kodutha perugu vara ninainthothaan tham perumai kazhal penum oru neriyil varugnanam koduppathanukku udanirundha arumaraiyaal udaiyavalai aliththarula arul seivaar.” Did He remember the great boons He had granted to Sivapadahridhayar and Bhagavati Ammaiyar, and the sacred scriptures? To bestow the unique knowledge that comes from following the path of worshipping His feet, He bestows grace with the Lady of the rare Vedas, Parvati. This refers to the birth of this child.

The Lord gave birth to Pillaiyar.

The Lord brought forth Pillaiyar for the refutation of other religions and the flourishing of Shaivism. Is it to fulfill these boons that the Lord appears here with the Goddess? If grace is to be bestowed upon the weeping Pillaiyar, then the presence of Parvati, the Lady of the Vedas, and the Lord Himself would suffice.

But now, the Lord not only manifests but also intends to give Gnanaponakam (food of wisdom). This also serves to fulfill the boon given to Sivapadahridhayar and Bhagavati Ammaiyar. How so? By giving Gnanaponakam, it will manifest as Tamil Vedas, the Devaram verses, leading to the eradication of other religions and the creation of Shaivism. This knowledge will be the cause for all future events.

Therefore, the Lord, having thus conceived, manifests to bestow grace. Pillaiyar is one who never forgets the holy feet of the Lord.

Therefore, to bestow the knowledge that comes from diligently following the path of worshipping the Lord’s feet, the Lord manifests with the Goddess.

Thus, it is also conveyed here that even divine knowledge does not come on its own as a result of worshipping the holy feet; it comes only if the Lord bestows it, a truth affirmed by the sastras. For this purpose, the Lord manifests with Parvati, the Lady of the sacred Vedas. The Vedas themselves are the general form of the Lord, and the Goddess is the primal one who governs the knowledge enshrined within those Vedas. She, the Goddess, is the embodiment of the Vedas, the primal source of knowledge. The Vedas are knowledge, so the Goddess, as the primal source of knowledge, is capable of bestowing it. As the Goddess bestows this knowledge upon Pillaiyar, Pillaiyar will offer those words of knowledge as the sacred verses of Devaram.

Now, the next verse: “Azhukindra pillaiyar thamai nokki arutkarunai ezhukindra thiruvulla iraiyavar thaam evvulakum thozhukindra malai kodiyai paarthu aruli thunai mulaigal pozhukindra paal adisil pon vallathu vootu enna.” This means the Lord, whose heart swells with compassion, looks at the mountain creeper, Uma, worshipped by all worlds, and commands her, “Nourish him with the milk flowing from your twin breasts in a golden bowl.” This is the next verse. The Lord’s heart is filled with divine compassion. The heart in which divine grace arises is a heart filled with compassion. Grace and compassion are one and the same. In Sanskrit, ‘karuna’ and in Tamil, ‘arul’ are two words that convey the same meaning. Sekkizhar uses both ‘arul’ to explain the greatness of Lord Shiva’s grace in Tamil usage and ‘karuna’ to explain it in Sanskrit usage.

He uses both terms to emphasize the Lord’s immense grace.

Therefore, the Lord’s heart is a heart filled with divine compassion, a heart that is completely an embodiment of grace. Only grace occurs in that heart, nothing else.

Therefore, a heart where divine compassion arises. The Lord’s heart is the birthplace of grace. That grace itself is Ambikai. The grace that exists when souls are bound in the state of Petha (bondage), entangled in worldly attachments, is known as Marakkarunai (material grace). In the state of Mukti (liberation), the grace that exists in the form of Parashakti is Arakkarunai (divine grace).

Here, the compassionate heart of the Lord that arose when Pillaiyar wept is Arakkarunai, which exists in the form of Parashakti in the state of Mukti.

Thus, the Lord, whose heart is filled with arising divine compassion, looks with grace upon Uma Devi, the mountain creeper worshipped by all worlds. ‘Malai Kodi’ refers to Parvati Ammaiyar. She is the mountain creeper worshipped by all worlds. There is no living being, in any form, that does not desire to attain power and wisdom. There are no living beings that do not desire to attain the power and wisdom they yearn for. Ambikai is she who accepts this desire for power and wisdom as their worship and bestows compassion.

Therefore, she is the Mountain Creeper worshipped by all worlds, meaning all living beings.

Thus, the Lord looks upon Parvati Ammaiyar and says, “Thunai mulaigal pozhukindra paal adisil pon vallaththu vootu.” He instructs Parvati Ammaiyar, “Collect the milk-nectar flowing from your two sacred breasts in a golden bowl and feed it to this child.” The twin breasts of the Goddess are indispensable aids for souls to grow in knowledge and attain salvation. The two breasts of the Goddess represent Para Gnanam and Apara Gnanam. The milk flowing from them is the milk-nectar of knowledge.

The Lord instructs, “Take it in a golden bowl and feed it to the child.” The sacred breast of Uma Ammaiyar is not to be directly consumed by mouth but is to be collected and fed by her. That is why the Divine Mother is known by the Sanskrit name “Apeetha Kuchamba” and in Tamil as “Unnamulai” (She whose breasts are not directly consumed). It is for this reason, that it cannot be consumed directly but must be collected and fed by her, that this is said.

The Lord did not say to feed him milk directly, but rather to collect it in a golden bowl and feed it. In the Skanda Purana, in the Saravanappadalam, it is stated that Kaveri takes Lord Murugan, her beloved son, from Saravana Poigai, embraces him, collects the milk flowing from her breast in a golden bowl, and feeds him. The verse is, “Kongaiyil pozhi paal eethilaathathōr kurumaṇi vaḷḷam meethu yēttru kaathal maamakarkku anpinaal aruththinaal Kavuri.” Just as a mother breastfeeds her child according to its maturity, so too is knowledge, guided by the Mother of the World, Gnana Valli, bestowed by the Lord’s command, according to the maturity of souls. If not fed by the Mother. Just as a child unfed by its mother cannot obtain milk, souls cannot acquire knowledge on their own; it must be fed to them. This is the meaning.

Thus, as the Lord commanded, the next verses are: “Aranam ulakelum eendraruli anaiththinukkum kaaranamay valam perugu karunai thiruvativana seer anangu Shivaperuman aruluthalum sendru anainthu vaarinangu thirumulai ponvallaththuk karantharuli ennarriya sivagyanaththu innamutham kulaiththaruli unnadisil enavootta umaiyammai ethirnokkum kanmalar neer thudaiththaruli kaiyil ponkinnam aliththu annalai angu azhukai theerththu angananaar arul porindhaar.” This refers to how the Lord bestows His grace. The next two verses describe how, as Lord Shiva commanded to offer the milk-nectar in a golden bowl, the Mother collected the milk from her sacred breast in a golden bowl and offered it. She is the one who gave birth to the Vedas and all seven worlds. ‘Aranam’ refers to the collection of texts like the Vedas and other scriptures. She gave birth to that knowledge for the souls. She is the one who gave birth to the seven worlds. The ‘seven worlds’ refers to the collection of seven universes, and similarly, the collection of souls born in the seven types of births.

The phrase ‘gave birth’ here means to bring souls bound in the state of ‘kevala’ (primal state) into the ‘sakala’ state (state of activity) by awakening their consciousness and guiding them.

Thus, the Mother is the one who gave birth to the Vedas and all seven worlds. She is the cause of everything.

Here, ‘cause’ acts as an instrumental cause, meaning she serves as an auxiliary cause to the efficient cause, the Lord, providing bodies, instruments, worlds, and experiences from Maya. Through this, she enables souls to experience and exhaust their karmic fruits, thereby leading them to salvation.

Thus, she is the cause of everything. She is the embodiment of flourishing grace. ‘Valam’ refers to the wealth of enjoyment (bhoga) and liberation (moksha). Her very form is the grace that leads to the attainment of enjoyment and liberation. Such is the glorious goddess, the Mother. She, the Mother, who brings forth the Aranas (Vedas), and the seven worlds, and who is the embodiment of grace, does all this for the sake of these souls. This concept is elaborately explained in the words of Tayumanavar Swamigal, who states: “Aivagai enum bhoothamaadhiyai vaguththu athanul achcharachchara bedhamaana yaavaiyum vaguththu nal arivaiyum vaguththu maraiyaathi noolaiyum vaguththu.” Such a Mother, whose very form is grace, upon the command of Lord Shiva, goes to Pillaiyar and collects milk from her sacred breast in a golden bowl.

The Great Goddess, having thus collected it, mixes the sweet nectar of immeasurable divine knowledge with the milk. She wiped the tears from the lotus-like eyes of Pillaiyar, who was looking at her, and offered the golden bowl to his hand, asking him to partake of the milk-nectar.

Thus, Lord Shiva, who is Angananar, put an end to Pillaiyar’s weeping and bestowed his grace. Our reflection on this continues.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 16 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 563, ‘Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam’, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, recounts the history of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Nayanar. Uma Ammaiyar, the Great Goddess, mixed the sweet nectar of immeasurable divine knowledge with milk, wiped the tears from the lotus-like eyes of Pillaiyar who was looking at her, and offered the golden bowl to his hand, asking him to partake of the milk-nectar.

Thus, Lord Shiva, who is Angananar, put an end to Pillaiyar’s weeping and bestowed his grace. The mixing by the Goddess refers to the sweet nectar of immeasurable divine knowledge. We saw earlier that the two, Para Gnanam and Apara Gnanam, These Para Gnanam and Apara Gnanam serve like adjuncts. Shiva Gnanam is superior to them, like medicine mixed in an adjunct.

Therefore, to indicate Shiva Gnanam, which is superior to these Para and Apara Gnanam, Sekkizhar Peruman uses the term ‘ennariya Shivagnanam’ (immeasurable Shiva Gnanam) in this sacred verse. Shiva Gnana Siddhiyar states that knowledge like the Vedas, Shastras, Smritis, Puranas, arts, and all forms of manifest speech, even up to the ultimate sound, are ‘Pasa Gnanam’ (knowledge of bonds), and that Shiva Gnanam is distinct from these. Shiva Gnanam is also referred to as ‘Tiruvadi Gnanam’ (knowledge of the sacred feet) and ‘Oli Gnanam’ (knowledge of light). This Shiva Gnanam instructs both Para Gnanam and Apara Gnanam.

Therefore, the knowledge bestowed upon Pillaiyar by the Mother was of the nature of both Mother and Father. It is for this reason that the sacred verses of Devaram emanate from Pillaiyar’s holy mouth for the benefit of the world. We can understand this from the nature of the Devaram verses. For instance, the Panchakshara Tiruppathigam, which revealed the conclusions of the Vedas to the Vedic scholars; and the Namasivaya Tiruppathigam, which helped those of Sakti Nipada attain Shiva’s feet and helped them merge with Shiva; and also the fact that even palm trees were blessed to attain union with Shiva through the Lord’s words, and other such truths, are found in the Devaram verses that emanated from the Lord’s sacred mouth.

Therefore, what the Goddess mixed and gave him It is the sweet nectar of immeasurable divine knowledge. ‘Amudam’ here signifies that which can bestow immortality and freedom from rebirth. This sweet nectar of immeasurable divine knowledge is mixed with milk and fed to Pillaiyar. Before that, she wipes the tears flowing from his lotus-like eyes. Children tend to look at the giver’s face when offered milk or other things.

Similarly, Pillaiyar looks at the Mother who comes to feed him the milk-nectar in a golden bowl.

Thus, the Divine Mother first wipes the tears flowing from the lotus-like eyes of Pillaiyar, who was looking at her.

After that, she feeds him the milk-nectar, which is mixed with the sweet nectar of divine knowledge, in a golden bowl. All these actions are performed by the Mother according to the divine command of Lord Shiva. The implication here is that Lord Shiva is the one who inspires and directs everything. Although the Mother’s actions alleviated Pillaiyar’s weeping, all these are truly the actions of the Lord. Such a Lord is Anganan. ‘Anganan’ means one who possesses immense compassion for all living beings.

Thus, Pillaiyar, having consumed the milk-nectar given by the Mother, becomes Gnana Sambandar. Sekkizhar Peruman explains this in the following verse: “Yaavarkkum thanthai thaai enum avar.” Since they are the Father and Mother to all, they appeared themselves and bestowed it, thus he became Aludaiya Pillaiyar, and the unique, flawless Shiva Gnana, which is incomprehensible to all gods and sages, became connected to him, just as Shiva Shakti stands in ‘tadatmyam’ with Shiva. He became Shiva Gnana Sambandar, having attained the explanation of Shiva Tatatmyam Sambandha, absorbed within it. This is the meaning of this sacred verse. In this verse, the sacred names of Pillaiyar, such as Aludaiya Pillaiyar and Thiru Gnana Sambandar, Sekkizhar Peruman describes and explains the meanings of the sacred names Aludaiya Pillaiyar and Thiru Gnana Sambandar in this verse.

The Mother and Father are the father and mother to all. ‘Yavarkkum’ means to all beings. Even though it is stated in terms of higher beings, they are also the Mother and Father to lower beings. Referring to the Lord as Father and Mother is a conventional usage.

Thus, they, who are the Father and Mother to all beings, appeared in this form and bestowed the food of wisdom upon Pillaiyar. Although Shiva and Shakti are shown as two, their essence is one.

Therefore, as Uma Ammaiyar fed him, Lord Shiva bestowed his grace. Uma Ammaiyar and He thus appeared in their manifested forms, came forward, offered milk, bestowed knowledge, and claimed Pillaiyar as their own. This is how the Lord bestows grace upon the category of souls known as Pralayakalas. The scriptures divide souls into three categories: Sakalas, Pralayakalas, and Vijnanakalas. Sakalas are those who possess the three impurities: Anavam (ego), Kanmam (karma), and Mayai (illusion). Pralayakalas are those who possess only Anavam and Kanmam.

Vijnanakalas are those souls who possess only Anavam. Among these three types, Pralayakalas.

Thus, the scriptures state that the Lord will come in a manifested form to bestow grace. The Kandar Kali Venpa mentions, “Kanma malaththarkku malar kan moonrum thaazh sadaiyum van mazhuvum maanum udan maal vidai mel minnidaththu pootha pavalapporuppondru vaitthanaiya theiva vadivaahi muththa karuma mala kattaruththu kan arul seithu” (For those with karmic impurities, the Lord, with three lotus eyes, matted locks, a mighty axe, and a deer, appearing on a mighty bull in a divine form like a coral hill blossomed in a lightning flash, cuts off the ancient karmic bonds and bestows sight/grace). Shivagnana Siddhiyar states that for the first two categories of souls among these three, namely Pralayakalas and Vijnanakalas, the Lord, being Niradhara (without support) and beyond all, bestows grace through the descent of His Shakti, destroying their impurities. The ways in which the Lord bestows grace by appearing before them are also many. In a similar manner of bestowing grace, the Lord appeared in a manifested form with the Goddess on a white bull to Pillaiyar.

Thus, because he was claimed by the Lord, Pillaiyar becomes Aludaiya Pillaiyar. ‘Aludaiya’ means that which is owned by the Lord.

Therefore, Pillaiyar shines as Aludaiya Pillaiyar, the child claimed by the Lord. There is also an implication that Pillaiyar is of the nature of a guru, who claims souls and leads them to salvation. That is, the first meaning is Pillaiyar claimed by the Lord. The second meaning is that Pillaiyar is of the nature of claiming all souls as his own and leading other souls to salvation. Why is he called Pillaiyar? He is called Pillaiyar because he was given milk and knowledge by his mother and father, and his weeping ceased, thus acquiring the status of a child.

We can recall here that in the Puranas of Chandikeswara Nayanar, Chandikeswara Nayanar also acquired the status of a child and was called Sengalvar Pillaiyar. ‘Aludaiya’ here refers to the master-servant relationship, where one is claimed as a servant or slave. Thirugnanasambandar Peruman himself has sung this as an internal evidence in his Devaram verses: “Bothaiyaar ponkinnaththu adisil pollaathenadhu thaathaiyaaru munivar thaanena aandavan.” This is Sekkizhar Peruman’s explanation for the name Aludaiya Pillaiyar.

Similarly, Sekkizhar Peruman also explains the name Gnana Sambandar in this verse. Shiva Gnanam is a truth that is difficult for even the Devas and Munis to comprehend. Shiva Gnanam is knowledge bestowed through divine grace.

Therefore, it is extremely difficult for Devas, Munis, or anyone else to comprehend. Such a thing is Shiva Gnanam. It is flawless Shiva Gnanam, unparalleled and unique.

Therefore, it is flawless Shiva Gnanam, a Shiva Gnanam that is incomprehensible to Devas and Munis. Since the Goddess bestowed that Shiva Gnanam mixed with milk, Pillaiyar became Gnana Sambandar. Even in his previous state, he was Gnana Sambandar.

However, here that Gnana Sambandam manifests explicitly.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he became Sivagnana Sambandar. Sivagnana Sambandar means one who has a connection like that of Sivagnanam. What does Sivagnana Sambandam mean? It means a connection that is united with Sivagnanam. That is, Sivagnanam is Shiva Shakti. The connection between Shiva Paramporul and Shiva Shakti, where Shiva Shakti is united with Shiva Paramporul in a state of Tatatmyam, is Tatatmyam Sambandam.

What is Tatatmyam Sambandam? Madhava Sivagnana Swamigal states in Sivagnana Mapadiyam that Tatatmyam is a state where two things exist as one without separation in a certain way. Sivagnana Mapadiyam states that Tatatmyam is the quality of being entitled to exist in two ways without separation. Tatatmyam is the relationship between a quality and its possessor. This is an eternal and inseparable relationship. Tatatmyam Sambandam is called ‘one in two’ in Tamil.

Its explanations are elaborately discussed in the Sivagnana Bodham and Sivagnana Bodha Mapadiyam texts.

Therefore, here Pillaiyar, like Shiva Shakti, merged within it and attained the explanation of Advaita Sambandam, which is Shiva Tatatmyam. This complete understanding of this Sambandam is attained only in the Nirumala Thuriyaatheetha state. That is why Sekkizhar Peruman describes it as ‘therivariya’ (difficult to comprehend).

Thus, this Sambandam will be fully understood only in the Nirumala Thuriyaatheetha state. In the states below this, it is very difficult to understand all these explanations.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman sings. At that transcendent state, when one is immersed in the ocean of supreme bliss, the knowing, knowledge, and knowable (Gnatru Gnana Sangalpa Gnanangal) and the knowledge of the arts (Kalaignana), which serve as means for contemplation, do not arise. Such is the state that Pillaiyar currently realized. If so, how did he realize it in that state? Pillaiyar is Aludaiya Pillaiyar, one who came into this world.

Therefore, he realized them for the sake of the people of this world. We can see this in Thiru Gnanasambandar Peruman’s hymn, beginning with “En ullam kavar kalvan” (The thief who stole my heart), where he describes the truth of that Advaita fusion of Shiva Ananda.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman provides commentary on the sacred name Aludaiya Pillaiyar and his becoming Sivagnana Sambandar, which is Gnana Sambandar or Thiru Gnana Sambandar. We shall continue our reflection.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 17 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 564, ‘Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam’, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, recounts the history of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Nayanar. Sivagnana Sambandar became Aludaiya Pillaiyar. Sekkizhar Peruman describes how he attained knowledge in the next verse: “Sivanadiye sindhikkum thirupperugu sivagnanam pavamathanai aramaatrum paanghinil ongkiya gnanam uvamaiyilla kalagnanam unarvariya meignanam thava muthalvar sambandhar thaam unarnthaar annilaiyil.” This song is one of the crown jewels among the songs in the history of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman sings in this song that Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman understood both Apara Gnanam and Para Gnanam. Sambandar, the foremost of ascetics, realized Kala Gnanam (knowledge of the arts), which is Apara Gnanam, and Meignananam (true knowledge), which is Para Gnanam.

In this verse, “Sivanadiye sindikkum thirupperugu sivagnanam” (the flourishing Shiva knowledge that meditates on Shiva’s feet) is an adjective for “uvamaiyilla kalaignanam” (unparalleled knowledge of the arts). “Pavathanai aramaatrum paanghinil ongkiya gnanam” (the exalted knowledge that completely removes karma) is an adjective for “unarvariya meignananam” (incomprehensible true knowledge). These are also referred to as Aparoksha Gnanam and Paroksha Gnanam. “Uvamaiyilla kalaignanam” refers to Apara Gnanam, and “unarvariya meignananam” refers to Para Gnanam. “Sivanadiye sindikkum thirupperugu sivagnanam” is an adjective for unparalleled knowledge of the arts. “Pavathanai aramaatrum paanghinil ongkiya gnanam” is an adjective for incomprehensible true knowledge.

For this verse, Kachiyappa Munivar has elaborated on this verse in the Thiruttanigai Puranam, in the chapter on receiving Agathiyar’s grace.
