In Shivaprakasam, Umapati Sivachariyar has stated in the Shivaprakasa Payiram: “Uyar gnanam irandaam maraa malar magala agalaadha mannu bodha thiruvarul ondru ondru athanai theliya pothum sivagamam endru ulagariya seppu noole” (Higher knowledge is twofold, that which removes enduring impurity and that which reveals eternal wisdom; one is divine grace, the other is the Sivagama that explains it for the world to know). The Paushkara Agama, in its Pati Padalam, states: “Sivasiya samavetaaya shaktir gyanathmikaamala shaivagyanam iti proktham shabdanthanumaamakam” (The pure, inherent knowledge-power of Shiva is called Shaiva Gnanam, which is conveyed by words and inference).

Thus, there are two types of knowledge: Para Gnanam and Apara Gnanam. Among them, Apara Gnanam is referred to here as ‘uvamaiyilla kalaignanam’ (unparalleled knowledge of the arts). Due to its characteristic of revealing tattva gnana (knowledge of principles), it surpasses other forms of knowledge of the arts. The Vedas and Agamas stand as exemplary foundations for all other knowledge of the arts.

Here, ‘kalaignanam’ signifies the Mukti Panchaksharam, but in a secondary sense, it refers to the Vedas, Sivagamas, and all other branches of knowledge that expanded from them. Such is the unparalleled knowledge of the arts, which is Apara Gnanam. It is the flourishing Shiva Gnanam that meditates on Shiva’s feet. It is the Shiva Gnanam that causes prosperity to grow. ‘Thiru’ means divine essence, which bestows Shiva-ness, liberation, and divine wealth. Panchaksharam means the Vedas and Sivagamas.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman realizes Apara Gnanam, which is the flourishing Shiva Gnanam that meditates on Shiva’s feet. At that moment, Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he attains Para Gnanam. He sings that he realized ‘unarvariya meignananam’ (incomprehensible true knowledge), which is the exalted knowledge that completely removes karma. This means that Para Gnanam is the knowledge that completely eradicates impurities.

Thus, even the karmic impurities that cause rebirth are completely destroyed in that state, and rebirth completely ceases.

Thus, the exalted knowledge that completely eradicates rebirth is Para Gnanam. It is also the knowledge that matures the root impurity of ignorance, which is the cause of rebirth. It is this knowledge that stands exalted in such clarity.

Thus, the exalted knowledge that completely eradicates rebirth is ‘unarvariya meignananam’ (incomprehensible true knowledge). That is Para Gnanam. It is unknown by Pasu Gnanam (knowledge of the individual soul) and Pasa Gnanam (knowledge of bonds), hence it is incomprehensible true knowledge. Those who attain that Para Gnanam will remain as that, their individual consciousness dissolved. This is incomprehensible knowledge, this Para Gnanam.

Therefore, Para Gnanam can only be realized if the Lord Himself, as the guru, reveals it; it cannot be realized through any other means. That is true knowledge.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman sings here that it is ‘unarvariya meignananam’ (incomprehensible true knowledge). The means to attain this Para Gnanam are ‘thelithal’ (clarity) and ‘nishtai kooduthal’ (meditation/abidance).

Therefore, ‘paangku’ (manner) here refers to clarity, and ‘unarvariya’ (incomprehensible) refers to meditation. These two are Para Gnanam.

Therefore, ‘bhavamathanai aramaatrum paangku’ (the manner that completely removes karma) is understood to lead to the destruction of bonds (pasa kshayam), and ‘unarvariya meignananam’ (incomprehensible true knowledge) is understood to lead to the attainment of Shiva (sivapperu).

Thus, Sambandar, the foremost of ascetics, realized both Para Gnanam and Apara Gnanam in that state. That state means the state of becoming Sivagnana Sambandar, having attained the experience of Sivananda and the pure Turiyaatita state upon consuming the food of wisdom, thereby becoming Sivagnana Sambandar. In that state, for the benefit of the world, both types of knowledge became manifest to him.

Therefore, Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman is not one who attained Apara and Para Gnanam in the sadhaka state like others. This is the implication here. Sambandar realized both Para Gnana and Apara Gnana because he is a ‘thava muthalvar’ (foremost ascetic).

Therefore, ‘thava muthalvar Sambandar thaam unarndhaar’ (Sambandar, the foremost ascetic, realized it) implies that ‘thava muthalvar’ indicates the reason why he realized it in that manner. It points to the reason for his manifestation as Thiru Gnana Sambandar at this time due to his past ascetic merit. We can recall here what we previously observed, that the term ‘thava muthalvar’ refers to one who never forgets the holy feet of the Lord. Such a one, possessing immense ascetic merit. Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman, therefore, the Lord, with three eyes, four arms, and a blue throat, along with other attributes, revealed his natural form, which performs the three actions, as a guru. The great penance of Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman, which was instrumental in the Lord, as the primordial being, revealing higher knowledge to the Pralayakalas, is explained through the word ‘thava muthal’. ‘Thavam muthal’ can also be taken as ‘first penance’, referring to the supreme merit of Shiva, standing at the sixteenth stage of ‘Sakthi Nipadham’ (descent of divine power), at the peak of intense maturity of the soul.

Such a ‘thava muthalvar’ (foremost ascetic) is Sambandar; therefore, he attained this state. The means to knowledge are listening, contemplating, clarifying, and abiding, which are four according to Sivagnana Siddhiyar. In Sanskrit, these are called Shravanam, Mananam, Nidhidhyasanam, and Nishta. Among these, the first two, listening and contemplating, belong to the Apara Gnanam category, and the latter two, clarifying and abiding, belong to the Para Gnanam category, as categorized by the Gnana Shastras. Why are these four divided into two like this? The first two, listening and contemplating, rely on scriptures, and thus are placed in the Apara Gnanam category.

The latter two, clarifying and abiding, occur due to divine grace, and thus are placed in the Para Gnanam category.

Therefore, knowledge obtained through the Vedas and Sivagamas is Apara Gnanam, and direct realization through divine grace is Para Gnanam.

Furthermore, among the four mentioned here, listening, clarifying, and contemplating are means to attain the knowledge that leads to liberation. One can learn by listening to instruction. One can also understand what has been heard by contemplating it through appropriate proofs. Having contemplated it thus, one can also understand it by clarifying it perfectly through Shiva Gnanam in one’s intellect. By this, one can destroy bonds, attain Nishta (abidance), and also experience Sivananda. Sri Madhava Shivagnana Munivar thus explains it to us.

Therefore, listening, clarifying, and contemplating—these three are gateways to attaining knowledge. Knowledge is a gateway to attaining liberation, which is implied here.

Therefore, knowledge is There is only one knowledge, but when categorized, it is two: Para (higher) and Apara (lower). The ways to attain it are four: listening, contemplating, clarifying, and abiding. It can also be five, in the form of Gnana Velvi (sacrifice of knowledge): studying and teaching sacred texts, making others listen to good principles, listening oneself, and contemplating flawless truths. This can also be eight, categorized as true Charya, Upaya Charya, true Kriya, Upaya Kriya, true Yoga, Upaya Yoga, true Gnana, and Upaya Gnana. These eight further expand into thirty-two, starting with Charyayil Charya. These are also explained as the ten దశకారியம் (Dasakaryam).

And in many other ways, knowledge expands. Even though all these exist, they are all subsumed within the two primary types of knowledge: Para and Apara. Sambandar, the foremost ascetic, realized such knowledge in that state. Generally, everyone would ask if Pillaiyar attained knowledge even without penance. To negate this, Sekkizhar Peruman uses the term ‘thava muthalvar Sambandar’ (Sambandar, the foremost ascetic) here.

Moreover, he describes the various classifications of the complete knowledge that he realized through this sacred verse.

Thus, Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman, the foremost ascetic who realized these two types of knowledge, arose. How did he arise? He arose, pulverizing the conclusions of other impure religions, each according to its understanding. He arose, pulverizing all the conclusions of other impure religions, which act according to their own understanding, without the awareness that the Lord is the one who directs all things, and without the knowledge that the true essence is the Lord and His devotees. Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman consumed the milk-nectar of wisdom, and thereby understood both types of knowledge. He was a foremost ascetic.

That very wisdom which entered him produced this sense of knowledge. That sense of knowledge that arose in Thiru Gnana Sambandha Peruman was of two types. This awakened state arose for the benefit of the world and its living beings. When this feeling arises in others, it benefits only them, but when it arose in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, it arose for the benefit of the living beings of this world. The wisdom that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman embodied is of two kinds.

Therefore, that wisdom itself arose as two kinds of wisdom, as feeling and as knowledge. It is this wisdom that rises to shatter the impure conclusions of those of other religions into dust. The one who creates everything is Isan. Isan refers to Lord Shiva, the primal being, known as Pati. The Choodamani Nikandu states the truth that Isan and Bhagavan refer to Lord Shiva. Such an Isan alone is capable of creating everything; this understanding is essential.

For living beings, the two entities apart from Pati are Pasam and. Pasu.

Here, creation, in the context of Pasu (souls), means guiding those souls to be subject to the five functions such as creation. To create Pasam (bondage) means to activate the mala of Maya and render the mala of Anava powerless so that souls may experience the fruits of their actions.

Therefore, the understanding here is that God, Isan, is the creator of both Pasu and Pasam, and attaining this Isan is the ultimate goal. This is what the tenth sutra of Sivagnanabodham refers to as Pasakshayam (the destruction of bondage).

Thus, the wisdom gained by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman serves primarily to achieve Pasakshayam for these souls, and it is also intended to refute all other religions. That resolve is also conveyed here as the first type of benefit.

Now, the second benefit is that the fruits of this knowledge are manifested in the form of the Linga, the Guru, and the devotee, known as the Jangama. Among these, the Guru and Linga forms are the Lord’s forms. The Jangama is the devotee’s form. The understanding that these two are the only forms is the second type of benefit, signifying the attainment of Shiva and the removal of residual impurities. This conveys the conclusions of the eleventh and twelfth sutras of Sivagnanabodham.

Therefore, the two types of wisdom embodied by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman yield these two types of benefits. To summarize, the first benefit is the refutation of other religions, and the second is the establishment of Saivism. Lord Shiva, in His compassionate heart, desired that all beings in the world should attain salvation through these two benefits. He had Thirugnanasambandha Peruman born here and nourished him with the milk of wisdom, thereby elevating these souls.

Now, the child, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who partook of the milk of wisdom, is seated on the bank of Brahmateertham. Sivapatha Hirudayar, who went to bathe in the teertham for Akamarshanam, emerges.

Let us continue to reflect on the sacred history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 18 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, part five hundred sixty-five, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vambara Varivandu Sarrkkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Sivapatha Hirudayar, having completed all his rituals, including Akamarshanam, comes out and looks at the child seated on the bank of the teertham.

The child appears immersed in supreme consciousness, shining with the unparalleled, singular light of Shiva’s wisdom, which is complete knowledge. This wisdom manifests as an outward light. Sivapatha Hirudayar looks at such a child and angrily asks, “Whose milk did you drink?” Milk is a food item that anyone can offer.

Here, however, Sivapatha Hirudayar becomes angry. Generally, one should not accept and consume food from just anyone, as it is not a good practice.

Moreover, milk, in particular, is not something to be received from just anyone. This is because the physical and qualitative traits of the mother would be present in that milk, and if it comes from someone else, those traits would transfer to the child consuming it.

Furthermore, due to the impurity of the vessel and many other reasons, it is not a good practice to accept and consume milk from just anyone, according to our custom. Especially for children, extreme caution must be exercised when giving milk and other initial. food items, otherwise, for children, that is, for children who drink milk given by others besides their mother, that milk can cause diseases and changes in disposition, among other things.

Therefore, one must be extremely cautious when receiving milk from others and giving it to a child. It is for these reasons that Sivapatha Hirudayar becomes angry. Not only that, many wicked people would wish harm upon a good child.

Therefore, this too contributed to Sivapatha Hirudayar’s anger and concern.

Thus, angered, Sivapatha Hirudayar further asks the child, “Show me the person who gave you this milk, allowing it to be defiled by their saliva,” and says, He took a small stick in his hand and raised it as if to strike. He held the stick and raised his hand as if to strike.

Here, ‘saliva’ refers to harm. He asks, “Show me the person who gave you this milk, mixing harm into it.” Why does he ask, “Show me the one who gave it to you?” Because if the item given might be harmful, he asks this in order to nullify that harm.

At that moment, the great little child stands on one leg, tears of overflowing joy streaming from his eyes, and points with one sacred finger of his raised hand towards the sky. The child. was a great little one. In form and age, he was small, but in nature, he was great.

Hence, the great little one.

At that time, in his father’s thoughts, he was considered a small child, but here there is also an indication that he possessed great glory that was then unknown to his father. From the sacred eyes of that great little child, tears of joy rained down. Tears poured from his eyes like rain due to joy. Just as it is said, ‘Is there a lock for love? The tears of the eager will proclaim it,’ here, tears of joy flow from the sacred eyes of the child. When asked, ‘Who gave you this milk?’, in response, the child.

The child raises one sacred finger of his sacred hand and points it upwards. He points it high above because, at the very moment the father questions the child, Thoniyappar, having fed the child milk, having assuaged his cries, continues to rise and bestow His vision upon the child. He descends from the heavens with Uma Devi on the bull, Rishabam. The father comes and asks the child this. That vision, however, is visible only to the child. Even though the Lord and the Goddess are in the sky, it is a sight not seen by Sivapatha Hirudayar.

The father, Sivapatha Hirudayar, could not see the Lord and the Goddess, but he only saw the mark of milk on the child’s lips. Sivapatha Hirudayar saw.

Therefore, he asks, “Whose milk did you drink?” The child had to point out the Lord, who stood above, unseen by his father.

Thus, he raised his finger and pointed upwards. He raises his sacred hand and points upwards to the Lord and Goddess standing above. Although the Lord is omnipresent and can be pointed to in all directions, here the child points upwards because, in the hierarchical steps of philosophy, the idea is to awaken and elevate the lower souls. This sacred act occurs through Sivapatha Hirudayar.

Therefore, he points upwards, raising the lower souls to the highest point.

The child raises his sacred hand to the highest point, intending to bestow grace upon the lower souls, bringing them to the supreme state.

Here, ‘highest point’ refers to the Lord who stands at the apex of the three aggregates of worlds—Asuddha Maya, Suddha-Suddha Maya, and Suddha Maya—that pure Sivaloka.

Furthermore, ‘highest point’ also refers to the Veda Siras, meaning the Lord Shiva, who is the fruit of the Upanishads and Agamas at their culmination. To indicate Him, he raises his sacred hand towards the highest point and lifts one sacred finger. That sacred hand is a unique sacred hand. The sacred hand which received the golden plates inscribed with the five letters, the sacred hand of the child of the Vedas, who came for the salvation of all worlds. Sekkilār Peruman sings, ‘It is but one.’ Those are the hands that bore the golden plates inscribed with the five sacred letters.

Therefore, they are sacred hands. These sacred hands are the hands that applied sacred ash to the body of the Pandya king to cure his fever. Those sacred hands are the hands that upheld Saivism by putting the sacred manuscript into fire and retrieving it, thereby arranging the sacred verses. Those beautiful sacred hands are the hands that cast the leaf into the river in earlier times to save us. Those sacred hands are the hands that offered water for the salvation of Buddhists and others.

Thus, the glories of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred hands are many. From those sacred hands, he takes. He raises one sacred finger, pointing upwards. That sacred finger is the index finger, which points and offers assistance.

Therefore, the index finger is special. It is a special part of the body that aids in the characteristic of an acharya. That sacred finger helped to point out the Lord, who is the meaning within the Sreepanchaaksharam, as ‘He is this one.’ Now, what does that five-letter Sreepanchaaksharam declare? It shows the nature of the soul to be freed from bondage, to understand its servitude to the Lord, to reach the Lord’s feet, and to attain salvation. This is Sreepanchaaksharam.

Thus, it is this very finger that helps to indicate the soul, devoid of attachment, in the mudra of silence. It also helps to show the unattached soul. The Sivagnana Sastram states that everything that can be pointed out and understood is Asat (non-existent), according to the saying ‘point out the knowledge that surrounds you.’ However, as an exception, here the unique sacred finger of the child points out and conveys Shiva, the Sat (existent) entity. This is the specialty of that finger of knowledge. Sekkizhar Peruman composes these verses: ‘Show me who gave you this milk mixed with defilement,’ he said. (Echchilmayangida unakku eethittarai kaattu enru kaicchiriyathu oru maaru kondu kaaleduthae achiriyapperumthakaiyaar aanandha kanthuli peythu ucciyin mel eduttharulum oru thirukkaiviralsutti vin niraintha perukozhiyaal vilangu mazhavidai mele panniraintha arumaraykal panintheththappavaiyudan e). (En niraintha karunaiyinaal nintraarai edirkkaatti un nirainthu pozhindhu ezhundha uyar gnana thirumozhiyaal ellaiyilaa marai muthal meyyudan eduttha ezhuthu marai mallal nedum thamizhaal immaanilaththorkku urai sirappa palluyirum kazhi koora tham paadal paramarpaal sellum murai peruvatharkku thirucceviyai sirappiththu semmai pera eduttha Thodudaiyaseviyan enum meymmei mozhi thiruppathigam piramapuram mevinaar thammai adaiyaalangaludan saatti thaathaiyaarcku emmai ithu seythapiraa ivananre ena isaiwiththaar.) The truthful pathigam titled ‘Thodudaiya Seviyan,’ which praises the sacred ear and was taken to perfection for his song to reach the Supreme Being, so that all beings might greatly rejoice and that the message for the people of this land might be excellent, was composed in rich, grand Tamil, drawing from the boundless Vedas, with the primal truth.

He identified Him who resides in Piramapuram with His characteristics and made his father agree, saying, ‘This is the Lord who made us thus.’ When Sivapatha Hirudayar asked, “Who fed you this milk?” the child, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, pointed to the Lord who appeared in the sky and sang the first unique pathigam, “Thodudaiya Seviyan.” Sekkizhar Peruman recounts this divine history through these sacred verses. In the sky of wisdom, the Lord appears with the Goddess on Rishabam. His manifestation is in the sky of wisdom, illuminating all beings according to their differing levels of maturity and helping them grow in knowledge. That is the expansive sky of wisdom.

The child sees that light. Even with that light present. The father stands there, unable to see.

Then, when the child speaks and points, Sivapatha Hirudayar somewhat understands and resolves, contemplating the meaning of that rare Tamil pathigam and all the events that transpired.

Thus, the Lord grants His vision with Umaiyammai on the ever-youthful Rishabam in the sky of wisdom, with all the rare Vedas bowing and praising Him. All these bowing Vedas are now about to come forth as Tamil pathigams from the sacred mouth of the child.

Therefore, as the rare Vedas bow and praise, Lord Shiva bestows His vision there. He grants His vision with Umaiyammai, out of boundless compassion. The Lord’s task was to soothe the child’s cries. It was indeed the Lord’s purpose, and it has been fulfilled here. Even after the fulfillment of the task for which He manifested, the Lord continues to grant His vision in the sky of wisdom, with the Goddess on Rishabam. Why is this so?

It is due to the Lord’s immeasurable, profound compassion for living beings. Because it was by the Lord’s manifestation with the Goddess on Rishabam and His granting of vision that the child was able to point to the Lord with those identifying marks and sing the pathigam. When Sivapatha Hirudayar, the father, heard this, all the living beings of this world, by hearing through him, will now benefit by chanting the pathigam ‘Thodudaiya Seviyan’.

Therefore, for the immense compassion that beings should benefit in this way, the Lord, who came to soothe the child’s cries, continues to grant His vision with Uma Devi on Rishabam in the sky of wisdom even after soothing the child’s cries.

Thus, pointing to the Lord manifested in the sky of wisdom, the child’s knowledge, becoming entirely one with the nature of that Lord, overflows with that supreme wisdom, and he is about to sing the Tamil pathigam ‘Thodudaiya Seviyan’ with divine verses. Sekkizhar Peruman conveys this to us through his divine verses.

We shall continue our reflection on this.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 19 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, part five hundred sixty-six, authored by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. The Thirumurai are significant authoritative texts in Saiva Siddhanta. They are compiled into twelve Thirumurai by Nambiyandar Nambigal Perumaganar. The first three Thirumurai were composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The first pathigam in the first Thirumurai, which begins with “Thodudaiya Seviyan,” is the first pathigam that the child, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, sang, pointing to the Lord who granted vision in the sky of knowledge, in response to Sivapatha Hirudayar asking, “Who fed you this milk?” Therefore, that.

Sekkizhar Peruman describes the sacred history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s singing. (Ellaiyilaa marai muthal meyyudan eduttha ezhuthu marai mallal nedum thamizhaal immaanilaththorkku urai sirappa palluyirum kazhi koora tham paadal paramarpaal sellum murai peruvatharkku thirucceviyai sirappiththu semmai pera eduttha Thodudaiya Seviyan enum meymmei mozhi thiruppathigam piramapuram mevinaar thammai adaiyaalangaludan saatti thaathaiyaarcku emmai ithu seythapiraa ivananre ena isaiwiththaar.) These are the verses composed by Sekkizhar Swamigal. For these verses, Sivakavimani Ayya provides a very. very subtle interpretation. The pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, beginning with “Thodudaiya Seviyan,” starts with the letter ‘Tho’. This letter ‘Tho’ is formed when the consonant ‘Ith’ (த) combines with the vowel ‘O’ (ஓ). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begins this pathigam with this letter. Sekkizhar Peruman explains it.

How does Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begin this pathigam? He begins by taking the first letter of the boundless Vedas with its consonant. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he begins by combining the first letter of the Vedas with a consonant. Those Vedas are referred to here with the epithet ‘boundless Vedas’. Boundless Vedas means that the Vedas are such that they discard all things by saying ‘Neti, Neti’ (not this, not this) and proceed without limit. These Vedas are revered as ‘unwritten scriptures’ because they cannot be measured, confined, or written down in their expansive nature.

They are transmitted through generations via oral tradition, through the ears, as instruction.

Therefore, they are called ‘Sruti’ in Sanskrit and ‘Othu’ in Tamil. Since they are not confined to written form but come as an oral tradition through recitation and instruction, they are called ‘Othu’ in Tamil. Since it comes through the ear, passed down through generations by way of oral instruction, it is called Sruti.

Thus, the four Vedas are boundless in nature. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begins the pathigam by taking the first letter of such Vedas, combined with a consonant. The first letter of the Vedas is the primal ‘Om’ of Pranava. When chanting the Vedas, there is a tradition of beginning with ‘Om’ in Pranava and ending with ‘Om’ in Pranava.

Therefore, the Veda is an expansion of Pranava. So, the first letter of the Veda is the ‘O’ sound, the first letter of Pranava. This is a vowel. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings this by combining it with a consonant. Sekkizhar Peruman states. That consonant is the letter ‘ith’.

When the pathigam begins with the letter ‘Tho’ as in “Thodudaiya Seviyan,” the ‘ith’ consonant is what Sekkizhar Peruman refers to here.

Therefore, combining the consonant ‘ith’ with ‘O’, the first letter of Pranava and the Vedas, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begins with ‘Tho’, as in “Thodudaiya,” and sings the pathigam. The ‘ith’ consonant that appears here refers to Thagaravidhya. Thagaravidhya is one of the thirty-two Vidyas mentioned in the Vedas. Just as Satvidhya, Homavidhya, and Varunividhya exist, Thagaravidhya is also a Vidya mentioned in the Vedas.

Therefore, the ‘ith’ consonant here. The consonant ‘ith’ here refers to this Thagaravidya. Thagaravidya is the true state of Sivashakti.

Furthermore, this ‘thagaram’ (த்) is the concluding letter of the Gayatri Mantras.

Moreover, in the Vedas, the supreme Brahman is referred to by the term ‘Sat’. In the Chandogya and other Upanishads, the term ‘Sat’ is used to denote Brahman, and the final letter of ‘Sat’ is also the consonant ‘ith’. The Vayu Samhita states that the first letter ‘sa’ in the word ‘Sat’ is the form of Shakti, and ‘ith’ is the form of Shiva. With this consonant ‘ith’, which possesses such distinctions, combined with ‘O’, the first letter of the Vedas. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begins the pathigam with ‘Tho’, as in “Thodudaiya Seviyan.” Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the pathigam, Tevaram, sung by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, beginning with “Thodudaiya Seviyan,” as a ‘written scripture’. We saw that the four Vedas are ‘unwritten scriptures’.

Here, the Tevarams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman are ‘written scriptures’. The Vedas describe the attributes of Brahman in an expansive manner that cannot be limited or confined. They are unwritten scriptures.

Here, the Tevaram, a written scripture composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, was able to limit and point out the Lord. This is indicated by Sekkizhar Peruman, who refers to the Vedas. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the Vedas as boundless scriptures and the Tevarams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as written scriptures. The wisdom of ‘thagaram’ is superior to life itself and elevates it.

Therefore, he sings by combining the ‘thagaram’, which brings forth this specialty, with ‘okkaram’. Even in Siva Agamas, the presiding deities and benefits associated with the matruka letters for ‘okkaram’ and ‘thakaram’ are mentioned.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes this ‘written scripture’ in rich, grand Tamil. ‘Mallal’ means richness or abundance. It refers to the generosity or abundance that provides what is desired, as and when desired.

Here, Tamil possesses a similar quality.

Therefore, this is. It becomes ‘mallal nedum tamizh’ (rich, grand Tamil). This is ‘nedum tamizh’ (grand Tamil) because it possesses the Thirumurai, which serve as instruments for discerning the ultimate reality, Lord Shiva. This brought the special distinction of ‘nedum tamizh’ to Tamil. That is, Tamil has the glory of conveying the true philosophy of the world. How did this glory come to Tamil?

It is because the divine work called Iraiyanar Akapporul, composed by Lord Shiva, is in Tamil. The divine works like Tevaram and Thiruvasagam, which the same Lord Shiva composed through the Nayanmars whose knowledge became Shiva, and the Gnana Sastras like Meikanda Sastras, were all composed in Tamil and bestowed by the Lord. Tamil attained that divine quality.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with such rich, grand Tamil, composed the Tevaram pathigam, the pathigam of “Thodudaiya Seviyan.” He composed these pathigams in such Tamil so that the people of this land might benefit and their words be excellent.

Here, ‘people of this land’ refers to human beings with six senses, because it is such people who benefit from the ‘Vasaga Diksha’ (initiation through words).

Therefore, so that these souls might benefit by listening to, contemplating, and reciting the Tevaram pathigams, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this pathigam in Tamil, so that the words of the people of this land might be excellent. Not only that, but sentient beings with six senses should benefit. Not only should they benefit, but all other beings, beyond those with six senses, should also greatly rejoice and attain bliss. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blesses them in this way. How does he bless them? He begins by praising the sacred ear of the Lord, starting with “Thodudaiya Seviyan.” This is because, for the people of this land to receive ‘vasaga diksha’ (initiation through words) and for many souls to rejoice, his song must go to Lord Paramar (Shiva).

These pathigams must reach the sacred ear of the Lord.

Therefore, he begins by praising the sacred ear of the Lord.

Thus, the meaning and benefit of the Tevaram pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman are for the living beings of this world to be freed from suffering and attain joy.

Thus, it is understood that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed all these pathigams for the living beings of the world, and not for himself.

Therefore, for all these souls to chant the Tevaram pathigams that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman now begins, and for these sacred verses to reach the sacred ear of Lord Paramar, he begins by praising the ear of the Lord, saying “Thodudaiya Seviyan.” We can understand that the human souls of this land were blessed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s pathigams through his Panchakshara pathigams, Thiruneetru pathigam, Thirupassuram, Kolvaru pathigam, and other pathigams. All other beings. We can see that other beings also benefit, as mentioned in the Thiruvottur pathigam and other pathigams. In the Thiruvottur pathigam, we will soon see histories such as the male palm tree becoming a female palm tree without bearing fruit and then attaining Shiva. Through that, we can understand.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings by praising the sacred ear, so that all beings may find rest and that the Tevaram pathigams may reach the sacred ear of the Lord.

The Lord has sacred limbs such as His sacred feet. Without mentioning them, he praises the sacred ear by saying, “Seviyan Thodudaiya Seviyan” (He with the ear and the ear-ornament), because the ‘thodu’ (ear-ornament) is an adornment worn by the Mother, who is the power of grace.

Therefore, the Mother. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begins this pathigam by first praising the Mother. Sekkizhar Peruman then continues to explain how he composed it.

Our reflection on this continues.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 20 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

He begins by praising the sacred ear of the Lord, starting with “Thodudaiya Seviyan.” This is because, for the people of this land to receive ‘vasaga diksha’ (initiation through words) and for many souls to rejoice, his song must go to Lord Paramar (Shiva).

These pathigams must reach the sacred ear of the Lord.

Therefore, he begins by praising the sacred ear of the Lord.

Thus, the meaning and benefit of the Tevaram pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman are for the living beings of this world to be freed from suffering and attain joy. The meaning and benefit of the Tevaram pathigams are for the living beings of the world, not for ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman himself.

Therefore, it is understood that these living beings, by reciting the Tevaram pathigams that ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman is now beginning, should have these verses reach the sacred ears of the Supreme Lord. For this purpose, he begins by praising the Lord’s ear as ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’ (one with an earring). The fact that human beings on this earth were blessed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman’s pathigams can be known through pathigams like Panchatchara pathigams, Thiruneetrupathigam, Thiruppasuram, Kolattupathigam, etc. Many lives and other beings are benefiting, as can be known through pathigams like the Thiruvoathur pathigam. In the Thiruvoathur pathigam, we will see the history of a male palm tree becoming a female palm tree without a cluster and attaining Shiva, and other similar events. Through this, we can understand.

Therefore, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman praises the Lord’s ear so that all beings may find rest and that the Tevaram pathigams may reach the sacred ear of the Lord.

The Lord has sacred feet and other sacred limbs, but without mentioning all of them, he praises the ear as ‘Seviyan Thoduudaiya Seviyan’ because ‘thodu’ (earring) is an ornament worn by the divine Mother, Arulshakti.

Therefore, the Mother Ayai is first praised, and then ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman begins this pathigam. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to describe how he sang it.

Let us continue our reflection.

Chapter 21 — ThirugnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 566, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam’, ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar Puranam. The Thirumuraikal, which are important authoritative texts in Saiva Siddhanta, are compiled into twelve Thirumuraikal by Nambiandar Nambigal Perumaganar. The first three Thirumuraikal are composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman. The first pathigam in the first Thirumurai begins with ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’. When Sivapadahayar asks, “Who fed you this milk?” the Child of God points to the Lord who appeared in a vision in the sky of wisdom and sings his first pathigam, this ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’ pathigam.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman describes the divine history of ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman singing that pathigam. The pathigam ‘ThiruThoduudaiya Seviyan’, which begins with the truthful words that praise the ear, is presented perfectly so that the boundless Vedic truths, taken with a body of truth, and the abundant, vast Tamil may benefit the people of this world, and that all lives may rejoice, and that his songs may reach the Supreme Lord. Sekkizhar Swamigal’s verses are: ‘He pointed out the Lord who graced Bramapuram with his attributes, saying, “Is this not the Lord who made us for our father?”’ Sivakavimani Ayya has given a very subtle commentary with all sorts of meanings. The pathigam composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, which begins with ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’, starts with the letter ‘Tho’. This letter ‘Tho’ is formed when the consonant ‘Ith’ and the vowel ‘O’ combine. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman begins this pathigam with this letter.

Sekkizhar Peruman explains it. How does ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman begin this pathigam? He begins with the first letter of the boundless Vedas combined with a consonant. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that he begins with the first letter of the Vedas combined with a consonant. Those Vedas are boundless Vedas. is mentioned here with the adjective. Boundless Vedas means that the Vedas, by eliminating all things with ‘neti, neti’ (not this, not this), are boundless and uncontained.

These Vedas are praised as unwritten scriptures, because these Vedas cannot be measured and written. They are boundless in nature and cannot be written. They are transmitted from generation to generation through oral instruction, through the ears.

Therefore, they are called ‘Shruti’ in Sanskrit and ‘Othu’ in Tamil. Because they are transmitted orally through instruction and not contained in written form, they are called ‘Othu’ in Tamil. Since it comes through the ear, passed down from generation to generation by instruction, it is called Shruti.

Thus, the four Vedas are boundless in nature. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman begins the pathigam by combining the first letter of such Vedas with a consonant. The first letter of the Vedas is the primordial ‘Omkara’. When chanting the Vedas, it is customary to begin with ‘Om’ from the Pranava and end with ‘Om’ from the Pranava.

Therefore, the Veda is the expansion of the Pranava. Hence, the first letter of the Veda is ‘Omkara’, the first letter of the Pranava. This is a vowel. ThiruGnana Sambandha Peruman combines it with a consonant, as Sekkizhar Peruman states. That consonant is the consonant ‘Ith’. The pathigam ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’ begins with the letter ‘Tho’, and the consonant ‘Ith’ that appears there is what Sekkizhar Peruman refers to here.

Therefore, by combining the consonant ‘Ith’ with ‘O’, the first letter of the Vedas and Pranava, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman begins by singing ‘Tho’ as in ‘Thoduudaiya’. The consonant ‘Ith’ here refers to Thagara Vidya. Thagara Vidya is one of the thirty-two Vidyas mentioned in the Vedas. Just as there are Sat Vidya, Homa Vidya, Varuni Vidya, Thagara Vidya is also a Vidya mentioned in the Vedas.

Therefore, the ‘Ith’ here the consonant ‘Th’ here refers to this Thagara Vidya. Thagara Vidya is the true state of Shiva-Shakti.

Furthermore, this ‘Th’ is the concluding letter of the Gayatri Mantras.

Moreover, in the Vedas, the supreme reality, Brahman, is referred to as ‘Sat’. In the Chandogya and other Upanishads, the term used to denote Brahman is ‘Sat’, and its final letter is also this consonant ‘Th’. The Vayu Samhita states that the first letter ‘Sa’ in the word ‘Sat’ is the form of Shakti, and ‘Th’ is the form of Shiva. With such special qualities, the consonant ‘Th’ is combined with ‘O’, the first letter of the Vedas. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman begins the pathigam ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’ by combining the ‘O’ (Omkara) to form ‘Tho’. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this Tevaram pathigam, which ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman begins as ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’, as ‘Ezhuthum Marai’ (written Veda) here.

We saw that the four Vedas are ‘Ezhuthamarai’ (unwritten Vedas).

Here, the Tevarams composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman are ‘Ezhuthum Marai’ (written Vedas). The Vedas describe the attributes of Brahman in an immeasurable and boundless way, they are ‘Ezhuthamarai’ (unwritten Vedas).

Here, the Tevaram composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, which is a ‘Ezhuthum Marai’ (written Veda), was able to point out and define the Lord, implying that Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the Vedas as ‘boundless scripture’ and the Tevarams composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman as ‘written scripture’. The knowledge of ‘Thagara’ is superior to life itself and elevates life.

Therefore, to express that special quality, he combines ‘Thagara’ with ‘Omkara’ and sings. Even in the Shivagamas, the presiding deities and benefits of the Matrukavarnas corresponding to Omkara and Thakara are mentioned.

Thus, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman composed this ‘written scripture’ in ‘Mallal Nedum Tamil’. ‘Mallal’ means richness or abundance. It refers to the quality of being generous, providing whatever is needed, whenever it is needed.

Here, Tamil also possesses a similar quality.

Therefore, it is Mallal Nedum Tamil. This epithet ‘Nedum Tamil’ came to Tamil because it contained the Thirumuraigal, which serve as a measuring tool to ascertain Shiva, the ultimate reality. That is, Tamil has the greatness of explaining the true philosophy of the world. How did this come to Tamil? The sacred text ‘Iraiyanar Agapporul’, composed by Lord Shiva, is in Tamil. The Tevaram, Thiruvasagam, and other divine texts composed by Shiva through the Nayanmars, whose minds were Shiva-like, and the Jnana Sastras like Meikanda Sastras, were also composed in Tamil, having been blessed by the Lord.

Tamil has attained that divine quality.

Therefore, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman composes the Tevaram pathigam, the ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’ pathigam, in such ‘Mallal Nedum Tamil’. Through such Tamil, he bestows grace so that the people of this earth may excel in their understanding and benefit. ‘People of this earth’ here refers to sentient beings, because only such sentient beings benefit from the ‘Vasaga Diksha’ (initiation through words).

Therefore, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman composes this pathigam so that these beings may benefit by listening to, reflecting on, and reciting the Tevaram pathigams, so that the people of this earth may excel in their understanding. Not only that, sentient beings It is not just that they should benefit, but also that ‘all lives should rejoice’. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman bestows grace so that other beings, besides the six-sensed humans, should also experience great joy and bliss. How does he bestow grace? He begins this pathigam by praising the Lord’s sacred ear, starting with ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’. This is because, for the people of this world to receive verbal initiation and for many lives to rejoice, his song should reach Paramanaar, Lord Shiva.

Since these pathigams should reach the sacred ear of the Lord, he begins by praising the Lord’s sacred ear.

Therefore, for the living beings of this world to be free from suffering and attain bliss, that is the purpose of the Tevaram pathigams composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman. The meaning and benefit of the Tevaram pathigams are for the living beings of the world, not for ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman himself.

Therefore, it is understood that these living beings, by reciting the Tevaram pathigams that ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman is now beginning, should have these verses reach the sacred ears of the Supreme Lord. For this purpose, he begins by praising the Lord’s ear as ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’ (one with an earring). The fact that human beings on this earth were blessed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman’s pathigams can be known through pathigams like Panchatchara pathigams, Thiruneetrupathigam, Thiruppasuram, Kolattupathigam, etc. Many lives and other beings are benefiting, as can be known through pathigams like the Thiruvoathur pathigam. In the Thiruvoathur pathigam, we will see the history of a male palm tree becoming a female palm tree without a cluster and attaining Shiva, and other similar events. Through this, we can understand.

Therefore, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman praises the Lord’s ear so that all beings may find rest and that the Tevaram pathigams may reach the sacred ear of the Lord.

The Lord has sacred feet and other sacred limbs, but without mentioning all of them, he praises the ear as ‘Seviyan Thoduudaiya Seviyan’ because ‘thodu’ (earring) is an ornament worn by the divine Mother, Arulshakti.

Therefore, the Mother Ayai is first praised, and then ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman begins this pathigam. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to describe how he sang it.

Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 22 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 569, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam’, ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar Puranam. The second verse of the first pathigam, which begins with ‘Thoduudaiya Seviyan’, is as follows: (Mutral aamai ila nagamodu ena mulaikkompu avai poondhu vatral oadu kalanaa bali theerndhu enadhu ullam kavar kalvan katral kettal udaiyar periyar kazhal kaiyal thozhudhaertha petram oorndha piramapurameviya pemman ivan andre) “He, who wears the old tortoise shell, young snakes, and the boar’s tusk, and collects alms with a dry skull-bowl, is the thief who stole my heart. Is he not the Lord who resides in Bramapuram, riding the bull, worshipped by great sages learned in scriptures, with hands that touch his feet?” In this verse, the Lord’s attributes are identified through the ornaments he wears. ‘Mutral aamai’ means an ancient tortoise. It refers to the shell of the ancient tortoise, the Koorma avatar of Vishnu. ‘Ila nagam’ refers to Ananthan and other snakes that have an age of several Chatur Yugas. ‘Ena mulai kombu’ refers to the tusk worn by Vishnu in his Varaha avatar.

The Lord wears all of these as ornaments on his sacred chest. ‘Vattral oadu’ is the dried skull of Brahma.

The Lord carries it in his sacred hand as a begging bowl.

Thus, the Lord who seeks alms in Brahma’s skull is the thief who stole my heart. Such a Lord, who appears on the bull in a state of grace for those great sages learned in knowledge who worship his feet with their hands, is he not? ‘Katral kettal udaiyar’ refers to those who are proficient in spiritual knowledge and learning, and by implication includes meditation, clarity, and absorption. He is the Lord worshipped by such great ones.

Lord Shiva grants visions on the bull and resides in Bramapuram.

Now, the third verse: (Neeranda nimir punjadai mel or nila ven madhisoodi erparandha ina velvalai sora en ullam kavar kalvan oorparandha ulagin mudhalagiya oor idhu enna perparandha piramapurameviya pemman ivan andre) “He, who wears a crescent moon on his flowing, matted red hair filled with water, making the conch bangles slip from my hands, is the thief who stole my heart. Is he not the Lord who resides in Bramapuram, renowned as the first and foremost city in the world?” ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman is singing. This is a song in the akapporul (love poetry) genre. When the heroine suffers in thoughts of the hero, her body wastes away, and the bangles on her hands slip off – this is the scene in akapporul.

Here, all souls are heroines, and the Lord is the hero of these souls.

Thus, this song is set in the mood of heroine and hero. “This thief who stole my heart, he is the Lord who resides in Bramapuram.” This Bramapuram is a unique city that remained indestructible in this world during the great deluge. It is a unique city that was not destroyed even during the water deluge. That is why it also has the name Thonipuram.

Thus, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman composes this third verse. The fourth verse: (Venmagizhndha madhil eydhadhum anri vilangu thalaivo) On his head, rejoicing, he begged for alms, and came and stole my heart, the thief! Is he not the Lord who resides in Bramapuram, who, with a chest adorned with the revered serpent and blossoming konrai, joyfully holds the feminine in his chest?“ In this, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman sings about the destruction of the Three Cities (Thiripura Samharam) accomplished by the Lord. He was the one who held a single arrow to destroy the three walls that joyfully and proudly flew in the sky, but he burned them with his gentle smile without using that single arrow.

Thus, he was like one who aimed an arrow to burn those three walls. He is the thief who stole my heart. He is the one who joyfully holds Umaiyammai in the left part of his mountain-like chest. He is the Lord who resides in Bramapuram.

Now, the fifth verse: (Orumai penmai udaiyan sadaiyan vidai) He is one with a combined male and female form, with matted hair, riding a bull. The companions say, “He is so wonderful to describe,” and he is the thief who stole my heart. When the dark sea swelled and engulfed this world at the time of the great dissolution, he, the Lord who resided in Bramapuram, who was great and floated as a boat, is he not?” This is the meaning of this verse.

The Lord is one who granted the left side of his body to Umaiyammai in one sacred form. He has matted hair. He rides on a bull. The companions describe the beauty of the Lord in these ways. He is the thief who stole my heart, who came just as the companions described. He is the Lord who resided in Bramapuram, who was great and floated like a boat when the dark-colored sea swelled and engulfed this world during the great dissolution.

This is the meaning of this verse.

Now, the sixth verse: (Maraikkalandha oli paadalodu aadalaraagi mazhu aendhi iraikkalandha ina velvalai sora en ullam kavar kalvan karaikala) He, who, singing and dancing to the sound of the Vedas, holding an axe, came and stole my heart, making my shining white bangles slip. He, who resides in Bramapuram, wearing a crescent moon that shines light in the dense groves with tall trees and thick foliage. This is he.

Now, the seventh verse: (Sadaimuyangu punalan analan eriveesich sadhirvaidha udaimuyangum aravodu thandhanadhu ullam kavar kalvan kadanmuyangu kalisoozh kulir kaanal amponnam sirakannam pedaimuyangu piramapurameviya pemman ivan andre idhan porul) He who has the Ganga intertwined in his matted hair, fire in his sacred hand, and a serpent tightly bound over his garment, danced, showering flames, and came and stole my heart. Such a Lord resides in beautiful Bramapuram. That Bramapuram is surrounded by salt pans embracing the sea, possesses cool coastal groves, and is home to beautiful-winged swans that roam with their mates. Such a Bramapuram is where my Lord resides.

Now, the eighth verse: (Viyar ilangu varaivundhiya tholgalaiviram vilaiyaviththa uyar ilangai araiyan vali setru enadhu ullam kavar kalvan thuyar ilangum ulagil pala oozhigal thondrum pozhudhellam peyar ilangu piramapurameviya pemman ivan andre idhan porul Kailai malaiyai peyarthu thanadhu peru) He, who crushed the strength of the mountainous shoulders of Ravana, the illustrious king of Lanka, who lifted Mount Kailash to display his great valor, is the thief who stole my heart. He is the Lord who resides in Bramapuram, whose name shines forth, undestroyed, in this world of sorrow, through many eons whenever they appear. In the Tevaram pathigams of ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, the eighth verses will always speak of Ravana and describe the pathigam in that way. The ninth verses will always praise the greatness of Shiva, whom Vishnu and Brahma could not find. The tenth verses will always condemn external religions like Buddhism and Jainism.

In the eleventh verses, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman will establish them as Thirukkadaikaappu (concluding verses). he will make it a Thirukkadaikaappu. This method is mostly followed in all the Thirukkadaikaappu pathigams composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman explains the reason for this. Why does ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman sing about Ravana in the eighth verse of his pathigams? Sekkizhar Peruman explains this reason, saying, (Mannulagil vaazhvaargal pizhaithaalum vandhu adaiyil kannudalan perungarunai kai kollum ena kaatta ennamilaa val arakkan eduthu murindhu isaippada annal avarkku arul purindha aakkappaadu arul seidhaar endru) “Even if those who live on earth commit mistakes, if they come and seek refuge, the Lord with the eye on his forehead will embrace them with his great compassion.” To show this, the powerful, thoughtless demon Ravana lifted Mount Kailash, broke his body, and then sang. The noble Lord bestowed grace upon him.

This act of grace was expressed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman in the eighth verse of his pathigam.

Therefore, if beings who have committed mistakes truly realize their error, accept responsibility for their wrongdoings, and make a firm resolve not to repeat the mistake, and pray to the Lord with sincere devotion, the Lord will forgive and grant grace. To make us realize this, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman narrates the story of how Ravana’s arrogance was quelled, placing it in this eighth verse, as Sekkizhar Peruman shows us. Thirukkadaikaappu. This convention is followed in most of the Thirukkadaikaappu pathigams composed by ThiruGnanaSambaman. Sekkizhar Peruman explains the reason for this. Why does ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman sing about Ravana in the eighth verse of his pathigams?

Sekkizhar Peruman clarifies the reason: (Mannulagil vaazhvaargal pizhaithaalum vandhu adaiyil kannudalaan perungarunai kai kollum enak kaatta ennamilaa val arakkan eduthu murindhu isaippaada annal avarkku arul purindha aakkapaadu arul seidhaar endru) “Even if those who live on earth make mistakes, if they approach, the great compassion of the Lord with the eye on his forehead will embrace them.” To demonstrate this, the powerful, thoughtless demon lifted and crushed the mountain, then sang, and the Lord bestowed his grace upon him. Sekkizhar Peruman thus explains this reason. Even if beings living on this earth commit mistakes, if they surrender to him, Lord Shiva, who has an eye on his forehead, will, with his great compassion, forgive them and hold them by the hand. To show this, the thoughtless demon Ravana lifted Mount Kailash, broke his body, and then sang, and the glorious Lord bestowed grace upon him. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman composed this in the eighth verse of his pathigam.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman shows us that ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, to teach us that if beings who have committed mistakes truly realize their error, take responsibility for their wrongdoing, and make a firm resolve not to repeat the mistake, and pray to the Lord with sincere devotion, the Lord will forgive and bestow grace, places the story of Ravana’s arrogance being quelled in this eighth verse.

Now, the ninth sacred verse: (Thanudhal sei thirai kaaniya maaloodu thandhamaraianum neenudhal seyilayan nimirndhaan enadhu ullam kavar kalvan vaanudhal sei magalir mudhalagiya vaiyaththavaretha pezunudhal sei maapuram eviya pemman ivan andre idhan porul Thirumalum naanmuganum sivaperumanadhu thiruvadigalaiyum mudiyaiyum kaanbadharkaga panriyaagavum annamaagavum thedi seyalatru vizha annamalayaay nimirndhavan em peruman atthagaiya peruman en ullam kavargindra kalvanaga vilangugindran magalir ullitta ulagaththavargal anaivarum thudhika virumbudhalai seiyum piramapurameviya peruman ivan andre endru ivvaaru onbadhaavadhu thiruppaadal in porul amaigindradhu Thirugnanasambandha Perumal ivvaaru thanadhu) Throughout his pathigams, in the ninth verse of each pathigam, he has sung about the unique great quality of the Lord that Vishnu and Brahma could not find. Sekkizhar Peruman explains why ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman structured it this way. (Thozhuvaarkke aruluvadhu Sivaperuman ena thozhaar valuvaana manaththaale maalaaya maalayanum ezhivaagum karuvilangum paravaiyumai eydhaamai vizhuvaargal anjezhuthum thudhiythuyndhappadi viriththaar) Vishnu and Brahma sought the Lord. Although they knew that the Lord grants grace only to those who worship him, they, not worshipping our Lord, became deluded by a wrong mindset. Vishnu became a lowly boar and Brahma became Brahma, as an eagle, went up and down but could not find him and fell.

Later, they were saved by praising the five sacred letters. To explain this, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman structured this sacred history in the ninth verses of his pathigams. He reveals to us the truth that Lord Shiva grants grace only to those who worship him. If ‘granting grace’ means revealing the truth and helping the soul to quickly attain liberation, does it mean that Lord Shiva grants grace only to those who worship him and not to those who don’t? That is not the case. The greatly compassionate Lord gives the appropriate medicine to each soul according to its illness of ignorance, and liberates them.

Therefore, this too is the grace of the Lord. The former is known as ‘Arutkarunai’ (grace of compassion), and the latter as ‘Marakkarunai’ (grace of transformation). The Jnana Sastras state this: ‘Protecting those who cling, and being without malice, allowing devotees to do their own deeds and for others to complete their karma.’ Vishnu, who is in a high position, tries to see the Lord’s sacred feet by taking the lowly form of a boar. Brahma, who is in a high position, tries to see the Lord’s sacred crown by taking the lowly form of a swan and flying upwards. The degradation of taking the form of a swan, according to this sacred history, was that he lied and committed an offense. Both of them, after this, attained salvation by chanting the Lord’s sacred name, the five sacred letters.

In the previous verse, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman’s composition based on Ravana’s act was an instruction for those living on this earth. In this verse, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman’s composition based on the story of Vishnu and Brahma is an instruction for the devas (heavenly beings) to attain well-being.

Let us persist in our reflection.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 23 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 570, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam’, ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar Puranam. The tenth verse of the first pathigam is as follows: (Buddhrodu poriyil samanum purangura nerinillaa ottha solla ulagam bali theerndhenadhu ullam kavar kalvan mattha yaanai marugavuri porththadhor maayam idhu enna piththarpolum piramapurameviya pemman ivan andre) In this tenth verse, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman says that the Buddhists and Jains stray from the path laid out by the sages, propagating their own mistaken ideas, and that Shiva is the thief who stole his heart by going to all the worlds and receiving alms. He wonders if Shiva is not the Lord residing in Bramapuram, who, making a wild elephant tremble, flayed its hide and wore it, making it seem like a magical act, like a madman. making it confused and flaying its skin to wear, making it seem like a magical act, like a madman. Is he not the Lord residing in Bramapuram? ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman says this.

The Buddhists and Jains, due to their lack of good karma and merits, would speak ill of the Saiva religion and propagate their own erroneous ideas that they deemed appropriate for their intellect. In this tenth verse, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman condemns the Jains and Buddhists. This same pattern is found in most of ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman’s pathigams, meaning that the tenth verse contains a condemnation of the Jains and Buddhists. Why did ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman structure it this way? Sekkizhar Peruman explains why ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman structured it this way: (Vethakkaaranayavennbirai ser seyya sadai naathan neri arindhu uyyaar thamile nalam kollum bodhamilaa saman kaiyar putthar vazhi pazhiyaakkum edhame ena mozhindhaar engal piraan Sambandhar endru) Sekkizhar Peruman explains why ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman condemns the Jains and Buddhists, who are external religious practitioners, in the tenth verse of his pathigams.

Lord Shiva is the cause of the Vedas. ‘Vedhakaranar’ means he is the primordial composer of the Vedas. It also means that Shiva is the instrumental cause, as described by the Vedas. The Vedas praise Shiva as the instrumental cause of this world.

Thus, Lord Shiva, the cause of the Vedas, Those who do not know his path and do not attain salvation are external religionists. The Jains and Buddhists are among those external religious groups who wander without attaining the good fortune of clinging to Saivism and attaining salvation. They are those who do not consider the Vedas composed by the Lord as authoritative but praise what they have created and spoken with their own intellect.

Therefore, the paths they speak of, the paths they follow, are harmful paths that bring disgrace. What disgrace do they bring? The disgrace of betraying trust by misusing the intellect, which the Lord created for good, in wrong ways. Such is the path followed by Jains and Buddhists.

Thus, our Lord Sambandhar spoke. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that our Lord Sambandha Peruman, who is the revered Acharya of the Saiva faith, speaks thus.

Therefore, this verse explains the meaning of the tenth verse in ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman’s pathigams. The rejection of the evils of the external religions like Jainism and Buddhism, and the propagation of the glory of the sacred ash, these two are the objectives of Pillaiyar’s incarnation. All these objectives begin and manifest from this first pathigam composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman. In it, the tenth verse is known as ‘Samanpaattu’ (the verse of equality). The great Acharya, who explained the sacred five letters and other Saiva tools in the preceding two verses, In this tenth verse, he emphasizes what is to be explained as ineffectual.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman explains the tenth verse.

Now, the concluding verse of this pathigam, known as Thirukkadaikaappu, the eleventh verse: (Aruneriyamarai valla muniyagan poigai alar meya peruneriyap piramapurameviya pemman ivan thannai oruneriyamanam vathunargnanasambandhan urai seidha thiruneriyatamil vallavar tholvinai theerthal ezithame) The meaning is as follows: Brahma, who is proficient in the precious, world-giving Vedas, worshipped Lord Shiva at Bramapuram. Bramapuram is located on the bank of the Brahma Theertham, where wide lotus flowers bloom. Lord Shiva, who resides in such Bramapuram (Sirkazhi), is the Lord who leads souls to the path of liberation. For those who are skilled in this sacred Tamil path, which is a precious path, spoken by GnanaSambandhan, who understands such Lord Shiva with a mind of single-minded devotion, it is easy to remove all their ancient karma, their accumulated karma (sanchitha karma). This is the meaning of this concluding verse.

Thus, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman concludes this pathigam, which contains ten pathigams, by declaring the eleventh verse as Thirukkadaikaappu. lotus flowers have bloomed, that is Bramapuram. Such a Lord Shiva resides in Sirkazhi, which is Bramapuram. He is the Lord who leads souls on the path to liberation. It is easy for those who are skilled in this sacred Tamil, which is a precious path, spoken by GnanaSambandhan, who understands such a Lord Shiva with a single-minded devotion, to eliminate all their old karmas, which are accumulated karmas. This is the meaning of this concluding verse.

Thus, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman completes this pathigam, which has ten pathigams, by declaring the eleventh verse as Thirukkadaikaappu. Thirukkadaikaappu means that after completing a pathigam, The eleventh verse is the one that articulates his name and the benefit of the pathigam, imprinted with his seals, as a way to conclude and mark it. The eleventh verse is called Thirukkadaikaappu.

Therefore, in all the pathigams composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman, the concluding verse is a Thirukkadaikaappu, and in it, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman has imprinted his name and the benefit of reciting the pathigam as a seal. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman refers to the pathigam as ‘Thiruneriyathamizh’, which means Tamil that shows the path of Shiva.

Therefore, this name ‘Thiruneriyathamizh’ applies not only to this pathigam but also to other Saiva Thirumuraikal like Tevaram and Thiruvasagam. methods.

Thus, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman concludes, with his seal, that those who are able to recite this pathigam, composed by ThiruGnanaSambandhan, who understood Lord Shiva, the Lord residing in Bramapuram, with a single-minded devotion, will have their ancient karmas easily resolved.

Here, ‘resolving ancient karmas’ is stated by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman as the benefit of the pathigam. ‘Ancient karma’ is also called ‘pazhavinai’ (old karma). It is referred to as ‘Sanchitha Karma’. This is the karma that remains to be experienced and exhausted. That is the old karma. ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman states that this accumulated karma (Sanchitham) will be resolved if this pathigam is recited.

Therefore, Sanchitha Karma If it is resolved, the karma that is the seed for future births will be gone.

Therefore, the Lord teaches that there will be no more births and that liberation is certain. Even though the removal of past karma (Sanchita Karma) is the benefit of this pathigam, it also means that Agamiyam (future karma) and Prarabdha Sedam (remaining Prarabdha karma) will also be resolved. It is also evident here that Pillaiyar incarnated as an Acharya to remove the suffering of birth from living beings and show them the path to liberation. In this first pathigam, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman points to the Lord saying, ‘Pemman Ivanandre’ (Is he not the Lord?). In his concluding pathigam, ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman imparts the sacred five letters and shows the path to liberation.

Therefore, for the living beings who recite the Lord’s pathigams, for those souls, there is certainly no rebirth, but only liberation. Regarding this concept, the author of Thiruvichaippa has spoken of Pillaiyar’s nature as an Acharya in Thiruvichaippa, saying, ‘He cured all our binding karmic illness and rules over us, Sambandhan.’ ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman has similarly bestowed the benefits of the pathigam in other pathigams. We can also see the truth that these pathigams grant those benefits to the souls who recite them from then until now.

Thus, the meaning of the first pathigam composed by ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman is concluded. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: “After completing the pathigam, and having sealed it with Thirukkadaikaappu, Pillaiyar, the master of Rig Vedic hymns, stood reverently, worshipping, and seeing the grace of the Lord’s divine compassion, all the celestials rejoiced greatly in the sky, shouting and showering fragrant flowers,” says Sekkizhar Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman sings that Pillaiyar, the master of Rig Vedic hymns, who sang the complete pathigam and also composed the Thirukkadaikaappu, stood worshipping the Lord. ‘Irukku Mozhi’ means Rig Veda.

Here, it refers to all four Vedas, indicating the generality of the Vedas. Sekkizhar Peruman states this to show that Pillaiyar’s sacred words are the Vedas. Sekkizhar Peruman tells us that the Vedas, which are the Lord’s words, came from Pillaiyar’s sacred mouth.

Furthermore, ‘Irukku Mozhi’, understood as ‘Irukkum Mozhi’ (the existing word), also conveys the implication of a word that eternally exists without destruction. The term ‘Irukku Mozhi’ also implies that it is a word of grace that will make those who study this pathigam reside in Shivaloka, taking it as a causative verb (‘iruththum’).

Furthermore, Saiva elders state that ThiruGnanaSambandha Peruman’s Tevarams are the essence of the Rig Veda. Sekkizhar Peruman also mentions this here as ‘Irukku Mozhi Pillaiyar’. The idea that Pillaiyar belonged to the Rig Vedic tradition is also subtly implied here. Even Arunagirinathar Peruman, in Thiruppugal, praises Pillaiyar’s sacred words in various ways as ‘Agama Veda Purana Nool’, ‘Shruti Thamizh Kavi’, ‘Aranaga Keetha Kavithai’, and ‘Upanishad Madhura Kavithai’.

Thus, after composing the first pathigam, he stands worshipping Lord Shiva. The child-saint stated that the celestials perceive the grace of Lord Shiva, who is the gracious lord. Although grace and compassion are one, here Lord Shiva, in His Ardhanarishwara form, bestows grace and compassion as two words that convey a single meaning. Though the words are two, their essence is one, and similarly, though Ardhanarishwara appears as two, their essence is one. To signify this, Sekkizhar Peruman uses the sacred name ‘Thiruvalan’ for the Lord in this verse. ‘Thiruvalan’ means the one who rules the prosperity of liberation; ‘Thiru’ here refers to the prosperity of liberation. This name is exclusive to Lord Shiva and great saints who have attained His nature.

Thus, the compassionate lord, Shiva, The celestials behold the grace of Lord Shiva. They gather in the sky, shouting with joy, showering divine, honey-laden flowers as a rain.

Our reflection now resumes.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 24 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Volume 571, by Sekkizhar Swamigal, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. As soon as Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recited his first pathigam, the Vedas themselves resounded. The light of the Vedas had diminished due to the external religions of Jainism and Buddhism.

Now, those very Vedas, through the child-saint’s words, would emerge as revealed scripture. From this pathigam onwards, the Kadai Kappu pathigams, as they issued from the child-saint’s lips, would clearly proliferate and grow, just as the formerly diminished Vedas now illuminated the world.

Thus, the Vedas themselves reverberated with a resounding sound. In the sky, the crowns of all the devas collided with each other, They shattered, and their gems scattered, falling to the earth like dew drops, covering the world. Crowds of ascetic sages, whose lives were always filled with truth and burgeoning peace, gathered like an ocean. Thoniyappar and Ammai, who had emerged from Thiruthoni to assuage the child-saint’s tears, now, after the child-saint had completed his pathigam, were again enshrined in Thiruthoni. Thoniyappar is compassionate, bestowing His two sacred feet as a sweet raft to devotees who approach Him with maturity and devotion, enabling them to cross the incomparable, powerful ocean of birth. Thoniyappar bestows His two feet, representing His gnana shakti (power of knowledge) and kriya shakti (power of action), upon the devotees gathered in Sirkazhi.

These feet serve as a raft, helping devotees cross the ocean of birth.

Thus, Thoniyappar enables devotees to reach His two raft-like feet through the pathigams composed by the child-saint.

Now, through the history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, we will see the lives of those devotees who, by holding onto the Lord’s feet through the child-saint’s pathigams, crossed the ocean of birth.

The Lord Himself bestows the knowledge that enables devotees to grasp His sacred feet; only the Lord can grant it.

Thus, by revealing His sacred feet, The Lord and Lady, who bestowed grace, are again enshrined in the Thiruthoni temple. To soothe the child-saint’s tears, the Lord appeared, feeding him the milk of wisdom. When his father later approached in anger, the Lord, by the child-saint’s pointing and the singing of his pathigam, had revealed His divine form in the sky all that time, an act of great compassion. This manifestation was to bestow upon devotees the nature of His two feet as a raft. This is because the child-saint’s pathigams, which are his great spiritual teachings, possess the quality of a raft. Until the child-saint pointed Him out, the Lord and Lady, Thoniyappar and Ammai, who had manifested their divine form in the sky, returned to Thiruthonipuram, showing that they were the very essence of those pathigams.

The Lord and the Goddess Seeing them thus enshrined in Thiruthoni at the Sirkazhi temple, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with ever-increasing love, entered the beautiful Thiruthoni temple from the bank of Brahmateertham, his mind, having entered through his eyes, remaining inseparable. From the bank of the pond, the child-saint saw the Lord, and due to his ever-increasing desire to continually unite with the Lord, as the Lord became enshrined in Thiruthoni, the child-saint also entered the Thiruthoni temple. The vision, having been granted in the form of Ardhanarishwara and through the feeding of the milk of wisdom, had imprinted itself in the child-saint’s heart. Captivated by this vision, the child-saint wished to see and worship again within the Thoni where Ardhanarishwara was enshrined, and so he proceeded to the Thiru The child-saint enters the Thoni temple. The child-saint’s father, Sivapadahridayar, performed immense austerities to become the child-saint’s father. He attained the blessing of being called ‘father’ by the child-saint.

Previously, he had raised a stick as if to strike him in anger, but from that state, the stick slipped from his hand, and he clapped his flower-like hands in joy and danced with bliss. Sivapadahridayar follows the child-saint, delighting in the sweet meaning of the ‘Thirunerith Thamizh’ (righteous Tamil) that the child-saint pointed out, having seen and heard it. He sees Lord Shiva and sees that Lord Shiva is enshrined in the Thoni, and follows Him. Like the child-saint, his father did not see Lord Shiva, Even though he had not directly seen Shiva, he perceived the signs of divine grace that occurred through the child-saint’s pathigam.

Therefore, with a heart overflowing with desire, he followed his son, who was walking ahead of him, believing it to be the grace of the Lord of Thonipuram. It is not proper to walk ahead of one who has received divine grace, so the father walked behind the child-saint who had received grace.

At that time, those who had seen what transpired, and those who, though not seeing, had heard, along with the Brahmanas wearing the sacred thread, wondered where else such a miraculous event had occurred. They gathered at the entrance of the Thiruthoni temple, where Lord Shiva, with his coral-red matted locks, was enshrined, their hair standing on end. They narrated this sacred history many times. Many people speak thus, and as they speak, they gather before the entrance of Thoniyappar’s temple. The child-saint, who had partaken of the nectar of wisdom, enters the Thiruthoni temple and stands before Thoniyappar and Periyanayaki Ammaiyar, before their sacred presence. He recites a pathigam expressing the sentiment, ‘Where is the Lord who owns me, along with Umadevi?’ and worships Him.

The pathigam recited by the child-saint now begins with ‘Naravanirai Vandarai,’ it is the 74th pathigam of the first Thirumurai, set to the Takkesi tune. This pathigam, which is one of the twelve names for Sirkazhi, bears the name ‘Puravam.’ On the bank of Brahmateertham, The Lord and Goddess emerged and bestowed grace, and then they were again enshrined in Thiruthoni.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes this pathigam, centered on the idea that the Lord Shiva, who revealed Himself and took him as His own, is present here in this Thiruthoni temple with Uma. Thiruthoni is the shrine on the second floor of the Sirkazhi temple where Thoniyappar and Periyanayaki, the Lord and Lady, are enshrined.

Here, the Lord is enshrined with Uma, and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes this pathigam, alluding to this fact.

Therefore, throughout the verses of this pathigam, he concludes each verse with ‘Imaiyor Etha Uamaiyodu Iruntane’ (The celestials praise Him, residing with Uma), as a crown. He bestows this pathigam. This is the second pathigam to emerge from the child-saint’s sacred words. It is the first pathigam recited within the Thiruthoni temple. This pathigam has eleven verses. Its first and concluding verses are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. (Naravanirai vandarai tharkondrai nayanthu nayanathal suravan seirivankodiyon udalam podiya vizhiseythan puravam urai vanpathiya mathiyar puramoonru eriseytha iraivan aravan imaiyor etha umaiyodirunthane ponnar mada needum selva puravam pathiya minnar idaiyal umaiyallodum iruntha vimalanai than arvam sey thamilin virakan urraiththa tamilmalai pannal padiyada piri)

Thiruchitrambalam (Thiriyaparalokanthane).

Thus, the first and concluding verses of this pathigam are structured.

After the Lord accepted the child-saint as His own, the child-saint, having been thus accepted, experienced and praised the nature of servitude to the Lord throughout the verses of this pathigam. With love, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, whose sweet mouth exuded the fragrance of the nectar of wisdom, departs from the temple, accompanied by many Vedic Brahmins, to perform the sacred service of singing rich Tamil pathigams, imbued with melodious seven notes, as offerings to Lord Shiva, through the discipline and grace of servitude. Although Thirugnanasambandha Peruman departed from the temple, he was bound by servitude, He emerges without parting from our Lord, as if bound. This is the devotion Thirugnanasambandha Peruman held for the Lord’s feet. That very devotion, coupled with desire, manifests as the nectar of wisdom, as fragrant words of wisdom and love mixed, in the form of pathigams.

Moreover, these pathigams, like the Lord’s own words (the Vedas), are filled with the harmony of the seven musical notes. Without effort, they spontaneously gathered and harmonized in the child-saint’s words.

Thus, before the child-saint, who had received the Lord’s grace, and after he emerged from the temple, the devotees of Lord Shiva and the people of Thiruthonipuram gathered at the temple entrance and praised the child-saint. They came forward to praise the child-saint as he emerged from the temple, in the following manner: (Kaliyir thavame kauniayar thaname kalagnanath thalliya kadale athanida amuthe adiyar mun vazhiya vanthu immanmisai vanor thaninathan eyilisai mozhiyal than thiruarul perranai enbar marai valar thiruve vaithika nilaiye valar gnana poraiyanimukile pukaliyar pukale porponniththuraiparumaniye suruthiyin oliye veliye vanthu iraiyavan umaiyalludan arulthara eyithinai enbar punniyamuthalai punaimani arainanodu pothum kannirai kathire kalaivalar mathiye kavinmevum punniyal kathiyai paruvamathoru moovarudathe enniya porulai ninravar arulperranai enbar) Thus the devotees and the people of Sirkazhi praised the child-saint with these words. Sekkilap Peruman arranges these words of praise as verses.

Let us go on reflecting.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 25 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Volume 572, by Sekkilar Swamigal, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Brahmins, the people of Sirkazhi, and devotees of Shiva praise Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in many ways. They praise him as one who embodies the fruits of the penance of those residing in Sirkazhi. They say that the people of Sirkazhi received this blessing first, before anyone else in the world, to have him in their midst.

Therefore, they praise him as the fruit of the penance of the people of Sirkazhi. They praise him as ‘Kauniyar Thaname,’ meaning he is the treasure of the Kaundinya lineage, having been born into that gotra. They praise him as ‘Kalagnanath Aazhiya Kadale,’ meaning the ocean of artistic and spiritual knowledge. They praise him.

Here, ‘Kalagnanam’ refers to the compilation of aparajnanam (lower knowledge). This knowledge is extremely rare for others who have not received Shiva’s grace.

Thus, they praise him as one who emerged like nectar amidst this ‘Kalagnanam.’ Nectar removes aging and birth. The nectar mentioned here refers to the ineffable true knowledge, which is parajnanam (higher knowledge). He attained the fruit of aparajnanam, which was parajnanam, and beyond that, he attained sacred grace, and even beyond that, he attained it for the benefit of the world. Devotees of Shiva praise him in this sense.
