This pathigam speaks of the glory of the Lord, stating that Thirumaraikkadu is His abode, and describes the special features of the place. This pathigam was given to the people of the world, instructing them to go and worship there.

Now, the fourth pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman for the sacred site of Thirumaraikkadu is the seventy-sixth pathigam of the third Thirumurai, which belongs to the Thiruviragam category, set to the Sadari Pann. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. “My Lord, who performs a great dance in the forest and collects alms from women, is said to reside in Vedavanam, where the mighty, stormy ocean casts forth pearls like mountain peaks, and where courtesans with bow-like eyebrows gather.” “Mandalamura wangadal valankezhuvu Kaali pathi mannu Kavuni venpodi neer aniyum Vedavanamevu Sivana in arulinal santhamevai thandamilin innisaiyena paravu paadal ulagil bandhan urai kondu mozhivaargal payilvaargal uyarvaan ulagame Thiruchitrambalam.” The note for this pathigam is that the Lord’s abode is Vedavanam.

Thus, these two great masters reside in Vedharanyam, also known as Thirumaraikkadu.

Now, Sekkizhar Peruman begins to narrate the preface to the sacred history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s avatar, which is the journey to Pandya Nadu, where he would eradicate Jainism and establish Saivism, and the subsequent divine events. Let us persist in our reflection.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 135 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 682, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. During the time when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman resided in Thirumaraikkadu, Jainism flourished in Pandya Nadu, and Saiva Vaidika tradition was suppressed. The divine event of the child-saint’s avatar, which includes the refutation of other religions, condemnation, and the exposition of Saivism, is now about to unfold. Sekkizhar Peruman begins to narrate it. This section is the central part of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s Puranam, spanning one thousand two hundred and fifty-six verses.

This section is contained in verses five hundred and ninety-nine and six hundred. Sekkizhar Peruman, following the narrative of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred life thus far, now begins the section where the child-saint’s avatar’s purpose is fulfilled in Pandya Nadu. Verses five hundred and ninety-nine and six hundred are as follows: While they were there, in Pandya Nadu, the land of the Southern King, where the true path was lost due to the accumulated karma, and Jainism flourished, causing turmoil before the rightful ways ceased, the Southern King, due to the karma he had accumulated, considered that path as the right one and remained firm in it. The established truth of Saiva Vaidika tradition, which is the good path, was abandoned and replaced by the evil path. These are the verses. While worshipping the Lord at Thirumaraikkadu, in Pandya Nadu, the evil consequences of accumulated karma led to the rise of Jainism.

The good ethical principles of Saivism were suppressed, causing everyone to be distressed. Never before had Jainism flourished like this, nor would it again. During this intermediate period, Jainism was flourishing there. This Pandya Nadu, at the time this history unfolds, During the period this narrative unfolds, Pandya Nadu was entirely under the control of the Pandya kings. The Cholas also ruled Pandya Nadu for some time.

But this was a period when the Pandya kings, as Southern rulers, governed the land.

At that time, Jainism had greatly flourished during this interim period. The Chola dynasty was always a lineage that followed Saivism without fail.

However, the Pandya lineage was associated with Jainism. During the intermediate period, Jainism flourished in this Pandya Nadu. The Chola dynasty, which came from the lineage that followed established Saivism, and whose land was enriched by the Ponni River, always remained steadfast in the Saiva tradition. In this Pandya Nadu, at this time, Jainism was flourishing. “We are servants who perform deeds and praise the Lord’s feet” is a saying from the Thevaram. The land of Pandya was in turmoil because the Saiva path, which includes the paths of Chariya, Kriya, Yoga, and Gnana, and the discipline of adhering to it, and the exposition of the glory of the sacred ashes, were not upheld, and Jainism flourished.

“Just as all seeds sown in a rainy season sprout at the same time and then wither away together in the dry season,” says a verse from Sivagnana Siddhiyar. Generally, in the rainy season or other seasons, the same type of seeds sprout and grow at the same time, remain for a short period, and then wither away together. We observe all these.

Similarly, most living beings in a country experience the same type of karmic results at the same time. The karma of those beings is collectively bestowed by the Lord at the same time, and such karmic results come to the beings worthy of experiencing them.

In the same way, in Pandya Nadu, most living beings at that time were influenced by the fruit of evil karma to follow Jainism, by the Lord’s will.

At that time, the Pandya king, also due to the fruits of his past evil karma, considered the Jain path as the true dharma and followed it. All good morals in the country declined, and evil morals increased.

Similarly, the Pandya king, the ruler of Pandya Nadu, due to the fruit of his past evil karma, was destined to align himself with Jainism. If there was past evil karma, the Lord would bestow the fruit of that evil karma accordingly. Due to the fruit of that evil karma, evil thoughts and subsequent evil actions would occur. If there was good karma, then due to the fruit of that good karma, good thoughts and subsequent good actions would similarly be brought about by the Lord – this truth is stated in the Gnyana Sastras. Although the Pandya king was born into the noble lineage of Saivism and a Saiva royal family, His conversion to Jainism during this period was due to the decree that he had to experience the fruits of his past evil karma. He adopted Jainism, believing it to be the path of righteousness.

Therefore, it is implied here that it was not truly the path of righteousness.

Thus, when Jainism flourished, the good path of enduring Saiva Vaidika tradition was lost and changed in Pandya Nadu. Saivism in Pandya Nadu is Vaidika Saivism, which is an eternal and imperishable form of Saivism. The truth that underlies the Vedic tradition is the Saiva path. The essence of the Veda is Saivism. Its truth is the path prescribed by the Siva Agamas and Vedas, which originated from the Lord’s sacred word “Sat.” Even though it is prescribed by both Saiva Agamas and the Vaidika Vedas, both Saiva Agamas and Vedas lead to the same conclusion.

Therefore, great souls celebrate Saivism by calling it Vaidika Saivism. Vaidika Saivism is praised by the exalted as “Azhagidhu Antho” (how beautiful it is!).

Thus, the Vaidika Saiva tradition, the good path, is an eternal good path.

The Lord is eternal and unchanging.

Similarly, His sacred words, the Vedas and Siva Agamas, are also eternal. Yet, in Pandya Nadu, at that time, due to the karmic experiences of those beings and the fruits of evil karma, Jainism flourished and Saivism was suppressed. To uplift this Vaidika Saiva good path, the child-saint incarnated. Sekkizhar Peruman has thus composed the introductory verse in the child-saint’s Puranam, stating, “May the Vedic path flourish, may the abundant Saiva tradition shine.” In accordance with this, through the sacred words of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the evil path of Jainism will be removed, and Saivism will flourish there.

Now, the evil path has spread. Because when that good path of Vaidika Saivism changed, it not only changed but also allowed the evil path to act like the good path in Pandya Nadu, thus Jainism flourished. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: “The peerless sacred places in the Tamil land of the Northerners all became ruins and many Jain schools, like groups of darkness, surrounded by hair-peacocks and water-vessels in hand, filled with Jains.” This is the six hundred and first verse. Pandya Nadu is called Tamil Nadu. Generally, all countries where Tamil is spoken, such as Chola Nadu, Thondai Nadu, Nadu Nadu, Kongu Nadu, and so on, All those countries are also Tamil Nadu. Even though the name Tamil Nadu is a common name for all those countries, it is uniquely attributed to Pandya Nadu by scholars.

Although Tamil Nadu can be a descriptive name applicable to other countries, it is specifically reserved for Pandya Nadu as a proper noun with inherent meaning. In the one thousand five hundred and fifty-fourth verse, Sekkizhar Peruman sang that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s arrival in Pandya Nadu was an arrival in Tamil Nadu. Because Lord Siva, the supreme deity, presided over the Sangam and nurtured Tamil, and because Agastya, the Tamil sage, still resides in the Podhigai mountains, and for many other reasons, Tamil Nadu refers specifically to Pandya Nadu. In such a Tamil Nadu, all the Saivite holy places were in ruins, meaning they became places with Jain ruins and schools. All the Saivite holy places in Tamil Nadu became desolate, turning into Jain monuments and schools. The glorious places in Pandya Nadu, such as Thiruppoovanam, Thirunelveli, and Thirukutralam, were filled with Jain monuments and schools.

“Paazhikal” refers to temples built by Jains for worship. “Palli” refers to places where Jain gurus gathered for study and resided.

In addition, There are also separate places for Jain gurus to reside in the monasteries. Generally, Paazhi and Palli are names given to our Saivite temples. These names have been in use since ancient times. We can still see Saivite shrines like Arathai Perumpali and Sembhon Palli.

However, Jainism, which emerged later, adopted these terms, Paazhi and Palli, for its own places and made it a custom. There, in those Paazhis, Jains gathered like groups of darkness. In their hands, peacock feathers shone like groups of darkness. In their hands, they held a Kamandalam, a water pot. Jains generally used to sprinkle water from the pot they held in their hands, stroke with peacock feathers, and chant mantras; this was one of the customs of Jain gurus. Not only that, but they also used peacock feathers to gently brush aside small creatures like ants from their path so as not to harm them.

Such Jains swarmed in the Paazhis and Pallis. Just as flies swarm around beehives, people also swarmed in these Paazhis and Pallis because the king was a Jain follower.

Therefore, people also followed the king and embraced Jainism.

Moreover, the teachings of Jains were based on non-violence as a superficial principle.

Therefore, those Captivated by the deceitful charm of those beautiful, superficial teachings, people became Jain followers and thronged to the Jain monasteries and schools.

Thus, while Jain gurus resided in monasteries and schools, Jain followers roamed everywhere, carrying peacock feathers, bamboo mats, and triple parasols. The triple parasol held by Jains is a symbol of their deity. It is made of gold, gems, and pearls, with a single staff. It is customary for Jains to mark their bodies with this symbol, like the emblem of their deity, on their chest, forehead, shoulders, and other places. These triple parasols of the Aragu deity are The Jains claim their beliefs are eternal bliss and encompass everything. They wander around carrying peacock feathers, water pots, mats, and umbrellas.

These Jains cling to the doctrines they found in their external religion, considering them the ultimate truth, and are content within those boundaries. They remain unresponsive even when they know a superior Saivite path exists, which is contrary to their own. Though Jainism had spread like darkness everywhere, two great people shone as the brilliant lamps of Saivism: one was our empress, Mangaiyarkkarasiyar, and the other was our lord, Kulachirai Nayanar. These two great individuals cherished and protected the Saivite path there. For the well-being of the Pandya king, who was a southerner, and to ensure his salvation, Queen Mangaiyarkkarasiyar, the auspicious daughter of the Cholas, and Kulachiraiyar, the great minister, shone as the brilliant Saivite lamps and served as pillars of support for the Saivite path.

Let us dwell further on this.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 136 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periyapuranam, Part Six Hundred Eighty-Three, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, titled ‘Vambarav Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam’. The esteemed daughter born to the Chola king in the Chola country was the Pandya Queen Mangaiyarkkarasiyar. She was indeed the daughter born to the Cholas for the salvation of the Pandyas. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman himself, in his sacred words, has exalted our empress, the Pandya Queen, in a pathigam, referring to her as ‘Ammaiyar Mangaiyarkkarasi Valavarkon Pavai’. In the Pandya country, while the Pandya king, the husband of the Pandya Queen, was leaning towards Jainism, the Pandya Queen remained steadfast.

She steadfastly followed the Saivite path. Kulachirai Nayanar Peruman, the minister of the Pandya king, also stood firm in the Saivite path.

Thus, while the Pandya king leaned towards Jainism, the Pandya Queen and Kulachirai Nayanar Peruman stood firmly in the Saivite path. Saivism found its support only in these two individuals in the Pandya country. The Pandya king mentioned here will henceforth be revered as one of the Nayanmars, Nedumara Nayanar, through the grace of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman has depicted the situation of the Pandya country and the state of Saivism at that time, placing these three great individuals within a single verse. Sekkizhar Peruman stated this in the six hundred third verse: (Varrisilai Thennavan than Uytharku valavarkoman thiru uyirtharulum selvap pandimadeviyarum kuraikazhal amaichanaram kulachirayarum enum iruvartham pangum anri Saivam angu eythataga) meaning, apart from the Pandya Queen, the fortunate daughter born to the Chola king for the salvation of the southern king with the strong bow, and Kulachiraiyar, the minister with the ankleted feet, Saivism did not flourish anywhere else there.

Thus, Saivism was firmly established only in the Pandya Queen and Kulachirai Nayanar; it did not reach other places. Although it is stated that Saivism existed only in these two, the Pandya Queen and the great minister Kulachirai Nayanar, they sent some envoys to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. These envoys were also devoted to the Saivite path.

Later, when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visited and worshipped the Lord of Thiruvalavai, the devotees serving him welcomed him with reverence. They too were followers of Saivism in the Pandya country at that time.

Therefore, even though Saivism existed among some individuals, the great people who served as protectors of Saivism were the Pandya Queen Mahadevi and the great minister Kulachirai Nayanar. That is why Peruman states that Saivism did not flourish anywhere else except with these two. Saivism had no other place to find support; it depended solely on these two in the good land of Pandya. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: (Angavar thangal angann arumperal Tamil Nadu utra theenginukku alavuthetra sindaiyil parivukonde ongiiya Saiva vaaymai ozhukkathil nindra tanmai poongazhal sezhiyin munbu pulappadaa vagai kondu vaythar enbathu adutha thiruppadal) meaning, the next verse states that these two great individuals, Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi, and the great minister Kulachirai Nayanar, deeply distressed by the immense harm that befell this rare Tamil country, nurtured the lofty truth of Saivite conduct in their hearts, keeping it hidden from the king. The harm that befell the rare Tamil country, the Pandya land, refers to the decline of Saivite conduct and the widespread prevalence of Jainism. Tamil and Saivism are intricately linked; if it is Tamil, it is Saivism, and if it is Saivism, it is Tamil, both being inseparably intertwined and signifying special connections.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman does not say that it is a harm that befell the Saivite country, but rather refers to it as a harm that befell the Tamil country.

Thus, whether it is the Saivite country, the Tamil country, or the Pandya country, it all refers to the same meaning here. Some modern researchers, unaware of all these distinctions, distortedly claim that the superiority of Jainism is the superiority of Tamil. Sekkizhar Peruman here emphasizes that the glory of Tamil lies in guiding people towards a path of devotion.

Lord Siva as Iraiyanar, Lord Muruga as Kumaravelar, Agathiyar, and many other divine poets flourished Tamil in this land. This means that the greatness of Tamil lies in the supremacy of Saivism, not in the supremacy of Jainism. That is why Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the harm that befell Saivism as the harm that befell the Tamil country. As the Saivite country, the Pandya land, was thus afflicted, Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi and Kulachirai Nayanar contemplated in their hearts about when this suffering would end and how to find a solution. Even though the desire for Jainism to disappear and Saivism to return was a policy contrary to the king’s command and opinion, they felt obliged to ensure the flourishing of Saivism in this country and to protect it. Queen Pandi and Kulachirai Nayanar firmly upheld the true conduct of Saivism.

They maintained their Saivite path without the king’s knowledge. If these two individuals upheld the Saivite path in this manner, it was for the benefit of this country. This is because the command of God is enshrined in the Vedas and Sivagamas, and the essence of these scriptures is that all living beings should adhere to the true conduct of Saivism.

Therefore, it is also the king’s duty to guide the people towards the true Saivite conduct, which is the ultimate teaching of the Vedas and Sivagamas revealed by God. However, the king here practices a different religion.

Therefore, in this situation, while the king’s command is aligned with the Jain religion, these two great individuals adhere to the true Saivite path, contrary to the king’s command, but without his knowledge. This is because God’s command is superior to the king’s command and is worthy of being followed.

Therefore, even though the government had changed and stood on a different path, the Queen, Pandi, and the minister, Kulachirai Nayanar, followed the Vedic Saivite path, which is a higher command than that of the king. It is true that they followed the Saivite path in this way. If righteousness is not upheld and if one does not follow the king, then righteousness will not prevail in this world. The world cannot function without the king’s command. It is the minister’s duty to enforce the king’s command.

Furthermore, following the husband’s path is the essence of chastity. The world should be shown that following the husband’s path is indeed the essence of chastity. Those in leadership positions, such as the king and queen of a country, must exemplify these virtues to their people. It is also the duty of the queen, Pandi, to do so.

Therefore, they had the responsibility to practice Saivism discreetly, without the king’s knowledge, for the sake of the country’s worldly order under the king’s rule. This was for the sake of the worldly order.

At the same time, for the sake of guiding the souls in this country away from the harm of Jainism and towards Vedic Saivism, their adherence to Saivite conduct was necessary there. Even though the king’s religion was different, the welfare of the souls in the country lay in Saivite conduct, and thus they had to stand firm.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman has presented all these nuances very subtly. These two individuals, having themselves stood firm in the Saivite path, were now about to send envoys to Pillaiyar to ensure others also embraced it.

Thus, their unwavering commitment to Vedic Saivism and their fervent desire for all souls to attain salvation by following Vedic Saivism are evident here.

Now, Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse: (Innneri ozhugugindraar ezulagugazhi venthar) (Vaitika vaaymai Saiva sen neri vilakkugindrar thirumaraikkadu serntha nannilai kanni nattu nalvinai payathal kettar) Thus, in this situation where Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi and Kulachirai Nayanar were present, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided at Thirumaraikkadu, illuminating the pure path of Saivism in this world. These two great individuals heard of this situation. The Pandya Queen and Kulachirai Nayanar Peruman heard this news. It is due to the good fortune of the Pandya country that they heard and learned of this. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is the great one who came to save the seven worlds.

He is the great one who came to illuminate the true path of Vedic Saivism. If it is said that he came here, it means that he incarnated here. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman had no personal reason to come to this world. He incarnated here solely for the benefit of the souls of this world. The two sacred feet of the Lord are Jnana (knowledge) and Kriya (action). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman incarnated as an Acharya (spiritual teacher) so that devotees could embrace these two sacred feet and attain the Lord’s sacred feet.

Until now, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman had undertaken pilgrimages to various countries like Chola Nadu, Nadu Nadu, Kongu Nadu, composed pathigams, and performed many miraculous acts of grace, thereby bringing salvation to these lands. Pillaiyar is now about to go and save the Pandya country, and also to establish all worlds in the path of sacred ash for their salvation.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Pillaiyar here as the glorious king who came to save the seven worlds. The Pandya Queen and Kulachirai Nayanar hear the news that Pillaiyar is illuminating the Saivite path in Thirumaraikkadu. Their hearing of this news signifies that the time has come for the good penance previously performed by the Pandya country to bear fruit.

Therefore, they hear this news. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing about how overjoyed they were upon hearing this news: (Kettappozhuthe sindai kilarnthezhu magizhchi ponga narpozuthu alarnda senthamarai nagaimugatharaaki vatpadai amaichanarum mangaiyarkkarasiyarum serpadu pulathaarenum sendradi panindharotar) meaning, upon hearing the news, immense joy surged in the hearts of Kulachirai Nayanar and Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi, and their faces bloomed like red lotuses freshly opened. The arrival of Pillaiyar, who is like the sun, is about to happen. Due to the arrival of Pillaiyar, who is like the sun, the faces of these two bloomed like red lotuses. Although Thirumaraikkadu is a long distance from the Pandya country, these two great individuals felt as if they had personally gone to Thirumaraikkadu and worshipped Pillaiyar’s sacred feet. They placed their minds there and worshipped the sacred feet; only their bodies remained here.

Sekkizhar Peruman then composes the next verse: (Kadhalal mikkor thangal kai thozhu karuthinale pothavil pugazhi kavalanar seyya pathangal panimin endru parisanamaakkal thammai maathavam sruthi seytha mamaraikkattil vittar) meaning, Queen Pandi and Kulachirai Nayanar, who had immense love for Pillaiyar, sent their servants, their retinues, to Thirumaraikkadu with the intention that they themselves should meet and worship Pillaiyar. They instructed them, “Go to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred feet and worship him.” They had previously worshipped Pillaiyar in their minds, but now they desired to meet and worship him in person.

Therefore, considering it as if they themselves were going to meet, worship, and submit their plea, they commanded their retinue to go there. They sent them with instructions to go there, prostrate at Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s feet, and submit their plea. That plea was a request to remove the harm that had befallen their country. These envoys were intelligent messengers.

Therefore, they fully understood the subtle message conveyed by the queen and the minister. They were blessed with the good fortune of worshipping Pillaiyar and submitting their plea.

Thus, even without the queen and the minister explicitly stating it, they understood their inner thoughts. They were capable of acting according to the task assigned to them. That is why Sekkizhar Peruman refers to them as ‘intelligent individuals’ in the next verse.

Now, accepting the command of the queen and the great minister, these envoys set off towards Thirumaraikkadu in the Chola country. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to narrate this.

Let us go on pondering.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 137 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periyapuranam, Part Six Hundred Eighty-Four, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, titled ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam’. Sekkizhar Peruman describes how the Pandya Queen and Minister Kulachirai Nayanar sent intelligent envoys to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. He states: (Angavar vida mun pontha arivudai manthar angann neengi van Tamilnattu ellai pirpada neriyin ekii gnangark neer nadum kadu nathigalum kadanthu vandhu thengamizh kaithai neythal thiru maraikkadu sernthar enbathu aru nuru ettavathu thiruppadal) This is the six hundred eighth verse.

Thus, those envoys who were sent were intelligent individuals. They were highly intelligent, and also It is also worth noting that they were fit to undertake this great task of bringing salvation to the Pandya country. They departed from there, meaning they left Madurai, the capital city of the Pandya country, Thirualavai, crossed the rich Tamil country’s border—here Tamil country refers to the Pandya country, a fertile Tamil land. The fertility of Tamil lies in its generous ability to guide those who study it to the path of God, bestowing upon them the three benefits of this world, the next, and the hereafter. Crossing the border of such a Tamil country, the Pandya land, these envoys entered the Chola country. This route is considered to pass through Melur, Thirupputtur, Aranthangi, and Athiveeraramapattinam, located northeast of Madurai.

The route by which Aludaiya Pillaiyar came to Madurai was from Thirukkodungunram, also known as Piramalai. This is another route. This route comes from the north towards Madurai and is a bit longer. As they crossed the Pandya country, they reached the Chola country, which is known as Neer Nadu (watery country). The regions of the Pandya country, with their many forests, small rivers, and tributaries, all flow into the eastern sea. It is mentioned here that these envoys crossed all these.

The names of places like Anappair Melpanaikadu, Maravakkadu, Thiru Idumbavanam, and Thirumaraikkadu reflect the nature of this region. The small rivers flowing here include the Mutha River, Thenaru, Pamparu, Thenvellaru, and Agniaru.

Thus, crossing the Pandya country and the intervening fertile plains of the Chola country (Neer Nadu), the envoys reached Thirumaraikkadu. The fragrance of screwpine flowers seemed to welcome them, wafting for a long distance in Thirumaraikkadu. Thirumaraikkadu is a coastal area, referred to as Neythal Nilam (coastal region). Having crossed the fertile plains of the Chola country, which is a watery land with abundant paddy fields, these envoys reached Thirumaraikkadu, a sacred place located in the eastern coastal region. Sekkizhar Peruman sings: (Thirumaraikkadu nanni sirapura nagaril vantha arumarai pillaiyar tham amarnthu inithu arulum selva perumadatthu anaiya vandhu perugiya viruppil thangal varum murai tanmayellam vayil kavalarukku sonnar) Having reached Thirumaraikkadu, they approached the great mansion where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided and bestowed his grace. The mansion where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resided is a great mansion of wealth.

It is a mansion where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman lovingly resided. It is a great mansion where Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously resided, bestowing sattbhavana (pure thoughts), which includes all initiations, for the welfare of this world. Since Peruman graciously resided there, Since he gracefully resided there, it became a great mansion of wealth that bestows liberation from worldly bonds (pasakshayam) and the supreme state of Shiva (Sivapperu). It was no ordinary mansion; it was a great mansion, meaning a mansion endowed with greatness. Its greatness lay in being a place where assemblies of devotees gathered. This mansion gained the distinction of being a place where Pillaiyar resided for many days after the miraculous event of the sacred door of Thirumaraikkadu opening and closing again.

This sacred mansion is of great significance as it is the starting point for Pillaiyar’s journey to the Pandya country, where his Avatar’s purpose of refuting other religions (parasamyana nirakaripum) and illuminating Saivism (Saivasamay vilakkam) would take place.

Therefore, this sacred mansion becomes equal to the sacred mansion where Pillaiyar resided in Thirualavai, Madurai. The envoys arrived at the exterior of that great mansion. With great devotion, they explained the reason for their visit to the doorkeepers of Pillaiyar’s sacred mansion. These envoys, out of immense devotion to Queen Pandi and the minister, conveyed their purpose to the doorkeepers of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred mansion. It is the doorkeepers who have the right to enter the sacred mansion and inform Pillaiyar appropriately in his presence.

Therefore, the envoys conveyed this matter to the doorkeepers. Peruman then composes the next verse: (Matra avar sendru pukku valavarkon magalar thennan kotravan theviyarum kulachirayarumeva porkazhal paniyavanthom ena silar puraththu vandhu sottranar enru potri thozhudu vinnapam seythar) This verse describes how the doorkeepers of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred mansion went inside and submitted this news to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in the form of a plea. The doorkeepers themselves had the right to enter the sacred mansion and announce any news. They stood before Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and submitted their plea, saying, “Oh Lord, outside our sacred mansion, the envoys sent by the daughter of the Chola king, the Queen of the Pandya king, and Kulachirai Nayanar, say that they have come to worship your golden feet.” Thus, the doorkeepers submitted their plea to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. When speaking about Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi, they first refer to her as the daughter of the Cholas and the Mahadevi (great queen) of the Pandya king, placing the Cholas first. They mention the Pandyas next.

Pillaiyar also belonged to the Chola country, and Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi was also the daughter of the Chola king in the Chola country.

Therefore, the doorkeepers first mention the connection between them, emphasizing the rights and uniqueness of this country, and then refer to her as the Pandya Queen, mentioning her connection to the Pandya country second. When Manikkavasaga Peruman, also known as Thiruvathavur Adigal, resided in a hermitage in Thillaiyambathi and Lord Shiva desired to obtain and write Thiruvachagam, he appeared as a Brahmin. When he came, he announced that his country was the Pandya country to Manikkavasaga Peruman. Manikkavasagar Peruman was also from the Pandya country.

Therefore, by announcing that he too was from the Pandya country, he created a connection based on their native land, fostering closeness. This incident comes to our mind here. These doorkeepers first mentioned the Chola country connection between Pillaiyar and Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman himself, in his sacred pathigam, first refers to Mangaiyarkkarasi as ‘Mangaiyarkkarasi Valavarkon Pavai Varivalai Kaimadamani Pangayachelvi Pandimadevi’, meaning the daughter of the Chola king, and then as Pandi Mahadevi, the queen of the Pandya country, thus following this order.

Thus, the doorkeepers stood before Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, submitting their plea. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse: (Pugazhi kavalar tham kettu poruvila arul mun kura agamalarndhu avargal thammai azhaiyum endru arulicheyya nagaumuch sevvii nokki natrava manthar kuva thagavudai manthar pukku thalaiyinal vanangi nindrar) Hearing what the doorkeepers said, Pillaiyar, the leader of Sirkazhi, was filled with divine grace. This incomparable grace overflowed within him. This divine grace was already kindled by the Lord from within even before they arrived and submitted their plea. When they submitted their plea, that grace surged and overflowed. This grace is instrumental in the flourishing of the sacred ash path and the removal of the opposing religions that hindered it.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it as ‘incomparable grace’. With this divine grace overflowing, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously spoke, commanding, “Call them here.” Seeing the special radiance of Pillaiyar’s joyful face, the good and devoted individuals, the servants, went outside and invited the envoys to come. These invited servants were intimate devotees of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. They were endowed with the merit of serving Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as intimate devotees, and also the merit of being present and assisting at the beginning of the divine grace event that was about to unfold in the Pandya country. Such devoted servants went outside the sacred mansion and invited the envoys to come inside. The intelligent envoys from the Pandya country also entered the sacred mansion.

How much merit did these envoys possess? They possessed great qualities of intelligence, love, and other virtues, making them worthy envoys to remove the great harm that had befallen the entire Pandya country, which was the Saivite path. Such worthy envoys entered the sacred mansion, and before Pillaiyar, they prostrated themselves on the ground, bowing their heads, and then rose to their feet. Addressing those who stood there, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously spoke. He composes the next verse: (Nindravardhammai nokki nigaril seer Champaivendhar mantalanguzhaliiyaram maniyar thamakkum manakunrenan nindra meimai Kulachirayar thmakkum nandrithan vinavikuri narpatham potruvarkal enbathu padal) meaning, the verse describes how Pillaiyar, the king of Sirkazhi, addressed the envoys who stood before him after bowing, and graciously inquired about the well-being of Mangaiyarkkarasi Ammaiyar, whose fragrant hair was adorned with flowers, and Kulachirai Nayanar, whose truth stood like a mountain. It was Pillaiyar’s divine will to inquire about the welfare of the people of the Pandya country.

He first asked if Ammaiyar and Kulachirai Nayanar were well. Because these envoys were sent by them.

Furthermore, the well-being of Queen Mangaiyarkkarasi and Kulachirai Nayanar was to be the cause of future good for the Pandya country and its king.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously inquired about the well-being of the Pandya Queen and Kulachirai Nayanar. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Kulachirai Nayanar as ‘Kulachiraiyar, whose truth stood like a mountain of honor.’ Kulachirai Nayanar was unwavering in his adherence to the Saivite path, no matter what obstacles arose, and he protected his conduct.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman compares his unwavering adherence to the path of conduct to a mountain. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus inquired, and the envoys who had come to convey the message replied. Peruman composes the next verse: (Kanni nattu amanar thammal kattazhindhu ilindhu thangal mannavanum avargal mayathu azhundha mahadeviyarum konnavil kulachirayarum kudi innilai pugazhivendarku iyampum endru irainjivittar enbathu thiruppadal) The envoys stated, they pleaded, saying, “The Kanni country, the Pandya land, has been ruined and debased by the Jains. Our king is also submerged in their illusion. Seeing this, the Pandya Queen and Kulachirai Nayanar were greatly saddened and distressed. They told us to go to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the king of Sirkazhi, and convey this situation to him, and to worship and plead with you.”

The envoys conveyed this message. Hearing what they said, all the devotees of Lord Shiva who were surrounding Thirugnanasambandha Peruman submitted a plea at Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred feet. They pleaded that he should defeat the Jains and make the Vedic path flourish everywhere, and that he should also make the king wear the sacred ash, thereby establishing Saivism in the Pandya country.

The devotees of Lord Shiva who were there submitted this plea at Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred feet. We shall continue pondering.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 138 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periyapuranam, Part Six Hundred Eighty-Five, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, titled ‘Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam’. All the devotees of Shiva who were seated with Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in the sacred mansion were full of love, as ‘love is Shiva’.

Therefore, when these envoys came and spoke about the prevalence of Jainism and the suppression of Saivism in the Pandya country, they were heartbroken to hear about the suffering that had befallen Saivism and the Pandya country. These devotees were interested in the flourishing of Saivism, the divine path.

Therefore, all of them submitted a plea to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. They pleaded that he should show compassion as requested by the people of the Pandya country. Our Lord, Lord Shiva, They implored him to defeat the Jains who did not worship the sacred feet, to make the Saivite path, which is the path described in the Vedas, flourish everywhere, to make the Pandya king embrace the sacred ash and transform him into a Saivite king, and to guide the Pandya king and his people to the path of God’s grace. They pleaded with Pillaiyar to make all practices in the Pandya country flourish as Saivite practices. Peruman then composes the next verse: (Matra avarkku arul purindhu pillaiyarum vakkesa munivarudan kuda sendru petram uyarthavar patham panindhu ponthu periya thirukkooupurathul irundhu thennadutru sei) (Pandimadeviyarum urimai amaicharum uraithuvitta varthai sottrani mannavarukku pugazhi mannar solli ezhuntharulutharkuth thuninthapodhu arasar arulicheygindrar pillaiy antha amankaiyar vanjanikkor avathiyillai urai seyvathu ulathu urukol thanum theeya ezhuntharula udanpaduvathu onnathu enna parasuvathu nam peruman kadalgal endral pazhudhu anaiyathu ena pagarnthu paramar seiya virai sey mal thal potri pugazhivendhar veyurutholiyai eduthu vilambinarre enpathu aduthu amekindra irandu thiruppadalgal) Thus, the envoys requested.

The following two verses describe this. After giving his grace to them, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, accompanied by Thirunavukkarasu Peruman, went and worshipped the sacred feet of the Lord in Vedharanyam (Thirumaraikkadu). They then came out and sat in the great Gopuram in front of the Lord.

At that time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman conveyed to Thirunavukkarasu Peruman the message that the Pandya Queen and Minister Kulachiraiyar had sent to him about the state of the Pandya country.

Thus, he stated that he had decided to go to the Pandya country as per their request. Hearing this, Thirunavukkarasu Peruman replied, “My son, there is no limit to the deceitful acts of the Jains.

“Moreover, at present, the planetary positions are also unfavorable; they are evil.

“Therefore, it would not be right for me to agree to your going there.” Thirunavukkarasu Peruman spoke. Pillaiyar, the leader of Sirkazhi, replied, “When we consider that we worship the sacred feet of the Lord, no harm will befall us. If we worship the sacred feet of our Lord, no harm will come to us.” Saying this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed the pathigam ‘Veyuru Tholipaangan’ (the one with the bamboo-like shoulder), which begins with these words. This is the essence of these two verses. The envoys from the Pandya country made their plea.

“Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bestowed his grace upon the envoys from the Pandya country and the devotees who were present and worshipped there.

“Later, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman went from the sacred mansion to the Thirumaraikkadu temple, also known as Vedharanyam. Before telling Thirunavukkarasu Peruman the news from the Pandya country, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman went with Thirunavukkarasu Peruman to worship the Lord and receive his grace, and also to inform Thirunavukkarasu Peruman about it. After worshipping the Lord, they came out and went to one of the great Gopurams located in the courtyard directly in front of the Lord. Generally, within a temple, there is praise, glorification, and singing of the Lord. The rule for visiting Shiva temples is that only essential discussions should take place, and no other conversations are permitted.

“However, Thirugnanasambandhar wished to discuss all these matters concerning the Pandya country with ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman before the Lord.

“Therefore, without speaking inside or immediately outside the temple, they met beneath the great gopuram between the two areas. There, Pillaiyar recounted all the historical events to ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman, explaining that he intended to travel to the Pandya country for these reasons. Upon hearing this, ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman addressed Thirugnanasambandhar, saying, “Pillai!” Thirugnanasambandhar always considered Appar Peruman as his spiritual father, addressing him as “Appare” from the very beginning.

“Therefore, from the position of a protective father ensuring no harm would come to Pillaiyar, ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman spoke, saying, “The Jains are extremely deceitful. Their treachery knows no bounds. Even the positions of the nine planets are currently unfavorable and are in a harmful state.

“Therefore, it would not be advisable for you to proceed to the Pandya country under these circumstances.” Upon hearing this, Thirugnanasambandhar replied, “If we praise the feet of our Lord, no harm will befall us.” He declared, saying and asserting this, and then blessed a pathigam that begins with “Veyuru Thozhippangan.” This pathigam, known as Kolaru pathigam, is so wonderfully divine that there are no people unfamiliar with it. The theme of this pathigam is “If we praise the feet of our Lord, no harm will befall us,” which is also its crowning statement.

“Thus, through this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandhar not only answered ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman’s objection but also praised the supreme Lord, ensuring His support. This Kolaru pathigam is truly remarkable. It holds great significance. Those who regularly recite it will find their misfortunes dispelled. Travelers who remember this pathigam before embarking on a journey will complete it successfully and without harm, a truth still evident today. This pathigam is included in the “Agathiyar Thevara Thirattu.” Each of its verses describes the Lord’s inseparable presence with the Mother and the benefits thereof.

“Thirugnanasambandhar, beginning with “Veyuru Thozhi Pangan,” starts by praising the Mother, stating that the Lord has Umaiyammaiyar, whose shoulders resemble bamboo, on His left side. Thirugnanasambandhar’s beginning by praising the Mother also signifies the essence of the Thiru Alavai temple. This pathigam is the eighty-fifth pathigam in the Second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Piyanthaikandarap. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. On the fourteenth day of the month, at dawn, The two months, Jupiter and Saturn, along with the serpent planets, will surely bring good things; good things will happen to devotees where there are sweet-smelling rice fields, jasmine, and abundant gold. The divine sage, the ascetic born in Piranmapuram, where the Vedas originated, has sung a garland of words so that the planets and days do not cause harm to devotees.

“Those who recite these verses will rule the heavens; this is our command.

“Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar composed this pathigam. Let us continue to ponder the explanation of the verses of this pathigam.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 139 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam by Deivasekkizhar Peruman, Volume 686, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandhar composed the Kolaru pathigam. This pathigam is the eighty-fifth pathigam in the Second Thirumurai, set to the tune of Piyanthaikandaram. This pathigam is also included in the Agathiyar Thevara Thirattu. Kayappakkam Sadasiva Chettiyar has written commentaries for the pathigams compiled in the Agathiyar Thevara Thirattu.

Kayappakkam Sadasiva Chettiyar taught Periya Puranam to Sivakavimani C.K. Subramania Mudaliar, the commentator of Periya Puranam. Kayappakkam Sadasiva Chettiyar attained divine grace by performing Shiva Puja in strict accordance with Agamic principles and by ceaselessly reciting and understanding the twelve Thirumurais many times. He was skilled in delivering discourses on Periya Puranam. This great personality stayed in Coimbatore for four years, teaching and explaining Periya Puranam. Sivakavimani Ayya, who received direct instruction from this venerable master, took notes at that time.

These notes later proved to be of immense help to Sivakavimani Ayya in publishing a comprehensive commentary on Periya Puranam.

Therefore, we can reflect a little on the explanation of the verses of this pathigam by combining the explanations written by Kayappakkam Sadasiva Chettiyar, the guru of our Periya Puranam commentator Sivakavimani Ayya, and the insightful commentary provided by Sivakavimani Ayya. The first verse of this pathigam is as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. “Veyuru Thozhi Pangan Vidamunda Kandhan miga nalla veenai thadavi Maasaru Thingal Gangai mudimel anindhu en ullamE pugundha adhanal Gnayiru Thingal Sevvai Pudhan Vyazhan Velli Sani Pambu irandum udanE Aasaru nalla nalla avai nalla nalla Adiyar avarkku migavE.” This is the first verse. Thirugnanasambandhar composed this pathigam, beginning with Umaiyammaiyar, calling the Lord “Veyuru Thozhi Pangan,” meaning the Lord who has Umaiyammaiyar, whose shoulders resemble bamboo, on His left side.

Additionally, Thirugnanasambandhar sang in each verse about the Lord residing with the Mother. He said that because the Lord, who has Umaiyammaiyar with bamboo-like shoulders on His left side and whose throat is adorned with the poison He drank, gently plays the excellent veena, and wears the flawless moon and the Ganga on His head, entered my heart—meaning, because He took residence in my heart—the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and the two serpent planets, Rahu and Ketu, Thirugnanasambandhar declares that these planets will cause no harm to devotees and will instead be benevolent towards them. When ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman raised the objection to Thirugnanasambandhar that the days and planets were not in a favorable state, Thirugnanasambandhar composed this pathigam as a reply.

Therefore, in the very first verse, Thirugnanasambandhar, using the nine planets and seven days, declares that they will only bring good things to devotees. It is because of this declaration that this pathigam came to be known as Kolaru pathigam, signifying that the days and planets are subservient to the Lord’s command. How can they be good to devotees? Our Nayanmars are all those who have transcended the senses and sought refuge in the feet of Shiva, thereby severing the cycle of birth and death. All the Thirutthondar Nayanmars are capable of experiencing the immaculate turiyatita state even in a waking state. Understanding this requires direct instruction from wise teachers; their meanings must be learned and comprehended from a guru.

Therefore, the Thirutthondar Nayanmars stand in such a state. They have no actions of their own but are solely agents of Shiva’s will. They are capable of doing everything, in accordance with the saying, “He creates for His devotees.” Therefore, if even the foremost deities seek the commands of these Thirutthondar, then what can these ordinary days and planets do to the Thirutthondar? This is the underlying meaning. In this verse, Thirugnanasambandhar concisely included the seven days, starting with “Gnayiru Thingal,” and the nine planets, demonstrating his divine poetic skill. That these great and extensive powers of the planets and days were subdued and made to serve is a testament to Thirugnanasambandhar’s grace.

The harm caused by these planets will cease for devotees. If it means that the harm caused by these will cease for devotees, what does it imply? It means that even the harms caused by them will turn into benefits. This is because, according to the Satkaryavada (the theory of pre-existence of effect in cause) accepted by Saivism, existing things have no destruction.

Therefore, the harms caused by these planets and days will transform into benefits. For the planets and days themselves, harm will also cease.

Moreover, unlike for others, they will bring only good benefits to devotees; this is its meaning. This also contains the subtlety of the upcoming historical events. “Aasu Arudhal” (removal of blemish) refers to the incident in Madurai when the Jains set fire to the monastery where Thirugnanasambandhar resided, but it did not affect him at all.

Therefore, the phrase “Aasu Arudhal” implicitly contains this historical outcome. Next comes “Nallana Agum” (will become good). In Madurai, the Jains are defeated in the three debates – Suravadam (fever debate), Analvadam (fire debate), and Punalvadam (water debate) – and Saivism triumphs.

Thus, “Nallana Adhal” (becoming good) encompasses this historical reference. With the removal of Jainism, the Pandya king and the people of the Pandya country embraced the sacred path of Saivism and applied holy ash.

Therefore, Saivism is about to gain three great devotees: the Pandya queen, the minister, and the king. This verse implicitly conveys all these historical events. This verse states that the Lord plays an excellent veena. This phrase refers to the Lord creating the world by producing sound through the veena.

Therefore, the Lord playing the veena signifies creation. The fourth Thirumurai, 112th pathigam, seventh verse, composed by ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman, states: “When the vast oceans overflow and the universe perishes, when Brahma too departs and his body is submerged, and the dark-colored Vishnu’s body is also gone, our Lord, holding the skull, plays an excellent veena, standing on the ocean.” Therefore, the meaning here is that the Lord plays the sound of the veena to bring about the re-creation of the world after dissolution. It is a Saiva tradition to state that during dissolution, the Lord plays the veena, signifying the first manifestation of Pure Maya as sound, to bring forth the world that had merged within Him.

Therefore, just as “veena thadavi” (playing the veena) signifies re-creation after dissolution, here it also implies the dissolution of opposing religions, specifically the removal of Jain impurities, and the re-creation of Saivism. It is mentioned here that all these events occur due to the Lord’s grace. This is based on the state of losing one’s ego. Sekkizhar Peruman has explained this very idea to us by saying, “If we worship the feet of our Lord, no harm will befall us.”

Therefore, the days and planets are good for the Thirutthondar, the devotees of Shiva, and thus they are also good for themselves; this is the implicit meaning.

Now, the second verse: “Enpodu kombodu Aamai ivai marbu ilanga Erudheri ezai udane Ponpodi maththa malai punal soodi vandhen ullamE pugundha adhanal Onpodu ondrodu ezhupathinetodu aarudam udanaya nalgal avaidham Anpodu nalla nalla avai nalla nalla Adiyar avarkku migavE.” This is the second verse. The bones, tusks of a boar, and tortoise shells adorn the Lord’s chest. He wears a garland of golden Cassia flowers and the Ganga on His head. He comes mounted on a bull with Uma, and because He entered my heart, Because the Lord, adorned with bones, boar tusks, and tortoise shells on His chest, wearing a garland of golden Cassia flowers and the Ganga on His head, came riding on a bull with Uma Devi and entered my heart, the ninth, tenth, sixteenth, eighteenth, and sixth days, and all other days counted along with them, will all do only good things with great love for the devotees. This is the meaning of this verse. In this verse, Thirugnanasambandhar uses the numbers nine, one, seven, eighteen, and six to denote days.

Astrology texts generally specify which days, or rather, constellations, should be avoided for travel. There is an astrology text called “Jyotisha Graha Chintamani” which contains a verse under the heading “Kooda Naal” (inauspicious days): “Aathirai Parani Karthikai Ayilyam Muppooram Kettai Theethuru Visakam Sothi Chittirai Magam Eeraarum Maathanam Kondaar Thaaraar Vazhinadai Pattaar Meelaar Paaythanil Patuththaar Theraar.” Sivakavimani Ayya has cited this verse from “Jyotisha Graha Chintamani” under the heading “Kooda Naal” in his commentary here.

Therefore, in this verse, the numbers nine, one, seven, eighteen, and six appear. These are numerical references to the inauspicious days or constellations for travel. Bharani, Karthigai, Thiruvaathirai, Ayilyam, Magam, Pooram, Chithirai, Swathi, Visakam, Kettai, Pooradam, Poorattathi are considered inauspicious constellations for travel. The verse mentions nine, one, and so on. Generally, counting starts from Ashwini, but there is also a tradition of starting from Krithikai. If we count Krithikai as one, then nine refers to the Pooram constellation, one to Krithikai, seven to Ayilyam, and eighteen to Pooradam.

Therefore, these four constellations correspond to nine, one, seven, and eighteen. The number six then refers to the days that accompany it, meaning the remaining constellations not previously mentioned, such as Magam, Kettai, Bharani, Swathi, Visakam, Aathirai, and Chithirai. This signifies the twelve inauspicious days we have already discussed. There is another way to denote these constellations. According to Kayappakkam Sadasiva Chettiyar’s commentary, nine refers to the Ayilya constellation, ten to Magam, sixteen to Visakam, eighteen to Kettai, and six to Thiruvaathirai. “Udanaya Naalkal” (accompanying days) refers to the other seven days, totaling these twelve constellations.

There are various ways of counting them. However, Thirugnanasambandhar’s divine word states that all such days will bring only good to devotees.

Now, the third verse: “Uruvazhar Pavalameni oli neeru anindhu umaiyodum vellai vidaimel Murugalar kondrai thingal mudimel anindhu en ullamE pugundha adhanal Thirumagal Kalaiyathurthi Sayamathu bhoomi thisai deivamana palavum Arunedhi nalla nalla avai nalla nalla Adiyar avarkku migavE.” In Shiva’s radiant coral-like red body, which shines with beauty, He wears radiant holy ash. The Lord, adorning His head with a fragrant konrai garland and the crescent moon, and riding on a white bull with Uma Devi, entered my heart. Because of that, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Durga, Bhoomadevi, and all the various directional deities will do only good things for the devotees. In this, Thirugnanasambandhar declares that Lakshmi, Saraswati, Durga, and the directional deities like Indra, Agni, Yama, Niruthi, Varuna, Vayu, Kubera, and Isana, along with other deities, will only bring good things to the devotees of Shiva.

Now, the fourth verse: “Mathinuthal mangaiyodu vadapal irundhu maraiyodhum engal Paramana Nadhiyodu kondrai malai mudimel anindhu en ullamE pugundha adhanal Kodhiyuru Kaalan Angi Namanodu thoodhar kodu noigal ana palavum Athigunam nalla nalla avai nalla nalla Adiyar avarkku migavE.” Our Shiva, who, with Uma Devi, whose forehead resembles the crescent moon, resides in the north and recites the Vedas, wore the Ganga and a konrai garland on His head and entered my heart. Because of that, the wrathful Kala, the fire god Agni, Yama, Yama’s messengers, and all terrible diseases will only bring good things to the devotees. Kalan mentioned in this verse is one of Yama’s ministers, and the messengers are Yama’s attendants.

Therefore, it is stated here that Yama, Yama’s messengers, and others will only do good to devotees.

Now, the fifth verse: “Nanjani kandhan endhai madavalthanodu vidaierum nangal Paraman thunju irul vanni kondrai mudimel anindhu en ullamE pugundha adhanal Venjina avunarodum urum idiyum minnum migaiyana pooththam avaiyum Anjidum nalla nalla avai nalla nalla Adiyaravarkku migavum.” Our Lord, whose throat is adorned with poison, our father, who rides a bull with Uma, wore the dark Vanni and Konrai flowers on His head and entered my heart. Because of that, the fierce Asuras, terrifying thunder and lightning, and all other beings will fear devotees and will only bring good things to them. Our Lord, whose throat is adorned with poison, our father, who rides a bull with Uma, wore the dark Vanni and Konrai flowers on His head and entered my heart. Because of that, the fierce Asuras, terrifying thunder and lightning, and all other beings will fear devotees and will only bring good things to them.

Now, the sixth verse: “Vaazhvari athalathada varigovanaththar madavaazhthanodum udanai Naal malar vanni kondrai nadhisoodi vandhu en ullamE pugundha adhanal Kolari uzhuvaiyodu kolai yanai kelil kodunagamodu karadi aal.” Our Lord, who wears a tiger skin as a garment, along with Uma Devi, adorned His head with fresh Vanni flowers, a Konrai garland, and the Ganga, and entered my heart. Because of that, fierce lions, tigers, killer elephants, boars, poisonous snakes, bears, and human-like monkeys will all do only good things for devotees. This is the divine word of Thirugnanasambandhar.

Now, the next verse, the seventh verse: “Seppu izha mulai nan mangai oru bhagamaga vidaieru selvan adaivar Oppizha mathiyum appu mudimel anindhu en ullamE pugundha adhanal.” Our Lord, who sits on the bull with the youthful Uma Devi, whose breasts are like shining metal, and who is approached by those who worship Him, wore the peerless moon and water on His head and entered my heart. Because of that, Because the Lord, the wealthy one who rides the bull with the excellent, youthful Uma Devi, whose breasts are like shining metal, and who is adorned with the incomparable moon and the Ganga on His head, entered my heart, heat, cold, vaatham, excessive pitham, and other evil karmas will not afflict devotees; instead, they will bring only good to them. This is the meaning of this verse.

Now, the eighth verse: “Velpada vizhiseythanru vidaimel irundhu madavaalthanodum udanai Vaazhmathi vanni kondrai malar soodi vandhu en ullamE pugundha adhanal.” Because the Lord, who once opened His eye to burn Manmatha to ashes, came riding on His bull with Uma Devi, wearing the beautiful moon, Vanni, and Konrai flowers on His head, and entered my heart, the troubles caused by Ravana, the king of Lanka surrounded by seven seas, and the deep seas themselves, and other difficulties, will not afflict devotees. Instead, they will bring only good things to the devotees.

Now, the ninth verse: “Palapalavedam agum paranari bhagan pasu yerum engal Paramana.” Our supreme Lord, who assumes various forms, whose left half is a woman, and who rides a bull, adorned His head with the Ganga and Eruku flowers and entered my heart. Because of that, Brahma, who sits on the lotus, Vishnu, the Vedas, other deities, the revolving time, the turbulent seas, and Mount Meru will all bring only good to the devotees.

Now, the tenth verse: “Koththalar kuzhali yodu visaiyarkku nalgukunamaya vedavikirthan Maththamum mathiyum nagam mudimel anindhu en ullamE pugundha adhanal Pudhdharodu amanaivadaththil azhivikkum annal thiruneeru semmai thidame Aththagu nalla nalla avai nalla nalla adiyaravarkku migavE.” The Lord, who has Uma Devi with fragrant, clustered hair, and who appeared as a hunter to grant grace to Arjuna, adorned His head with the Datura flower, the moon, and a snake, and entered my heart. Because of that, the holy ash of the great Lord will surely defeat Buddhists and Jains in debates, causing their destruction. This is the truth, this is certain. By that virtue, the harm coming from other religions will not affect devotees; they will only experience good. This verse indicates Pillaiyar’s reason for going to the Pandya country and that holy ash will be his support there. The Thiruneetru pathigam, which begins with “Manthiramavathu Neeru,” which Thirugnanasambandhar is about to sing in Madurai, first defeats the Jains in debate.

Later, it properly led to their execution by impalement and destruction.

Therefore, this tenth verse implicitly refers to that.

Now, the eleventh verse, the Thirukadaikaappu: “Thenamar pozhilkol alai vilai sennal thunni valar sempon engum nizhala.” In Brahmapuram, the sacred town of Sirkazhi, where golden wealth abounds, and honeyed groves, sugarcane, and red paddy grow densely, was first worshipped by Brahma. The wise and learned Thirugnanasambandhan, born in this Brahmapuram, composed this pathigam, this garland of words, ensuring that the planets and days would not trouble devotees. Those devotees who recite this pathigam, The devotees who recite this pathigam, this garland of words that grants benefits, which Thirugnanasambandhar proclaimed so that the planets and days would not cause harm to devotees, will rule in the heavens. This is my command, thus Thirugnanasambandhar blesses this Thirukkadaikaappu (concluding verse) as his own decree. According to the gracious command of Thirugnanasambandhar, who possesses all knowledge, both worldly and transcendental, everything mentioned in this pathigam will bring good to devotees.

For devotees who possess Shiva-Karanas and realize the immaculate Turiyatita state even in a waking state, all these will bring good.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandhar, as one of those devotees, blesses this remarkable pathigam, stating that these things will only bring good to him. There is another historical event associated with this pathigam and our nation, India. It is a contemporary history. In August 1947, according to the English calendar, legal arrangements were underway to grant India independence.

At that time, Governor-General Mountbatten called Jawaharlal Nehru and asked how India would symbolically receive its independence. Nehru was confused about what symbol to use to receive independence. Nehru sought advice from the elder statesman C. Rajagopalachari. Rajarishi Chakravarti Rajagopalachari explained how the tradition of assuming governmental responsibility and how a new king takes office was observed in India, especially in Tamil Nadu. The Rajaguru would present the Sceptre to the newly appointed king, thereby signifying the transfer of power.

Therefore, we should similarly receive a Sceptre from the British through one of our gurus, which would symbolize the transfer of power from the British to us, he advised. Nehru agreed. Time was short. Rajagopalachari contacted the Thiruvavaduthurai Adheenam, one of the ancient Saiva Adheenams in Tamil Nadu, belonging to the Thirukailaya Paramparai Sri Meykanda Devanayanar Santhanam, and conveyed this news. This message was submitted to the then Gurumaha Sannidhanam.

At that time, Sri-la-Sri Ambalavana Desika Paramacharyar Swamigal was ruling as the twentieth Gurumaha Sannidhanam of Thiruvavaduthurai Adheenam. Rajaji requested them to perform the auspicious ceremonies for the transfer of power in India.

At that moment, the Gurumaha Sannidhanam was suffering from a severe fever but agreed to perform the event. The Adheenam instructed Chennai UMID Pangaru Chettiar Jewellery, which was famous at the time, to make a silver Sceptre plated with gold, engraved with Saiva symbols. The Sceptre was prepared. The Gurumaha Sannidhanam summoned Sri Math Kumaraswami Thambiran, who was then the junior pontiff (Thambiran Swamigal) of the Adheenam, handed him the Sceptre, and commanded him, along with the Oduvars and the renowned Nadaswaram artist Thiruvavaduthurai Rajarathinam Pillai, to proceed to Delhi.

At that time, the Oduvamurthigal submitted a request to Sri-la-Sri Gurumaha Sannidhanam of Thiruvavaduthurai, asking which pathigam should be recited entirely when receiving the Sceptre during the transfer of power. In response, the Thiruvavaduthurai Gurumaha Sannidhanam commanded that the Kolaru pathigam, beginning with “Veyuru Thozhi Pangan,” should be recited in its entirety. He commanded that the entire pathigam beginning with “Veyuru Thozhi Pangan,” known as Kolaru pathigam, should be recited. Thirugnanasambandhar’s divine word states that if this pathigam is recited, the planets in the sky will always bring good to us.

Therefore, he ordered that this pathigam be recited. In a private airplane arranged by the wise C. Rajagopalachari, the Thiruvavaduthurai Thambiran Swamigal, the Oduvamurthigal, and Thiruvavaduthurai Rajarathinam Pillai all traveled to Delhi. On August 15, 1947, at midnight, as India awaited the golden moment of liberation from slavery, the Thiruvavaduthurai junior pontiff, Thambiran Swamigal, received the Sceptre from Mountbatten, which had been blessed and sent by the Thiruvavaduthurai Adheenam Gurumaha Sannidhanam. The junior pontiff of Thiruvavaduthurai Adheenam, Thambiran Swamigal, received the scepter from Mountbatten. The Oduvamurthigal purified the scepter with holy water and then fully recited the Kolaru Thevaram pathigam, which begins with “Veyuru Thozhi Pangan Vidamunda Kandhan.” As he finished reciting the last line of the eleventh verse, “Adiyaragal vaanila arasaazhvar aanai namathe” (Our devotees will rule the heavens, this is our command), Sri Thambiran Swamigal handed the scepter to Nehru.

This event took place with the accompanying music of the Nadaswara Chakravarti Thiruvavaduthurai Rajarathinam Pillai. A black and white photograph of this event still exists in the Thiruvavaduthurai Adheenam monastery. The photograph is dated August 15, 1947, and shows Nehru holding the scepter, along with Sri-la-Sri Thambiran Swamigal of Thiruvavaduthurai Adheenam.

Therefore, it is a very important point that this pathigam, composed by Thirugnanasambandhar, was recited when India attained political independence.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandhar composed this pathigam both as a reply to ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman and as a means of seeking the grace of the Lord. From Thirumaraikadu, also known as Vedharanyam, Pillaiyar’s journey to the Pandya country is about to begin.

Let us keep pondering.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 140 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam by Deivasekkizhar Peruman, Volume 687, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandhar composed the Kolaru pathigam. After listening to this pathigam, ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman gave his consent. He agreed and consented to Thirugnanasambandhar going to the Pandya country. Before hearing the Kolaru pathigam, ThiruNavukkarasu Swamigal had refused consent for Pillaiyar to go to the Pandya country, but after hearing the pathigam, he agreed to Thirugnanasambandhar’s visit to the Pandya country.

In this Kolaru pathigam, Thirugnanasambandhar concluded with a command in the Thirukkadaikaappu, did he not? That command is indeed the command of Shiva. Because Thirugnanasambandhar declared, “The holy ash of the Lord will destroy Buddhists and Jains in debate,” and “The garland of words I utter ensures that no harm from planets or days will come to devotees,” ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman became convinced that no harm would befall Thirugnanasambandhar in the Pandya country and that the Jains would be eradicated.

Therefore, ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman now consented. Was ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman previously hesitant because he did not wish for the removal of evil from the Pandya country, or was he afraid of the Jains? Neither was the case. He was not without conviction in divine grace.

But why did he not consent to Pillaiyar’s departure before? It was purely out of paternal love for the Lord. It was that fatherly affection for Thirugnanasambandhar that caused ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman to prevent Thirugnanasambandhar from going to the Pandya country. Now that those doubts have been dispelled after hearing the Kolaru pathigam, he gives his consent. He is pleased because until now, ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman and Thirugnanasambandhar had journeyed together to sacred sites from Thirupukalur.

First, ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman would go. Subsequently, Thirugnanasambandhar would reach that place. Upon reaching the place, both great individuals would visit the temple together and sing pathigams. This was the established tradition. ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman also thought that this tradition would continue, and he intended to accompany Thirugnanasambandhar to the Pandya country.

However, Thirugnanasambandhar, looking at Appar Peruman, said, “Appare, please stay in this Chola country,” and with folded hands, he bowed, thus preventing ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman from coming to the Pandya country. There is a saying, “There is no mantra greater than a father’s word.” Thirugnanasambandhar regarded Appar Peruman as his spiritual father.

Thus, even though ThiruNavukkarasu Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman tells Thirunavukkarasar Peruman, who was filled with paternal affection, that he should stay in the Chola country, and reverently makes this request, avoiding the act of coming along. Hearing this, Thirunavukkarasar Peruman, understanding that the words of the child were indeed divine, bows in farewell to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Thirunavukkarasar Peruman, with a rare generosity of heart, agrees to this.

First, he agreed to the child going to the Pandya country.

Now, he also agrees to their separation and to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman traveling alone. Sekkizhar Peruman then proceeds to compose the next verse. This is the six hundred and eighteenth verse: “To foster the Vedas and enlighten Saivism, the jewel of Vedavanam again entered, bowed at its feet, rose, sang praises, and having received grace and permission, returned. Having respectfully taken leave of Vakeesar of great penance, who remained unswerving, and having given him permission, the Lord of Kazhi, with enduring love, intimately departed and reached the adorned palanquin.” The child, Pillaiyar, incarnated to foster the Vedas and enlighten Saivism. He incarnated solely to accomplish these two things. Both of these are now about to take place in the Pandya country.

Therefore, at this moment, as he begins his journey to the Pandya country, the child’s incarnate purpose, which is to uphold the Vedic path. “...to make the path flourish,” as stated at the beginning of Pillaiyar’s Purana, Sekkizhar Peruman mentions it again in this verse, saying, “to foster the Vedas and enlighten Saivism.” This is because the central event of Pillaiyar’s Purana and the reason for Pillaiyar’s incarnation begins from here, and so Sekkizhar Peruman composes it this way. Fostering the Vedas means performing Vedic sacrifices. Enlightening Saivism means cherishing the explanation of spiritual practices. Is it not the Lord of Thirumaraikkadu, the Lord of Vedavanam in Vedharanyam, who is capable of fostering the Vedas and bringing enlightenment to Saivism? He is the one who opened the doors that the Vedas had closed and guarded.

Did not the Lord residing in Vedharanyam, by His grace, foster and illuminate both the Vedas and Saivism, exhibiting His character and wisdom?

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman goes before that Lord, sees Him again, praises Him, sings pathigams, and extols His glories.

At this time, the pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is not available to us. There, in Vedharanyam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman receives divine permission from the Lord. Generally, it is customary to receive divine permission from the deity before leaving any temple site.

Accordingly, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman now receives divine permission from the Lord of Vedharanyam. Thirunavukkarasar Peruman, who possessed great penance, worshipped him in such a way that he could not be refused, granted grace to him, and then. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman gives him leave and departs, conversing affectionately with great love. Thirunavukkarasar Peruman, who shines as a great ascetic sage, a sage of wisdom, and a supreme sage, embodying both past and present penance. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously permits that Lord to remain there without accompanying him, and gives him leave. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman asked Thirunavukkarasar Peruman, who had continuously accompanied him from Thirupukalur and was still poised to follow, to stay in the Chola country, and made him agree to his departure, which was very difficult for Thirunavukkarasar Peruman to bear.

Therefore, Thirunavukkarasar Peruman, who was staying in the Chola country, departs from the Chola country. Pillaiyar bids farewell to Thirunavukkarasar Peruman. We pondered upon the news of Thirunavukkarasar Peruman taking leave of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, as the Lord graciously revealed it in Thirunavukkarasar Peruman’s Purana.

Here, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bids farewell to Thirunavukkarasar Peruman. Although these two great spiritual masters are now separating, the love between them remains undiminished. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who journeys to the Pandya country, will complete all the events there and then, when he resides in Thirukkadavur, having worshipped there, he will hear that the great sage Vakeesa Muni is residing in his city. The story of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s journey to Thirupunduruthi to meet him is yet to unfold.

Therefore, he now bids farewell to Thirunavukkarasar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman bids farewell and departs from there. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse. Thirunavukkarasar was also there.

Now, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman ascends the palanquin adorned with bright pearls, and with a heart yearning for the unique name upon the head of the One who raised the bull, he recites the five sacred letters, and worships the divine form glowing with sacred ash in his mind. The six hundred and nineteenth verse states: “The ocean of devotion, filled with love that melts the heart, surged with the roar of the great ascetics.” Thirunavukkarasar Peruman remains there in the Chola country.

Now, Pillaiyar departs from Vedharanyam, seated on the pearl palanquin. Until now, all those who had been listening to the Purana. The focus was on both Thirunavukkarasar Peruman and Pillaiyar. From now on, Thirunavukkarasar Peruman will remain in the Chola country, and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman will begin his journey to the Pandya country.

Therefore, from now on, the full attention of those listening to the Purana should be directed towards Pillaiyar.

Thus, Sekkizhar Peruman, by stating that Thirunavukkarasar Peruman was there, gracefully illustrates the beauty of the Purana by indicating that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman now proceeds in this direction. Pillaiyar, with a heart cherishing the sacred feet of Lord Shiva on his head, recites the unique name of the Lord, the five sacred letters, and worships the divine form adorned with sacred ash. He contemplates and bows.

Therefore, when Pillaiyar ascended the palanquin, he placed the Lord’s feet upon his head. In his mind, he recites the unique name, the five sacred letters. Reciting means reciting with a focused mind, meditating intently. The five sacred letters can be recited in three ways: mentally (manatham), softly (mantham), and audibly (urai). What Thirugnanasambandha Peruman recited now falls under the mental recitation category. He mentally recited the five sacred letters, and with the same mindset, he audibly praised them.

At the same time, he envisioned and worshipped the Lord’s divine form adorned with sacred ash, as he ascended the pearl palanquin. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. All the devotees chant the name of Hara Hara, roaring like an ocean. The name of Hara Hara echoed there.

Let us go on contemplating.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 141 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part Six Hundred Eighty-Eight, authored by Theivasekkizhar Peruman, Vambarav Varivandu Saroppam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Purana. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman undertakes a pilgrimage from Thirumaraikkadu towards the Pandya country. Devotees surge everywhere, praising Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Auspicious instruments resound loudly in all four directions. The sound of the Vedas spreads everywhere.

Various auspicious instruments like padakkam, beri, tharai, kalam, and thalam are played. A shower of flowers falls everywhere. Devotees and people carrying full pots, lamps, and incense welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman wherever he goes. He journeys towards Madurai, also known as Thiru Alavai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman journeys on.

However, he worships all the temples along the way. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing how Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, having departed from Vedharanyam, worships the temples on the way to Madurai and composes pathigams. This is the six hundred and twenty-second verse: “The Lord of Thonipuram, surrounded by devotees, reached Thiruvagathiyanpalli, on the seashore surrounded by vast waves, worshipped the sacred feet of the Lord of the Devas, and sang a great Tamil Vedic song, praising the Lord.

“Then, he worshipped the Lord of Thirukkodikkuzhagar, surrounded by clouds of sand dunes, and joined the devotees.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman journeys to Thiruvagathiyanpalli, a temple located on the seashore. This temple is among those on the route from Vedharanyam to Madurai. Among them, the first temple is Thiruvagathiyanpalli. This temple is located on the seashore, where the sea is calm and clear, without churning or agitation. It is a land rich in saltpans, an area of the coast not heavily populated. This region is a forest area, the abode of Durga, with sand dunes accumulated by sea breezes, rising high like mountains.

“These are truly magnificent coastal landscapes. Even today, these areas with sand mountains and rain are worth seeing. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who incarnated in Sirkazhi, arrives at Thiruvagathiyanpalli, located in this area. He reaches Thiruvagathiyanpalli, the one hundred and twenty-sixth temple on the south bank of the Kaveri. This is the place where Agastya performed penance to witness the Lord’s marriage.

“Hence, it is known as Agathiyanpalli. An idol of Agastya Peruman is installed and worshipped in the temple. The Lord’s name is Agasteeswarar, and the Goddesses’ names are Bagampiriyal and Mangai Nayaki. Agastya Theertham, Agni Theertham, the ocean Theertham, Agni Pushkarani, and Yama Theertham are the sacred waters.

“The Lord faces east, and the Goddess faces west. This temple is located near Nagapattinam, south of Vedharanyam, and close to Kodiyakkarai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who journeyed here, composed a pathigam. It is the seventy-sixth pathigam of the second Thirumurai. The pathigam is composed in Kantharappann. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam.
