Instead of going as fire, let the form of the fire change into a fever and slowly reach the Pandya king. Even that fever, even that affliction, quickly If it attacks, harm will occur.

“Therefore, Pillaiyar commands that it should go slowly so that such harm does not happen. We saw that in “agave,” “aga” is a word of blessing. In the second verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman addresses Lord Shiva, Alavay Sokkanathar, as “Siththane.” Here, it is hinted that the Lord performed divine sports as an all-powerful Siddhar in the Thiru Alavay temple in Madurai. Because of his nature as a Siddhar, he has the power to transform the fire set by the Samanars into a fever and inflict it upon the Pandya king. It is also hinted that he is capable of all other things. “Anjal” refers to fear.

“This fear arose for the sake of the devotees, out of concern that some harm might befall them. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman makes a plea to remove that fear. In the third verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises Alavay Sokkanathar as “Dhakkan velvi thagarthu arul Alavai sokkane” (Alavay Sokkanathar who destroyed Daksha’s sacrifice and showered grace). Just as Alavay Sokkanathar destroyed Daksha’s sacrifice and showed grace, he is capable of destroying the deceit and cruelty of the Samanars—this is the historical reference here. In the fourth verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises Alavay Sokkanathar Peruman as “Attamurthiyane” (Lord with eight forms), meaning that the Lord has eight forms, and fire is one of them. He is the one who has fire as one of his eight forms and is going to protect from the upcoming fire ordeal.

“Thus, the entire pathigam Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed and sang.

“Thus, as Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praised Lord Shiva, who dwells as medicine in Thiru Alavay, and composed a pathigam, by the grace of Alavay Lord, that intense fire, the heat of the fire, reached the Pandya king as a fever. That fire, known as fever, reached the Pandya king. At that very moment, we will continue to contemplate.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 158 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
The Periya Puranam, part seven hundred and five, from the Vambara Varivandu chapter, composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, the Purana of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. We saw that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed a pathigam, praying to Alavay Sokkanathar Peruman. That pathigam was not motivated by evil thoughts such as enmity or hatred, but with the sole purpose that the king and the country should be reformed. In it, he praised Lord Shiva, who resides in Alavay as medicine. If a disease is to be cured, medicine must be administered internally.

Therefore, in this pathigam, he has enshrined Lord Shiva, who acts as the medicine of Thiru Alavay. This is indeed Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s grace. Is the king’s illness the Lord’s divine grace? Otherwise, to cause the ripening of the accumulated karma, to provide enjoyment, to stop the deluding power, to protect and bestow grace, and all other actions cannot be praised without grace, says the eighteenth verse of Sivaprakasam. Is it grace to cause someone to fall ill?

Here, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman blesses that the fire should slowly go and turn into a fever for the Pandya king. Does he make someone ill? What does medical science say? It says that the diseases that come into our body arise from the body’s natural tendency to remove the accumulated harm within us.

Therefore, it is a manifestation of the Lord’s grace. For living beings, Why do diseases come? Diseases come as a result of the sins committed by those living beings.

Thus, the Lord bestows disease and thereby resolves the sins already committed by those living beings.

Therefore, even disease is the Lord’s divine grace. The historical account of Thirunavukkarasu Peruman being afflicted by a severe stomach ailment and subsequently graced comes to our mind here. As soon as Pillaiyar made this divine pronouncement, the disease reached the Pandya king there. Pillaiyar made the appeal, and the divine grace within that divine pronouncement brought this about. If one asks if the fire went as Pillaiyar’s divine pronouncement commanded, yes, Pillaiyar’s divine pronouncement, filled with Shiva’s power, caused this to happen in many ways. That fire, which emerged and spread outwardly in various forms, retained its heat.

That fire, which remained subtle, reached the Pandya king with the same nature. That fever afflicted the Pandya king’s body. This happened at the very moment Pillaiyar commanded in his divine speech. The Samanars had set fire to the monastery where Gnana Pillaiyar, the son of Lord Shiva with the red sacred body, resided. That night is now fading. The sun rises over the eastern sea.

As morning arrives, the evil deed committed by those wicked Samanars the previous night is announced to Pandimadevi and Kulachirai Nayanar. Upon hearing the news, both the Queen and Kulachirai Nayanar are distraught. They think, “We invited Pillaiyar to this country where these evil people live. Is that why this offense befell Pillaiyar?

“Therefore, the atonement for this offense must be for us to take our own lives.” Both are confused. Those who came say that the Samanars set fire to Pillaiyar’s monastery, but it has been extinguished. Upon hearing the first part of this news, that the Samanars set fire to Pillaiyar’s monastery, Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti felt in her sacred heart, “We caused this; therefore, taking our own lives is the atonement for this.” Because the Queen’s love is of the highest degree, where milk spontaneously flows upon hearing Pillaiyar’s sacred words.

“Therefore, upon hearing that evil deed, upon hearing that evil news, the Queen became afraid and trembled for her life.

“Thus, she was confused, thinking it better to take her own life. This is the highest love. When one hears that something bad has happened to one’s beloved, one’s life is at risk; that is the nature of the highest love.

“Thus, upon hearing the first half of the news, Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumattiyar became distraught. They immediately tell her the next part of the news: that the fire set by the Samanars has been removed, and no harm has come to Pillaiyar’s monastery or anyone else. Upon hearing this news, Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumattiyar and Kulachirai Nayanar recover from their agitation and become clear again.

“Thus, the same news, in two successive parts, is conveyed. Between the first and second parts of the news, the Queen became distraught.

“Then, upon hearing the second part, her agitation subsided, and she became somewhat clear, though still filled with increasing fear and trembling, they both grieved. While they were contemplating how the outcome of this evil committed by the Samanars would be, the next news arrives. The servants who are very close and guard the king very closely come and say that the king has a fever. To Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumattiyar and Kulachirai Nayanar, The Pandya Queen, the mistress, becomes agitated because her husband has a fever. She hurries to find a solution. This is a sin against Shiva, so Pandimadevi’s fear intensified due to doubt about how its resolution would be.

“The intensity of the fever burns the king, causing his body to tremble. Like a fire emitting heat, it quickly spreads both inside and outside the king’s body. Even those outside the palace where the king is located are affected by the fever. Due to this heat, the king’s body dries up and shrinks. The king’s body collapses. The consciousness, that sense of awareness, slowly leaves the king.

“That vital consciousness was set aside. Even those who stood close to the king could not bear the heat and stood far away from him. When diseases like smallpox or severe fever occur, they would lay the patients on tender banana plants.

“Similarly, here, if tender banana plants are brought, they burn and shrivel, indicating the immense heat emanating from the king’s body. Doctors well-versed in medical texts arrive. They perform the best medical procedures and treatments mentioned in the medical texts they have studied. Medical texts extensively describe types of diseases, methods to cure them, types of methods, and how diseases manifest. Medical science branches into many disciplines. As the Kural states, “Diagnose the disease, find its cause, discover the cure, and administer it effectively.” In this manner, experts in various arts implement the best treatments and medicines prescribed in those medical texts for this disease.

“They attempt to treat the king; they provide treatment. However, none of it proves effective. Instead, the fever continued to intensify for the king.

“Thus, the king has been afflicted with a very severe disease. The Samanars, upon hearing of the king’s condition, sigh and grieve. The Samanars suspect that this might be the result of their actions the previous night. Nevertheless, hiding their shame and humiliation, they approach the king. Upon hearing that the king had fallen ill, the queen was agitated, and the minister was afraid. They immediately arrive at the king’s side.

“These actions were born of their love. However, the Samanars, even though they heard the news earlier, arrive very slowly, at the very end. This highlights the deceitful nature of their hearts. They arrive, suspecting that the act they committed the previous night is manifesting in this way.

“Therefore, they suspected that what they did was an evil sin. The Samanars, however, did not believe that Pillaiyar was capable of causing such a consequence. Nevertheless, they suspected it because their act occurred the previous night, and at the same time, the king was afflicted with the fever.

“Thus, the Samanars suspect this due to the continuous occurrence and the related connection. The Samanars are adherents of a very confusing doctrine. They declare seven types of substances through the Anekantavada argument and do not provide a definitive conclusion regarding the nature of reality. The Samanars The Samanars, who are confused about their own principles, now come to the Pandya king and try to cure the disease. Medical texts state that those who attempt to cure a disease must understand the disease itself, its origin, and its cause.

“But here, the Samanars come and see that the king has a fever, yet they try to cure the disease without even realizing that its origin comes from their evil deed. The Samanars, with their Anekantavada, hold confusing principles; they try to cure the disease without knowing its origin and without even attempting to know it. The Samanars chant mantras in the name of their deity and perform what is called ‘mantra-treatment.’ They always carry a bunch of peacock feathers in their hands. When someone falls ill, they perform mantra-treatment with it. This is a tradition of Samanar gurus. They also carry a staff along with the peacock feathers.

“So, they took out the peacock feathers to rub on the Pandya king’s body, chanting their mantras with the staff and peacock feathers. At that very moment, it caught fire, scattering sparks and burning. Due to the intensity of the Pandya king’s fever, the peacock feathers also burned, and the staff caught fire and burned as well. The king’s fever was so severe. The Samanars, observing this, were extremely afraid. The Samanars sprinkle the water from the kundi they always carry on the Pandya king and repeatedly chant, “May Arihan protect you.” Arihan is the deity of the Samanar religion.

“As they sprinkled the water from the kundi, chanting the mantra, the water, like ghee poured on fire, greatly intensified the fever.

“Therefore, the Pandya king ordered them to leave immediately, saying, “None of you should be here; go at once.” At the same time, the king lost consciousness and fell into a state of oblivion. At that very moment, Pandimadevi addressed Kulachirai Nayanar, She says, “Is it not the evil committed by the Samanars the previous night against Pillaiyar, who was born in Sirkazhi and has graced us, that has ended in this manner?” Upon hearing this, the minister Kulachirai Nayanar humbly addresses the Queen, saying, “Certainly, it is the action of these Samanars, the offense committed against Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the beloved of the Lord, that has thus reached the king. If the Samanars try to cure this disease, it will only worsen.” Kulachirai Nayanar continues to contemplate.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 159 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
The Periya Puranam, part seven hundred and six, from the Vambara Varivandu chapter, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, the Purana of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Pandimadevi, Mangaiyarkkarasi Ammaiyar, addresses Kulachirai Nayanar, who had taken on the responsibility of minister, saying, “Is it not the evil committed by the Samanars at night against Pillaiyar, who was born in Sirkazhi and has graced us, that has ended in this manner?” The verse states that Pandimadevi, filled with fear, asks the minister who had taken on the burden, “Has the evil committed by the Samanars at night against him who came from Pugazhi and graced us, ended in this way?” Pandimadevi is filled with fear. She fears, contemplating her husband’s unconscious and speechless state. She fears, contemplating her husband’s life and consciousness being pushed to the side. She fears, seeing that the heat is not subsiding but intensifying, threatening his life.

She also fears, realizing that this situation is a consequence of an offense committed against a devotee of Shiva. She is anxious about what might happen next. The Queen, thus fearful, addresses Kulachirai Nayanar, who has taken on the burden of minister. Kulachirai Nayanar is the one who bears the burden of minister. The ministerial skill is to foresee the past, present, and future and to possess the ability and duty to avert all harm that may befall the government. Such a burden of ministerial responsibility has been taken on by Kulachirai Nayanar, and it is he who is capable of knowing what is needed and executing what is required here.

That duty is very great, very rare.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it as the ‘burden of minister.’ Appar Swamigal’s Thevaram, in the pathigam dedicated to Arur Araneri, states that ‘those who are loved will also bear burdens.’ Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, born in Pugazhi, came here out of compassion for the Pandya kingdom, having graced Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti and Kulachirai Nayanar. Such is the nature of She asks Kulachirai Nayanar if the offense committed by the Samanars against Pillaiyar is the cause of this. The next verse states, “The king’s minister, Kulachiraiyar, humbly replies, ‘The cruelty of these deceitful ones, the evil they committed against the beloved of the one who destroyed the three cities, has completely afflicted the king. If they (Samanars) try to cure it, it will only worsen.’” The minister answers the doubt posed by the queen. The evil committed by the Samanars has completely afflicted the king here. The same evil is now about to befall the Samanars as well.

If the Samanars try to cure this fever that has afflicted the king, it will not work; it will only grow worse, because a disease If the very substance that caused the disease is reintroduced into the body, it will intensify and worsen the disease, as stated in medical texts.

Similarly, if the Samanars, who are the root cause of this fever that has afflicted the king, come and attempt to cure it, it will only increase the disease, says the great minister.

Therefore, this is certainly a result of the offense committed by the Samanars against the devotees. Hence, the power to cure this disease resides only with the devotees of the Lord, the devotees of God.

Therefore, in the same way, the devotees of Shiva, who are the beloved of Lord Shiva, who previously destroyed the three cities, will go and eliminate the enemies.

Therefore, Pillaiyar Only one person can cure this fever and show compassion, says the great minister. After saying this, Mangaiyarkkarasi Perumatti and Kulachirai Nayanar stand before the king. They pay homage. Both sides bow before the king and say, “This fever has come because of the evil deed committed by the Samanars in Madurai against the benevolent one who came from Pugazhi. The grace of Pillaiyar is the solution to this.” (kayamum manamum masu kazhuvudal seyyar seyyum mayamum indha noyay valarpathe valar ven thingal meya veniyarpal gnanan pettravar virumbi nokkil theeya ippiniye andri piravi) These are the two verses Sekkizhar Peruman presents here.

Both sides stand humbly before the king.

Here, the two sides Sekkizhar Peruman refers to are the Queen and the minister. This term ‘both sides’ should be understood as referring to the Queen and the minister individually. The Queen’s ‘two sides’ refer to her duty to protect the Saiva faith and her duty to ward off the current evil.

Therefore, Pandimadevi is ‘two-sided.’ Similarly, Kulachirai Nayanar, who embodies both Saiva faith and ministerial authority, also represents these ‘two sides.’ Both of them stand before the king, humbly bowing. The king, however, is in a state of lost consciousness and awareness. Standing before him, Kulachirai Nayanar humbly explains to the king why this fever has come: it arose and intensified due to the harmful act committed by the Samanars upon seeing Pillaiyar, the benevolent one who came from Sirkazhi and arrived in Madurai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is a benevolent person. He came to Madurai on his own to bless the people of the Pandya kingdom. Even when the Samanars set fire, Pillaiyar did not deviate from righteousness or get angry.

He resolved to grace and correct the king and the people of the country. These Samanars committed an improper act against Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Out of tradition not to speak evil, Kulachirai Nayanar refers to it as an “improper act.” Therefore, Kulachirai Nayanar says that Pillaiyar’s grace is the solution. The Thirukkural states: “Diagnose the disease, find its cause, discover the cure, and administer it effectively.” In accordance with this, Kulachirai Nayanar describes this severe illness that has befallen the king. He states that it resulted from the evil and improper act committed against Pillaiyar.

Thus, Kulachirai Nayanar identifies the root cause of the disease. He states, Similarly, he states that the solution is Pillaiyar’s grace, following the principle of “identifying the means of cure.” What needs to be done, as mentioned in the Kural, “the effective action,” Kulachirai Nayanar will explain in the upcoming verses.

Therefore, in accordance with the Kural beginning with “Diagnose the disease,” Kulachirai Nayanar, who is excellent in ministerial wisdom, thus declares. These Samanars are those who accumulate dirt on their bodies by not bathing, fearing that tiny creatures on their bodies might die. Just as their bodies are dirty, their minds are also filled with impurity and deceit. Those Samanars, without revealing the truth that this resulted from their deceitful evil act, pretend to know nothing and try to cure the disease. Such deceitful Samanars, therefore, their actions will only worsen the disease. The solution to this is that if Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who attained knowledge from Lord Shiva with the crescent moon in his matted hair, looks upon him with grace, this severe illness will be cured, and also the cycle of rebirth will end, says Kulachirai Nayanar.

That moon, which was in a dying state, waning in its phases, was nurtured by the compassionate Lord.

The Lord has wisdom, and Ganesha possessed that wisdom from Him.

Therefore, Ganesha is capable of saving the king here, too. His grace alone will cure this burning disease for the Pandyan king.

So, the disease came from Ganesha’s cruel intention; it will be cured by Ganesha’s benevolent intention and also end rebirth, says Kulachirai Nayanar. (iru nokku ival un kan ullathu oru nokku noy nokku ontu annoy maruntu) is a verse from Thirukkural.

Similarly, this disease came from Ganesha’s cruel intention. The explanation here is that it will be cured by Ganesha’s benevolent, graceful intention. When Ganesha’s graceful intention falls upon someone, the impurities of the soul are removed, and the means to liberation are granted. Such is the power of Ganesha’s graceful intention. He is the ultimate Guru, so a mere glance from Him removes impurities and grants the means to liberation. When even incurable rebirth is cured, it goes without saying that this burning disease will be cured.

This is what Kulachirai Nayanar says.

Then, Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verses: “(Minavan seviyinodu mey unarvu alippor koora Gnanasambandar ennum nama mandiramum sella anapothu ayarvu thannai akanrida amana)”. He began to speak. The queen and the minister told the Pandyan king, as we saw in the previous part, that Thirugnanasambandar’s graceful glance alone would cure this disease.

At that time, didn’t the sacred name and mantra, Thirugnanasambandar, exist within their words? As soon as he heard that sacred name, the Pandyan’s weakness disappeared. When the sacred name Thirugnanasambandar reached the ears of the Pandyan king, who was in a state of unconsciousness and loss of speech, his weakness was removed. The king, having lost consciousness, was in a state of hidden thought and forgotten words.

Therefore, it was necessary to convey this message close to his ears.

Thus, Mangaiyarkarasi Perumatti and Kulachirai Nayanar conveyed it. This is also the method of a Guru initiating a mantra. Sekkizhar Peruman says, “(Nama mandiramum sella Gnanasambandar ennum nama mandiramum sella)”. According to the sacred words of Thevaram, “(Anchezuththin Namathan Kan)”, the sacred five-letter mantra, Panchatcharam, is the name of the Lord.

Here, Gnanasambandar is also a five-letter word. If you remove the silent letters from Gnanasambandar and count them, there are five letters.

Therefore, Gnanasambandar is also a five-letter word, and thus it is also a mantra.

Similarly, we saw there how the five-letter word Navukkarasu became the mantra that saved Appoothiyadigal Nayanar. Just as the Lord’s name is the sacred five-letter word, as Thirukkazhippadiyar says, “(Than cheyyum thanmaikalum akki yidum anbarkku aran)”, so too is the name of the devotees a sacred five-letter word. This means it protects those who remember it. The definition of the word mantra in Sanskrit is stated as “(Mananath trayate iti mantra)” (that which protects one who contemplates it). Its meaning here is to protect those who remember it.

Here, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman explains the nature of this name, Gnanasambandar, becoming a mantra. This is because the name Thirugnanasambandar is embedded within the messages spoken by the minister and the queen. When that word reached the king’s ears, it dispelled his weakness. From this point, the king begins to walk on the path of truth.

Therefore, through this, we can understand that the name Thirugnanasambandar becomes a mantra. It wasn’t just the message spoken by the two great individuals that entered his ears; this mantra also entered, protecting those who remember it. is the nature of a mantra, and it is at work here. Immediately, the weariness disappears. This is the benefit that came as soon as the power of the mantra began to operate. This mantra is the operation of Shiva’s power.

Therefore, it produced results merely by thought.

After his weariness was dispelled, the king speaks a message to the shameless Jains who were present there. Let us go on contemplating.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 160 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periyapuranam, Part 707, authored by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, “Vambara Varivandu Cherukkum Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam.” The next verse describes the Pandyan king addressing the Jains present there. The verse is: (Mannavan avarai nokki matra ivar seykaiyellam innavaru eydhu noykke ethuvayinana enru enni manniya Saiva neethi mamaraich chiruvar vanthal annavar arulal innoy akalume ariven enran.) The king looks at the Jains and, thinking in his mind that their actions were the cause of this disease, says to them, “If the boy, the great Vedic scholar of established Saiva tradition, comes here and this disease is cured by his grace, then I will be enlightened.” Thus says the king. The phrase “(Maniya Saiva Neethi Mamaraich Chiruvar)” in this verse is from the king’s speech. Jainism, which emerged in the middle, has now perished. Saivism, however, is a religion that has existed beyond measure, so ancient that it cannot be said when it originated.

Therefore, the phrase “(Maniya Saiva Neethi)” comes from the king’s own words.

Moreover, here he refers to Thirugnanasambandar in the plural as “(Mamaraich Chiruvar)” (children of the great Vedas). Previously, when he was swayed by the Jains, he referred to Ganesha in the singular as “(Mamaraich Maithan)” (son of the great Vedas).

But now, he refers to Thirugnanasambandar in the plural as “(Mamaraich Chiruvar)”. He refers to him in the plural as “(Mamaraich Chiruvar)”. Previously, the king’s state was as if his ego was non-dual with the Jains. The king, being under the influence of the Jains, was angered when he heard Ganesha’s name from their mouths. Being swayed by the Jains, Ganesha’s name, when uttered by them, angered the king and made him refer to him in the singular as “son”.

Here, the very name-mantra, Gnanasambandar, reaching the king’s ears through the words of Mangaiyarkarasi Perumatti and Kulachirai Nayanar, brought about true understanding and made him refer to Thirugnanasambandar as “(Maa Maraich Chiruvar)” in the plural.

Moreover, that very sacred name removed the mental delusion of the king, who had been enslaved by the words of the Jains, and gave him the wisdom to discern between good and evil.

Therefore, he tells the queen and Kulachirai Nayanar that if Thirugnanasambandar comes here and this disease is cured by his grace, he will attain clarity. He further states this in the next verse. The king’s mental delusion, which was subservient to all the words of the Jains, was dispelled, and he gained the wisdom to discern between good and evil.

Therefore, he tells the queen and Kulachirai Nayanar that if Thirugnanasambandar comes here and cures this disease by his grace, he will attain clarity. He further says, as the next verse states, (enru mun kuri pinnim yan utra pinaiyai theerthu venravar pakkam serven virakundel azhaiyum enna anravar uvakai pongi arwathal anaiyai nokki chenra neer vellam polum kathal vellathil selvar) which is the 723rd verse. The king, having spoken thus, further continues, addressing the minister and the queen, saying, “I will join the side of whoever cures this disease that has come upon me and triumphs.

“So, if there is a way to cure my disease, call him, call Thirugnanasambandar,” he tells the queen and the minister. The king first said, “If he comes and cures my disease by his grace, I will attain clarity,” in the first verse. That was a response to what the queen and the minister had said earlier.

“Here, the king says, “Call Thirugnanasambandar,” which is an order and command to Pandiyadevi and Kulachirai Nayanar. It is the duty of ministers to act without the king’s command to find a solution when the king is in a state of unconsciousness.

“Therefore, Kulachirai Nayanar could have brought Thirugnanasambandar then itself. However, Even though the king was in a state of diminished consciousness, he was previously strongly aligned with the Jains.

“Therefore, the king was in a state of both seeing and hearing with skepticism. So, the minister thought it was not right to bring Ganesha by himself at that time, and he spoke to the king face-to-face. As a result, the king regained some consciousness, and now, by the king’s own word, the order to bring Thirugnanasambandar is given.

“Moreover, the king says here, “I will join the side of the victor.” This indicates a mindset where he has abandoned his allegiance to the Jains and stands neutrally, without any bias.

“Therefore, the king is currently in a state of impartiality. The king’s mind is in a state of impartiality. The king asks, “If there is a way to bring that great Vedic scholar, bring him.” This is because the king had a doubt in his mind whether Thirugnanasambandar would come, as he was not someone who would come seeking royal wealth. If the king summons someone, who would come immediately? Only those who desire the king’s wealth or authority would come immediately upon being summoned.

“However, Thirugnanasambandar is beyond such things; he does not consider these matters important.

“Therefore, the king had doubts whether he would come when summoned. The king had doubts.

“Furthermore, he doubted if he would come among the Jains, who blasphemed Shiva. There were also doubts as the Jains had previously mistreated Ganesha. With so many doubts, the king ordered them to see if there was any way to bring Ganesha. Just as the king doubted, Ganesha, even after being summoned, did not go directly to the king but went to the Lord of Alavay, prayed to Him, understood His divine will, and only then appeared before the king.

“Therefore, when the king commanded Mangaiyarkarasi Perumatti and the minister to bring Ganesha, they received it with great joy. The two great individuals had, until that day and for a long time previously, longed and worried to bring this king and country to the path of Shiva. The queen and the minister experienced joy today. They felt joy because grace was about to manifest in the future and bring about good. The flood of their love and passion, which had been dammed up until then, flowed like a torrent when the dam broke. Just as naturally flowing water is dammed up and made to stagnate, so too did the king’s deviation from the path of Shiva obstruct the natural flow of Saiva dharma.

“Now that the king’s situation has changed, their love flows like a flood breaking a dam. The queen and Kulachirai Nayanar, having been grieved and saddened by the evil deeds committed by the wicked Jains in the monastery, quickly go with great eagerness to worship the noble feet of their leader, Ganesha, to dispel the sorrow in their hearts. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse: (Mannavan idumbai theera matra avan pani merkonde anna men nadaiyinarrum animani sivikaiyeri minnidai madavar choozha verpadai amaichanarum mun anaintha eka sanpai muthalvanar madathai sarnthar.) To alleviate the king’s suffering, and taking up his work, the queen and the chief minister, who had previously been at odds with the king, now execute his command to summon Ganesha. To fulfill this command, the queen travels in a palanquin surrounded by women. The chief minister rides a horse and goes ahead of the palanquin. Traveling in a palanquin surrounded by women was a custom among noble families in those days.

“These customs are appropriate for the queen’s high status. The verse states that the queen travels in a palanquin surrounded by women. These are not only maidservants but also armed women guards and female attendants. The queen proceeds surrounded by them. The queen proceeds there. This is a royal command.

“According to the royal command, it would be enough for the minister to go to receive Ganesha. However, the queen also goes due to her overflowing love.

“Thus, both of them go to the monastery where Thirugnanasambandar is residing. The next verse says: (Thirumadam sarach chenru seyarik kanninar mun varupari ezunthu ninra amaichanar vanthapanmai sirapura pillaiyarkku vinnappam cheyveer ena parisanaththavarum pukku patham arinthu unarthukindrar.) After approaching the monastery, the chief minister, who came on horseback, dismounts and tells the attendants at Ganesha’s monastery, “We have come here. The minister tells the attendants, “Please convey our request to the Ganesha of Sirkazhi.” The attendants take this message and, standing before Ganesha, convey their request to him. They consider Ganesha’s presence to be like the presence of the Lord himself, and thus they make their request. They convey that the queen and the benevolent minister have arrived. When they inform him that the queen and the benevolent minister have come, the Lord says, “Bring them here.” They then return to summon them with great urgency.

“The attendants inform Ganesha that the queen and the benevolent minister, Kulachirai Nayanar, have arrived again. They, having arrived and welcomed Ganesha the previous day, also showed him the monastery and established him there.

“So, they have come again today.

“Therefore, the attendants inform Ganesha that these two have arrived again. As they convey this, Ganesha, the leader of Sirkazhi, graciously commands them to bring them immediately. The attendants then go with great eagerness to summon the queen and the chief minister. The queen and Kulachirai Nayanar enter the monastery. Upon entering, they behold Thirugnanasambandar and hear that wonderful verse. Sekkizhar Peruman then composes the next verse, which begins with “(Gnanathin thiruvuruvai)”.

“We shall proceed with our contemplation.””
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 161 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periyapuranam, Part 708, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, “Vambara Varivandu Cherukkam Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam.” Mangaiyarkarasi Piratti and Kulachirai Nayanar enter the monastery where Ganesha resides and behold the divine form of Thirugnanasambandar. Sekkizhar Peruman composes a beautiful verse, the 728th verse, describing how they beheld him: (Gnanaththin thiruvuruvai vanaththin misaiyanri mannil valar mathikkozhunthai thenakka malarkkonrai senjadayar seertodukkum kanaththin ezhupirappai kankalippa kandarkal.) The queen and the minister beheld him. This verse portrays how the queen and the minister beheld Ganesha on that day, exactly as they perceived him in their minds. The queen and the minister had seen Ganesha both individually and together the day before. The state in which they saw him then was different, and Sekkizhar Peruman clearly shows in this verse that the state in which they see him now is different due to the events that have occurred in between and the various thoughts that have arisen in their minds concerning them.

Previously, the queen and Kulachirai Nayanar had a general vision; now they have a special vision. The special always encompasses the general and elaborates on it.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman sings extensively here.

Moreover, the state in which Mangaiyarkarasi Piratti and Kulachirai Nayanar behold Ganesha here is the very state in which Ganesha is about to appear before the king, cure his disease, and bestow knowledge upon him, after worshipping the Lord of Thiruvalavai and receiving His divine grace. In this state, Ganesha is about to appear before various people and Jains in Madurai, who will benefit according to their respective merits. He is about to grant a vision that will benefit them.

Furthermore, he is in the state of appearing as a Guru to save the king and the people of the country through the bestowal of knowledge.

Therefore, Mangaiyarkarasi Piratti and Kulachirai Nayanar behold him in this manner. Just as Sekkizhar Peruman describes Ganesha’s divine vision here, similarly, he describes the vision in which Ganesha will later bestow the true words of wisdom to all who attend the sacred wedding at Thirunallur Perumanam, granting them the ultimate liberation.

Here, Ganesha appears as a Jnana Desikar, bestowing “(Bhavana Diksha, Chakshu Diksha, Sparsha Diksha, Vachaka Diksha)” etc., upon the Pandyan king. The stories of Thirugnanasambandar making the Vaigai riverbed a Diksha mandapa, removing past karma, granting the ability to know the Primeval Lord, and placing His divine feet are yet to unfold. (Vinaikal oththu thulaiyana nirathalale) and (Alavayilan palathayinar Gnanamazhavare) are sacred verses from Thevaram which contain this idea. The great author of spiritual texts, in the Thirukkaliththuppadiyar, explains this concept by saying, (Manra pandiyan ketpa kizhakkum meijnanaththin atpalavarkku arul enpathai ariyee) in the Irupayirupattu. All these are spiritual teachings.

Therefore, the author Sekkizhar Peruman himself describes them there. We can also note Sekkizhar Peruman’s intention to change the poetic structure from the historical narrative style to the Narcheeradi Kochaga Kalippa from now on. The four phrases, from “(Gnanathin thiruvuru)” to “(Kanathin ezhupirappu)”, implicitly refer to the four paths of Saiva faith: Gnana (knowledge), Yoga (discipline), Kriya (action), and Charya (observance). In that way, the state in which Ganesha stands as a true guru, guiding the way to attain the Lord through these four paths, is explained here. Sivakavimani C.K.S. Aiya writes that the greatness of this verse, which contains so many rare references, should be heard and pondered upon from the mouth of an experienced guru.

Moreover, Sivakavimani Thirumaganar also delivers a wonderful commentary on this verse. The queen and the minister behold Ganesha, who is present in that state, as the embodiment of knowledge. “Embodiment of knowledge” means one who has a divine body formed by Shiva-knowledge. Thirugnanasambandar is a chief ascetic who realized true knowledge through consciousness, which is difficult to comprehend.

Therefore, while others perceive through worldly and illusory knowledge, Thirugnanasambandar, through divine knowledge, always remembers and beholds the feet of the Lord. He is one who has completely realized true knowledge, which is the fulfillment of those feet. This was explained in the context of the pathigam “(Veyuru Thozhippangan)”, and specifically through “(Thiruneeru Chemmay Thidame)” (the sacred ash is pure and steadfast) in that pathigam, by which the Buddhists’ arguments were destroyed, and also in many other places.

Thus, the timeless, all-knowing, divine true knowledge of Shiva is all-powerful.

Therefore, it is capable of removing all great obstacles and bringing salvation. This is indicated implicitly. Thirukkazhippadiyar states this: (Unarvariya kalangal chellatha kathaludan niruthi kalangal munrinaiyum kandu). We will see these qualities in the upcoming sacred history.

Next, after “(Gnanaththin Thiruvuruvinai)”, comes “(Nanmaraith Thaniththunaiyai)”. The queen and Kulachirai Nayanar beheld him as one who, with the help of Shiva-knowledge, restores the Vedic tradition and the Saiva path from the treachery of the Jains.

Next, thirdly, they saw him as (vanaththin misaiyanri mannil valar mathikkozhunthai) a growing crescent moon on earth, not just in the sky, as Thirugnanasambandar. There will be imperfections in the moon in the sky.

Here, Thirugnanasambandar is like a growing moon without any imperfections. The moon in the sky waxes and wanes; this moon, however, is always growing. The moon in the sky gives physical light; this moon, Thirugnanasambandar, gives the light of wisdom. The moon rises up to sixteen phases and then wanes.

Here, Thirugnanasambandar is one who shines with a fullness of sixteen phases, unchanging. The physical moon in the sky nourishes crops. This moon, Thirugnanasambandar, nourishes the Saiva crop. All this is implied as they behold him as (vanaththin misaiyanri mannil valar mathikkozhunthai) (a growing crescent moon on earth, not just in the sky). They perceive him there as the embodiment of Thirugnanasambandar as (Thenakka malarkkonrai senjadayar seertadukkum kanaththin ezhupirappai). Shiva always wears the Konrai garland and has matted hair adorned with Konrai flowers.

Matted hair is a special characteristic unique to Shiva, and so is the Konrai flower garland. They saw the seven births of song in the music that praises nothing but the glories of Shiva. The music that Thirugnanasambandar sings is beautiful. Song (kAnam) originates and expands from seven types of musical notes.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to it as the seven births of song. There are musical modes known as “(palai irulu kottha pan)” and so on. There are also other derivative musical forms that spring from them.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the seven fundamental musical forms as “(Kanathin Ezhupirappu)”. Another musical tradition refers to these as Melakarta ragams and Janya ragams. Music (kAnam) is considered the Gandharva Veda, which is one of the four Upavedas. It brings joy to all deities. This Gandharva Veda, music, was used to sing about other deities and humans, and other beings, apart from Shiva. This music had longed to sing about Shiva and had been yearning for it.

Moreover, there was also penance.

Furthermore, after enduring seven births, these melodies finally found their fulfillment and purpose by being incorporated into the sacred pathigams that emerged from the divine words of Thirugnanasambandar, who was “(Konrayar adiyal peyna embiranar)” (our Lord who wears the Konrai flower and worships no other feet). The penance of those melodies, which longed to sing about Shiva, found its completion there.

Therefore, they beheld the seven births of song. They beheld all these things – the embodiment of knowledge, the unique support of the four Vedas, the growing crescent moon on earth, not just in the sky, and the seven births of song – with delight in their eyes. The queen and the minister (kannkalippa kandargal). “(Kazhiththal)” (delight) is a function of the soul’s consciousness. When the soul, through the external sensory organ of the eye and the mind, unites and perceives, a being experiences delight through that perception. The Sivagnanabodham, in its fifth sutra, explains that the five senses are perceived by the soul because the soul either unites with them to perceive, or they cannot function on their own.

Here, the delight experienced by the soul through the eye, a sensory organ, is referred to as “(kannin kazhippu)” (the eye’s delight) and “(kankalippa kandarkal)” (they saw with delight in their eyes).

Therefore, Sivakavimani Aiya summarizes the meaning of this wonderful verse as follows: “Just as a father and mother give birth to everyone, so too did Ganesha, who is the unrivaled, unique embodiment of Shiva-knowledge and who knows both artistic knowledge and subtle true knowledge, appear. They saw him as the very embodiment of that Shiva-knowledge. They saw that Shiva-knowledge as the unique support that protects the explanations of the scriptures bestowed by the Lord when they face obstacles. They saw Thirugnanasambandar as one who is like a crescent moon, born on earth, dispelling the burning heat of birth and radiating cool, wise light. They also understood that his graceful aid comes through his sacred words, which praise only the glories of the Lord with matted hair.

“Therefore, they comprehended that the seven births of song are embodied in Thirugnanasambandar’s divine form.

“Thus, Mangaiyarkarasi Perumatti and Kulachirai Nayanar perceived this with true understanding and experienced joy. The idea is that Thirugnanasambandar’s divine body, like tears and mother’s milk, is made of true knowledge, which is one of the qualities that cannot be grasped by superficial understanding. The bodies of others who have attained true grace, being illusory, are like a lamp in daylight; they are hidden within that graceful knowledge, becoming imperceptible.

“Therefore, Ganesha’s divine body is indeed made of knowledge. Sekkizhar Peruman has already described this as “Ganesha, who flows with great consciousness.” Thus, Mangaiyarkarasi Perumatti and Kulachirai Nayanar behold Ganesha, who is residing in the monastery. As they beheld him, tears flowed from their eyes like a stream, and they clasped their lotus-like hands together, prostrating themselves on the ground, touching his sacred feet, which were like lotus flowers. With faltering speech, trembling bodies, and troubled minds, they became oblivious to everything. They rolled on the ground, overwhelmed, and, like those who have fallen into the boundless ocean of sorrow and are clutching onto a shore to escape it, they clung to Ganesha’s lotus feet without letting go, due to their intense devotion, and lay there.

“We will continue to contemplate Thiruchitrambalam.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 162 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periyapuranam, Part 709, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, “Vambara Varivandu Cherukkam Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam.” Mangaiyarkarasi Perumatti and Kulachirai Nayanar behold Thirugnanasambandar. This sight, which delighted their eyes, immediately brought to their hearts the thought of the grave injustice and harm the Jains had inflicted upon such a Ganesha. This thought immediately dispelled the delight they had experienced from the vision and, moreover, brought forth an ocean of anxiety and sorrow, manifold greater. As this sorrow welled up in their minds, tears flowed like a stream from their eyes. Both of them clasped their hands and prostrated themselves on the ground.

Their speech faltered. Their bodies trembled, and they rolled on the ground. These are all physical manifestations. First came delight, followed by sorrow due to memory. These changed, and a state of knowing nothing, other than those two states, came upon them.

Therefore, they rolled on the ground, overwhelmed. Like those who have fallen into the boundless ocean of sorrow and are clutching onto a shore to escape it, they clung to Thirugnanasambandar’s sacred feet without letting go, due to their intense devotion, and lay there. Ganesha, the noble one who came to Sirkazhi, raised those two who were clinging to his feet with his sacred hand and consoled them. Thirugnanasambandar is the one who came to dispel the interruption that occurred when the Vedic path was about to begin, causing the Vedas to flourish and thrive. He lifted both of them with his sacred hands. We saw how they lay as if immersed in an ocean of sorrow.

Thirugnanasambandar lifts them out of that ocean of sorrow with his sacred hands. Phrases like “(ennai ippavaththil sera vakaiyethuththu inithamudaiya yeduththa porpatham edukkum makathai)” refer to that act of lifting.

Similarly, this place, where Thirugnanasambandar lifts them with his sacred hands, is filled with grace. Having thus lifted them and bestowed upon them his compassionate gaze, he says to them. Ganesha graciously asks, “Has any harm come to you, who are blessed with grace?” Thirugnanasambandar says, “(Arumarai vazh poompugali annalar adipoonda iruvaraiyum thirukkayal eduththuth thethidavum therumanthu theliyadarthamai nokki sirapparuli thiruvudaiyeer ungal pal theengullatho ena vinava venjamanaar mun cheytha vanchanaikku miga azhinthe anjinom thirumenikku adathu enre athu theernthom vanchakar matravar cheytha theethozhil poy mannvanpal enjalila kodu veduppay ezha ninrathu ena thozhuthu veiyya thozhil aman kundar vilaikka varum veduppavar tham cheyyum mathi mayaikalal theeramai thippiniyan)”. (Mayalurum mannavan mun matravarai venrarulil emaathu uyirum avan uyirum ena uraiththarkal.) Sekkizhar Peruman composes three verses here. Thirugnanasambandar asked if any harm had come to them. In response, both of them say, “We were greatly distressed and afraid of the evil deeds previously committed by the cruel Jains.

“We then firmly believed that they could not harm your sacred body. But the evil deeds perpetrated by those deceivers did not end there; they manifested as an unbearable burning disease in the king.” Thus they spoke and worshipped him. The fear that the fire set by the Jains would harm Thirugnanasambandar subsided, replaced by a firm conviction. The fear that it might harm Ganesha passed, replaced by a firm conviction.

“But unexpectedly, that fierce heat reached the king. We feared it would come to Ganesha, but it lacked the power to do so; thus, it reached the king instead. The queen and Kulachirai Nayanar, having said that the burning disease caused by the vile actions of the evil Jains could not be cured by the illusory remedies of the Jains, pleaded with Thirugnanasambandar that if he would conquer the Jains in front of the king, who was afflicted by that burning disease, then their lives and the king’s life would be saved. They tried to cure the Jains who had committed evil deeds, but the disease did not subside; instead, it intensified, and the king lay bewildered within it. They request that Thirugnanasambandar must conquer those Jains in the king’s presence. If Thirugnanasambandar does not show such divine compassion, the king’s life will be lost, and before that, their own lives will also be lost.

“They explain the existing circumstances and the actions that need to be taken, and they plead with him. Their plea contains hints that their lives are bound together with the king’s, and that it is the Lord’s primary duty to protect them, and for that purpose, the king’s life must be protected.

“Furthermore, if harm is to come to the king’s life, then harm will come to our lives first.

“Therefore, in this situation, we await your divine action, they say, and request him to conquer the Jains. Conquering the Jains is one action, and then bestowing grace is the next action. Bestowing grace upon the king is the next action. Conquering the Jains implies the removal of bondage, and then bestowing grace implies the attainment of Shiva. Conquering the Jains happens by defeating them in debates (Suravadam), in trials by fire (Analavadam), and in trials by water (Punalavadam) in the king’s presence. Bestowing grace is explained by Thirugnanasambandar giving sacred ash (Thiruneeru) and taking the king under his protection, and by teaching him the sacred verses of the Shivagamas (Shivagama Mantropadesham).

“These historical events are yet to unfold.

“Thus, Mangaiyarkarasi Perumatti and Kulachirai Nayanar submit their plea. Thirugnanasambandar, having listened to their plea, graciously tells them, “Do not fear. I will, by the command of the Lord, defeat the senseless Jains today for all to see, so that you may rejoice, and I will make the Pandyan king wear the sacred ash.” Thus, Ganesha graciously speaks the next verse. Hearing this, they first bowed and their faces bloomed. (Azhunthum idar kadalidai ninru adiyomai eduththarula chezhuntharulach chivikaiyin mel thennadu cheyvaththal ezhuntharula perudaiyom en peram ena thozhutalum en). As ThiruGnanaSambandhar thus spoke the verses, the Queen and the Chief Minister, hearing him, bowed before him, their faces beaming with joy. They said, “You have arrived on this beautiful pearl palanquin as a result of the great penance performed by the southern country, in order to lift us from the ocean of suffering in which we were deeply submerged.

“Therefore, we have received a great blessing. What more could we not achieve? We can achieve anything!” Mangaiyarkarasi Ammaiyar and Kulachirai Nayanar then bowed in reverence.

“We shall carry on with this discussion.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 163 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Volume 710, written by Deivasekkizhar Peruman, the section on the buzzing streaked bees, the biography of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman declares that by the command of the Lord, he will defeat the Jainas in debate and bring the Pandiya King to the path of the sacred ash. Mangaiyarkarasi Pirattiyar and Kulachirai Nayanar rejoice, considering this a great blessing bestowed upon them. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse: “Aavadhum azhivum ellaam avar seyal amanaraagum Paavakaarigalai nokkum pazhudhudan neenga vella Sevuyar kodiyinaardham thiruvullam ariven endru Poovalardh pozhil soozh Santhai puravalar podhuginraar.” (All that comes into being and all that perishes is His action. The protector of Santhai, surrounded by flower-filled groves, knowing the sacred will of the Lord with the bull banner, declares that he will conquer the sinful Jainas and remove the blemish.) All creation and destruction are the actions of Shiva.

The Vedas refer to Shiva with the word ‘Tat’, indicating Him. All creation and destruction are His actions.

Therefore, both the defeat of the Jainas, which is destruction, and the establishment of the Shaiva path in the Pandya country, which is creation, were desired by Mangaiyarasi Pirattiyar and Kulachirai Nayanar. These two actions, therefore, would not occur without the grace of Shiva. To emphasize this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states, “All that comes into being and all that perishes is His action.” The Jainas are sinners, those who commit sins. Even looking at sinners is a blemish. If we see those who do not apply sacred ash, we are afraid. As stated in Thiruvachakam, “Even seeing evil people is evil.” Justice scriptures also state, “Seeing evil people is evil.” The Jainas held the principle, “Do not see, do not touch.” To remove the blemish that came from the king looking at these sinners, and to defeat the Jainas, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds to Thiruvalavai Temple, saying, “I know the sacred will of the all-powerful Shiva.” The evil of looking at sinners, debating with them, and then subsequently defeating and destroying them – all these actions must be performed.

Therefore, he ponders on the sacred will of Thiruvalavai Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman resolves that he must know and receive the grace and consent of Thiruvalavai Peruman before undertaking the evil of debating with the Jainas. To understand the sacred will of Thiruvalavai Peruman concerning engaging in debate, he addresses Thiruvalavai Peruman with the pathigam “Thiruvullamae” (Is it Your sacred will?).

Then, to perform the actions of defeating and destroying them, he sings another pathigam to Thiruvalavai Sokkanatha Peruman, asking, “Is it Your sacred will to conquer and destroy in debate?” As the Thiruvachaka Dasangam states, “Your undefiled unique banner, which stands out brightly, overcoming the afflictions of strangers,” Shiva is the one with the bull banner. This bull banner is a banner that conquers those who are without attachment.

Therefore, to understand the intent of Thiruvalavai Peruman, who has such a high bull banner, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman enters the Thiruvalavai Temple. Sekkizhar Peruman describes this in the next verse: “Vaiyagam uyya vandha vallalar madathinindru Meiyani neetru thondar vellamum thaamum poonthu Kai inai thalaiyin meedhu kuviya kan malarchi kaatta Seychadaiyar mannum thiruvalavaiyul pukkaar.” (The generous benefactor who came to save the world, along with a throng of devotees adorned with sacred ash, came from his monastery. With joined hands raised above his head, and his eyes beaming with joy, he entered the sacred Thiruvalavai where the Lord with the reddish matted hair resides.) Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the generous one who took incarnation and came to this world, came to the Pandiya kingdom. By his arrival in the Pandiya kingdom, the world would be saved; that is, Shaivism would flourish, evil would recede. All will be enveloped by Dharma. Such a generous Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds from his monastery to the Thiruvalavai temple, surrounded by a multitude of devotees adorned with the brilliance of sacred ash.

He enters the temple with his hands joined above his head in worship. His eyes radiate joy. This is a sign of bliss as he approaches the Lord. The blooming of the eyes is an outward expression of inner joy.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman enters the Thiruvalavai temple. Deiva Sekkizhar Swamigal then composes the next verse: “Nokida vidhiyilaarai nokki yaan vaadhu seiya Theekanmal meniyaane thiruvullamae endraennil Baakkiya payanaay.” (O Lord with a fiery body, is it Your sacred will that I debate those who are not destined to be seen?) This is the 738th verse. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman stands before Thiruvalavai Sokkanatha Peruman and says, “O Lord with a body like fiery embers, O Lord with a body like fire, is it Your sacred will that I debate the Jainas, who are not destined to be seen?” Like the fruit of blessings, the child-like Balaraavayar, looking at the truth, sings a pathigam, a garland of rich Tamil verses.

The Lord has a body like fiery embers. Both ‘thee’ (fire) and ‘kanal’ (embers) refer to the same meaning.

Here, ‘theekkanal’ (fiery ember) denotes its intensity. Fire both cooks and protects through burning. Excessive fire takes lives, and the absence of fire also takes lives.

Therefore, here, fire has the power to both destroy and protect. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman addresses Sokkanatha Peruman as ‘Theekkanal Meniyane’ to signify that the Lord possesses a form capable of both destruction and protection. The burning fire is superior to the fire set by the Jainas and produces its effect.

Therefore, addressing the Lord as ‘Theekkanal Meniyane’, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman asks, “Is it Your sacred will that I debate with the Jainas, who are unworthy of being seen?” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that the Jainas are unworthy of being seen or being seen by. They were not destined to receive the grace of Pillaiyar at that time. One should not look at the Jainas, nor should one debate with them.

Therefore, both these actions are explained in Shaiva scriptures. We have already seen the subtlety of the rule that one should not even look at wicked people. If one should not look at or debate, why does Pillaiyar attempt these actions here? Because, as Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal states, “For those with confused minds who debate, and for all those whom the poor call ‘gods,’ there is no other god but Mahadeva.” The truths of other religions are absorbed as parts and aspects within Shaiva dharma.

However, Shaiva dharma cannot be contained within anything else. When religions that held only a few doctrines arrogantly rose, claiming to know the whole truth, and deceived the people of this world, plunging them into the pit of other faiths, it became the duty of great elders, who guide the world, to stand by divine grace, debate, and reveal the true nature of those religions so that the world would not be deceived but saved.

Furthermore, when adherents of other religions seized and occupied our great treasures, the Shaiva temples and Shaiva principles, it also became our duty to reclaim and protect our heritage. All that Pillaiyar is about to perform falls within this framework. All external religions should remain within their boundaries. When they do not remain within their boundaries but rise up and begin to seize other religions, the Vedic religions, it becomes the duty of Pillaiyar and Thirunavukkarasu Peruman to protect the world from being deceived by such actions. Pillaiyar and Arasu performed these as acts of grace. Destroying any religion is a difference in maturity.

The true harmony of Shaivism is to find everything in its proper place, step by step, according to the difference in maturity. Without this, clinging to a few words and ideas and saying that everything is one, demonstrating harmony. Such a display of harmony is false harmony. These pseudo-explanations prevail due to a lack of proper instruction from teachers who truly understand Shaiva truths and a lack of adherence to experiential practice.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman appeals to Shiva, asking, “Is it Your sacred will to see the Jainas and defeat them in debate?” Whether it is the Lord’s sacred will can be understood by the concept in Shivagnana Bodham: “He stands as one, knowing and seeing, as if he himself is the Lord within the very truth of the Lord.” In that state, the Lord will grant grace so that people can understand. Without His grace, they do nothing, and the great souls who see only Shiva’s grace as their eye. The great souls who perceive only Shiva’s grace as their guide are capable of seeing everything encompassed within Shiva’s pervasiveness. This state is very difficult for others who do not abide in it to comprehend. The customs prevalent these days, such as understanding omens, casting lots, discerning intentions, and seeking flower oracles, are all practices that have evolved from the aforementioned truth, each according to their respective level. In a later part of this narrative, the event where Pillaiyar himself took up the Thirumurai with his sacred ash-stained hand and saw the divine manifestation written on the palm leaf of the Thirunallatru pathigam, is also based on this very concept.

Thus, the fruit of countless blessings, meaning the fruit of the countless penances performed by countless souls, is this: It is to receive Gnanasambandha Peruman.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Swamigal refers to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in this verse as “Balaraavayar, the fruit of countless blessings.” Srimath Madhava Shivagnana Munivar also uses this same phrase, praising Sekkizhar Peruman as “Sekkizhar, who lives in Kunrai, the fruit of our blessings.” Such a Balaraavayar is Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. If we say Balaraavayar, it means that his sacred mouth, from which the fragrance of the milk of wisdom fed by the Divine Mother continuously emanates, gives rise to words of wisdom.

Therefore, Sekkizhar Peruman uses the name Balaraavayar here to indicate that, by that divine wisdom, he perceived the sacred will of the Lord. Along with the Lord who was seated on the beautiful golden boat. We can recall the teacher’s explanation of this meaning in the 1995th verse: “The consort with golden bangles, whose sweet words are like the milk from her sacred breast, and whose mouth is like coral.” Realizing the significance and rarity of this name, later elders bestowed the name Balaraavayar upon their children. Our divine Sekkizhar Peruman’s younger brother also bore the name Balaraavayar. Such a Balaraavayar composes a pathigam, a garland of powerful Tamil verses. The richness of this powerful Tamil garland pathigam is its ability to guide souls to salvation by following the path of grace, standing firm in righteousness.

At this time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sang two pathigams. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to explain how Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed those pathigams.

Let us resume our reflection on this.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 164 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Volume 711, written by Deivasekkizhar Peruman, the section on the buzzing streaked bees, the biography of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. To defeat the Jainas in debate, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman asks Thiruvalavai Peruman for His sacred will and sings two pathigams before the Lord. Sekkizhar Swamigal explains this in two verses: the 739th verse and the 740th verse. “Kaannidai aaduvaararai kaattu maavuri mun paadi Thennalar kondraiyaartham thiruvula nokki pinnum Unnamil vetha velvi endru eduthu uraiyin maalai Maanamill amanam thammai vadil vendrazhikka paadi Aalame amuthaga undu vaanavarukku azhithu kaalanai Maarkandarku kaaynthanai adiyerku indru Nala nin puzhae aga vendum nanmaraigal etthum Seelame aalavazhil sivaperumane endrar endru.” (Singing before the Lord who dances in the forest, wearing the hide of an elephant, looking at the sacred will of the Lord adorned with honey-blossoming Konrai, and then singing the garland of words beginning with “spotless Vedic sacrifice” to defeat and destroy the dishonorable Jainas in debate. You drank poison as nectar, saved the celestials, and punished Yama for Markandeya.

Today, only Your glory should prevail in the world, O Shiva Peruman of Aalavai, whom the four Vedas praise.)

The Lord is one who dances in the forest. This signifies both destruction and re-creation.

Therefore, it indicates the disappearance of the darkness of Jainism and the re-flourishing of Shaivism.

Here, the Lord is referred to as ‘Kaannidai aaduvaar’ (One who dances in the forest). He sings the pathigam beginning with ‘Kaattumaavuri’ (elephant hide) to worship such a Lord. He sings before the Lord to understand His sacred will. Among the pathigams he sang, the first one began with ‘Kaattumaavuri’. This pathigam that begins with ‘Kaattumaavuri’. Why does he compose two pathigams?

One pathigam is to ascertain the Lord’s sacred will regarding whether to engage in debate with the Jainas. After understanding the Lord’s sacred will to debate, the second pathigam is to ask the Lord if it is His sacred will to win that debate and destroy Jainism.

Therefore, in the first of the two pathigams composed now, the one beginning with ‘Kaattumaavuri’, Pillaiyar asks the Lord, “Is it Your sacred will to debate?” In the second pathigam, he prays to the Lord, “Is it Your sacred will to win and destroy in debate?” Only after Pillaiyar perceived in his heart that the Lord had graciously consented to the debate. Only then did he ask, “Is it Your sacred will to win and destroy in debate?” If he had not received the Lord’s consent to debate, there would be no need to further inquire about the Lord’s will to win and destroy in debate.

Therefore, after praying to the Lord with the first pathigam, “Is it Your sacred will to debate?” and realizing through divine grace that debating was indeed the Lord’s sacred will, Pillaiyar then prays to the Lord in the second pathigam, “Is it Your sacred will to win and destroy in debate?” Pillaiyar, who had resolved, “I will know the sacred will of the Lord with the bull banner to conquer and remove the blemish from those who look at sinners,” and then entered the Thiruvalavai temple to inquire, proceeds further only after the Lord’s sacred will has given consent.

Therefore, it is understood through this that the Lord’s sacred will indicates consent to Pillaiyar.

Thus, the subsequent religious debate, the victory related to it, and the destruction of the Jainas all occurred by the command of Shiva’s sacred will. It is also understood that all of Pillaiyar’s actions were Shiva’s actions because he stood in divine service, becoming one with the Lord, as if he himself was the Lord. All those from other religions who doubt Pillaiyar’s compassion and the excellence of Shaivism should clearly understand this. Taking the verse, “Singing ‘Kaattumaa uri’ first, and then singing ‘Vedha Velvi’”, it is noteworthy that the pathigam ‘Kaattumaa uri’ signifies the rejection of other religions, and the pathigam beginning ‘Vedha Velvi’ signifies the creation of the path of sacred ash, both sought to understand the sacred will.

Here, a crucial point is to understand the state. These two—the destruction of bonds and the attainment of Shiva—are the core ideas of the tenth and eleventh sutras of Shivagnana Bodham, representing two different types of grace bestowed by the Lord upon souls. We have already seen that these are also the divine purpose of Pillaiyar’s incarnation.

Therefore, one pathigam is requested for the destruction of bonds, which is the rejection of other religions, and another pathigam for the attainment of Shiva, which is the establishment of the path of sacred ash.

Thus, the defeat and destruction of the Jainas are Pillaiyar’s sacred will, and also the Lord’s sacred will, and are known here to be a part of the destructive action that causes these souls to experience the fruits of their karma. The two pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman are the fourth and fifth pathigams dedicated to the Thiruvalavai temple. The first pathigam, which begins with “Kaattumaavathu Oripodthuda,” is the 47th pathigam of the Third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Kausikam. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: “Vendkaiya.” “Thiruvullave Senthum Thirunale endru Vallamanna Sarasandamizh ketamayana sol pagarum bali neenga velam kariyuri portha kadavule nokkida vidiyillatha aman kaiyarai nokki naan otti vaathu seithal thevareerukku Thiruvullame” means, “Is it Your will, O Lord, that I should debate with those who have no destiny, having heard the words that say ‘Thiruvullame Senthum Thirunale,’ and having discarded the elephant’s hide as clothing?” This verse expresses the Lord’s divine will and grace. Having understood the Lord’s will, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this pathigam.

The second pathigam composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman on this occasion is the fifth pathigam dedicated to the Thiruvalavai temple. It is the 108th pathigam of the Third Thirumurai, beginning with “Veda Velviyai,” and is set to the tune of Pazhampancharam in the Nadimel Vaippu meter. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: “Amalodu therthil thiru.” “Ayaparamaney alam niyo pugazhe miga vendum sen Aalavayil uraiyum maadiriye koodaalavaai konai vidai kondu vaadal mene amalarai vaattida maada kaali sambiththa ippadal vallavar bakkiya vaazha ye Thiruchitrambalam.” This verse states that those who can recite this song, praising the fame of the Lord who resides in Aalavai, will live prosperously.

Pillaiyar, having inquired, “Is it Your will that I should debate?” and having understood through a divine sign that the Lord had consented, believed that if a debate were to take place, it must end in victory, and the wicked must be destroyed. This second pathigam was composed to request the Lord’s will for these two outcomes. By this pathigam, he discerned the Lord’s will and felt it within his heart, just as he had desired and inquired. This is evident from the section where he heard Tamil in the first pathigam, and from the eleventh verse of the second pathigam, which states, “Vidai kondu vaaden meniyamanarai vaattida maadakkaali sambandan mathiththa.” From these, we can understand this. It is further affirmed here that Pillaiyar is a refined soul, directly guided by the Lord.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who bestowed these pathigams upon us, understanding the will of Thiruvalavai Sokkanatha Peruman, further addresses Thiruvalavai Peruman, saying, “O virtuous one, praised by the four Vedas! O Lord Shiva, enshrined in Thiruvalavai! You consumed poison as nectar and bestowed grace upon the celestials.

“Furthermore, for Markandeya, You kicked and rolled Yama. Today, I seek knowledge. Today, let Your fame spread across this entire world.” He appeals to the Lord by calling Him the virtuous one praised by the four Vedas and Lord Shiva of Aalavai, invoking these two qualities. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman here praises the two acts of grace: consuming poison as nectar and saving the celestials, and subduing Yama for Markandeya. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, witnessing these, prays, “I, Your servant, also desire that today, all this knowledge, all this grace, may spread Your fame.” He addresses Lord Shiva as the virtuous one praised by the four Vedas. The virtue praised by the four Vedas signifies the Lord’s unique characteristic of being the embodiment of the Vedas.

“Secondly, he addresses Him as Lord Shiva of Aalavai, which represents the Lord’s general characteristic as the inner essence of the five divine functions. Consuming poison as nectar and bestowing it upon the celestials is an act of pure compassion, while subduing Yama is an act of fierce compassion.

“Here, too, these two acts are mentioned. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman thus expresses that the Lord should perform these actions. As Thirukkovaiyar states, “Aalame amuthaga undu aalathinaal amirthaakiya kon,” meaning, “He who consumed poison as nectar and transformed it into immortality.” This implies that by purifying the hindering principles, these obstacles become aids for achieving divine experience.

“Thus, Lord Shiva, by consuming poison as nectar, saved the celestials. This applies generally to the Saivite world and specifically to the people of the Pandya kingdom. Just as He contained the overwhelming poison that arose to delude the celestials, He should subdue the false doctrines of Jainism and Buddhism that deluded the Pandya king, the people of the Pandya kingdom, and the devotees, causing falsehood to prevail, the Vedic traditions to diminish, and the glory of sacred ash to be disregarded. The request by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, that “He who consumed poison as nectar and gave it to the celestials,” implies that these evil paths should be suppressed and contained within their respective limits. The act of subduing Yama for Markandeya’s sake, representing the annihilation of time, was not only for Markandeya and the celestials but also for the devotees, showing Shiva’s divine compassion. Since these two acts were for the devotees as well, it implies that today, this divine compassion should also be bestowed upon His humble servant, and its benefits should reach all devotees.

“This is the underlying message. Just as Yama came to torment Markandeya.

“Here, we can also observe how the Jains, like Yama, came to torment Pillaiyar by engaging in wicked deeds. He prays, “May Your glory alone fill the world for this humble servant.” This reference, “Gnyanam nin pugazhe miga vendum Then Aalavayil uraiyum em aadiye,” appears in the second pathigam. When addressing the Lord as “The embodiment of virtue praised by the four Vedas,” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman here refers to the Lord’s compassion, as He stands as Shiva and Shakti, bestowing grace upon all beings. “Virtue” here denotes the Lord’s divine quality. By saying, “May Your glory alone fill the world with knowledge,” it implies that due to the spiritual ripeness of the souls at that time, the Lord’s glory was diminished and not widespread, and Pillaiyar prayed to remove that state and spread the Lord’s glory throughout the world. It is also understood that Pillaiyar prayed, as stated in the ThirupPasuram, “Aazhga theeyadhellam Aran naamame soozhga” (May all evil be dispelled, and may the name of Aran encompass all).

“When he addresses Lord Shiva of Aalavai, it signifies that Thiruvalavai is the place where the Lord’s omnipresent and eternal grace manifests. The Tevaram states, “Mannagaththum vaanagaththum engumaam thinakagath thiru Aalavai” (Thiruvalavai is firm and present everywhere, on earth and in heaven). Having received the Lord’s divine sign in advance and experiencing the joy of realizing that grace, he prays to the Lord that the name of Aran should always and everywhere encompass everything. After receiving the Lord’s gracious permission, he arrives at the first gateway of the ancient Thiruvalavai’s Kapilamadhil with a brilliant and glorious form, adorned with the sacred ash on his forehead. Surrounded by loving devotees, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives at the first gateway of the ancient Thiruvalavai Kapali fort. To bestow grace upon Pandimadevi and Minister Kulachirai Nayanar, Pillaiyar mounts a pearl palanquin adorned with red gems.

“The limitless cheers of the devotees, chanted from all sides, filled the three worlds and all other worlds. Let’s continue to contemplate this.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 165 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar.

Thiruchitrambalam.
The Periya Puranam, composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, Part 712, in the Vambaravaru Vanda Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeds towards the palace in a palanquin. Various auspicious musical instruments play. Surrounded by devotees, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives. The radiance of the sacred ash worn by the devotees seems to rise upwards like a radiant halo.

Pillaiyar, shaded by a pearl umbrella, proceeds in a pearl palanquin. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the 744th verse: “Kanniukku aniyay ullar ezhuchiyil kaatchi petrar nanniya samayam veru nambinar enum munbu punniya thavangalin kol.” That verse states, “Panchavan thanjam mevi punniya murthi vandhu Maduraiyil pugutha endraal.” Pillaiyar’s majestic presence serves as an adornment for the eyes. Pillaiyar appears immensely beautiful to the visual sense. People adorn their ears and hands with ornaments, but no one adorns their eyes. The eye is a sense organ with a unique distinction, so it deserves the best adornment.

That best adornment is to behold Pillaiyar’s beauty. Just as Thirunavukkarasu Peruman says, “Navinukku arungalam Namasivayave” (The precious ornament for the tongue is Namasivaya), and Thirukkural states, “Kannukku anikalan kannottam” (The adornment for the eye is compassion), here, for the visual delight of the eye. Pillaiyar, who appeared immensely beautiful, became the ornament for the eyes. The people of Madurai witnessed this glorious sight. These people, who now see Pillaiyar’s majestic presence in the streets of Madurai, are Jains by faith but were originally Saivites before converting to Jainism. They now behold Pillaiyar’s majestic arrival.

There are Jain gurus who hold cruel doctrines and must be defeated in debate. There are also those who, swayed by Jain gurus, did not witness Pillaiyar’s majestic arrival.

Furthermore, some, driven by envy, ignorance, and other negative emotions, hid themselves and did not behold Pillaiyar’s divine sight. Apart from those who hid, the people of Madurai who now witnessed Pillaiyar’s majestic arrival were blessed. For those who behold Pillaiyar’s majestic arrival are those who have performed spiritual austerities in their previous births. It is not enough to have performed austerities only in this birth; one must have performed them progressively. This is explained by Madhava Sivagnana Munivar in his commentary on the eighth Sutra of Sivagnanabodham, referring to “austerities performed earlier.” Similarly, the people of Madurai who now witness Pillaiyar’s majestic arrival must have performed austerities in various ways, not just one, to be able to witness such a divine sight. Such people, who had performed prior austerities, beheld Pillaiyar’s majestic presence.

The sight itself is. The first event in internal emotional experiences. In internal experiences, first comes sight, then doubt, then clarity, then appreciation, then acceptance, and then rejoicing in the divine. The nature of these events is extensively discussed in literary works on internal experiences like Thirukkovaiyar and in works on grammar.

Here, the people who were blessed by Pillaiyar’s arrival, receiving good fortune, wonder and discuss what good fortune they must have had in the past for this sacred figure, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, to come to Madurai, bestow his vision upon them, and take them as his own. The fire set by the Jains did not harm Pillaiyar; instead, by Pillaiyar’s command, it became a disease affecting the king of Madurai, who had consented to the fire. That disease. Pillaiyar’s grace comes here as a command to cure. Witnessing this, the people who beheld Pillaiyar’s majestic arrival were freed from their former delusion. This is the initial stage where Pillaiyar bestowed grace upon the people of Madurai who had basic spiritual maturity.

Later, by Pillaiyar’s command, the fiery disease left the king, and the king was saved.

Then, the people of Madurai also witnessed the victory of Pillaiyar’s grace in the fire debate.

Following that, the women of the city who witnessed Pillaiyar coming forth victorious in the water debate are present. These people are of a higher level of spiritual maturity than those mentioned earlier.

Now, there are even more spiritually mature people in Madurai. Who are they? During the water debate, when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, acting as the great guru to the Pandya king at the banks of the Vaigai, a place of initiation, bestowed spiritual instruction through his verses and took the Pandya king under his protection by giving him sacred ash, he also achieved victory in the water debate.

At that time, he not only embraced the Pandya king but also gave sacred ash to the people of Madurai present there, taking them under his protection. These people of Madurai, who were now taken under his protection, were of a higher level of spiritual maturity.
