Thus, we can joyfully witness the various forms of grace bestowed by our spiritual master, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, upon souls of various levels of spiritual maturity. The Saivite principle that a guru bestows grace in different ways upon souls of various levels of maturity is explained here. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. As Thirugnanasambandha Peruman embarks on his journey, the Pandya Queen follows him in a palanquin, and Minister Kulachirai Nayanar walks ahead of Pillaiyar with a throng of devotees.

Thus, the queen follows Pillaiyar, and the minister walks ahead in the procession. According to custom and royal tradition, the queen follows in a palanquin. The minister, however, dismounts from his horse and walks with the devotees.

In this manner, they reach the palace of the king of Kanninadu. “Kanninadu Udaiyan” means the king who rules over a protected land.

Also, since Meenakshi Devi, as Tadathagai Pirattiyar, ruled there, the Pandya kingdom is known as Kanninadu. Pillaiyar thus arrives at the palace of the king of such a Kanninadu. Kulachirai Nayanar informs the king of Pillaiyar’s arrival. “When Kulachirai Nayanar reached the king and announced the arrival of the lord of Chanbai, surrounded by golden walls, the king’s sorrow diminished slightly, and he commanded that a jeweled throne be placed beside his crown.” Kulachirai Nayanar quickly goes ahead, enters, and informs the king that Pillaiyar is arriving. Upon hearing the good news of Pillaiyar’s arrival, the Pandya king’s sorrow, which he had before, diminishes slightly. As soon as his sorrow lessens, the king commands that a suitable golden throne, adorned with many jewels, be placed for Pillaiyar’s arrival beside his own head.

The king commands that the fully jeweled golden throne, a suitable seat for Pillaiyar, be placed beside his head. It is our custom to arrange a proper seat for important persons before they arrive. The king, who is lying down, commands that the golden throne for Pillaiyar be placed beside his head. The king orders Kulachirai Nayanar to go and escort Pillaiyar.

First, an altar is prepared, then the deity is invited and installed upon it, and then worshipped. According to this custom, the king issues an order to Kulachirai Nayanar to arrange a suitable seat for Pillaiyar and to have Pillaiyar installed upon it. The king gives an order to Kulachirai Nayanar. Previously, when the king was under the sway of the Jains, he lamented, saying, “Hear, hear!” upon hearing of Pillaiyar’s arrival.

At that time, he had agreed when the Jains suggested setting fire to Pillaiyar’s monastery. He had intended to expel Pillaiyar from the city. All of that was the king’s former state, the state he was in until the previous night. That state is like a blind child in utter darkness; similarly, the soul, immersed in the darkness of ego, bound by impurities, is in that state. The soul in that state does not discern between good and bad; it considers good to be bad and bad to be good. That is the state of souls.

That was the state the king was in before, under the sway of the Jains. The Saiva Siddhanta scriptures state that when the Lord’s concealing power (Tirodhana Shakti) acts through the cycle of birth, a disease-like process, the darkness of ego gradually recedes, and good knowledge progressively emerges, guiding the soul towards good actions.

Here, too, the fire set by the Jains acts as a disease, as grace, “Paivaiye Sendru Pandiyarku Aagave,” in the king. The king’s previous state, where he harbored only hatred and wished to expel Pillaiyar, has now changed. The king is pleased with Pillaiyar’s arrival. When Kulachirai Nayanar says that by uttering Pillaiyar’s name mantra and wishing for his presence, not only this illness but also the illness of rebirth will be cured, the king expresses his joy, saying that if Pillaiyar comes and cures his illness by his grace, he would be delighted. This is the grace of Pillaiyar himself, the grace that prompted the king to send someone to him.

Now, upon hearing the news that Pillaiyar is coming to the palace, it is Pillaiyar’s gracious gaze that makes the king command that a pedestal be placed next to his own throne for Pillaiyar.

Furthermore, it is Pillaiyar’s gracious gaze that causes Kulachirai Nayanar to be sent to receive Pillaiyar, and the king, who until now had agreed to everything the Jainas had said, changes his stance and decides that he will no longer speak deceitfully but will remain impartial. When he sees Pillaiyar arrive, he raises his hands in worship and points to the pedestal next to his throne.

Thus, as grace settles, darkness gradually dissipates, and blessings arise in various places, as exemplified by this historical account. As soon as the king gives this command, Kulachirai Nayanar is overjoyed. Until now, Kulachirai Nayanar, on behalf of the king, had carried out the royal duty of welcoming guests as instructed by the Queen.

Now, the king himself agrees to welcome Pillaiyar and to arrange a pedestal for him and to send someone to receive him. Kulachirai Nayanar is exceedingly happy. Kulachirai Nayanar, with great joy, goes out from the palace to bring Pillaiyar. Kulachirai Nayanar goes very quickly to escort Pillaiyar into the palace.

Our reflection now resumes.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 166 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part Seven Hundred Thirteen, authored by Thirudeva Sekkizhar Peruman, Vambaravarivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. As soon as Kulachirai Nayanar goes to welcome Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, all the Jainas surround the Pandya king. The Jainas, who consider the Aragu god under the Ashoka tree as their deity, approach the Pandya king and say, “Is this the way to establish our religion? How can you do this?” They say to the Pandya king, “This religion is the Jaina religion, and it is your religion. You must protect your religion; it is your duty.

“This religion is your possession, and protecting your possession is your duty.” They lay out this premise. Having said this, the Jainas further state, “You have invited him, that is, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, here. Let it be. He and we will try to cure your illness together in front of you. Even if your illness is cured by him, you must say that your illness was cured by the method we employed.” Thus, they speak to the king with great deceit. They are those who consider falsehood as truth.

“But the Pandya king does not agree. Until now, he had been subservient to the Jainas and had acted unilaterally in their favor. Now he does not agree to this deceit of the Jainas because The benefit of the penance previously performed by the Pandya king is now ripening and bringing good results.

“Therefore, he does not agree to the deceit of the Jainas. The scriptures state that the truth is that the fruit of penance manifests and becomes useful only when it ripens and comes to fruition; God will bring about the fruit of that penance.

“Accordingly, until now, the time for that penance to ripen and come to fruition had not arrived, so he was under the sway of the Jainas. Now is the time for the Pandya king’s previous penance to bear fruit.

“Therefore, the Pandya king does not now agree to the deceit of the Jainas. The Pandya king tells the Jainas, “You both try to cure this disease through your deities. I The Pandya king declares that he will not deviate from impartiality and speak deceitfully. When the king says this, the Jainas are very saddened and remain there.

“At the same time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who is like the essence of the penance performed by the southern Tamil country, the Pandya kingdom, reaches the gate in front of the Pandya king’s palace, dismounts from his pearl palanquin, and enters. This is described in the seven hundred and fiftieth verse: (avan uraippa kundar ennangirundha ellai thenn thamizh naadu seythavakk kozhundu pOlvaar van thani pavana munnar vaayilul anaindhu maadu pon thigal tharala paththi sivikai ninru ezhundhu pukkaar) As Kulachirai Nayanar previously arrived, the queen, Kottravan Deviyar, also rose from her place and went. The next verse says that the king of the cool Tamil country saw the Kaundinya lord, who resembled the full moon with abundant arts, who had come to the earth to dispel the long darkness, standing in the sky. After informing the king, Kulachirai Nayanar arrives before Pillaiyar. The queen also comes inside the palace and descends from her palanquin. The Pandya king, the ruler of the cool Tamil country, sees Pillaiyar, the Kaundinya lord, who resembles the full moon with abundant arts, who has come to the earth to dispel the long darkness, as if from the sky.

“When Pillaiyar sets out from Thirualavai temple, the chief minister arrives with a large retinue of devotees before him. As they approach the palace, the minister separates from the crowd and quickly goes ahead, enters the palace, informs the king of Pillaiyar’s arrival, arranges a pedestal for Pillaiyar according to the king’s command, then leaves the palace again, receives Pillaiyar, brings Pillaiyar into the palace, and stands there. The queen also arrives there. The Pandya king, the ruler of his Tamil country, sees Pillaiyar coming. The Peruman mentions the inherent coolness that will cure his fever. He refers to the king as the ruler of his Tamil country, including the Pandya country, because of the coolness that the Podigai mountains bring to the Pandya country.

“The Pandya king sees Pillaiyar arriving like a full moon rising from the sky to dispel the long darkness, like the internal darkness of Jainism being dispelled, like a shining moon that neither waxes nor wanes in the ethereal sky. The Sekkizhar Peruman compares Thirugnanasambandha Peruman to the moon because he brings coolness with his divine arts and ambrosial arts. Since the sacred ash’s divine light shines everywhere when Pillaiyar arrives, it is compared to the white light of the moon. The Pandya king sees Pillaiyar arriving thus. Until the previous day, the king had been saying things like ‘see and touch’ and ‘hear and touch.’ Due to the benefit of his previous penance, this situation changes, and he sees Pillaiyar with great desire and love. Among the inner meanings, sight is the first thing that occurs.

“The king sees Pillaiyar. Sekkizhar Peruman describes what he did upon seeing him. The next verse states: (kanda appozhudhe vendhan kaiyedutthu eytha nokki than thunar mudiyin paangar thamaniya peedam kaatta vandhamizh viragar mevi adhan misai irundhaar maayai konda valla amanar ellaam kuripinul achcham kondaar) Immediately upon seeing Pillaiyar, the king raises his hands in worship and shows the elevated pedestal to Pillaiyar. The king, suffering from his illness, is unable to stand up and worship with folded hands, so he worships with folded hands from his seated position. He also points to the pedestal, indicating for Pillaiyar to be seated there. He points with his hand.

“The method of invoking the deity in Shiva puja involves actions such as Avahanam (invocation), Sthapanam (installation), and Sannirodanam (confinement), which are performed by showing specific mudras (hand gestures). We see a similar situation occurring here. When the king requested this, Pillaiyar graciously ascended and sat upon the elevated seat. The Jainas, whose religious principles included deceit and falsehood, felt fear within their hearts. They were afraid. The next verse is: (Chezhiyanum Pillaiyardham thirumeni kaanappetru vizhiyura nokkalaale vemmayinOy sirithu neengki azhivurum manam nernirkka anthanar vaazhvai nokki keluvuru pathi yaadhu enru viruppudan ketpOdhu)

“This is the seven hundred and fifty-third verse. The king saw Pillaiyar, and Pillaiyar’s gracious gaze also fell upon the king.

“Therefore, the king’s fever now recedes a little further. Earlier, when the name mantra entered the king’s ears, his exhaustion subsided slightly.

“At that time, the king expressed his joy, saying he would be happy if this illness was cured by the arrival of this young sage, and he would join their side.

“Later, when he was informed of Pillaiyar’s impending arrival, the illness receded a little further, to the extent that he ordered a pedestal to be placed next to his throne. He had also refrained from speaking deceitfully to the Jainas, which was another stage in the illness receding.

“Now, upon seeing Pillaiyar and receiving Pillaiyar’s divine gaze, his fever further recedes a little, and the king’s mind becomes clear. He looks at Pillaiyar with great desire and asks him, “What is your native place?” He gains the strength to ask this.

“Thus, it is explained here that the gradual relief from illness and the enlightenment of wisdom are attained by a soul through the grace of the Supreme Guru, Pillaiyar. Previously, the mind, which was disturbed and lost due to the severity of the illness, is now steady. With such a mind, he looks at Pillaiyar and asks, “Where is your village?” Is it not still a tradition to ask, “What is your village?” and begin conversation when welcoming a new person? When the king asked this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman replied, (Ponni valandharu naattu punar pazhana purampanai) surrounding the beautiful town of Kazhumalam, which we consider our home. Thirugnanasambandhar, the child who has the excellent twelve names, thus sang a pathigam to the southern king, as described in the seven hundred and fifty-fourth verse. Pillaiyar replies, “Ponni Valandharu Nadu is the Chola country, my country.

“In the Chola country, irrigated by the Kaveri river, surrounded by fertile fields and wetlands, the child composed a pathigam, Thirukazhumalam, which is Sirkazhi, which we consider our home.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman replies, “Kazhumalam is the town we praise.” In the pathigam he just sang, “Kazhumalam is the town we praise,” is the concluding line of every verse. Kazhumalam is the town we praise. In each verse, this serves as a crown. Among the twelve sacred names of Sirkazhi, he mentions the other eleven sacred names and the twelfth name, Kazhumalam. In each verse of this pathigam, Pillaiyar thus blesses. Sekkizhar Peruman refers to this pathigam as a pathigam that embraces and praises the twelve names.

“This pathigam, which begins with Piramanur Velupuram, praises the twelve names of Sirkazhi in each verse. It is a pathigam set in the Gantharam tune and is in the style of Thiruchakkaramaatru. Piramapuram, Venupuram, Pugazhi, and so on are the twelve sacred names of Sirkazhi. In this pathigam, the first verse begins with Piramanur, and the second verse begins with the second name, Velupuram. The third verse begins with the third name, Pugali.

“In this way, each verse begins with one of those names, and Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has arranged the twelve names in the same order in each verse. This is a pathigam composed in the Thiruchakkaramaatru style, which is the seventieth pathigam in the Second Thirumurai. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thonipuram. (theraai ponnam sirappu sampai arulmal than kali kochchai vayam ullitta aathiyaai pannirandaai nindra theere kazhumalam naam paravum oore kaavimalaa pOraiyum kanna kazhumalathin peyarai naaLumbhaaviyasee pannirandum nalluzha) This pathigam was composed in the king’s palace to console him when he asked, “What is our village?” Although this pathigam belongs to Sirkazhi, it was composed in Madurai. Let’s continue our reflection.””
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 167 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part Seven Hundred Fourteen, authored by Thirudeva Sekkizhar Peruman, Vambaravarivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Pillaiyar is seated on the golden pedestal.

At this time, the envious Jainas approach Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Hiding the fear in their hearts, their faces ablaze with anger like fire, and their eyes red like embers, they approach Pillaiyar. The hearts of the Jainas were filled with envy. The Thirukkural states that righteousness is formed by avoiding these four: envy, desire, anger, and harsh words.

At this point, the commentator Parimel Azhagar explains envy as not tolerating others’ prosperity.

Here, the envy among the Jainas is the desire to suppress Shaivism and to flourish themselves. They outwardly display their principles of non-violence, etc., but in reality, their mindset is to suppress Shaivism through deceit, falsehood, and other cunning means and to thrive themselves. This is the mindset of the Jainas, and this is called envy. Envy means jealousy. Because of this envy, the Jainas’ eyes turn red, and they utter many harsh words. From envy, desire arises.

When that desire is not fulfilled, anger arises. Due to that anger, harsh words are spoken. All these are interconnected and cause and effect each other, as Thiruvalluvar states in the Thirukkural about the four things: envy, desire, anger, and harsh words, which are integral to righteousness. We see this in these Jainas here. Their eyes red with envy, they utter many harsh words. If envy takes hold in one’s heart, it leaves no room for any other good qualities.

This evil quality of envy has the nature of completely taking over the heart.

Thus, the Jainas speak there. They possess both external and internal darkness. The internal darkness in their hearts consists of evil qualities like envy. All evil qualities arise from the quality of tamas, and the color of tamas is said to be dark. We can recall this here. Due to that envy, it is as if the fire of anger leaps out from their faces and eyes.

Generally, anger is referred to as fire because this anger will burn and consume those who are overtaken by it. Burning means that anger will torment those who are angry in many ways, both internally and externally.

Thus, the dark-skinned Jainas surround Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who shines like a red-gold light of Shiva knowledge. This is like clouds surrounding the rising sun in the morning. Since Sekkizhar Peruman refers to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as the sun here, we can understand that the previous Jaina darkness was like night, and when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, like the sun, rises, the surrounding Jaina darkness is dispelled. Just as the clouds surrounding the sun lose all their strength and cannot stand, so too the Jainas surrounding Thirugnanasambandha Peruman diminish before the light of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s Shiva knowledge in a little while. Generally, we refer to a dog barking as ‘kuraippathu.’ In the same way, the Jainas bark meaningless and very loud insults. Earlier, Sekkizhar Peruman referred to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as the sun.

Now, he describes the loud and meaningless harsh words uttered by the Jainas as dogs barking. The proverb “a dog barking at the sun” comes to mind here. Generally, those who lose in an argument make noise, speak evil words, and shout loudly. The Jainas, filled with envy, anger, and other evil qualities, shout loudly in this manner, without any thought for the Pandya king who is suffering, and without any regard for time or place. Pillaiyar, hearing them, says, “Speak properly, as is appropriate to your truth.” However, the foul-mouthed, frenzied Jainas leap up and, in a large group, surround and clamor and cry out. The young lady, seeing this, cannot bear it and trembles within.

She looks at the southern king and says, “It seems like the divine body is fragile. This gracious Pillaiyar, and these countless Jainas, O King, our Lord will surely dispel the delusion of your illness.

“Afterwards, these Jainas will be submerged. If they are strong, let them speak,” says Sekkizhar Swamigal, composing two verses here. Pillaiyar looks at the Jainas who are surrounding him and barking, and says, “You should speak in an orderly manner. Do not bark like this.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman says, “Speak as a religious debate should be conducted.” Pillaiyar says, “Let the debate proceed according to the rules.” Those who engage in religious debate should present their religious principles, the definition of God according to their religion, the principles of epistemology, what life means according to their religion, what liberation means, and so on, in a systematic and logical manner, with valid proofs. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states, “Explain all your truths and the meanings expressed in your religious texts.

“Do not shout like this.” Therefore, the Jainas surrounded Pillaiyar and challenged him to a debate and shouted. Pillaiyar tells them to speak in an orderly manner, according to the rules of debate, and not to shout or speak in a disorderly fashion. Nevertheless, those foul-mouthed, frenzied Jainas jump up. Many of them rise and surround him, panicking and crying out improperly. They engage in actions that do not conform to the rules of debate. Instead of entering the debate fairly as Pillaiyar instructed, they act improperly.

“Seeing this, Pandimadevi is unable to bear it and trembles within. The previous night, the Jainas had committed evil deeds in secret.

“Now, the same Jainas are misbehaving even when they meet Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in person.

“Therefore, Pandimadevi fears what might happen. The queen Mangaiyarkkarasi reaches a state where she cannot bear to see it, and her mind is filled with trepidation. This is also an outcome of her maternal quality of compassion. This gracious Pillaiyar is of a tender form, while these cruel Jainas come in a crowd and shout. These Jainas are capable of wicked deeds. Because of their strength in numbers and the burning anger of their envy, they will attempt to do anything they wish.

“This thought arises in Pandimadevi’s heart, and so Pandimadevi says to the king, “This Pillaiyar is a young boy, but the Jainas are innumerable, O King. Our Pillaiyar will cure the delusion of your fever.

“After that, these Jainas can debate if they are able.” Pandimadevi thus requests the king. Pillaiyar is of a tender form, The Jainas are in a group. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman will cure your illness.

“After that, the Jainas can debate. The Queen, with these four thoughts in her mind, speaks thus. The first thought among these four is about Pillaiyar’s divine form. This shows the motherly love and the profound love of Mangaiyarkkarasi Pandimadevi. When Pandimadevi speaks thus, the king replies to Pandimadevi, saying, (maaranum avaraai nokki varundal nee enru mattra veruvaadhu enkOl enmel veppu ozhitthu arughar neerum aaranich sadayinaarukku anbharaam ivaru ninggal theariya dheivatthanmai ennidath therippeer enraan) This is the seven hundred and fifty-ninth verse.

“The Pandya king replies. He calls the Queen, who was trembling inside, and first tells her, “Do not fear.” He tells her, “Do not be sad.” He says, “You need not grieve,” and then the Pandya king further says, “What other debate is needed? You, the Arhats, and this devotee of Shiva, who wears the Ganga in his matted hair – you both remove this fever from me.

“After that, you explain to me the true nature of your deities.” The Pandya king mentions them separately, not together.

“Therefore, the Pandya king tells them both to individually try to cure this disease and show the truth. This is also because of Pillaiyar’s gracious gaze, which further reduced the Pandya’s fever, allowing the king to speak this way.

“Here, he refers to Pillaiyar with great respect and high regard as “this devotee of Shiva who wears the Ganga in his matted hair.” He speaks this way, with his illness and delusion removed, because he heard Pillaiyar’s name mantra, saw Pillaiyar’s divine form, and received Pillaiyar’s gracious gaze.

“At the same time, when the king spoke thus, Pillaiyar looks at Pandimadevi and speaks words of grace, saying, “You need not grieve.” (Gnana aaramudhum undaar natsavuruvai nokki) (vizhiyinaay kel mattra ennai baalan enru nee nani anjavednda nilaiyilaa amanarkku enrum yaan ezhiyaan aleen enrumezhundirupathigam paadi pertiyaal arulic cheytha pillaiyaar thamakkum munnam surtru nindru alaitthal ovaa arugarkum thennar kOmaan itrai naaL ennai uttra piNiyai neer ikazhitththeerum tetrrana theerththaar vaadhil venranar enru seppa) These are two verses composed by Sekkizhar Peruman. Pillaiyar looks at Pandimadevi and says, “Do not be afraid,” and at this time, he also composes a pathigam. “O lady with eyes like a deer, listen. You need not greatly fear me, thinking I am a child. I am never weak before these transient Jainas,” he sang that pathigam with this sentiment.

“Let us go on reflecting.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 168 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part Seven Hundred Fifteen, authored by Thirudeva Sekkizhar Peruman, Vambaravarivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, addressing Pandimadevi, says, “Do not be afraid. Do not think that I am a child and be afraid. Aalavai (Siva) is our protector, so I will not be weak before these Jainas.” He then composes a pathigam, beginning with “Maani Ner Vizhi Maadaraai.” “Maani Ner Vizhi Maadaraai” means “O queen with eyes like a frightened deer, listen, O great Queen, wife of the Pandya king. This child has pure, sweet words.

“Do not become anxious thinking that I am merely a child. Since Thirualavai is our protector, I will not be weak before these Jainas.” He thus composed the pathigam. Pillaiyar addresses the Pandimadevi as “Maani Ner Vizhi Maadaraai” in this pathigam. This is the only pathigam in which Pillaiyar addresses a specific individual directly. Such is the special nature of Pandimadevi. This pathigam is the sixth pathigam dedicated to Thirualavai, the thirty-ninth pathigam in the Third Thirumurai, set to the Kolli tune.

“The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (veli maadaraai vaLa vikkumaa perum devi ke paaLavayOru baala eevan enru nee paRi vedhi aaLai maamizhaiyaadhiyaaya idanggalaai pala azal chenarugeLi enallen thiru aaLavaai aruL nirkkave ekkara maN kaigaRu keLiye nallen thiru aaLavaai sokkaniyal uLLirukkave thuLangum mudhi) Thirugnanasambandha Peruman addresses Pandimadevi as “Maani Ner Vizhiyal” and begins this pathigam. “Maani Ner Vizhi” means eyes like a frightened deer. The queen, Mangaiyarkkarasi, trembles at the thought of what might happen to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s divine body and speaks to the Pandya king.

“At that time, she is trembling and has a frightened look in her eyes. It is to such a queen that Pillaiyar addresses and sings. He says that these Jainas are transient Jainas, meaning that they are confused, holding principles where something can be both false and true, unable to define their principles, wandering as confused individuals. He states, “I am not weak before them,” and thus composes this pathigam. (Maani ner vizhi maadaraai vazhudhikkum maa perundhevi keL paanalvaai oru baalan eengu ivan enru nee paRiv eydhidhel aanai maamalai aadhiyaaya idangaLil pala allal ser eanarkku eliyen alen thiru aalavaai araN nirkkave) This beautiful first verse is thus structured. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings to the Queen and blesses her. “O great Queen, wife of the Pandya king, listen.

“Do not consider me easy, thinking I am a child with sweet, pure words. Thirualavai is our protector, so I am not weak before these lowly ones who cause much suffering in places like Anaimalai and other such places,” thus declares Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. We had previously seen that the Jainas had gathered in Anaialai and other mountains. We had seen that upon hearing of his arrival, Jainas from various parts of the Pandya kingdom gathered in large numbers in Madurai. There are eight hills surrounding Madurai: Elephant Hill, Pig Hill, Snake Hill, Cow Hill, etc. In each of these eight hills, a thousand Jainas, making a total of eight thousand, lived there, having established Jaina schools.

“They lived in caves and on rock beds in these hills. All of them, eight thousand Jainas living in these eight hills, came to Madurai. Throughout the pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman exposes the true nature of the Jainas. He explains how they lead their lives by holding false principles and outwardly displaying non-violence. He explains how they live by displaying non-violence outwardly. The language spoken by these Jainas was Prakrit, a corrupted form of Sanskrit.

“They did not even speak it properly. There are Vedic scholars who are proficient in Sanskrit and other languages, having thoroughly studied the Vedas, Agamas, and mantras. These Vedic scholars were ashamed when these Jainas spoke, distorting the Sanskrit language and using Prakrit, making a lot of noise. The Vedic scholars, who had thoroughly studied Sanskrit, the Vedas, Agamas, and mantras, were ashamed that these Jainas were distorting the language. These Jainas were accustomed to distorting all these languages and speaking with much clamor, as stated in the second verse. they are accustomed to distorting all these languages and speaking with much clamor, as stated in the second verse. In the third verse, he condemns the principles of the Jainas.

“The Jainas hold the principle of ‘asti-nasti’ (is-is not). If asked if God exists, the Jainas would say it cannot be definitively said that He does or does not, speaking in a confusing manner, unable to define their principles, wandering as confused individuals. They wander unclothed, making observers ashamed. In the third verse, it says that these Jainas roam around with names like Candrasena, Indrasena, Dharmasena, Gandhasena, Kanakasena. Whether it is Sanskrit or Southern language, Tamil, if one properly learns these two languages, the truth one will realize is that Shiva is the supreme God and Shaivism is the excellent religious path. This understanding will come to one.

“If one properly learns these North Indian and South Indian languages, one will realize this. But these Jainas, without properly learning these two languages, are unable to understand the Vedic path and the Shaiva path. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman explains in the fourth verse that these Jainas are blind-eyed and wander around. These Jainas compose books like Eliviruttam, Kiliviruttam, Nariviruttam, etc., and deceive people by claiming their contents are true. They outwardly portray themselves as doing many good deeds. They desire the wealth that comes from these deeds and accumulate riches.

“Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states in the fifth verse that he is not weak before such Jainas who seize wealth in this manner, and that our Aalavai Lord will always bless us. In the next verse, he mentions various types of Nandis, such as Kanakanandi, Pushpanandi, Bhavanandi, Kumanamasunakanandi, Kunakanandi, Divananandi, and states that these Jainas consider evil itself as penance. In the seventh verse, he says that these Jainas claim to have no attachments or relations but do not adhere to faultless moral conduct. They adhere to unjust paths. He states that he is not weak before such Jainas and Buddhists, because the Lord of Aalavai always protects us. In the eighth verse, he states that Ravana believed there was no one superior or equal to him, but Shiva destroyed Ravana’s arrogance.

“He sings that he is not weak before those Jainas who, without bowing to Shiva, practice false penance, carrying a water pot and peacock feathers, tucking a mat under their armpit, walking with fear and trepidation one after another, lest they harm any small creature, considering this their principle, because the Lord of Thirualavai protects him. In the ninth verse, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states that the Jainas are those who do not worship the sacred feet of Shiva, the holy one whom Brahma and Vishnu could not comprehend. They perform rituals for the deceased as if offering water to the dead. In the tenth verse, he states, “I am not easy for the Jains who pluck out their hair, subject their bodies to penance, causing suffering through false asceticism, and utter meaningless words, because the fortress of Thiruvalavay is my inner support.” He proclaims that Shiva is unknown to these Jains and Buddhists. Our leader, Shiva, has beautiful red feet. Abandoning His worship, they have embraced false asceticism, ignorant of the path taught by good texts, and not standing on that path.

“They speak like scholars but utter words of blame. “I am not easy for those Jains, for the fortress of Thiruvalavay stands within me,” he sings in the eleventh verse, which serves as the final verse.

“The Lord of Thiruvalavay, Sokka Natha, my Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who graciously declares, “Since the Lord of Thiruvalavay dwells in my heart, I am not easily swayed by the arrogant Jains,” states that those who recite this pathigam, graciously uttered by Gnanasambandhan, the Tamil Lord born in Thiruppukazhi in the presence of the Pandya king, will face no suffering.

“Thus, in the eleventh verse, he sets the palasruthi for this pathigam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman condemns the doctrines of the Jains and Buddhists in this pathigam. Both these paths stood against the Vaidika Sanatana Dharma, seeking to negate the Vaidika Dharma.

“Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this pathigam. Pillaiyar incarnated to make the Vaidika path and the Vedic way flourish, and the Shaiva Sect to shine brightly, didn’t he?

“Therefore, he composed this pathigam. As soon as Pillaiyar composed the pathigam, the Pandya king began to speak. Addressing Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and the Jains, the Pandya king said, “Today, you two must individually try to cure this burning disease that has afflicted me. Whoever cures this disease will be victorious in the debate.” Pillaiyar is characterized by his connection to grace. He does nothing without His grace; being under the sway of grace, Shiva’s actions manifest as his own. This is the nature of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, Thiruvalava Didn’t Pillaiyar sing in the pathigam, “Though Arun stands, Sokka is within me”?

“Pillaiyar is such a person. The Pandya king speaks to him and the Jains. Upon hearing the king’s words, the Jains rush forward. They say to the Pandyas, “We will cure the disease in the left side of your body. We will cure it through our divine efforts, by chanting mantras.” The Jains rush forward first because if Gnanasambandha Peruman were to come forward first and cure the Pandya king’s disease with his grace, he would win.

“So, to prevent that, the Jains rush in and say they will cure the burning disease on the left side of the Pandya king’s body. The Jains say, “We take the left side; we will chant mantras to cure the burning disease on the left side.” According to anatomy, the left side of a man’s body is considered the female part, and the right side, the male part.

“Therefore, a disease on the left side of a male Pandya king’s body is a part that is easily curable. However, curing a strong disease that has taken hold would require significant effort. The disease would be severe, and curing it would not be so easy.

“Therefore, the Jains took the left side of the Pandya king because a male Based on the medical truth that a disease on the left side can be easily cured, the Jains chose the left side of the Pandya king’s body. The Jain gurus, who always carry peacock feathers, apply their efforts there. They stroke and chant mantras over the Pandya king’s left side with their peacock feathers. As they do so, instead of the disease subsiding, the burning disease intensifies further. The Pandya king cannot bear it.

“Thus, unable to endure the suffering, the king looks at Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Conveying through eyes is one of the characteristics of kings.

“Accordingly, as the disease worsened due to the actions of the Jains, As the disease intensifies, the Pandya king, unable to bear it, looks at Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The meaning of that gaze is that the Jains tried to cure the disease and failed; they could not cure it.

“Now, you should present your side of the argument. The Pandya king expresses this silently through his gaze as the burning intensifies and he can no longer speak. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the wealthy one of Thirukkazhumalam, observes the Pandya king’s condition. Seeing this, he determines that the sacred ash of the Lord of Thiruvalavay, Sokka Natha Peruman, the Lord of Thiruvalavay, will act as a permanent mantra and medicine to cure the disease on the king’s right side. With that in mind, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings the Thiru Neetru pathigam, which begins with “Manthiramavathu Neeru,” praising and expounding the essence of the Vedas. Let’s continue to contemplate.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 169 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periyapuranam, Volume 716, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandhanainar Puranam, composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. The Pandya king looks at Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, begging him to cure the burning disease in his body. Sekkizhar Peruman composes the next verse. “Seeing the gaze of the Southern King, the wealthy one of Thirukkazhumalam (Sirkazhi) stated that the sacred ash of the Lord of Thiruvalavay would be the abiding mantra and medicine to cure the burning on his right side,” thus begins the 764th verse, praising the established Vedas and singing the sacred pathigam. “Thennavan” here refers to the Pandya king.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman observes the Southern King’s gaze. “Gaze” implies a hint. Seeing the Pandya king’s gaze, Pillaiyar, the wealthy one of Thirukkazhumalam, the wealthy one of Sirkazhi, states that the sacred ash of the Lord of Thiruvalavay will be the mantra and medicine to cure the burning disease on his right side. Bearing this in his heart, he sings the pathigam beginning with “Manthiramavathu Neeru,” praising and explaining the essence of the Vedas. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman believes that the sacred ash of the Lord of Thiruvalavay will be the mantra and medicine to cure the king’s burning disease. We can see that “Alavai Annal Neere” (The sacred ash of the Lord of Alavai) is the crown jewel of the pathigam he just sang.

We can see that the sacred ash of the Lord of Thiruvalavay, Sokka Natha Peruman, acts as a mantra and medicine, curing the burning disease. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously proclaims this. To cure diseases and karmic afflictions, there are three types of remedies: ‘mani’ (gems), ‘mantra’ (incantations), and ‘aushadham’ (medicine). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s words indicate that this sacred ash embodies all three. “Alavai Annal Neeru” (the sacred ash of the Lord of Alavai) signifies ‘mani.’ When he sings “marunthumay” (and as medicine), it refers to ‘aushadham.’ And when he begins to sing, it indicates that the sacred ash itself is the ‘mantra.’ Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, using sacred ash as a tool, chants mantras to cure the burning affliction on the king’s body and graciously composes this pathigam. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman structured this pathigam with an internal reference in its final verse, stating, “The ten verses recited for the healing of the burning affliction on the body of the Southern King.” Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, through this pathigam, designated the sacred ash as the means to achieve victory in this debate.

This sacred ash is praised in the established Vedas. That is, the Vedas venerate this sacred ash. The glory of sacred ash is extensively elucidated in the Upanishads, which are considered the head of the Vedas. Upanishads such as Basmajabalam, Kalagni Rudram, and others, praise and worship this sacred ash as ‘basmam,’ ‘rakshai,’ and ‘vibhuti’.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman also stated in the pathigam that the sacred ash is mentioned in the Vedas. This pathigam contains eleven verses. After singing the first six verses of this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman takes the sacred ash with his sacred hands and applies it to the right side of the Pandya king.

Thus, the first six verses of this pathigam were sung to cure the burning on the king’s right side. The remaining five verses of this pathigam, from seven to eleven, were then uttered to cure the burning disease on the king’s left side.

Therefore, in the first six verses, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who praised “The sacred ash of the Lord of Thiruvalavay,” structured this pathigam into two parts, fittingly praising “The sacred ash of the Lord of Alavai” in the subsequent five verses. The pathigam is one for both sides. This single pathigam was sung to cure the disease on both the left and right sides of the king’s body. In that single pathigam, the first six verses cured the disease on the right side, and the second five verses cured the burning disease on the left side. The great Sekkizhar then composes the next verse. This verse begins with “Thiruvallar Neeru Kondu Thiru Kaiyal Thadava” (Taking the sacred ash and applying it with his sacred hand), continuing from the previous verse, “annavan valappal veppai Alavai An We can understand the meaning of the 765th verse by connecting it with the preceding one: “The sacred ash of the Lord of Thiruvalavay, being both an unfading mantra and medicine, will cure the burning on his right side.” After singing the pathigam and taking the sacred ash in his hands, Pillaiyar applies it to the king’s body.

“It is called “Thiruvallar Neeru” because it is sacred ash. “Thiruvallar Neeru” means ash that fosters ‘Thiru.’ ‘Thiru’ here refers to Shaiva spiritual wealth. He considered ‘Thiru’ as grace. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman refers to this sacred ash as the embodiment of Parasakti in the eighth verse, stating, “Paravanamavathu Neer” (Water is the form of Parasakti). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman takes this sacred ash, the form of Parasakti, in his sacred hands and applies it to the king’s body on his right side. The Jains, however, had stroked the king’s body with peacock feathers without touching him.

“But Pillaiyar, with great compassion, took the sacred ash in his sacred hands and touched and applied it to the king’s body. This was like a Gnana Guru bestowing initiation through touch (Sparsa Deekshai). As Thirugnanasambandha Peruman applied it, that right side, free from the burning, became cool like a cold body of water.

“At the same time, The heat from the right side of the king’s body moved to his left side, and with both sides’ heat converging on the left, the king’s body became extremely hot on the left side.

“Thus, the Jains failed not only in their attempt to cure the disease on the right side but also in their method of preventing the disease from worsening on the left side, which was exacerbated by the heat from the right side. In both ways, the Jains suffered defeat. As the king’s left side glowed with intense heat, the Jains trembled, and the king’s burning disease affected them to such an extent that their peacock feathers burned, and they moved far away from the king. The king of Pukazhi, whom many worship, with one side To alleviate the fever, those excelling in wisdom in this vast world came in wonder and gathered there. The king of Pandya’s body, where coolness prevailed on the right and heat intensified on the left, now appeared as if all the coolness of the world had gathered on his right side, and all the heat of the world had gathered on his left side, as if coolness and heat had converged and settled in one place within the same body. His The body of the king then manifested this.

“The king spoke, “At this time, when I am esteemed, on one side there is a white hell, on the other side is the bliss of liberation. On one side there is bitter poison, on the other side is sweet nectar. I, in one form, have attained the nature of two opposites.” This is the next verse, the 768th verse. The king, filled with great wonder, says, “What a marvel, what a surprise!

“At the same time, on one side there is a cruel hell, and on the other, the bliss of liberation. It is as if on one side there is the experience of great poison, and on the other, the experience of sweet nectar! In my one body, I have attained these two contrasting natures,” he says. The same object cannot possess two contradictory, different Natures.

“But here, in my form, in my body, such contrasting natures have come together, the Pandya king marvels. “You, the Jains with your white garments, have lost. Leave me and depart. Oh benevolent leader of the Vedic lineage, who came and uplifted me, please bestow your grace upon me so that this burning disease completely vanishes,” he says, bowing in his mind. He becomes close to the path of good destiny. He tells the Jains, “You have lost.

“Leave me.” This was the punishment the king meted out to the Jains for losing the debate.

“At the same time, the king bows in his mind to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who uplifted him. “I did not desire or invite you, yet you, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, have come here on your own and blessed me. Oh benevolent one, who has cleansed me of the fruits of cruel karma and uplifted me, please also cure this burning on my left side,” the Pandya king prays. The next verse is the 770th verse. Please bestow your grace, O Benevolent One,” the Pandya king supplicates to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman with a bowed mind. As the king desired, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman assumes a state of grace and shows his divine compassion on his face.

“He reveals it through the radiance of his divine face. As his divine face displayed divine compassion, his divine hands displayed the sacred ash. Is not that sacred ash the form of grace? Is it not the form of Shiva’s power? Taking that sacred ash, to cure the disease on the right side, he sings the pathigam “Manthiramavathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is the mantra). As he sang the second part of that sacred ash pathigam, those five verses, praising the sacred ash to cure the disease on the king’s right side, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman applied the sacred ash to the king’s body with his sacred hands.

“The divine compassion he showed signifies bhavana (meditation). The pathigam he sang praising the Lord signifies mantra (incantation). His act of applying it to the king’s body signifies kriya (action).

“Therefore, we see here the three aspects: mantra, bhavana, and kriya. As Thirugnanasambandha Peruman performed this, the very moment he applied the sacred ash, the burning disease on the king’s left side also immediately vanished. This burning was a severe heat that had transferred from the right side to the left, The ailment, which the Jains previously could not cure, is now gone. The king attains the states of Malaparipagam and Iruvinai, as described in Saiva Siddhanta. This also implies that the cruel birth-affliction, born of strong karma and primal impurity, is also removed.

“Therefore, the Pandya king is now freed from that disease, and the birth-affliction, which was the root cause of the disease, is also removed.

“Thus, he attained the exalted state of being free from rebirth.

“Thus, the pathigam, in which Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with great divine compassion, praised the sacred ash, is revered as the Thiru Neetru Pathigam. This is the seventh pathigam dedicated to the holy shrine of Thiruvalavay. It is composed in the Gandhara tune, and is the 66th pathigam in the second Thirumurai. The king’s body was illuminated then. The king will speak, “At this time, when I am esteemed, on one side there is a white hell, on the other side is the bliss of liberation. On one side there is bitter poison, on the other side is sweet nectar.

“I, in one form, have attained the nature of two opposites.” This is the next verse, the 768th verse. The king, filled with great wonder, says, “What a marvel, what a surprise!

“At the same time, on one side there is a cruel hell, and on the other, the bliss of liberation. It is as if on one side there is the experience of great poison, and on the other, the experience of sweet nectar! In my one body, I have attained these two contrasting natures,” he says. Chapter 170 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periyapuranam, Volume 717, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, by composing the Thiru Neetru pathigam, cured the Pandya king’s burning disease and also freed him from the cycle of rebirth. Sacred ash is a symbol of Shiva for Shaivites, a Shiva mark. The two Shaiva ornaments are vibhuti and rudraksha. Shaivites, or devotees of Shiva, are those who worship Shiva with true love as Pasupati.

Just as a chaste wife wears the sacred marriage thread given by her husband as a symbol of her chastity, Similarly, those who worship Shiva as the Supreme Lord wear vibhuti and rudraksha as Shiva symbols, signifying their devotion. Just as a married woman desires to wear the symbol of the sacred marriage thread and does not hesitate to wear it, so too are those who eagerly wear the Shiva symbols of vibhuti and rudraksha, and do not shy away from wearing them, called Shaivites. Innumerable texts speak highly of vibhuti and rudraksha. In the four Vedas—Rig, Yajur, Sama, and Atharva—and their parts, such as the Ramarahasya Upanishad, The Kalagni Rudra Upanishad, Atharva Shiras Upanishad, Shandilya Upanishad, Jabala Upanishad, Brihat Jabala Upanishad, Taittiriya Upanishad, Svetasvatara Upanishad, and Vasudeva Upanishad, the glories of vibhuti are extensively discussed. The Basmajabala Upanishad, found in the Vedas, is exclusively dedicated to expounding the greatness of vibhuti. This Upanishad is specially dedicated to speaking about the glory of vibhuti.

Similarly, vibhuti is discussed in all Shaiva Agamas and their sub-divisions. The greatness of vibhuti is spoken of in all texts, including Vedic essence texts, Smriti texts, Puranic texts, and Itihasa texts. The Kandapuranam states that vibhuti and rudraksha are prescribed in the Vedas as a daily practice for Brahmins. The Skanda Purana states that wearing sacred ash and rudraksha is a daily requirement for Brahmins and others, as prescribed in the Vedas. The Suta Samhita states that whether one is a Gnanin (wise person), a Brahmin, or anyone else, they must wear sacred ash before engaging in their karmic duties. It states that one who desires liberation must continuously wear sacred ash.

Texts state that one should consider a person wearing sacred ash as Lord Shiva himself. Just as the glory of Lord Shiva is immeasurable, so too is the greatness of Shiva’s symbols immeasurable. Sacred ash is the solution to all sins, sufferings, and fears. One should not touch water, food, or anything else, nor perform any other ritual, without wearing sacred ash. Vedic rules state that a Brahmin, even due to tiredness, Should not chant the Gayatri mantra without wearing them.

Therefore, wearing vibhuti and rudraksha is not only part of occasional (naimittika), optional (kamya), and expiatory (prayaschitta) rites, but also a constant daily practice that everyone should adopt. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, praising such sacred ash, composed the Thiru Neetru pathigam, beginning with “Manthiramavathu Neeru.” It embodies all mantras, starting from the Sri Shiva Moola mantra. “Neeru” means that which is obtained through ritual purification. It has names such as vibhuti, basma, and rakshai.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings, “Manthiramavathu Neeru” (The mantra is sacred ash). “Vanavar Melathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is above the celestials) implies that since sacred ash is on exalted beings, The truth is revealed that sacred ash should also be on other worldly beings. “Sundaramavathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is beauty) means sacred ash bestows beauty. Those who apply vibhuti are capable of captivating anyone who sees them. The Thiruppallandu pathigam emphasizes this, saying, “Like the red kumkum on the young breasts of those with eyes like fish, the sacred ash adorns the chests of the virtuous, who are praised.” Next comes “Thuthikkap Paduvathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is to be praised). The Vedas praise and salute the sacred ash.

The Vedas praise the sacred ash, saying, “Salutations to this sacred ash, which is the seed for attaining wealth.” Thus, the Vedas praise the sacred ash.

Therefore, sacred ash is to be praised.

Next, it says, “Tantiramavathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is tantra). Tantra means a means or method. Sacred ash is one of the three means for curing diseases: mantra, tantra, and medicine, and it also embodies all three. As Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred words state, “Mantra, tantra, and medicine,” so does sacred ash shine. Mantra refers to the Vedas, and tantra refers to the Shiva Agamas. We can see that this sacred ash is adopted in some way in the worship of various religions.

Therefore, “it is present in all religions.” Such sacred ash is the sacred ash of Thirualavai, where Uma, with her red lips, is a part, as Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings. “Senthur Vaayumai” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings about the nature of Lord Shiva, who dwells as Meenakshi Sundareswarar in the holy shrine of Thiruvalavay in Madurai, with Uma, whose lips are red. He states that it is the sacred ash of that Lord Shiva of Thiruvalavay. In the second verse, he says, “Vedaththil Ullathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is in the Vedas). Just as the Vedas salute Lord Shiva, so too do the Vedas salute the sacred ash.

As we have seen before, Upanishads such as Basmajabalam and Kalagni Rudram praise the sacred ash. There are Vedic sayings that command, “Burn the forehead that is without vibhuti.” Thirunavukkarasu Peruman declares, “It is Thiruvaloor without sacred ash.” Sacred ash is the only symbol worn by everyone and bestows all blessings, removing all sufferings, including the misery of birth. The Vedas speak of it as removing all suffering and encompassing everything. Such sacred ash is also praised by Tamil Vedas.

Next, it says, “Vemthuyar Theerpathu Neeru” (Sacred ash removes harsh suffering). “Vemthuyar” means severe suffering, which refers to the suffering of rebirth. This suffering comes through three gates: Adhyatmika, Adhibhautika, and Adhidaivika. Sacred ash is what removes such sufferings. “Tharuvathu Neeru” (Sacred ash bestows) comes next. “Bodhath” means knowledge.

Although self-knowledge is also called knowledge, self-knowledge must be destroyed, and only Shiva-knowledge is desired by souls.

Therefore, here, “Bodhath Tharuvathu Neeru” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s gracious words refer to Shiva-gnana (Divine knowledge).

Next, he graciously states, “Punmai Thavirppathu Neeru” (Sacred ash removes impurity). This refers to the impurity that afflicts the soul and the body. The impurity of the body is disease; the impurity of the soul is ego (Anava Malam). Applying sacred ash removes all these impurities, called ‘punmai’ (lowliness). Wearing sacred ash is a practice to be learned through the guidance of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who is like a beacon of fire. Sacred ash is.

Next comes, “Unmaiyil Ullathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is in truth). “Unmai” here refers to true scriptures. True scriptures speak of the greatness of sacred ash.

Therefore, “Unmaiyil Ullathu Neeru.” Such sacred ash is the sacred ash of Thiruvalavay, surrounded by cool waters and fields, says Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in the second verse. In the third verse, he graciously states, “Mukthi Tharuvathu Neeru” (Sacred ash bestows liberation). Sacred ash is what grants liberation, also known as moksha. Next comes, “Munivar Anivathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is worn by sages). Sages also wear sacred ash. Sages are those who constantly hold the Lord in their thoughts.

Such sages also wear sacred ash. “Sathiyamavathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is truth), meaning it is reality. That is, sacred ash is the indestructible substance called Sat.

Next, comes, “Thakkor Pugazhvathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is praised by the worthy). “Thakkor” means great people. Great people praise sacred ash. Next comes, “Bhakthi Tharuvathu Neeru” (Sacred ash bestows devotion). Sacred ash also bestows devotion. “Paravai Iniyathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is sweet to birds) comes next.

Sacred ash becomes sweeter and sweeter as it is praised. Next comes, “Siddhi Tharuvathu Neeru” (Sacred ash bestows Siddhi). This means sacred ash bestows desired things. Siddhi also refers to the eight great Siddhis like Anima.

Now, in the fourth verse, “Kana Iniyathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is pleasant to behold). This ash is pleasant to see. “Kavinai Tharuvathu Neeru” (Sacred ash bestows beauty). “Kavin” means beauty. Previously, “Sundaramavathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is beautiful) appeared.

There, we saw that it means sacred ash is beautiful.

Here, “Kavinai Tharuvathu Neeru” means that sacred ash is not only beautiful itself but also beautifies whatever it is associated with. It is not only beautiful, but it also beautifies that which is adorned by it. “Peni Anipavarkkellam Perumai Koduppathu Neeru” (Sacred ash bestows greatness upon all who cherish and wear it). “Penuthal” means to appreciate, to desire. Sacred ash bestows greatness upon all who thus desire and wear it. “Maanam Thagaivathu Neeru” (Sacred ash upholds honor) comes next.

“Maanam” means dignity. “Thagaivathu” means to abide in that noble quality, not to descend from it. “Mathiyai Tharuvathu Neeru” (Sacred ash bestows intellect) is next. “Mathi” means intellect, which refers to worldly knowledge. “Bodhath” (true knowledge) was mentioned in the previous verse.

Therefore, the ‘mathi’ mentioned here refers to worldly knowledge. “Senam Tharuvathu Neeru” (Sacred ash bestows elevation) is next. “Sen” means the higher world. Sacred ash also bestows the beautiful joys of that higher world. The fifth verse begins with “Poosa Iniyathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is pleasant to apply). Sacred ash is pleasant to wear.

“Punniyamavathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is righteousness). Sacred ash is the embodiment of righteousness. “Pesa Iniyathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is pleasant to speak of). Sacred ash is pleasant to speak of repeatedly. “Perunthavaththorkkellam Aasai Keduppathu Neeru” (Sacred ash destroys the desires of great ascetics). For great ascetics who desire liberation, sacred ash serves as a means to liberation, free from attachments.

This vibhuti bestows all worldly pleasures, such as merit, upon householders who approach it with a desire for worldly enjoyments. It also serves as a means to liberation for great sages who are attached to supreme bliss, by cutting off their attachments.

Therefore, it is said to destroy desires. “Anthamavathu Neeru” (Sacred ash is the end) is said. All things ultimately The next verse praises sacred ash, stating that it is praised by everyone in this land. It is the sacred ash of Thiru Alavaayan. The verse also states that sacred ash is wealth, as ‘aruttham’ means wealth. Sacred ash removes suffering, as ‘avalam’ means suffering.

Sacred ash alleviates distress. Sacred ash bestows the heavenly realm. Sacred ash is suitable for all good things, meaning it is a means to achieve all benefits. It is the white ash worn by the virtuous. ‘Punniyam’ refers to Shiva’s virtue, and ‘punniyar’ are those who possess it.

Furthermore, Shiva himself is known as Punniyar.

Therefore, the virtuous apply white ash. Such sacred ash is the sacred ash of Thiru Alavaayan, surrounded by majestic mansions.

Next, in the seventh Thiruppadal, it says, “Eyilathu attathu Neeru,” meaning this ash incinerated the three cities. “Irumaikkum Ullathu Neeru” signifies that this ash supports both earthly and heavenly pursuits. “Irukkum Neer” means that this ash is wealth. “Thuyilai Thaduppathu Neeru” means that this ash prevents sleep. “Thuyil” also means death, and in this context, it implies preventing forgetfulness of Shiva. Sacred ash ensures that one does not forget Shiva.

“Suththamathu Aavathu Neeru” means that sacred ash is pure. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman declares, “Ayilai Politharu Suzhaththu Alavaayan Thiruneere,” meaning it is the sacred ash of Thiru Alavaayan, who possesses sharp weapons. The eighth Thiruppadal says, “Iravanan Melathu Neeru,” meaning sacred ash was on Ravana’s body. Ravana, the son of Visravasu, was a great rakshasa. He was crushed under a mountain and cried for a long time, earning him the name Ravana, meaning ‘one who cries,’ bestowed by the Lord. He was a great devotee of Shiva.

Therefore, his body was adorned with sacred ash. “Ennaththakuvathu Neeru” means that sacred ash is considered distinguished.

Next, “Paravanamavathu Neeru” states that sacred ash embodies the essence of Parasakthi. ‘Paravanam’ means the color of the drum. ‘Para’ is a Sanskrit word referring to Parasakthi. In Tamil, ‘Parai’ is a name for Sivasakthi. This ‘Para’ being present means it is the form of Sivasakthi. “Pavamm Aruppathu Neer” means sacred ash removes sins. “Tharavanamavathu Neeru” follows, meaning sacred ash also embodies the color of the earth, ‘Thara’ being a name for the earth.

Next, “Thaththuvamavathu Neeru” states that sacred ash embodies the forms of principles. “Ara Vanangum Thirumeni Alavaayan Thiruneere” means that this is the sacred ash of Thiru Alavaayan, whose sacred form is worshipped by serpents, ‘Ara’ meaning snakes. In the ninth Thiruppadal, “Malodu Ayan Ariyaatha Vannamum Ullathu Neeru” means that sacred ash is an entity that even Brahma and Vishnu could not comprehend. “Melurai Dhevarhal Thangal Meyathu Vennpodi Neeru” signifies that sacred ash is also the white powder on the bodies of the celestials.

Next, “Yela Udambu Idarththeerkkum Inpam Tharuvathu Neeru” means that sacred ash removes bodily ailments and bestows joy. “Alamathu Undamidattril” This is the sacred ash of Thiru Alavaayan, who consumed poison. In the tenth Thiruppadal, “Kundikai Kaiyargalodu Sakkiyar Kootamum Kooda Kanndikai Pippathu Neeru Karutha Iniyathu Neeru” means that sacred ash bewilders even the Jain and Buddhist communities. It is delightful to contemplate. “En Dhisaipattta Porulaar Etthum Thakayathu Neeru” states that sacred ash is worthy of praise by the guardians of the eight directions, the Dikpalakas.

“Andatthavar Paninthu Etthum Alavaayan Thiruneeru Idhu Aakum” means that this is the sacred ash of Alavaay Chokkanathan, worshipped and adored by those holding high positions in the cosmos, ‘Andatthavar’ meaning those in charge of the cosmic realms. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman declares this.

Now, in the eleventh Thiruppadal, the final verse, “Aatral Adalvida Yerum Alavaayan Thiru Neetrai Por” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman concludes this pathigam with a benefit statement, saying that those who master these ten verses, which were sung to alleviate all diseases afflicting the body through sacred ash, will be good people. This is the sacred ash of Thiru Alavaayan, the Shiva who rides the victorious bull. Thirugnanasambandha, the Brahmin from Sirkazhi, states that those who can recite these ten verses from this pathigam, which he composed in worship, will be good people.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman explains the benefit of this pathigam.

Therefore, this sacred ash, by removing diseases of the body. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes this pathigam, stating that it cures all diseases, including the disease of rebirth caused by the impurity of the soul. We have pondered the explanations of the verses of this sacred ash pathigam, composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with the help of the commentaries of Kayappakkam Sadhasiva Chettiyar and Sivakavimani Ayya.

Let us continue to contemplate the sacred history.
