Chapter 171 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periyapuranam, Part 718, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, by Deivachikilar Peruman. The Pandya king’s fever is cured by the grace of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Upon his recovery, the Pandya Mahadeviyar and Kulachirai Nayanar worship the lotus feet of the young saint, placing them on their heads. The verse states that the queen and Kulachirai rejoiced, saying, “We have achieved greatness today, we are truly born, and the king has attained liberation from rebirth.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman eradicated evil, here referring to the Pandya king’s fever, and its root cause, the king’s alignment with the Jains. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman simultaneously eradicated these three evils: the king’s alignment with Jainism, the evil influence of Jainism, and the evil karma from the king’s past actions.

Both Pandi Mahadevi and Kulachirai Nayanar prostrate themselves at Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred red feet. They worship him, declaring, “We have achieved greatness today, we are truly born.” They say, “Today we are truly born,” meaning, “Today we have reaped the benefits of our birth.” The Devaram sacred text states, “Days not spent in devotion are days not born.” According to this, all previous days, when they could not serve the king, the devotees, or Shiva, were as if they were not born.

Therefore, they declare, “Today we are born, and we have reaped the benefits of our birth.” They praise the king, saying, “The king has attained liberation from rebirth.”

Now, the Pandya king, free from all his fevers, attains supreme bliss and worships Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, raising his hands above his head. The king performs this act when he is healed and saved. The king’s state is thus explained.

After the fever was cured, the actions of the queen and the minister were first explained by Deivasekkilar Peruman.

Then, it is explained what the king did. This is because the happiness of Pandi Mahadevi and the great minister, who had earnestly prayed to the Lord for the welfare of the king and the country, and had suffered greatly. The joy of Pandi Mahadevi and the great minister surpassed the joy of the king who was cured of his fever and regained health.

Therefore, their joys were mentioned first. Just as when a sick child recovers, the mother’s joy upon seeing its well-being is felt before the child’s, we see this even in the natural order of the world.

Therefore, after first narrating the joy of Pandi Mahadevi and Kulachirai Nayanar, Sekkizhar Peruman then narrates the king’s actions. All of the king’s fevers, both those that came and went, and those that lingered in his left side, had subsided. The fever of delusion, which was the root cause of his bodily fever, also subsided. The fever of past severe karma, which was its cause, also subsided. These were all interconnected. These were the gross and subtle causes and effects.

Once all his fevers subsided, the Pandya king attained supreme bliss. The supreme bliss mentioned here refers to the bliss of liberation. This is because this very Pandya king will transform into Nindraseer Nedumaran, becoming one of the sixty-three Nayanmars, and as Nindraseer Nedumaran Nayanar, he will attain the state of a jivanmukta, liberated from rebirth and achieving supreme bliss. Sekkizhar Peruman alludes to this historical detail here. He states that the king attained supreme bliss. In reality, the removal of illness is a separate experience, and the experience of joy is separate.

Since illness obstructs the experience of joy, the removal of illness aids the enjoyment of bliss.

Therefore, the removal of illness is metaphorically referred to as having gained joy, even though the removal of illness is distinct from the attainment of joy. The Pandya king has now experienced the removal of illness. He will surely attain supreme bliss after receiving spiritual instruction from Thirugnanasambandha Peruman on the banks of the Vaigai. Sekkizhar Peruman confidently states here that the king attained supreme bliss. Srimad Madhava Sivagnana Munivar, in his Sivagnana Mapadiyam, explains that worldly pleasure, which is the experience of the mind deeply comprehending objects of enjoyment, is ‘sitrinpam’ (minor bliss), while deeply comprehending the manifestation of Shivathvam (Shiva’s nature) through spiritual wisdom is ‘perinpam’ (supreme bliss). He thus clarifies the distinction between ‘sitrinpam’ and ‘perinpam’.

Having shed all his fevers, the Pandya king. The Pandya king, with his hands clasped above his head, worships Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Earlier, we saw the Pandya king worshipping Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in his mind.

Now, having recovered, he worships with both hands raised. He says, “I have found peace by clinging to the feet of Gnanasambandha, who came to alleviate the severe illness before the Jains, who have no sense of honor.” Just as a furious elephant, freed from its bonds, charges forward, the Pandya king, who had been bound by the doctrines of the Jains, is now liberated from those shackles.

Now, the Pandya king comes forward directly and expresses the truth in this manner, causing all the Jains to fear. They feared when they saw that all the magical powers they possessed had completely lost their strength.

Now they ponder how to achieve victory and search for a way to succeed. Sekkizhar Peruman describes the thoughts of the Jains at that time in this Thiruppadal, saying, “Seeing the Saivite youth, through the victory of his words, and the fragrant garland of sweet words, remove the fever of that trickster, they thought among themselves that argument was useless.” The Jains witnessed that the fever of the Pandya king was completely cured by the Thiruppathigam of the Saivite youth, the young saint, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Therefore, the Jains directly witnessed that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s pathigam, the garland of words, worked such miracles, curing the fever. Hence, they thought that they could not defeat Thirugnanasambandha Peruman through religious debate based on logic. ‘Tharkavatham’ means to establish one’s own position.

So, they realized the truth that they could no longer defeat Thirugnanasambandha Peruman through such debates.

Therefore, they thought to themselves, “Now we will try to win in fire and water.” Fire and water are both inanimate objects. The Jains believed they could control the inanimate power of fire and water with the spiritual power of their mantras. They mention both fire and water here. If they truly had faith in their religion and their mantras, they would have mentioned only one.

But here, they want to win in both fire and water. This shows that they doubted if they could win with fire alone.

So, they included water. This is because they had previously seen that the fire they had unleashed through their mantras on the Thirumadam where the young saint was staying had failed to harm him and had lost its strength.

Therefore, they had doubts about fire. But even after knowing that, they included fire in their plan. This is because the fire ordeal they were now planning, the ‘Analavatham,’ was not to be directed at the young saint, but rather they needed to demonstrate their ability to control the inanimate power of fire with their mantraic power. They also failed to realize the truth that the fire, which had previously not obeyed their command, became the fever and afflicted the Pandya king when the young saint commanded it. That is why they decided to combine fire and water, and to overcome by controlling the inanimate power of fire and water with their mantraic power through the two debates, ‘Analavatham’ (fire ordeal) and ‘Punalavatham’ (water ordeal). The Jains plan this.

While they are still contemplating, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman addresses them, saying, “You should speak about the truths of your religion.” Earlier, before the fever was cured, when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived, the Jains, enraged, surrounded and belittled him. Even then, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman used these same words. Due to the commotion at that time, the debate did not take place.

Now, after the Pandya king’s fever is cured, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman suggests resuming the debate on religious truths from where it left off. Let us press on with our contemplation.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 172 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periyapuranam, Part 719, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, by Deivasekkizhar Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman initially challenged the Jains to a doctrinal debate, asking them to present the truths of their religion.

However, the queen intervened, saying that if the Jains were truly capable, they should speak after the king’s illness was cured.

Thus, according to the king’s command, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman first undertook the task of curing the illness and succeeded.

Therefore, after his initial invitation was interrupted, the young saint now called upon the Jains again to continue the religious debate. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the supreme spiritual teacher, invited them to declare the truth that their religion could not stand before the true religion of Saivism, thereby guiding the world towards salvation. He issued this invitation so that the world might come to know this truth and attain liberation.

At that time, minor religions, with their limited doctrines and worship of minor deities, had confused the world by differing from Saivism, which recognizes Shiva, the primordial cause and ultimate deity, as the supreme God and the repository of all ultimate truths. This confusion led to a proliferation of falsehoods, a decline in Vedic practices, and a diminishing of Saivite principles, with the significance of sacred ash not being fully understood. To rectify this situation and to establish the true standing of all religions. It is the duty of the spiritual teacher to accurately inform and define them.

Therefore, the young saint undertook this task only after consulting with and receiving the permission of Lord Chokkanatha of Alavaay. For these reasons, the young saint invited the Jains to speak about the truths of their religion. In this world, Saivism, which embraces the tenets of many religions that appear to be contradictory, and thus shows these religions as progressive steps without conflicting with any of them, does not hate, oppose, or destroy any religion.

However, why are refutation of other doctrines and religious debates present here? They exist for self-preservation and to reveal the truth as it is. We must understand that the young saint’s invitation to the Jains for a religious debate was out of compassion to enlighten them, who were obstructing Saivism and confusing the world with their falsehoods, and to guide this world to salvation. The subsequent history of the Jains being executed on stakes falls under the category of royal justice, a form of punitive justice implemented by the king. There is no connection between the young saint’s invitation to a religious debate and the king’s subsequent implementation of that punitive justice system. The Jains refused the young saint’s invitation to a religious debate and chose a debate based on direct experience.

They agreed to conduct a debate based on direct experience, and if they lost, they would be impaled.

Thus, the Jains brought about their own destruction through their actions and words. This matter of royal justice will be explained in detail later when that historical event unfolds.

In this way, the young saint invites the Jains to engage in a debate by presenting the truths of their religion. In response, the Jains state that debating the truth of a doctrine is an auditory matter.

Therefore, a debate that can be seen with the eyes is better, and they agree to such a debate. The king replies to the Jains with a sarcastic remark, saying, “When my entire body was burning with fever, you could not even alleviate it slightly; you failed.

“So, what debate do you have left?” The king’s tone implies, “Why do you need a debate when you have already failed?” However, the Jains take this as an inquiry into what debate they wish to engage in and respond. They propose an ‘Analavatham’ (fire ordeal), where both parties write the tenets of their religion on a palm-leaf manuscript and place it in a blazing fire. The manuscript that remains unburnt will prove the truth of its religion. The Jains propose this fire ordeal to the king. The Pandya king attempts to respond. Before he can speak, the young saint begins to speak.

“The young saint tells the Jains, “The method you suggested is very good. You say that if the leaf placed in the fire remains unburnt, it will prove the truth of the religious tenets written on it. I accept this challenge. In the presence of the Pandya king, we will conduct the debate as you have suggested and decide the outcome. Come!” The young saint says this before the king can reply to the Jains.

“This is because the Jains had challenged them to a debate. If the king were to try to prevent them from doing so, it would not be fair. If the Jains were invited to a debate and then refused, it would also imply that those who refused were not victorious.

“Therefore, the young saint, realizing that the king now understood the truth and would not agree to the Jain’s debate, informed the Jains that he accepted the challenge before the king could reply. He did not stop at curing the fever in the Pandya king’s body, but rather, by showing all possible ways for the Jains to agree to a religious or magical debate. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, with the intention that the world would be freed from the illusion of Jainism, that the harm done to Saivism would vanish, and that the light of sacred ash would shine, offered his response before the king could reply to the Jains. He challenged the Jains to a debate according to their own principles. The verse states, “Before the king could speak, the young saint said, ‘It is good what you said; if the leaf placed in the fire wins, you said the truth of the matter is real; then come before the king with the strong trunked elephant.’” Thus, when the young saint spoke, the king ordered his attendants to create a fire in the royal court. The 779th verse states: “As the opposing Jains arrived in unequal numbers, at the command of the guardian of Sanbai, whose fame was incomparable, the king, whose vast army was beyond description, ordered his servants to prepare a burning fire in the royal assembly.” In this verse, Deivasekkizhar Peruman praises Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as “Oppil Vanpugazh Sanbayar,” meaning the incomparable glorious one from Sanbai.

“Even though the king initially refused, he eventually agreed to what the young saint said. Such was the incomparable glory of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The term “Vanpugazh” (glorious fame) refers to his generosity, indicating that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, out of compassion for the Jains and the people of this world, bestowed grace without reservation.

“Thus, Deivasekkizhar Peruman praises Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as “Oppil Van Pugazh Sanbayar Kavalalar,” the guardian of Sanbai with incomparable glory. Accepting Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s words, the king commands that a good fire be made in the royal court. That court, just as the king reformed and understood the truth of Saivism, also reformed.

“Therefore, it was a reformed court, and a court that stood as a place for the world to witness and be reformed by this fire ordeal. It was customary for great matters to be decided before the king’s court.

“Accordingly, the king commanded his servants to make a good, hot fire in that royal court. The 780th verse describes: “The commanded men gathered firewood, arranged it, and lit the fire; the smoke rose, then vanished, and the fierce, burning fire god manifested his light; and the master of the three Tamils, seeking wisdom, arrived.” The men commanded by the king immediately brought cut firewood and arranged it in the royal court to create a fire. The fire began to burn, first releasing smoke, then emanating light.

“After the smoke dissipated, the fierce fire god revealed his light. The king had received the diksha of Thirugnanasambandha’s divine gaze, meditation, and touch, and had adorned sacred ash.

“Therefore, the king, having achieved the balance of good and bad karma, was destined to receive the fruits of his past penance.

“Thus, according to the pure thoughts of the king, the fire god appeared in that royal court. The young saint, the master of the three Tamils, approached the fire.

“Let us proceed with our contemplation.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 173 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periyapuranam, Part 720, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam, by Deivasekkizhar Peruman. The young saint stands before the fire prepared by the Pandya king in the royal court. Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing: “He praised the good arrangement of the melodious Thiruppathigams, which he had composed declaring that the Lord with the red-eyed bull is the only truth. He bowed, saying that our Lord is the Supreme Being, and with his hand, he took the manuscripts to his head and untied the protective cords.” This is the 781st verse. The Thiruppathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman were written down on palm-leaf manuscripts and collected.

These are referred to as the ‘Thiruppathiga Nanmurai’ (good order of Thiruppathigams). It is recorded that Sambandha Charanalar, the maternal uncle of the young saint, was the one who wrote down and carried the palm-leaf manuscripts of the Thiruppathigams as they were composed.

Thus, all the Thiruppathigams composed by the young saint so far were written on palm-leaf manuscripts and carried by the young saint’s entourage. Sekkizhar Peruman here names this collection ‘Thiruppathiga Nanmurai’.

Here, ‘Thirumurai’ is the traditional name given to the collection of Thevaram hymns. It is the customary practice of Saivite scholars to refer to all twelve Saivite divine scriptures as ‘Thirumurai’. Referring to or calling other texts by the name ‘Thirumurai’ is an incorrect practice. It is also a tradition. Such a Thiruppathiga Nanmurai, composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and set to music by him, remains eternally youthful, new, and yields endless benefits, just as it did when he sang it. The Thiruppathigams within this Thiruppathiga Nanmurai are sacred verses revealed by the young saint, instructing the world to understand that Shiva, who possesses the red-eyed bull, is the ultimate truth.

These Thiruppathigams, composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, emphasize that Shiva is the sole primordial entity, the only truth, and nothing else holds such significance. They exemplify the principle of not praising anyone other than Shiva, thus enlightening the world with this profound truth. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships the Thirumurai manuscript containing these Thiruppathigams. He bows, stating that Shiva, our Lord, is the supreme God, the ultimate reality above all others. He then takes the Thirumurai manuscripts in his sacred hand and places them upon his sacred head.

After that, he unties the protective string of the palm-leaf manuscripts. Untying the string signifies his intention to open the manuscripts, and whichever leaf, whichever Thiruppathigam, appears is the one he will place in the fire.

Thus, the young saint unties the protective string on the manuscripts, preparing for the ordeal. This method of discerning the Lord’s will is called ‘Kairu Saatri Paarththal’ (reading by drawing lots). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman is the first to perform this. This practice has continued from that day until now, where devotees consult the Thirumurais by drawing lots. This tradition of ‘Kairu Saatri Paarththal’ is also found in the Kanda Puranam, Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam, and other texts. The belief is that whatever appears when the Thirumurais are consulted in this way reveals the Lord’s will to us.

Here, when the young saint consults the Thevaram Thirumurai by drawing lots. The pathigam that appears must remain unburnt when placed in the fire, demonstrating the true essence of Saivism. It must refute other religions and elucidate Saivite principles, thereby liberating this world.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman unties the protective cord on the Thirumurai manuscript containing the pathigams, seeking to understand the Lord’s will. Before the avatar of Sri Meykanda Deva Nayanar, his parents, on the command of their family guru, Arulnandi Sivachariyar, performed ‘Kairu Saarti Paarththal’ with the Thevaram Thirumurai of Aludaiya Pillaiyar.

At that time, the Thiruvengattu Pathigam appeared, specifically the second verse of the Thiruvengattu Thiruppathigam. The palm-leaf manuscript containing the verse, “Peyadaiyā Piriveydhum Pillaiyinuḍu Uḷḷa Ninai Ayinavē Varamberuvar Aiyura Vēṇḍā Eṉṟum Vēyaṉa Tōḻumai Paṅgaṉ Veṇkāṭṭu Mukkuḷḷa Nīr Tōy Viṉaiyār Avartaṉṉai Tōyāvām Tīviṉaiyē” (Devils will not approach, separation will occur, children will attain their wishes, no need to doubt; those who bathe in the three waters of Venkadu, where Shiva, who shares his body with Uma whose shoulders are like bamboos, resides, will not be touched by evil karma) appeared. As written in that verse, Sri Meykanda Deva Nayanar’s parents went to Thiruvengadu, prayed for a boon, bathed in the Agni Tirtham, and worshipped the Lord, receiving the boon of a child. That child was Sri Meykanda Deva Nayanar. He attained divine wisdom at the age of two, leading to the creation of the Sivagnanabodham, a sacred text that refuted other religions and established Saivism. This text became available to the Tamil world and became the cause for the world’s salvation.

That history, even its foundation, is this sacred practice of ‘Kairu Saatri Paarththal’ in the Thevaram Thirumurai. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was the first to demonstrate this during this fire ordeal. Sekkizhar Peruman describes it in the next verse: “When he himself opened the Thirumurai, which bestows the spoken truth, with his sacred ash-covered hand, it happened that the Thiruppathigam ‘Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyaal,’ praised by the Lord with four mighty shoulders and the virtuous one, appeared.” This is the next verse.

The Lord unties the cord of the Thirumurai, as the manuscript is called Thirumurai. ‘Thirumurai’ means a book that expounds truths that lead to the sacredness of liberation. The term ‘Thirumurai’ is conventionally and definitively applied to the twelve Saivite divine Tamil scriptures compiled from Aludaiya Pillaiyar’s Thevaram up to the Periyapuranam, also known as the Thiruthondar Puranam. This is the tradition of Saivite elders. Our divine Sekkizhar Peruman, by applying this tradition to the young saint’s Thevaram, initiates the usage of the term ‘Thirumurai’ here. The Thirumandiram’s verse, “Paadum Thirumurai Paarvathi,” serves as evidence that only the Lord’s compositions are called ‘Thirumurai’.

Therefore, based on this concept, Umapathi Sivachariyar explains that these collections, from the Thevaram to the Periyapuranam, which are the Lord’s own utterances, are named ‘Thirumurai’ and categorized as the twelve Thirumurais.

Therefore, it is customary not to use the name ‘Thirumurai’ for compositions by other souls. Such a Thirumurai, which contains the spoken truth, refers to the spoken form of Shiva, the ultimate reality, as conveyed by the Vedas and other scriptures, and by great sages.

Therefore, the meaning conveyed by this word is the ultimate truth. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman himself, with his sacred hand adorned with sacred ash, examines that Thirumurai, which conveys the spoken truth. He performs ‘Kairu Saatri Paarththal’ (drawing lots). Without allowing anyone else to do so, he himself takes the manuscript, places the protective string across the Thirumurai manuscripts with his sacred ash-adorned hand, and opens them to perform ‘Kairu Saatri Paarththal’. The Thiruppathigam that appeared was the Thirunallatru Thiruppathigam. It is the Thiruppathigam that praises ‘Annalaar Maruvu Nallatru’.

It is the Thiruppathigam that begins with ‘Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyaal’. That Thiruppathigam that begins with these words manifests there. When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman performs ‘Kairu Saatri Paarththal’ with his Thirumurai, the Thiruppathigam that appears is ‘Nallatru Potrum Thiruppathigam’, which means the Thiruppathigam that praises ‘Annalaar Maruvu Nallatru’. This is because this entire Thiruppathigam, composed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, praises the holy site of Thirunallatru. The concluding phrase, “Nampemuman Meyathu Nallatru,” is embedded in every verse of this pathigam by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. “Nampemuman” is the first word of the first verse at the beginning of that pathigam.

Therefore, the first word of that pathigam that emerged in this manner. The word “Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyaal” reveals the divine will to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The reason this leaf remained unburnt and fresh when placed in the fire is also attributed to the beginning of the verse, “Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyaal,” which refers to the sacred breasts of Ambikai. The sacred breasts of the Divine Mother are considered as knowledge, nectar, and givers of enjoyment to living beings. This is the significance of “Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyaal,” and it is the reason why the leaf remained unburnt and fresh in the fire. “Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyaal” refers to Uma Devi.

“Bhogam Artha” Poṇmulaiaḷ means a woman with ornamented breasts, referring to Umadevi. The first verse of that Thirunallar pathigam, “Bhogamārtha pūṇmulaiyāḷ taṉṉōṭum poṉ nakalam pāgamārtha paiṅkaṇ veḷḷēṟṟu aṇṇal paramēṭṭi āgamārtha tōḷuṭaiyan kōvaṇa āṭaiyiṉ mēl nāgamārtha nampaḷavāṉ mēyatu nallārē,” begins by placing the Goddess Ambika first. Umadevi, also known as Ambika, is the inseparable Abhinashakti of Lord Shiva. Just as the sun in the sky shines as a magnificent ball of light on its own, yet at the same time, it helps us see the objects of the world by mingling with the light of our eyes.

Similarly, the supreme being Shiva, untouched by anything, stands as self-luminous Shiva, and when that supreme being helps souls and stands by their side, it is called Shakti.

Therefore, Umadevi is eternally inseparable from Lord Shiva. This form of Ardhanareeswara, called Umaiyorubaga Murthy, is described in the sacred texts. The Vajasaneyi Samhita of the Yajur Veda praises this divine form as “Ahoratre paashve” (day and night are its sides). This mantra describes Lord Shiva, whose entire body is covered in sacred ash, as day, and the dark body of Umadevi as night. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman states, “He possesses the quality of joining day and night” and “Our Lord is day and night.” Now, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman describes Ambika, who is the Abhinashakti of Lord Shiva, as “Bhogamārtha pūṇmulaiyāḷ” (she whose adorned breasts bestow enjoyment). In the Kanda Puranam, Umadevi’s breasts are referred to as “paramabodha neerathai” (the essence of supreme knowledge).

It is here explained that both forms of knowledge, Para (higher) and Apara (lower), are the breasts of Ambika, the universal Mother.

Therefore, “Bhogamārtha pūṇmulaiyāḷ” signifies the grace-bestowing Shakti, who nourishes souls with both Apara Gnanam (worldly knowledge) and Para Gnanam (divine knowledge). It is Lord Shiva who keeps such Umadevi on the left side of his beautiful body. He is the leader who has the bull Rishabam, with its green eyes and white color, as his vehicle. He is Parametti. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praises Lord Shiva as Parametti, stating, “Bhogamārtha pūṇmulaiyāḷ taṉṉōṭum poṉ nakalam pāgamārtha paiṅkaṇ veḷḷēṟṟu aṇṇal paramēṭṭi.” Just as the Tamil Vedas declare that Parametti means “the supreme one who transcends speech and mind,” and Siddhanta Sastra describes him as “the supreme one who is beyond the comprehension of patha gnanam and pasu gnanam,” Parametti is the name that reveals the exalted state of Lord Shiva. Though in such an exalted state, Lord Shiva, for the benefit of us, the souls, mounts the bull, which embodies dharma, captivating our eyes and minds.

He, with a beautiful form, graces us by being inseparable from Umadevi, who, as the divine grace-bestowing Shakti, has both Para Gnanam and Apara Gnanam as her breasts, all to provide us with enjoyment.

Thus, that verse says, Lord Shiva, out of compassion for souls, bestows both Apara Gnanam (book knowledge) and Para Gnanam (self-realization). He has Umadevi, the divine grace-bestowing Shakti, on the left side of his golden body, which captivates both eye and mind. He, as the rider of the dharma-symbolizing bull, shines in an exalted state, transcending worldly existence as Viswadhikari. He provides knowledge to souls, wearing the Vedas as his loincloth. He, the perfectly pure one who directly activates pure Maya, is our Lord, who ever dwells in Thirunallar. This is the meaning of the first verse of the Thirunallar pathigam.

That verse appears when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman examines the Thirumurais by drawing a thread. It is understood here that the reason this pathigam, beginning with “Bhogamārtha pūṇmulaiyāḷ,” remained green and unburnt in the fire. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman then lovingly worships this pathigam.

We shall continue our contemplation.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 174 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
The Periya Puranam, Volume 721, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, written by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, recounts the history of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman drew a thread to divine, the Thirunallar pathigam appeared. The next verse states that the leader of the Kauniyar, having lovingly received that pathigam and worshipped the Lord of Thirunallar, who has a dark, venomous throat, then joyfully took the sacred palm leaf from the sacred palm leaf collection into his hand. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, lovingly accepting that pathigam, worships the Lord of Thirunallar, who has a dark, venomous throat. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman remembers that pathigam in his heart, takes it upon himself, and holds it in his hand.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships the Lord of Thirunallar, who is praised in that pathigam. That sacred leaf contains profound truth. He removes that leaf from the sacred text, takes it separately, and his body filled with joy, he holds it in his hands. The leader of the Kauniyar, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, says, “The Lord of the truthful pathigam that leads to goodness, and the name of the Lord who enslaved me, is the eternal truth that will remain.” Sekkizhar Peruman composes two verses: “He, the trickster, saw the great assembly, and rejoiced when they offered the burning fire of falsehood to him, which delighted them.”

At this point, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, taking that leaf separately from the sacred texts and holding it in his sacred hands, declares it the Lord of the truthful pathigam that leads to goodness. Taking the leaf on which the Thirunallar pathigam was written, he contemplates and praises the meaning of “Bhogamārtha pūṇmulaiyāḷ aṇṇal paramēṭṭi,” which appeared therein and revealed a divine sign. He then composes the pathigam “Thaḷirilavaḷaruḷi.” Pillaiyar states that the Lord of Thirunallar is the Lord who enslaved him, and his name is the true essence. His sacred name is written on this leaf. He wants to show the Jains that the Lord’s name is the true essence.

Therefore, this should not burn in the fire. Believing it should be so, he commands and sings the pathigam “Thaḷirilavaḷaruḷi.” Now, for this historical narrative, this pathigam “Thaḷirilavaḷaruḷi” serves as a strong internal evidence.

Therefore, before placing this leaf in the fire, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman sings the pathigam “Thaḷirilavaḷaruḷi.” This pathigam is the 87th pathigam in the third Thirumurai, set to the tune of Sadhari. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: (malai makaḷ kuḷirila vaḷaru vaṭamuḷaiyiṉaiyaḷirila vaḷaru malu nalla viḷavaḷarō ivai paḻu tēvai ciṟṟaiyaṟi vaittam vaṉa muḷai naiyōṭu ciṟi) (taru attiram mūlu kalvalagaru gnana sambandha oṟṟapam ediriṉiyil īṭa ivai kūṟiya sottariyōru patum aṟivāval puyaiyūr tūya tirucci) This sacred leaf, bearing the Thirunallar pathigam, which he held in his sacred hand, contains the name of the Lord of Thirunallar in every verse. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman praised the leaf on which a pathigam was written, stating that if this pathigam is placed in fire, it will remain green and unblemished because of its association with the mountain maiden Umadevi’s beautiful breasts. This is the truth.

He said he praised it in front of the king for placing this leaf in the fire. This is the essence of this pathigam as well. To ensure that the leaf on which this pathigam was written remains green and cool, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has used words like “thaḷir” (tender leaf) and “naḷir” (coolness) in this pathigam. This demonstrates Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s firm resolve to cool the fire into which the leaf was to be placed. We can recall here the unwavering resolve of Thirunavukkarasu Swamigal, who, standing in the midst of a lime kiln, transformed it into a pleasant pond and felt the coolness of the Lord’s sacred feet. Just as the first verse of the pathigam begins with “Bhogamārtha pūṇmulaiyāḷ” and ends with “veḷḷēṟṟu aṇṇal paramēṭṭi,” here, in the Thaḷirilavaḷaruḷi pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman refers to the Mother’s sacred breasts by saying, “because of its association with the mountain maiden’s beautiful breasts.” In the Thirunallar pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman would have praised the Mother’s breasts only in the first verse.

However, in every verse of this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman would have sung about Ambika’s breasts using the phrase “vaṉamulai” (beautiful breasts). It is because he sang about Ambika’s breasts that the Thirunallar pathigam remained green and unburnt in the fire. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman has established this reason in every verse of this pathigam, “Thaḷirilavaḷaruḷi.” Pillaiyar’s sacred hands are reddish hands, redder than the inner petals of a red lotus. They are softer than the inner petals of a red lotus. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s sacred hands are very red because of their act of distributing the sacred ash, which is the essence of Shaiva truth. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman takes that leaf with the Thirunallar pathigam in his sacred hand.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman places that sacred leaf in the fire for all the members of the Pandian’s great assembly to see. Why does he sing the Thaḷirilavaḷaruḷi pathigam and then place it? In the past, in the Amarneethi Nayanar Purana, we saw how Amarneethi Nayanar recited the five letters and balanced himself on the scale, and how Thirunavukkarasu Peruman praised the sacred ash.

Similarly, when embarking on a great task, it is the tradition and custom of great individuals to recite the name of Shiva.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, If he praises and sings a pathigam and then puts this leaf into the fire, it is because he is not reciting the five letters but a pathigam. The five-letter mantra (Panchaksharam) is also a name of Shiva.

Here, Pillaiyar praised and entered with a name. Considering that this pathigam praised the name of the Lord of Thirunallar, not just Shiva’s name in general, he sang it and placed it in the fire. He put the leaf in the fire, singing the pathigam “Thaḷirilavaḷaruḷi,” which conveys the idea that Shiva’s name is the eternal truth, and to show the Jains that even if these are placed in fire, there will be no harm; this is the truth. The minds of the Jains, who were without clothes, were burnt and destroyed. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who came to redeem this world, understood the truth of the divine and incarnated to save this world. Pillaiyar, the leader of the Kauniyar, came to the Pandian kingdom to save it through this debate, and thus the world.

He joyfully understood that the name of the Lord of Thirunallar would not be harmed by fire and would bestow enjoyment upon the people of this world.

Therefore, he joyfully placed that sacred leaf in the fire. What happened when it was placed in the fire? The divine Sekkizhar Peruman then sang about it. The five elements—water, fire, wind, and ether—along with the sun, the moon, and the soul, constitute the eight forms (Ashtamurthi) of the Lord.

Therefore, that pathigam has Lord Shiva, who is such an Ashtamurthi, as its subject. Fire is one of these Ashtamurthis. Murthi means body. The one who lives as the soul within that body is the Murthiman. Fire is one of those Ashtamurthis, isn’t it?

Therefore, that fire is the body of the Lord.

The Lord is the soul of it. Without the soul, the body has no action. The body cannot function independently. The king is positioned before it. The soul is its life. These eight forms are the body of that living soul.

Fire is one of those eight forms.

Therefore, that leaf was green. It appeared because the leaf is the soul and the fire is the body.

Therefore, when the soul entered the body, the leaf settled there and shone green. Even before that, the fire was like that. Isn’t God all-pervading? So even before that, the fire was with life.

But the body, which is fire, not only in that extent, but including fire, now contains the Murthiman who has all the Ashtamurthis as his body.

Therefore, like God, that leaf not only did not burn in the fire but also shone green, gaining that existence. Water and air are also among those eight forms.

Therefore, the Ashtamurthi, which contains fire, water, and air, entered the essence. Didn’t it contain the fire of the deluge, the waters of the deluge, and the wind of the deluge?

Therefore, when the great fire, which contains the fire of the deluge, was there, it was able to quell this small fire. Thiruppugazh says that it can even burn fire.

Therefore, when the fire, which is the form that contains the fire of the deluge, was there, it happened that way. Lord Shiva, who has the mountain maiden in one part of his body, appears as an Ashtamurthi in this manner. When the leaf had to be placed in the fire, the song “Bhogamārtha pūṇmulaiyāḷ poṉ nakalam pāgamārtha paramēṭṭi” was written. Pillaiyar understood, through divine grace, that it was flawless.

Therefore, with that understanding, for “muḷaiyāl pāgamārtha paramēṭṭi,” he sang, “If placed in fire, it will be flawless because of the mountain maiden’s breasts.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman realized with divine grace that there would be no harm in placing this pathigam, which speaks of the mountain maiden’s breasts, in the fire.

Thus, he sang the pathigam “Thaḷirilavaḷaruḷi.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman realized that there would be no harm in placing this pathigam, which speaks of the mountain maiden’s breasts, in the fire.

Thus, he sang the pathigam “Thaḷirilavaḷaruḷi.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman realized that there would be no harm in placing this pathigam, which speaks of the mountain maiden’s breasts, in the fire.

Thus, he sang the pathigam “Thaḷirilavaḷaruḷi.” Due to its nature, that leaf remained green in the fire.

Here, the Peruman states that the leaf’s quality of not being damaged was due to the power of that pathigam. How did he perceive that power in the leaf? He saw the leaf and found the phrase “Pūṇmulaiyāḷ pāgam uṭaiya paramēṭṭi” (Paramēṭṭi, who has the ornamented-breasted one in his part). Within it, he saw the Lord of Thirunallar, who is its meaning. Such contemplation is knowing. And such a command is a mantra.

He made those actions become their true nature. “Muḷaiyōṭu kula vaḷiṉ” (if it associates with the breast) is a form of contemplation. The name itself is truth. “If placed in the fiery pit, there is no harm to these” is the mantra of command. How did it become a mantra? Tolkappiyam states that a mantra is a secret word uttered by a perfect sage.

By taking that leaf and meditating and sanctifying it eleven times through the eleven verses of the pathigam, he infused it with divine power, thus giving the leaf that quality. Sivagnanabodham, in its twelfth sutra, third adhikaranam, second example verse, says: “Just as one sees fire in a log by a single mantra, so too does one perceive the form that is not truly there, yet appears as such to those who see it that way.” According to this, we can reflect upon and understand the truth of Sivagnanabodham, which prescribes Shiva worship in stationary objects. Since Shiva manifested here, that leaf, being the very form of Lord Shiva, remained unharmed and shone green within the fire. As per Thirumantiram, “The great mad elephant hid the tree; the great mad elephant hid itself in the tree. The primordial elements hid the transcendent; the primordial elements hid themselves in the transcendent,” the name of the Lord of Thirunallar itself became manifest, and the words and the leaf that were there disappeared, as if they had never existed.

Therefore, it remained green.

Thus, the divine grace of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman manifested there. Our contemplation continues.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 175 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
The Periya Puranam, Volume 722, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, written by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, recounts the history of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirumandira Thiruvakku states, “There is no deity equal to Shiva; there is none equal to him here.” Saivism classifies religions into four categories: purappuram (outermost), puram (outer), akappuram (inner-outer), and akam (innermost). Among them, the principles of Harugata Jainism are unclear and confusing. They state that there are seven substances, beginning with Jeevan. When asked if these seven substances exist or not, they respond with “It exists, it does not exist, it exists and does not exist,” using terms like Asti-Nasti, thereby adopting the Aniekantavada (multi-faceted reality) as their principle.

They would not agree with the Vedas and Sivagamas, they were contrary.

Therefore, our spiritual teachers, upon seeing this, wanted to prevent these Jain principles from deluding the souls of this world. They desired that the souls of this world should find salvation by realizing the truths expounded in the Vedas and Sivagamas, which are the true and noble paths. For this reason, they refuted and condemned these heterodox religions, rejecting other doctrines and establishing the glory of Saivism. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was born for this purpose. In the fire debate, the leaf bearing the name of Lord Thirunallar, on which the Thirunallar pathigam was written, remained green.

Now, the Jains are those whose minds are clouded by illusion, who believe falsehood to be truth. This stems from the nature of their religious tenets. Such Jains took the leaf on which they had written their religious principles, which they held in their hands. They cast it into a intensely burning fire. Even as they cast it into the fire, they were filled with doubt and worry, wondering if it would remain unburnt or if it would survive. Only if this leaf remained unburnt would they be able to control the king and the country as before in the Pandian kingdom.

If this leaf does not survive, we will bring disrepute to our religion, they thought, and with fear and anxiety, they cast the leaf in doubt. As soon as the Jains threw their leaf into the fire, it turned black. It vanished like cotton catching fire. The Jains, who were worried with doubt about whether the leaf would survive before putting it in the fire, now saw that the leaf did not survive but turned black and disappeared. They were worried.

Therefore, they would no longer receive the benefits of their association with the king. They would lose all those benefits. Reflecting on all this, their spirits sagged. Even though their spirits sagged, they still held the peacock feather in their hands, because even when they realized that their religion was false and not the true religion, they stubbornly refused to accept the truth and clung to their belief that it was their religion.

At the same time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, Pillaiyar, the embodiment of knowledge, took the green leaf from the fire that was lit in the Pandian assembly. He took that leaf from the fire with his sacred hands. All these days, this assembly had watched in wonder as that leaf remained green. That leaf shone with freshness and novelty. The leaf on which the pathigam was written shone green. The meaning written on that leaf shone with novelty.

Unlike other objects that fall into the fire, this leaf remained fresh and unwithered.

Therefore, this Thirunallar pathigam, which begins with “Bhogamārtha pūṇmulaiyāḷ,” is known as the “Pachchai Pathigam” (Green Pathigam). Nambiyandar Nambigal Swamigal, in his “Aludaiya Pillaiyar Thiruthogai,” mentions this Pachchai Pathigam as “Peruman who explains the meaning” and praises Aludaiya Pillaiyar as the one who composed sixteen thousand verses. The novelty there is that the meaning written on that leaf, which was previously understood in a general sense concerning the general nature of God, is now, in the context of this historical event, specially understood and worshipped in relation to the specific nature of God.

Therefore, it was new. The leaf not only remained undestroyed but also became greener and newer than before.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman shows it there for all to see. He then places that leaf back into the sacred text, in the same way and in the same position as it was before. He once again places and arranges this leaf in the sacred text, fitting it in the same manner and order as he had removed it from the manuscript. Seeing this, the king now angrily addresses the Jains and tells them to show the leaf they had placed. The Jains saw that the leaf they had cast into the fire had been destroyed. Nevertheless, they approached the fire to retrieve their leaf.

At that moment, the fire burned them. Seeing this, the Jains retreated from the fire. The king then observes this. He is a king who does not deviate from justice.

Therefore, even after seeing the Jains defeated in this manner, to prevent them from suffering, he ordered the fire to be extinguished. He brought water to quench the red fire. This action reflects the king’s justice. His action was filled with both righteousness and compassion. After it was extinguished, the Jains looked there. There was ash that had burned, and there were pieces of unburnt wood left from the fire.

The Jains could not find or retrieve the leaf they had thrown in. There were only charred ashes and leftover pieces of wood. The Jains searched to see if any part was left unburnt, but there was none.

Therefore, the Jains stood there in dismay, unable to do anything further. They stood wringing their hands, unable to do anything else. Seeing this, the king, with a wry smile, said, “Look at that ash. You who came to explain the true meaning, taking falsehood as your support, depart!” Earlier, when they could not cure his left-sided ailment, the king had told them to leave him.

Now, even after their defeat, the king again tells them to leave. The king asks mockingly, “Earlier, I was saved from the fiery disease by Pillaiyar, and you were defeated in that debate.

“Now, the leaf you put in the fire did not endure; it burned. Do you still think you haven’t lost?” The Jains, not understanding the subtle meaning of the Pandian king’s mocking smile, and with their minds still unclear, the Jains continued to speak. “We have debated twice; we will debate a third time. In that third debate, we will win at least once.

“So, we have debated twice, and now we will have a third debate. In that, we will show our true skill,” say the Jains. There is also a worldly custom of trying something three times if one fails.

“So, these Jains also say they will prove themselves. Those who lose often say they will surely win.

“Similarly, these Jains also say this. They had already lost twice, and those were defeats. If we consider there to be three debates in total, these Jains had already lost in two debates.

“Therefore, they had already reached the state of defeat. Nevertheless, they said they would try a third time and that they would win. They said this with the intention of proving at least a part of their religion, if not entirely. If they were to win in that third debate, they would show that there was some truth in their religion, and thereby once again ensnare the royal court and the king. This conspiracy was evident. Hearing this, the Pandian king said, “You have lost twice, but you still have that desire.

“Even if you have a third debate, nothing will come of it.” However, the leader of Sirkazhi, whose body shone with the beauty of sacred ash and who was renowned, accepted the third challenge posed by the Jains and inquired about what the third debate would be. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, though victorious, was renowned for his compassion towards those who had lost. The saying, “The praise of one who speaks will rest upon the giver,” comes to mind. Even after the Jains had lost again, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman asked what the next debate would be. Even after the king rejected this third debate, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman accepted and inquired about the third debate.

“Thus, Pillaiyar, due to his immense compassion even towards those who had lost, shone with profound fame. Just as it was explained that fame at the place of “Iraivan Porul Ser Pugazh” (God’s fame that joins with meaning) is the true fame that is filled with divine qualities, such profound fame shone in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman shone there as the epitome of fame.

“Let us go on contemplating.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 176 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
The Periya Puranam, Volume 723, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, written by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, recounts the history of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman inquired about the third debate. In response, the Jains explained the nature of the third debate. Both parties should write their religious truths on a leaf, affirming the unchanging nature of the ultimate reality.

Then, these leaves should be placed in a flowing river. The leaf that does not drift away with the current but remains at the spot where it was placed, the one who placed such a leaf would be declared the victor, the Jains stated. These Jains said that when the leaf is placed in the river, it should not flow away with the water but remain in the same place where it was dropped.

However, in this water debate, Pillaiyar performs a great divine miracle for all the people of this world to see. What is it? The leaf written by Pillaiyar not only remains in the river current but also travels against the direction of the river current.

We will now see this history in detail through the words of Sekkizhar Swamigal. When the Jains said this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously said, “That is good, we will do it.” He accepted the third debate. When the Jains spoke, the victorious king, well-versed in fame, said, “We will do that, it is good,” and the spear-wielding minister said, “Whatever else they do, they are defeated anyway; let them do what they want to do.” When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously accepted, that it not only stayed in the current of the river but also moved against the direction of the river.

We will now see that history in detail through the words of Sekkizhar Swamigal. When the Jains said this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously said, “That is good, we will do it.” He accepted the third debate. Sekkizhar Swamigal states in his verse: “When the Jains said that the leaf should remain in the same place when placed in the river, the King of glorious fame graciously said, ‘That is good, we will do it.’ Then the spear-wielding minister said, ‘Whatever else they do, they are defeated anyway; let them do what they want to do.’” When Thirugnanasambandha Peruman graciously accepted, Then Kulachirai Nayanar comes and stands beside Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. He stands near the king, a little distance away. As Thirukkural says, “Like those who warm themselves by fire, neither too close nor too far,” an minister should neither approach the king too closely nor remain too far away. Just as someone warming themselves by a fire would stand at a suitable distance, neither too close to get burned nor too far to feel no warmth, so too should an minister be.

In accordance with Thirukkural, Kulachirai Nayanar, being a great minister, stands at a proper distance, neither approaching nor receding from the king, and speaks.

At the same time, the great minister resolves to put an end to this ongoing debate by the Jains. He believed that these Jains, having lost this third time, should not continue to prolong the debate with arguments for a fourth, fifth, and sixth time. A limit must be set, a decision made. With this duty in mind, as a government official, the great minister approached the king and said, “Those who lose in this upcoming debate should have their fate decided and announced immediately after this debate.” The great minister said that it should be decided now what the losers should do and what punishment should be meted out to them. Hearing this, the Jains became angry at the great minister. The next verses state that the Jain ascetics who heard this, overcome by surging anger due to jealousy, said, “If we ourselves perish in this solitary debate through our own verbal failings, then this king will hoist us onto the impaling stake.” The minister, the great elder, was an object of anger for these Jains.

Anger arose from jealousy. Unable to tolerate the prosperity of the Saivites, the Jains harbored envy, which is called alukkaru. Thirukkural states, “Alukkaru Udayarkku athu salum onnar vazhukkaiyum kedu enpathu” (Envy is enough to destroy those who possess it; it is also the ruin of their enemies). Thirukkural also says, “Alukkaru ena oru pavi thiruchchethru theeyozhi uyththuvidum” (The sinner called envy will lead one to utter destruction).

In this way, Thiruvalluvadeva Nayanar explains how those with this envious nature will be destroyed by their own envy.

Therefore, following that ancient saying, the Jains here, out of envy, bring about their own ruin. Those Jains themselves declare with their own mouths, “If we lose in this debate, then this king, this Pandya king, will hoist us onto the cruel impaling stake.” In the same manner, the Jains lost the water debate and were impaled.

Thus, the reason for the Jains being impaled was not the minister, nor the king, nor பிள்ளையார். It was a consequence they brought upon themselves, which we clearly understand here. They declared, “If we lose the debate, this king will impale us, and we agree to that.” The Jains declared this. Hearing their words, the Pandya king, ruler of Podhigai Malai, said to the Jains, “You have spoken thus in the heat of your anger, forgetting your own deeds.” He then commanded, “Go and gracefully place your palm-leaf manuscripts, containing the essence of truth, into the flowing waters of the Vaigai River.” As the king spoke, பிள்ளையார் descended from the golden throne where he was seated and mounted his pearl palanquin, setting off. The king then followed him on horseback, behind Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who was a great benefactor.

The Jains, who lacked the ability to truly understand and live by the truth, continued on their way. They proceeded with confusion in their minds. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, mounted on a pearl palanquin, departed from the palace and made his way towards the Vaigai River. In the main streets of Madurai city, the king followed Thirugnanasambandha Peruman on horseback. As Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived in his pearl palanquin, a multitude of people surged through the streets of Madurai city to witness the sight. The next verses state, “Thennavan veppu theerndhu sezhmani koyil neengi pinnura anaindapodhu Pillaiyar perugum selvam Manniya Madurai moothur marugil vandhu arulakkandu Thunniya madhar maindhar thozhudhu verinaiya sonnar.” When பிள்ளையார் arrived in the main streets of Madurai city, after the king’s fever was cured and he left the rich gem-studded temple, seeing the increasing splendor of பிள்ளையார் in the ancient city of Madurai, throngs of men and women worshipped him and offered praises.

The city of Madurai is praised by Sekkizhar Peruman as “perugum selvam manniya Madurai moothoor,” meaning a prosperous and ancient city. Madurai is the ancient city, overflowing with the wealth of grace, which is the benevolent gaze of Angayarkann Ammaiyar. This quality of being ever-present and growing can be seen even today. Thiruppallandu says that something is “pandum endrum endrum ulla porul” (a thing that was, is, and always will be), and this applies to the ancient city of Madurai. In the streets of such an ancient Madurai, crowds of people surged. As பிள்ளையார் arrived in his pearl palanquin, followed by the king on horseback, and the queen behind him, and the minister on one side, and on the other side, eight thousand Jains, the street of Madurai city was resplendent.

Thus, the streets of Madurai city gleamed. Seeing Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arriving in his palanquin, all the people cheered and were filled with enthusiasm. பிள்ளையார் had cured the Madurai king’s fever and had won the fire debate. These two events had spread throughout Madurai city very quickly.

Therefore, a large crowd had gathered there, wishing to behold பிள்ளையார், who had performed these two acts of grace. Even though there was a large crowd, Sekkizhar Peruman sings that it was the women who were at the forefront to worship and behold Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. All these people, who had until now believed in the alien religion. The people, who had previously trusted the Jain religion, now, through the gracious acts of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, have abandoned their belief in that alien religion. Their previous allegiance to Saivism in Madurai has been restored, and they now stand worshiping and beholding பிள்ளையார். This is because the adherence to Jainism was a temporary phase for the people of Madurai.

Their inherent nature was Saivism.

Therefore, after a brief period of detachment, they quickly re-embraced it.

Thus, the people of Madurai, especially the women, came forward to behold Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

At that time, all the people praised Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. Sekkizhar Peruman captures their praise in seven verses, which we will continue to reflect upon.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 177 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
The Periya Puranam, Part 724, “Vambarav Varivandu Serukkam,” composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, describes the puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives in a pearl palanquin in the streets of Madurai city. All the people behold him and praise him. Some say, “Look at this Nayanar, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar, who cured the fever of the Pandya king and relieved our suffering.” Those who recognized Thirugnanasambandha Peruman told those who did not, “This is our leader, known by the name Gnanasambandhar; behold him.” There were some who had only heard the name Thirugnanasambandhar. Many people stood there who had never before seen the sacred form of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman.

Therefore, those who had already beheld Thirugnanasambandha Peruman introduced him to all those who were seeing him for the first time. பிள்ளையார் had arrived in Madurai the previous day.

At that time, only a few had beheld Thirugnanasambandha Peruman when he came to the temple, and later when he went from there to the monastery.

Then, that night, when the Jains’ evil deed caused the fever, and பிள்ளையார் entered the temple and then the palace for that reason, only a few beheld him.

At that time, the Jain religion was a dense darkness that deluded three types of people. In that state, very few beheld Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The news that the fever was cured by பிள்ளையார்’s grace and the sacred ash, and that the palm-leaf manuscript placed by பிள்ளையார் in the fire remained unburnt, asserting the superiority of Saivism, and that the Jains were defeated in both these instances, and even after the king had ostracized them, they were coming for a third and final time to see the manuscript and be impaled – all this news spread throughout Madurai city like wildfire carried by the wind.

Therefore, a huge crowd of people had gathered to witness the glorious arrival of பிள்ளையார். Among these, as mentioned before. Only a few knew பிள்ளையார் by name and had seen his sacred form.

Now, they were introducing பிள்ளையார் to the many who had not seen him before. They explained his greatness, the pathigam he recited, the humiliation of the Jains he defeated, and other things.

In this way, those who had previously beheld Thirugnanasambandha Peruman were introducing him to the people who were now seeing him for the first time. As this happened, Sekkizhar Peruman presented all the praises that the people offered to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman in the following six verses. The verse begins, “Panarum kudhalai seiya pavalavay Pillaiyar thamm manaseer Thennadhu vazha vandhu annaindhar enbar” (Some say that பிள்ளையார், with a sweet, lisping, coral-like mouth, came to bless the great land of the South). Some say that பிள்ளையார், with a coral-like mouth uttering lisping words fragrant with milk, came here to bless the great and glorious Pandya kingdom.

Here, “manaseer nadu” refers to the Pandya kingdom. “Manaseer” means great glory. The Pandya kingdom is ancient, and the saying “Thenpandi nadu theli” (The southern Pandya land is clear) is a sacred utterance praised by great sages. The Pandya kingdom has the special glory of having the Lord, who is easily accessible to all beings, shining with immense grace and clarity. The glory praised by such great people, and the meaning of “manam” here, can be taken as greatness and the special quality of the Lord’s easy grace. This glorious Pandya kingdom, the land of the Southern King, came to thrive.

By its prosperity, they too gained benefit, and thus, everyone praised Thirugnanasambandha Peruman as the one who came to bless the Pandya kingdom. All the people spoke of how their Jain gurus had lost the fire debate to him. Some spoke of how they had seen with their own eyes that the sacred ash of Lord Shiva, with his matted locks, was the true reality. Some spoke of the beauty of பிள்ளையார் arriving in a palanquin made of pure gold, studded with brilliant pearls, saying, “What beauty!” Seeing this sight. Some said, “Our eyes have lived a full life seeing this.” Some said, “These Jain gurus are inherently evil; only evil came from them, and now we have seen it.” Some said, “The Supreme God is the Lord enshrined in the Thiruvalavai temple; rejoice in seeing him.” Some said, “To know the ancient Lord Shiva with three eyes is true wisdom.” Some said, “The Vedas and the sacred ash will spread everywhere and permeate all.” Some said, “The Lord in Thiruvalavai is Namban; go and see him.” Namban means one who is worthy of trust and refuge. This name, Namban, is attributive.

The name Nambi refers to Lord Shiva. The Thiruppathigam “Nambi” illustrates this. Others who trust and take refuge in lesser deities may obtain minor benefits from them, and such people do exist.

However, Shivagnana Siddhiyar states that other deities suffer, die, are born, and create further karma.

Similarly, the women of Madurai, seeing that the Arhat god, who had until now protected and benefited the Jains, was now abandoning them in the middle of a river, spoke thus: “The Lord of Thiruvalavai is Namban, worthy of trust and refuge.” They praised him, saying, “To know him is the ultimate wisdom, the wisdom of experience; he is the most ancient of all ancient things,” as the people understood and spoke. The people, looking at the Jains who were approaching on the other side, said, “Look how the faces of these Jains have withered!” Some spoke of how the cruel deceptions of the Jains had been destroyed. Some wondered about the change in the sharp-speared Pandya king’s allegiance to the Jain gurus. Some said, “The darkness of this cruel Jainism has departed, and now a new dawn has arrived for us all.” Some questioned, “Will those who lost in fire now win in water?” Some wondered, “Even if these Jains have hearts of iron, can they stand against this பிள்ளையார்?” Some said, “Look at the fate that awaits these Jains, who, abandoning subtle truths, only grasped coarse ones and were confined to that level.” The people say that these Jains understood only coarse matters. The Jains are those who only learned the texts that prescribe the virtues of animal dharma, but did not understand their subtle inner meaning.

The Jains do not understand sin and merit.

Therefore, these people say this. Their defeat has already been decided.

So, some say that Minister Kulachirayar has already prepared sharp impaling stakes for them. Some say that these Jains came to cast their palm-leaf manuscripts into the Vaigai River. Some wonder if a palm-leaf manuscript placed in flowing water will stop in one place without being carried away. Some speculated that பிள்ளையார், having attained supreme wisdom, could even stop those palm-leaf manuscripts. Some said, “ பிள்ளையார், whom the entire country can behold, will now arrive directly; just watch.” Generally, when an event takes place, people express such opinions.

Similarly, Sekkizhar Peruman beautifully illustrates how people were talking there. He states that பிள்ளையார் could stop the palm-leaf manuscript from flowing with the water.

Following this, another person said, “ பிள்ளையார் will arrive here shortly, and we will all see him win by stopping the manuscript in the flowing water. Look at that.” One person says, “See for yourself.” Some said, “Should the Jains be so bold as to agree that the losers must be impaled? The Jains should not have said that.” Some said, “This is befitting பிள்ளையார், who has demonstrated his gracious acts and possesses supreme grace.” Some said, “All the deeds that பிள்ளையார் has performed so far are beneficial to us.” The gracious act of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was performed with grace, untouched by negative qualities like anger. Even when the Jains set fire to Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s monastery, he did not get angry at them. Instead, he graciously blessed that the fire should go to the king who had erred in his duty.

Thirugnanasambandha Peruman possessed the grace to make the king experience his karma, cure his illness, and embrace him. Before entering the debate, he was endowed with the grace of entering the royal court only after inquiring about the divine will twice. Even there, when the king refused to give the Jains a place, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman intervened and graciously allowed the Jains to debate.

In this way, people praised the greatness of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s grace. Everyone who witnessed the Pandya king being freed from harm by the sacred ash would praise the power of Saivism.

Therefore, some urged everyone to embrace the Saivite path.

Thus, the people standing on both sides of the street spoke. There, a white umbrella with a beautiful golden handle, shining like lightning, cast its shadow from above, while பிள்ளையார், adorned in a palanquin studded with many gems, came to make the four Vedas prosper. He arrived to show the people of the Pandya kingdom the path of righteousness. As he thus arrived, many ceremonial instruments sounded.

We shall continue our reflection on this.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 178 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
The Periya Puranam, Part 725, “Vambarav Varivandu Serukkam,” composed by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, describes the puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. As Thirugnanasambandha Peruman proceeded through the streets of Madurai, ceremonial instruments sounded. The instruments praised the glories of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. The verse states, “Then thamizh vilangav vandha Thirukkalumala thon vandhan Manrullaar alitha gnana vattil vankaiyan vandhan Venru ulaga vaigaiyil velvan vandhan enru chinangal en thisai nerungiyenga.” (He who came from Thirukkalumalam to make beautiful Tamil shine has arrived. The strong-handed one who received the cup of wisdom given by those in the assembly has arrived.

He who will conquer in the Vaigai of the world has arrived, thus the ceremonial instruments resounded, filling all eight directions.) பிள்ளையார், who came from Thirukkalumalam to make beautiful Tamil shine, has arrived. The conch is still being played, heralding the arrival of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who came to illuminate southern Tamil. “Then” means beauty, so “Then Tamil” means beautiful Tamil. Beauty means to exist with eternal, unfading youth, and it also means that this Tamil, being full of knowledge, bestows an eternal and unchanging beauty leading to an affinity with Siva’s feet. This is extensively explained in the “Thiruthonda Thogai” which states “Then Tamil Payanai Ulla Thiruthonda Thogai Munpada”. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was born to spread Tamil.

The great Sekkizhar Peruman, describing Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s purpose of incarnation, states “Asaivil Sezhum Tamil Vazhake Ayal Vazhakin Thuraivalla” meaning, ‘whose unwavering rich Tamil path is adept in other traditions’. As he danced, he spoke. The conch sounds, announcing the arrival of Pillaiyar, who came to illuminate southern Tamil. The conch sounds, proclaiming the arrival of Pillaiyar, who received the golden bowl containing the Sivajgnana milk bestowed by Thillai Koothar, who dances in the assembly, and whose sacred hands grew with this grace. The conch sounds, heralding the arrival of Pillaiyar, who won the previous debates and will also win the upcoming debate by water in the Vaigai river.

Thus, the sound of these conches echoes intensely in all eight directions. The next verse is the 811th verse: “Pannmani Murasam Soozhndha Palliyam Iyamba Pinne Thennanum Theviyarum Udan Sella Thiran Sellum Pun Neri Amanar Veroor Pudai Vara Pugazhi Vendhar Manniya Vaigaiyatrrin Karaimisai Maruvandhar.” Sekkizhar Peruman, having sung about Pillaiyar’s sacred procession, now sings about the King and Queen’s procession. He also sings about the arrival of the Jain ascetics and then about Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s arrival on the banks of the Vaigai river. Pillaiyar goes ahead in a palanquin adorned with pearls, followed by the King.

The King makes his way through the street, so his musical instruments are played to mark his presence. Pillaiyar proceeds, followed by his retinue, and then the King and Queen join them. Until this point, that is, until the King’s illness was cured in the palace, the Queen and the minister had acted on their own initiative, without the King’s consent.

After that, the debate by fire took place, and now the debate by water is about to happen. Both of these debates, especially the debate by fire, occurred as a royal affair in the King’s court and presence. When royal affairs take place, the Queen must also be present.

Therefore, the Queen was present during the debate by fire in the palace court.

Similarly, now as the King comes to the banks of the Vaigai, the Queen also accompanies him. Here we can observe the tradition of the former day’s government, where royal affairs involved the King and Queen being together and acting in unison.

However, from the day the King adopted Jainism until he embraced Shaivism, it is not depicted that the King and Queen acted together. This is because the King stood apart on religious matters.

Now, both the Queen and the King are coming together.

Therefore, in these royal affairs concerning Shaivism, they are now both participating together. From today onwards, this is how it will unfold. As this sacred procession takes place, the Jains are also approaching on the other side of the street. Towards the banks of the Vaigai, during the fire debate in the King’s court, there were only a few Jain gurus.

But now, the debate by water is happening on the banks of the Vaigai.

Therefore, all eight thousand Jain ascetics are coming on one side of the Madurai street. As Pillaiyar proceeds with his devotees and retinue, the Jain ascetics, lacking the fortune to be associated with Pillaiyar and attain salvation, walk away on the other side. Pillaiyar thus makes his sacred procession through the holy street and arrives near the banks of the Vaigai river. This Vaigai river is sung by Sekkizhar Peruman as “Manniya Vaigai”. “Manniya” means permanent or established. “Mannudhal” means to be established.

It means to be established. This Vaigai river is a river established by fame, a river established by the merit of being associated with Siva. We learn from the Thiruvilayadal Puranam that the Ganga itself came as the Vaigai river at the command of the Lord for Kundotharan during the wedding of Meenakshiammayar. It was on the banks of this same Vaigai river that the Lord’s divine play of carrying soil took place. Appar Swamigal praises the Vaigai river in Thiruppoovan Thiruththāndagam, saying, “Aniyar Vaigai Thirukkottin Nindradhor Thiramum Thondrum” (The sight of the adorned Vaigai’s sacred bank will appear). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrives on the banks of such a glorious and established Vaigai river.

The King looked at the rapidly flowing river water, and the next verse states: “Aatru Neer Kadugavodum Marungura Arasan Nokki Neetrani Thigazhdhameni Niraimadhi Pillaiyarum Vetrhoru Arugar Neerum Vithitha Edu Idgiraan Thotravard Tholaar Endru Munnura Thunindhu Ittargal”. Pillaiyar and others reached the banks of the Vaigai river, went along the sandy path of the river, and arrived at a spot where the river water flowed very rapidly.

At that moment, the King looked at Pillaiyar and the Jain ascetics and said, “Pillaiyar, whose body shines with the beauty of sacred ash like a full moon, and you Jain ascetics, who are of a different form, as you both have agreed, cast your respective palm-leaf manuscripts into the river.” The Pandyan King, having attained salvation through sacred ash, was captivated by Pillaiyar’s sacred form, which was resplendent with sacred ash, considering it a magnificent form. He (Pillaiyar) is full of divine wisdom.

Now, as he is about to impart spiritual instruction to the Pandyan King, he is full of perfect wisdom and possesses all the characteristics of a guru. It is to imply this that the Pandyan King refers to Pillaiyar as “Pillaiyar, whose sacred form shines with the beauty of sacred ash like a full moon.” At the same time, he refers to the Jain ascetics as those who have a form different from that sacred form of sacred ash.

Thus, the Pandyan King instructs Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and the Jain ascetics to cast their respective palm-leaf manuscripts into the river. He says, “One who loses will not always lose”. Following this worldly wisdom, the Jain ascetics decide to cast their palm-leaf manuscript into the floodwaters of the river first.

We shall proceed with our reflection.
