Devendran created a sacred tank and worshipped here to absolve Sage Gouthama’s curse. Rama worshipped and received blessings here. All these historical events are elaborately recounted in the purana of this shrine. Since Kali resides in the rock-cut cave at the entrance of the unfinished tower (mottagopura vayil), and the deity is very fierce, this door is always kept closed.

“The purana of this shrine was composed by Thiruvarur Thiyagaraja Kavirayar. It is said that those who die in Kasi attain liberation, but Thiruppunavayil bestows Jeevan Mukti (liberation while living) by removing the sins of those who come and worship here, as stated in the Viruthapuri Mahatmiyam. The Viruthapuri Mahatmiyam is described in the Ekadasa Rudra Vaibhava Khandam of the Shiva Mahapurana. This shrine is also known by the names Indrapuram, Sathanandapuram, Vajradrumavanam, Vanamugam, Kaivalyapuram, and Viruthakasi. Among the shrines surrounding Thiruppunavayil, Thirthaandathanam is in the southeast, Paraiyathur in the northwest, Kalyana puram further northwest, Velimuthy in the west, and the shrine worshipped by Vasishtar in the north. The purana states that Viruthapureeswarar bestows grace in these places as well.

“The shrine’s purana states that Yama and his messengers will not enter the vicinity of Viruthapuri, and all who die here will attain Shivalokam. Five inscriptions from the period of the Pandya kings have been discovered at this shrine. In the inscriptions, the Lord is referred to as Thiruppunavasal Udaiya Nayanar. It also has other names such as Virathapathi, Virathakasi, Indrapuram, Brahmapuram, Vajravanam, Kaivalyagnanapuram, and Dakshina Thiruchitrambalam. This Lingamurthi is next in size only to the Brihadeeswarar in Thanjavur. Its height is nine feet, and its circumference is eight and a half feet.

“The Avudaiyar has a circumference of thirty-three feet, and the Gomukhi is three and a half feet long. In the Mahamandapam, to the south, Somaskandar, Nalvar, and Sekkizhar are seen. We learn from the puranas that on Vaikasi Punarpoosam, the flag is hoisted, on Swathi, the chariot festival takes place, and on Visagam, the Theerthavari (bathing ritual) occurs.

“Also, on Maasi Magam, the Panchamurthis come forth and perform the Theertham (sacred bath) in the Sharpanathi (Paampaaru). Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who arrived at this shrine, bestowed a pathigam. It is the eleventh pathigam of the Third Thirumurai, a pathigam set to the tune of Gandhara Panchamam. The first and concluding verses of this pathigam are as follows: (பேரைப் பள்ளியுள் பழிகள் போற்றும் அமரும் இடம்) (உணல் மாமூதி உணவாயிலே பொண்ணு தோடிய உமைப்பே உணவாயிலை கேட்டவர் துழுது ஏத்த நியஞான) The summary of this pathigam is that the Lord, praised for various qualities such as having a red matted lock and a white crescent moon, resides with the Goddess in the Punavaiyil, surrounded by punnai trees.

“Let us press on in meditation.”
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 213 - Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
The Periya Puranam, Part 760, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, the section on Vambara Varivanda Charukkam, the puranam of Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worships at the Thiruppunavayil temple and resides there for some days. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman continues to sing the 892nd verse: “Having praised many joyful abodes of the three-eyed Lord in the Pandya kingdom, a land filled with shrines, and having established the path of Vedic scriptures and bestowed elevated liberation through the essence of sacred ash, he came to live in Kalinagar. Surrounded by many devotees of the Lord with the eye on his forehead, and with the moon-crowned king revering him, he came to Manamelkudi, the town of the minister.” This verse describes how Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visits many shrines near Thiruppunavaiyil in the Pandya kingdom. He visits many shrines near Thiruppunavayil in the Pandya kingdom.

This Pandya kingdom is renowned for the Lord and the Goddess ruling as king and queen. It is a land where the Supreme Lord Himself reigns as sovereign. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman visits many such shrines in the Pandya kingdom. These shrines are believed to include Oriyur and others. Oriyur is a Vaippu Thalam (a shrine mentioned in devotional hymns but without a full pathigam dedicated to it). Having worshipped these shrines, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman travels to Manamelkudi, the town of Kulachirai Nayanar.

From Thiruppunavayil, traveling along the coast, usually northeast by road, one reaches Manamelkudi. Further along the coast from here, traveling north, this road passes through Ammanichatram, Sethupava Chatram, Rajamadam, Athiveeraramapattinam, and extends up to Mannargudi. In earlier days, this was the main road used by pilgrims coming to Rameswaram from the northern kingdoms. It was along this path that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman traveled from the Pandya kingdom back to the Chola kingdom. In the Pandya kingdom, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman established the path of Vedic scriptures and the elevated status bestowed by the sacred ash. Sekkizhar Peruman describes the path of Vedic scriptures as the “ordained path of Vedic scriptures.” The Vedas contain prescriptive statements like “Sathyam Vadha Dharmam Chara” (Speak the truth, practice righteousness).

Such prescriptive statements are prevalent in the Vedas. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, by commanding everyone to adhere to the discipline and path laid out by the Vedas and the scriptures derived from them, greatly promoted the Vedic way. He also removed all obstacles caused by external religions that condemned Vedic sacrifices and did not follow Vedic principles.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman emphatically stressed the Vedic path.

Next, the significance of the sacred ash: this is the path of the Agamas, the Saivite path, where the Saivite path leads to the highest liberation. The most excellent support for this is the sacred ash itself. The Saivite path and the sacred ash are inextricably linked. The sacred ash, as a symbol of rejecting other religions and upholding the Vedic path, and promoting the flourishing Saivite way, which were the core objectives of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s divine incarnation, were all established and fulfilled here in the Pandya kingdom by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman. These actions, which began in Madurai, were carried out throughout the Pandya kingdom. Having completed this, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, accompanied by all the devotees, arrived at Kulachirai Nayanar’s Manamelkudi.

Manamelkudi was, in earlier days, a part of the Pandya kingdom, a shrine on its border. It is near Aranthangi and is a town with a significant Muslim population. It can be reached about sixteen naligais southeast of Avudaiyar Koil. From Thiruppunavayil, it can be reached in about eight naligais northeast to Mimeesal, and from there, about seven naligais northeast. The Vellar River near Manamelkudi This Vellar river, also known as Swetha Nadi, served as the northern border of the Pandya kingdom in ancient times, separating and defining the boundaries between the Pandya and Chola kingdoms.

Therefore, this Manamelkudi was a shrine within the Pandya kingdom. It was to this Manamelkudi, the abode of our Kulachirai Nayanar, that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived. He was accompanied by the Pandya king, Mangaiyarkarasi Pirattiyar, and Kulachirai Nayanar. Sekkizhar Peruman then composed the next verses: “While he joyfully resided in that city, he visited the many shrines surrounding it. He returned and joined with the permanent holy devotees. The king, Mangaiyarkarasi, and Kulachirai, with his sharp spear, together worshipped his mighty feet and praised him with supplications.

“During the days when the Chief of Sirapuram, who praises the feet of the Lord adorned with the crescent moon on His head, joyfully resided there, he resolved to return to the Chola kingdom, the land of the surging Kaveri. Mangaiyarkarasi, the king of the South, and the minister, unable to bear separation from his sacred feet, wished to accompany him. Seeing this, he said, ‘If you agree to what I say now, you will be upholding the path of Shiva.’ Thus, to those who were greatly distressed, he gave suitable advice to prevent their distress. This Vellaru river, also known as Swetha Nadi, served as the northern border of the Pandya kingdom in ancient times, separating and defining the boundaries between the Pandya and Chola kingdoms.

“Therefore, this Manamelkudi was a shrine within the Pandya kingdom. It was to this Manamelkudi, the abode of our Kulachirai Nayanar, that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived. He was accompanied by the Pandya king, Mangaiyarkarasi Pirattiyar, and Kulachirai Nayanar. Sekkizhar Peruman then composed the next verses: “While he joyfully resided in that city, he visited the many shrines surrounding it. He returned and joined with the permanent holy devotees. The king, Mangaiyarkarasi, and Kulachirai, with his sharp spear, together worshipped his mighty feet and praised him with supplications.

“During the days when the Chief of Sirapuram, who praises the feet of the Lord adorned with the crescent moon on His head, joyfully resided there, he resolved to return to the Chola kingdom, the land of the surging Kaveri. Mangaiyarkarasi, the king of the South, and the minister, unable to bear separation from his sacred feet, wished to accompany him. Seeing this, he said, ‘If you agree to what I say now, you will be upholding the path of Shiva.’ Thus, to those who were greatly distressed, he gave suitable advice to prevent their distress. Having returned, the king, Mangaiyarkarasi, and Kulachirai, with his sharp spear, together worshipped his mighty feet and praised him with supplications. During the days when the Chief of Sirapuram, who praises the feet of the Lord adorned with the crescent moon on His head, joyfully resided there, he resolved to return to the Chola kingdom, the land of the surging Kaveri. Mangaiyarkarasi, the king of the South, and the minister, unable to bear separation from his sacred feet, wished to accompany him.

“Seeing this, he said, ‘If you agree to what I say now, you will be upholding the path of Shiva.’ Thus, to those who were greatly distressed, he gave suitable advice to prevent their distress.

“After this, they feared to disobey his command, and agreeing to return, they fell at his feet. They worshipped the child-saint, who had come for the salvation of the world, with an unbreakable bond of friendship. Praising the Lord who consumed the deadly poison, he departed from that land and began his journey back, as narrated by Sekkizhar Peruman in verses 893, 894, and 895. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, who joyfully resided in Manamelkudi, visited all the nearby shrines. They stood revering the child-saint, who had incarnated for the salvation of the world, with an unbreakable friendship.

“With an overflowing love that could never be separated in their hearts, they prostrated at the sacred feet of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and stood worshipping him. In the 896th verse, Sekkizhar Peruman begins to sing the divine history of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman entering the fertile land of Ponni Nadu (Chola kingdom) from the Pandya kingdom and commencing his pilgrimage there.

“Let us go on meditating.”””

It was at this shrine that Murugapperuman imparted the Panchakshara mantra to sixty thousand sages and Durvasa.

When the sage Sukala saw Kamadhenu, which he had raised, worshipping a Shiva Lingam by showering milk, he grew angry, fearing a decrease in his milk supply, and struck her. Kamadhenu, distressed by this, ran and worshipped, then collided with the Shiva Lingam as if to convey its plight, and fell into the Pasupathi Theertham in the northern street of this temple.

At that moment, the Lord appeared and brought the cow back to life. Because Kamadhenu struck it, the original deity is seen with three scars, appearing as three divisions. These three divisions are joined together with copper plates, and the Lord grants his divine vision. Dhananjayan, the serpent, worshipped the Lord here on the first day of Aippasi. Green grapes, mangoes, and mango juice are special offerings here. In the inscriptions from the time of Rajarajan, this shrine is referred to as Pambani Kutram, Pambani of Sutraveli Valanadu.

Sundaramoorthy Swamigal and Cheraman Perumal Nayanar, after worshipping Thirukandiyoor, saw Thiruvaiyaru appear on the north bank of the Cauvery River. Chapter 215 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, Part 762, by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, Vambara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. During the days when Thirugnanasambandha Peruman was residing in Thirukollambuthur after worshipping the Lord there, he desired to go to Thirunallaaru and worship the Lord.

The Lord of Thirunallaaru is the hero of the pathigam that remained unburnt and brought victory in the great fiery debate, the Annal Vatham, against the Jains in the presence of the Pandiya king in Madurai.

Therefore, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman obtained divine permission from the Lord at Thirukollambuthur and set out on a pilgrimage towards Thirunallaaru. Unable to bear parting from the Lord of Thirukollambuthur, he received divine permission and departed from there. He visits all the sacred places on the way from Thirukollambuthur to Thirunallaaru. Many sacred places like Thirukudavayil, Thiruvanchiyam, Thiruvambar, and Thiruppugalur are situated along the way. He visits all these places and reaches Thirunallaaru.

There, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reaches the temple of the Lord, who is widely praised and protects the land. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman refers to the sacred place of Thirunallaaru as a place that is widely praised by all directions. Even today, we see that those afflicted by sorrow and suffering come from all directions to Thirunallaaru, seek blessings, and find relief from their woes.

Therefore, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman praises such a Thirunallaaru as a widely praised sacred place. He worships before the Lord who owns the land. The name of the Lord of Thirunallaaru, Tharbharanyeswarar, is ‘Naddudai Nayagar’ (Lord of the land). The divine Sekkizhar Peruman explains the sacred story of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman worshipping the Lord of Thirunallaaru and singing a pathigam in the nine hundred and second verse: “With many devotees surrounding him, he descended from the pearl palanquin, bowed at the glorious sacred entrance of Thirunallaaru temple, and entered. He circumambulated the temple where the Lord with the crescent moon on his head is enshrined, entered with joy, and with lotus-like hands joined in reverence, he worshipped the benevolent Lord. With tears flowing from his eyes, he sang a pathigam beginning with ‘Paadaka Melladi.’” All the devotees surrounded him, and from that place, he descended from the pearl palanquin.

He bowed at the magnificent sacred entrance of Thirunallaaru temple and entered. He circumambulated the inner precincts of the temple where the Lord with the crescent moon on his head is enshrined, entered with joy, and worshipped with his lotus-like hands joined together. The worship performed by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman here was due to his insatiable remembrance of the immense grace that helped him internally in the royal court at Thirualavai. In this pathigam, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composes a pathigam beginning with “Paadaka Melladi,” making the great grace of the Lord of Thirunallaaru who came and resided in Alavai the refrain of each verse. Here too, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begins this pathigam by placing Ambika first, saying “Paadaka Melladi Paavaiyodum.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman begins this pathigam.

We saw that in the unburnt green pathigam, “Bhogamartha Poonmulaiyaal,” Ambika was placed first.

Similarly, we saw that in the pathigam “Thaliril Valaruli Umai,” which was composed before the king in Madurai with the written leaf placed before him, the Goddess Uma was placed first.

Similarly, here in Thirunallaaru, in this pathigam that links the Lord of Thirualavai and the Lord of Thirunallaaru, Ambika, the divine energy, is placed first, as “Paadaka Melladi Paavai.” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman composed this pathigam.

The Lord of Thirunallaaru is the benevolent one who manifested himself and came from the Chola country to the Pandiya country.

Therefore, to remove the Jains and enlighten Saivism, The Child, who returned from the Pandiya kingdom to the Chola kingdom, remembered it there and worshipped at Thirunallaaru.

Thus, in this pathigam, he questions, “What is this, that our Lord of Nallaaru resided in Alavai?” This pathigam, therefore, serves as a common pathigam for two sacred places, Thirunallaaru and Thirualavai. It is a question-and-answer pathigam. It asks, “What is it that the Lord who was in Thirunallaaru came and resided in Thirualavai?” This pathigam is set to the tune of Nattappadai. The first and last verses of this pathigam are as follows: “Paadaka Melladi Paavaiyodum Padu Pinakkadidam Patti Nindru Naadakam A.” “Nallaaru Udaiya Namberuman idhu enkol Sollay Sudaga Munkay Madandai Maargal Thunaivarudum Thozhu Ethi Vaazhtha Aadaga Madam Nerungu Koodal Alavayin Kan Amarndhavare.” “Anbudaiyaanai Aranai Koodal Alavay Meviyathu Enkol endru Nanponai Nadanai Nallaatranai Nayambera Potri Nalanguzhavum Ponpudai Suztharu Madakaali Poosuran Gnanasambandan Sonna Inbudai Padalgal Pattum Vallar Imayavar Ethi Irupparthame.” Thiruchitrambalam.

The divine Sekkizhar Peruman explains the summary of this pathigam in the nine hundred and third verse as follows: “In the debate conducted by the Jains before the Southern King, the leaf placed in the fire remained green, and you were my inner support, residing openly in Alavai, my wonder, my Lord!” Saying, “What is this wonder, my Lord?” he adorned it with Tamil verses, praised it, and resided there with his virtuous devotees. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman then departed from Thirunallaaru, having received divine permission from the Lord of Thirunallaaru, to worship other sacred places of enduring fame. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman states that previously, in the debate conducted by the Jains in the presence of the Pandiya king, the leaf placed in the fire turned green, and the Lord manifested himself in Thirualavai as an inner support within his heart. He praises the Lord’s compassion repeatedly by composing this pathigam of sweet Tamil verses, asking, “What is this wonder, my Lord, that you resided there with such affection?” After this, he came out of the temple and resided in Thirunallaaru, that sacred place, accompanied by his sweet and devoted followers.

At that time, other sacred places of enduring fame. Having received divine permission from the Lord of Thirunallaaru, he worshipped and departed from Thirunallaaru.

Thus, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman reached the sacred place called Thiruthalicheri. A special divine event was about to happen there. In Bodhimangai, near Thiruthalicheri, many Buddhists lived.

At that time, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman began to sing. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman composes the nine hundred and fourth verse: “As he reached Thiruthalicheri, rich in glory, and worshipped Lord Shiva, he approached Bodhimangai, where the unattainable Buddhists reside. When the Saivites learned of this, they gathered like a tumultuous crowd, sounding countless instruments, and proclaimed, ‘The victor over other religions has come!’” Thirugnanasambandha Peruman arrived at the sacred place called Thiruthalicheri, rich in glories, and there he praised Lord Shiva and composed a pathigam. Thiruthalicheri is the fiftieth sacred place among the temples on the south bank of the Cauvery that are praised in verses. It is currently known as Koyilpattu.

The sanctum faces west, and a Sun worship (Surya Puja) takes place in the month of Panguni. The special feature of this place, where Devas and sages come to worship, is praised in Thirugnanasambandha Peruman’s pathigam. The Lord’s name is Parvathivarar, and the Goddess’s name is Sakthiyammai or Parvathiyammai. The sacred pools are Surya Pushkarani and Parvathi Theertham. This place now forms part of Karaikkal town. This temple is located at the other end of the street where the Maampazheswarar temple stands in Karaikkal.

The pathigam (decade of verses) composed by Thirugnanasambandhar for this temple is the third pathigam in the second Thirumurai, set to the tune Indhalapann. The first and final verses of this pathigam are as follows: Thiruchitrambalam (PoovaLarnthana kondu muppodhum Porkazhal thevar vandhu vanangum miku theLichcheriyeer Mevorum thozhilaLodu keLal pin vedanam paavakam kodu nindrathu polum numpaanmaiye). (DikkuLam pozhil suzh theLichcheriyin selvanai Mikka kaaliyul Gnanasambandhan viLambiya thakka paadalgal pathum vallargal thadamudiththokka vanavar suzha iruppavar solli). This means: “O Lord of Thelichcheri, where devas come to worship your golden feet three times a day with blooming flowers! It seems you stood with the profession of a hunter, chasing a boar. Those who are skilled in these ten suitable verses, composed by Gnanasambandhan of Kaali, about the Lord of Thelichcheri, surrounded by groves in all directions, will be surrounded by celestial beings with grand crowns.”

This pathigam, composed by Thirugnanasambandhar, praises the Lord’s greatness, such as His going after a boar with the Goddess as a hunter, begging for alms everywhere, and adorning His head with the Ganga. As Thirugnanasambandhar thus worshipped Thiruthalichcheri and continued his pilgrimage, he passed through the nearby village of Bodhimangai. It was a village populated by Buddhists. As Thirugnanasambandhar traveled in the pearl palanquin bestowed by the Lord, accompanied by devotees blowing the trumpets and conches, and beating drums, he proceeded through the village of Bodhimangai.

We shall go on reflecting.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 216 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, composed by Dhivasekkilar, Part Seven Hundred and Sixty-Three, Vampara Varivandu Charukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. As Thirugnanasambandhar, after worshipping Thiruthalichcheri, proceeded on his pilgrimage, he passed through the village of Bodhimangai. This village of Bodhimangai was predominantly inhabited by Buddhists. As Thirugnanasambandhar proceeded through that village, seated in the pearl palanquin granted by the Lord, Shiva devotees and attendants, sounding the trumpets, conches, and other instruments given by the Lord, proclaimed the glory of Thirugnanasambandhar. This act of the devotees, attendants, and the general public, including the villagers, is a customary occurrence during all of Thirugnanasambandhar’s processions.

Therefore, as he passed through Bodhimangai, as always, Shiva devotees, in a fervor, blew conches, trumpets, and many auspicious instruments, proclaiming the glory of Thirugnanasambandhar as ‘ParasamyakolaRivan.’ ‘ParasamyakolaRi’ is an epithet praising Thirugnanasambandhar. ‘KolaRi’ means lion. ‘ParasamyakolaRi’ means one who is like a lion to the mad elephants of other religions.

Thus, singing praises, they proceed, immersed in this atmosphere. People traveling through public thoroughfares have the right to speak and act innocently, according to their own will. This is called freedom in modern times. In such a situation, the Jains in that village, unable to tolerate the words of praise for Thirugnanasambandhar and the sounds of trumpets, conches, and drums, gather together. They gather as if to obstruct the blessed procession of Thirugnanasambandhar. Overwhelmed by jealousy in their hearts, they are deluded and report this news to their leader, Buddhanandhi, and others.

They speak with great anger. The malice that arose in their hearts, the jealousy called ‘azhukkaaru’, clouded their intellect.

Thus, they went to Buddhanandhi, one of the foremost among their Buddhists, and spoke to him. Buddhanandhi is a traditional name for eminent and renounced Buddhists. Due to jealousy, as the Thirukkural says, ‘Azhukkaaru ena oru paavi thiruchattru theeyozhi uyththuvidum’ (Jealousy, that sinner, will completely lead one to evil). They are deluded due to this jealousy. For Buddhists, delusion means perceiving one thing as another and becoming confused. The Thirukkural describes this as ‘Porul allavatrai porul enru unarum marul’ (the delusion of perceiving non-existent things as existent).

While these Buddhists were thus reporting to their leader, Buddhanandhi, Thirugnanasambandhar’s procession approached. At that moment, the shouts of the devotees and the surging sound of the conches, along with the joyful exclamations of the Shiva devotees, reached Buddhanandhi’s ears. It was as if a sharp spear, heated in fire, had been plunged into his ears. Buddhanandhi, gathering all his followers, came before Thirugnanasambandhar’s assembly. Buddhanandhi angrily declared, “You hail your leader as ‘Parasama KolaRi,’ the conqueror of other religions, and sound trumpets as a sign of victory. You can only say that after defeating me in a debate!” Earlier, Thirugnanasambandhar had defeated the Jains in Madurai, which constituted a victory over all other religions.

However, Buddhanandhi, ignoring this, foolishly demanded that he too be defeated in a debate. He speaks out of ignorance, insisting he must be defeated in a debate. As Buddhanandhi spoke, what did he do? He obstructed the devotees in Thirugnanasambandhar’s procession that was approaching. He silenced the sacred conches they were blowing, claiming that conches should not be sounded in this village. He tried to use violence against the devotees, taking away their instruments.

Thirugnanasambandhar is a peerless pure sage of wisdom. He is the embodiment of compassion, devoid of hatred and attachment. This purity signifies inner cleanliness. The previous debate with the Jains and the upcoming debate with the Buddhists are not born of hatred towards external religions, nor are they due to affection for Shaivites. The compassion that Thirugnanasambandhar possesses is the compassion to reveal the true state of existence to all beings in this world and save them.

Therefore, he is a peerless pure sage of wisdom. These conches, trumpets, and other instruments were given by the true Lord; they do not proclaim false praises, but rather speak of the genuine and meaningful glories of Thirugnanasambandhar, the peerless wise leader.

However, when these instruments are sounded while passing through a public street, these Buddhists, believing themselves to be numerous in this village, unite and try to exert force, saying that such sounding should not occur and removing the instruments held by the devotees. Witnessing this, the true Shaivites become angry. In Shaivism, its path has always been one of patience and compassion.

However, when its state is encroached upon and obstructed by other religions, Shaivism also possesses the valor to not shrink from removing those obstacles and impediments through disciplinary action.

Therefore, these true devotees, becoming angry, thought that if they tolerated these outrageous acts of the Buddhists, the Buddhists would use more force. So they went to the palanquin where Thirugnanasambandhar was seated and informed the young child (Thirugnanasambandhar) of what was happening.

Here, we must remember one thing: whenever Thirugnanasambandhar visited any temple, a large crowd would surround him, preceding and following him, and the procession would extend for a great distance.

Therefore, this incident, this act of violence perpetrated by the Buddhists, occurred among the devotees in the front row of the procession.

Therefore, these devotees, becoming angry, walked back a long distance to where the young child (Thirugnanasambandhar) was coming and reported what was happening. They also recounted the violence committed by the Buddhists and the statement by Buddhanandhi that the praise ‘Parasama KolaRi’ would only be true after he was defeated in a debate. Thirugnanasambandhar, with a serene mind, considered that if these Buddhists spoke thus on the path where he was coming without any intention of debate, it was also for the good. He decided that he would expose the falsehood of Buddhanandhi and the true nature of their false doctrines. Thirugnanasambandhar thus graciously spoke to the devotees.

Therefore, this debate was not sought by them; it intervened on their path.

Thus, it was due to divine grace, and Thirugnanasambandhar, implying that divine grace orchestrates everything for good, decided to debate with these Buddhists and expose the true nature of their doctrines. As this was happening, Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal, who was accompanying Thirugnanasambandhar’s procession, was the young child’s maternal uncle. He was the one who, always present, collected and compiled all of the young child’s pathigams onto palm-leaf manuscripts. It is mentioned that those palm-leaf manuscripts containing the young child’s pathigams would always be carried with him. We already saw this during the fire debate. Sambandha Saranalayar witnessed the events unfolding here, the use of force and violence by the Buddhists.

Immediately, he consulted the palm-leaf manuscripts containing the pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandhar by drawing a string through them. The verse that appeared when he consulted the manuscripts in this manner was the tenth verse of the Panchakshara Pathigam, which begins with “Thunjalum Thunjalillatha Polthinam.” That tenth verse states: (Buddhar saman kazhukaiyar poikolla chithavargal theLinthu therina viththaka neeranivara vinaipagaikku aththiramavavana anjezhuththumae). This is the tenth verse of the Panchakshara Pathigam. What does it mean? It means that Buddhists and Jains, the false words they utter are not held in the minds of the clear-minded ones who recite with conviction the Sri Panchakshara. The divine five letters (Sri Panchakshara) are capable of striking like an arrow and destroying enemies who come to wage war against those who wear the sacred ash, which possesses all powers.

It says, ‘Aththiramavathu anjezhuththumae,’ meaning ‘the weapon is the five letters.’ In that verse, it is stated that ‘Aththiramavathu anjezhuththumae’ refers to the weapon for those who come to wage war with enmity against the wearers of sacred ash. As soon as ‘Aththiramavathu anjezhuththumae’ appeared upon consulting the Thirumurais, Sambandha Saranalayar considered this utterance to be the command of Thirugnanasambandhar, and taking this divine word as a command, Sambandha Saranalayar used it as a weapon. Unable to tolerate the slandering of Shaivism, devotees, and the Vedas by the Buddhists, Sambandha Saranalayar consulted the pathigams composed by Thirugnanasambandhar. When this particular verse from this pathigam appeared, he took it as a command and wielded it as a weapon. He declared that Buddhanandhi’s head should be struck by lightning and roll down, that his head should be severed and fall to the ground by a lightning strike. Dhivasekkilar, in the nine hundred and ninth verse, describes this: “The irresistible, powerful mantra, like a lightning bolt, that destroys obstacles opposing the order of the Shaiva path of the bull-mounted Lord, uttered by the truthful word of the devotee, tore the body and head of the Buddhist who came to engage in verbal battle into separate pieces.”

When this happened, the crowd of Buddhists scattered in disarray, filled with fear. The verse composed by Dhivasekkilar, the nine hundred and ninth verse, describes this. The divine command of the Lord of Shaiva tradition, who bears the bull emblem, was thus brought forth to dispel obstacles. The utterance of that devotee, filled with devotion, acted like an irresistible and powerful Shiva-weapon, a thunderbolt, that destroys and removes impediments to Shiva worship from all three sides – above, below, and in the middle. At that very moment, it shattered Buddhanandhi’s body and head into separate pieces. The word of the devotee manifested there as a Shiva-weapon.

A Shiva-weapon, according to the Agamas, is an Astra Mantra that, when used during Shiva Puja, unfailingly removes obstacles that hinder the puja from the above, middle, and lower regions, like a lightning strike.

Therefore, it is stated in the Agamas that one should remove all obstacles with that Shiva-weapon mantra and then begin the puja.

In the same way, that very Shiva-weapon, through the word of the devotee, caused Buddhanandhi’s body and head to separate. It was as if lightning had struck. Seeing this, the crowd of Buddhists was thrown into disarray, fled, and became filled with fear. Dhivasekkilar then states in the next verse, the nine hundred and tenth, that the others, seeing Buddhanandhi, who had challenged them to a verbal battle, fall with his head and body severed, and witnessing the devotees’ victory through that very word-weapon, came to the conclusion that this was the inevitable divine decree that had removed the impending obstruction, and they all began to proclaim: “Aran!” (Shiva). The sound of that proclamation reached the heavens. The next verse, the nine hundred and tenth, is composed by Dhivasekkilar.

The mantra of the pathigam, ‘Aththiramavathu Ainthezhuththumae’ (The weapon is the five letters), contained the weapon of Shiva as described in that verse. It was by this weapon that he fell, wasn’t it? The Sankalpa Nirakaranam states this: “The God of Kaunia in Kaali, with the joyful words of the devotees who compose excellent pathigams of divine wisdom, caused the head of the arrogant Buddhist to roll, not by wielding a sharp sword.” This incident, where Buddhanandhi’s head was struck by lightning and severed by the word of the devotee, Sambandha Saranalayar, occurred in the front row of the young child’s procession. The young child’s palanquin, however, was still progressing far behind.

Therefore, the devotees swiftly went to the young child and reported this event that had occurred in front. Thirugnanasambandhar heard it. When he heard that the Buddhist had died unexpectedly by a lightning strike, he declared that it was an act of Shiva’s grace, an inevitable divine decree, and urged everyone to praise Shiva. Thirugnanasambandhar proclaimed that the removal of the obstruction that had come upon their path, without them seeking it, was Shiva’s divine will (niyathi), and therefore, he asked everyone to chant Shiva’s name.

At that moment, the devotees in the procession chanted Shiva’s name, “Hara Hara,” which then reached up to the heavens. Let us go on reflecting. Thiru Thiruchitrambalam.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 217 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Periya Puranam, composed by Dhivasekkilar, Part Seven Hundred and Sixty-Four, Vampara Varivandu Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Buddhanandhi’s head fell separately from his body as if struck by lightning. Seeing this, all the other Buddhists were astonished and gathered among themselves, confused as to whether this event was caused by deception or was a result of the true power of the Shaiva religion. Pondering this in their minds and discussing it among themselves, they came to Thirugnanasambandhar, led by their leader, Sariputthan. Sambandha Saranalayar’s divine utterance caused that event, which was an act of sorcery.

Therefore, to perform that sorcery, these Buddhists, led by Sariputthan, approached the assembly of Shiva devotees and asked, “This is the truth of our religion, and we wish to debate it. Please agree to this.” The young child, born like a lion in the holy city of Seerkazhi, heard this, deemed it beautiful in his divine heart, and with great joy, quickly descended from his pearl palanquin. He ascended the mandapam (hall) of an inn there and sat with the Shaivites. In ancient times, inns were built along the routes for pilgrims from the North to Rameswaram. Thirugnanasambandhar, accompanied by his devotees, sat in the mandapam of one such inn.

Then, having obtained the young child’s consent, the Shiva devotees approached the Buddhist crowd and said, “Our victorious leader from Shambai, the head of the Vedas, and the master of the three Tamils, Thirugnanasambandhar, joyfully invites you. Please come and present the truth of your religion.” The Shiva devotees made it clear to the Buddhists that the one who invites them is a revered figure who upholds Vedic principles and who will conquer them by establishing those Vedic truths through the three Tamils. The Buddhists also They arrive before the assembly hall of that inn. Sariputta also arrives there. Sambandha Saranalayar then praises the sacred feet of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, the beautiful leader of Sirkazhi, receives his grace, and begins the debate. Sambandha Saranalayar asks Sariputta to speak and elaborate on the God, the leader of his religion, and the nature of liberation, which is the meaning of what that God proclaims.

Thus, the religious debate begins. In general, during a religious debate, there are said to be two excellent areas for determining victory or defeat: the God concept of that religion and its liberation concept.

Therefore, the two topics of the definition of God and the definition of liberation were considered the best parts for presenting the arguments of one’s religion and achieving victory or defeat in a religious debate. In this era, religious condemnation itself serves as a religious debate, which we also observe here.

Thus, Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal, praising the sacred feet of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman and beginning the religious debate, asks Sariputta, “What is the concept of God in your religion? What is the definition of liberation in your religion?” Sariputta replies. For Buddhists, there is one Adi Buddha, and including him, there are a total of twenty-four Buddhas. Of these, the twenty-fourth The last was Gautama Buddha, who is widely known.

So, when asked about the concept of God in Buddhism, Sariputta explains the concept of God related to the Adi Buddha. There are fourteen Saiva Siddhanta Shastras, and among them, there is a Shastra called Sivagnana Siddhiyar, a text composed and bestowed by Arulnandi Sivachariyar, one of the Saiva religious Santana Acharyas. This Sivagnana Siddhiyar has two sections: Subaksham and Parapaksham. Parapaksham contains sections that refute and reject other doctrines.

Here, in this section of our Periya Puranam, where the debate with the Buddhists occurs, Theivasekkizhar Peruman presents that debate in ten verses. Desikanar, Sivakavimani, who wrote a commentary on this, quotes all those sections from Sivagnana Siddhiyar Parapaksham that refute the Buddhists. There are four branches of Buddhism: Sautrantika, Vaibhashika, Madhyamika, and Yogachara. Arulnandi Sivachariyar has refuted and rejected all four of these in Sivagnana Siddhiyar Parapaksham. As we saw earlier, those who do not accept or reject our Vedas as authoritative refer to their scriptures as Pitaka texts. This Pitaka refers to the tradition of twenty-four Buddhas, including the Adi Buddha.

These are texts taught through the order of instruction, categorized into three types: Vinaya Pitaka, Sutra Pitaka, and Abhidharma Pitaka. These are also known as Tripitaka or Pitaka Thrayam. Pitaka means ‘basket.’ The Buddhist saying is that Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are three types of jewels. They recite this as a mantra: ‘Buddham Saranam Gacchami, Dharmam Saranam Gacchami, Sangham Saranam Gacchami, Namo Buddhaya, Namo Dharmaya, Namah Sanghaya.’ Because these texts carry these three jewels like a basket, they are called Pitaka. In response to Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal’s request, Sariputta begins to explain the concept of God in the Buddhist religion.

Therefore, the Buddhist God is said to be Adi Buddha, and the history surrounding him is that this Adi Buddha was born from his mother’s right hip and caused his mother to die six days after his birth. To save beings, he was born and died in countless Kalpas, through countless births, giving assurance to beings, and then, changing that state, he attained liberation. This is Adi Buddha, a historical note on the God of Buddhism. When speaking of time calculation, Kalpa is described as a very large unit of time, approximately 320 million years. In countless Kalpas, beings are born and die, entering countless wombs according to their karma, coming as humans, devas, Brahmas, nagas, animals, or ghosts, and are born and die. their principle is that after attaining certainty, that Buddha attains liberation.

Similarly, a key Buddhist principle is Kshanabhanga Vadam. This Kshanabhanga refers to a very short duration of time. One Kshana is defined as the time it takes for a needle to pierce eight out of a hundred stacked lotus petals. The nature that Buddhists describe here is the Kshanabhanga nature: that knowledge and knowable objects, like the light of a lamp, appear and perish in a moment, undergoing four types of destruction, which is called Kshanabhanga Vadam. As said before, the born Adi Buddha, having boundless good, initially was endowed with virtues and was a yogi. He attained liberation by overcoming faults through the knowledge of Trillakshana Bhavana, meaning the three bhavanas: ‘Sarvam Dukham,’ ‘Sarvam Anityam,’ and ‘Sarvam Shunyam.’ He is called Paramam and Adi Buddha.

Before attaining liberation, through knowledge arisen from asceticism, he fully understood everything and preached Dharma and gave instructions for the salvation of others.

Thus, Sariputta explains the concept of God.

Here, the four noble truths (Chatu Satyam) that Buddhists speak of—Dukkha, Dukkhotpatti, Dukkha Nivaranam, and Dukkha Nivaran Margam—are attained. This Adi Buddha, knowing all things, told the faultless old Pitaka text, which is worshipped and praised by even Devas, considering the suffering of others as his own suffering, in a world where the five great sins are murder, theft, lust, liquor, and falsehood. he himself is the Adi Buddha. According to their doctrine, the प्रमाणs (proofs) accepted by Buddhists, as stated in the Pitaka texts, are only two: Pratyaksha प्रमाण and Anumana प्रमाण.

Thus, all objects known through Pratyaksha and Anumana are perishable, and there are some other fundamentals. Sariputta thus explains the concept of God in Buddhism, the history of that Adi Buddha, how he died and was born, and died and was born again, and then attained liberation, and how he gave instructions. he states. Hearing this, Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal asks him to explain his definition of liberation. He asks, “You said your leader attained liberation, so what is the definition of liberation that your religion speaks of?” To this, Sariputta replies that the destruction of the five skandhas is liberation.

So, according to Buddhism and the Pitaka, liberation occurs when the five skandhas are destroyed; he states that destruction is liberation. When answering the first question about the doctrine, he said that Adi Buddha attained liberation. Taking this as a basis for the question, he asks, “What kind of liberation did he attain? What is the definition of liberation according to your religion?” To this, he states that the destruction of the five skandhas is liberation, and that is the definition of liberation according to Buddhist texts. The five skandhas mentioned in Buddhism are form (rupa), sensation (vedana), perception (samjna), mental formations (samskara), and consciousness (vijnana), which arise from the aggregation of these five conscious beings.

Therefore, the Buddhist doctrine states that the destruction of these five is liberation. Among these, the first, the Rupa Skandha, represents the material cause of all forms. This Rupa Skandha includes the four great elements: earth, water, fire, and air, the five sense organs, the five sense objects—form, taste, smell, sound, and touch—gender distinctions, and other similar elements, totaling twenty-eight principles. This is the first skandha, called Rupa Skandha. From this, what is understood is that these Buddhists do not accept Akasha as an element.

Next, they speak of the second as Vedana Skandha. This is the sensation arising from the contact between the sense organs and their objects. This sensation is of six types, corresponding to the five sense organs and the mind. Since each of these six types can be classified into three categories—kusala (wholesome), akusala (unwholesome), and kusala-akusala (mixed)—Vedana becomes eighteen types.

Thus, this Vedana Skandha is of eighteen types. The third, Samjna Skandha, is the knowledge required to identify and name objects using general and specific understanding, which arises from the six types of sensations associated with the six sense organs: body, mouth, eye, nose, ear, and mind. This skandha arises through the six sense organs.

Next, the fourth is Bhavana Skandha. This refers to the special maturation (paripaka vishesham) that the karmic instruments (karana) attain due to the differences in actions performed by the three instruments: mind, speech, and body. This skandha is said to be of fifty-two types and is also called Samskara Skandha. Fifth is Vijnana Skandha. The consciousness of sleeping beings, like a single agent, resides within conscious beings and is the consciousness principle that supports all their knowledge. This Vijnana Skandha is categorized into eighty-nine types based on the various types of thoughts, good and bad actions, which are its functions.

Thus, the five skandhas are described. These skandhas are impermanent. Form is said to appear and vanish instantly like foam. Sensation is like a bubble that appears and moves on water. The Samgna skandha is like a mirage appearing in the sun. The Samskara skandha is like a banana tree, lacking strength and stability.

The Vijnana skandha is said to appear like a magic show. All these details, as we have already seen, are extensively described in Sivagnana Siddhiyar Parapaksham, along with their refutations.

Similarly, in the Thiruvadavur Adigal Puranam, which narrates the sacred history of Srimath Manikavasaga Swamigal, there is a chapter called ‘Buddharai Vathil Venra Sarukkam’ (The Chapter of Defeating Buddhists in Debate). In Thiruchitrambalam, Buddhists come to debate with Srimath Manikavasaga Swamigal. Manikavasaga Swamigal makes the daughter of a king from Sri Lanka, who is mute, speak, and through her, defeats the Buddhists in debate. In that chapter, Buddhist doctrines and their refutations are also extensively detailed.

Therefore, learning and understanding these will help in understanding the Buddhist debate in this section of Periya Puranam. In the Manimegalai edition, regarding Buddha’s history, Buddha Dharma, and Buddha Sangha, Mahamahopadhyaya Thiruu. Ve. Saminathaiyar has extensively researched and compiled what many have written about them.

Therefore, the five skandhas that we have seen in detail, from the text Sivagnana Siddhiyar Parapaksham, as stated, Sariputta states that the destruction and annihilation of these five skandhas are the definition of liberation in the Buddhist religion. Immediately upon hearing Sariputta’s answer, our devotee Sambandha Saranalayar, having heard Sariputta’s words and assimilated them, now presents a counter-argument. Let’s continue to contemplate this.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 218 — Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
The Periya Puranam, authored by Theivasekkizhar Peruman, Part 765, Vampara Varivanda Sarukkam, Thirugnanasambandha Nayanar Puranam. Having heard Sariputta’s explanation of the true Buddhist principles of God and liberation from the Buddhist texts, our beloved Sambandha Saranalayar assimilates Sariputta’s words and then questions Sariputta based on his answers. He asks Sariputta, “You stated that your Adi Buddha attained liberation by extinguishing the five skandhas, including his knowledge. If the five skandhas are extinguished, then you build Buddha Viharas assuming your leader is present there, create images of him, and at those temples, you perform pujas. Tell me, who accepts these pujas and grand celebrations that you conduct with these large forms in your Buddha Viharas?” Sambandha Saranalayar begins to ask Sariputta.

A Buddha Vihara is the name for a Buddhist temple. It is customary for Buddhists to install large forms of Buddha in various postures—sitting, reclining, standing—in their temples. Even today, these can be seen in Buddha Viharas in Sri Lanka and in Buddhist temples and cave temples in North India. If you create such large forms and perform all the rituals of offering food, adorning with flowers, and requesting (like chanting), which you call puja, in those Buddha Viharas for that Buddha, believing that your leader is present there, do all these rituals become objects of your leader’s consciousness? For the puja to be perceived, which you perform with the thought that Buddha is here in this world and accepts the puja, he needs consciousness. For consciousness to arise, according to the principle you stated, there must be a combination of the five skandhas.

But your principle is that in liberation, those five skandhas are extinguished and perish.

Therefore, these things are not objects for your leader, who is in liberation. These will not be consumable items for your leader.

So, who accepts the puja that you perform believing he is here and receives it consciously? Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal raises questions. He asks, “You, Sariputta, said that your leader has entered liberation, discarding the body that possessed five types of consciousness due to good and bad karma. How can it be appropriate to build temples and hold festivals for someone whose consciousness and senses are extinguished? Because your leader, who has entered liberation, lacks the tools to perceive objects, such as eyes.

“Therefore, the absence of tools to perceive objects makes it impossible for him to experience consciousness,” argues Sambandha Saranalayar. He refutes them by taking their own principle: “Your leader, who has attained liberation, has no eyes or other senses to see; therefore, no consciousness arises in him.” To this, Sariputta replies. Sariputta says, “When one person reviles and kicks another who is sleeping without knowledge or consciousness, even if the sleeping person does not feel it, the evil karma resulting from kicking and reviling will accrue to the one who kicks.

“Similarly, even if our prime leader, Adi Buddha, does not perceive these pujas and festivals while in liberation, the benefit of performing puja to him will accrue to the one who performs it.” Sariputta thus answers, refuting the objection raised by Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal. Hearing these words from Sariputta, our beloved Sambandha Saranalayar again raises an objection, a question. He says, “Your leader, who accepts the worship you perform, lacks the faculties to perceive, and therefore has no likes or dislikes. In that case, he does not accept that worship,” replies Sambandha Saranalayar. “Either he should accept your worship with pleasure, or he should reject it with displeasure. Only if he possesses such consciousness can he bestow the appropriate benefit.

“Otherwise, since he is said to be in the state of liberation, where consciousness is extinguished, he is unable to accept that worship.

“Therefore, he will not provide the appropriate benefit,” Sambandha Saranalayar counters. To this, Sariputta replies. Sariputta states, For the fruit of karma to accrue, there is no need for a mental state of agreement or opposition, that is, likes or dislikes. Because a sleeping person, unaware, has neither likes nor dislikes for external events happening around him.

“But if someone kills that sleeping person, the sin of murder will accrue to them.

“Similarly, even though our Lord has no likes or dislikes for this worship, the benefit of this worship will accrue to us,” says Sariputta. To this, Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal replies with a counter-question: “You say it’s like the sin of murder that accrues when someone kills a sleeping person. In that case, wouldn’t the life separated by murder, the body it resided in, and the inner faculties that experienced the pain of murder be required for the one who was murdered?

“Similarly, for your Lord to bestow the benefit of worship, life, body, and faculties are certainly required. If you say that all these exist for your Lord in the state of liberation, then that is not the liberation that was said to be attained only when the five skandhas are destroyed. Your leader would not be one who has entered that liberation. It would mean he did not attain the liberation where, as you defined, the knowledge of the five skandhas also perishes. If the benefit of the performed worship is to be received, then for your primal Lord to enter liberation, these must have already perished.

“Thus, Sambandha Saranalayar reveals the contradiction in Buddha’s doctrine and the inconsistency of his example with his own principles.

“Thus, he concludes.

“Now, Sambandha Saranalayar refutes this definition of liberation in a second way. You stated that liberation is full of supreme bliss, and you spoke of your leader as having attained everlasting blissful liberation. If liberation means supreme bliss, then to attain that bliss in liberation, there must be consciousness. For consciousness to exist, according to the principle you stated, the functions of the skandhas are necessary.

“But you say that he entered liberation with his consciousness and knowledge extinguished. If he entered such liberation, there is no means to attain supreme bliss. Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal thus points out the contradiction in their stated principle.

“Therefore, your liberation becomes a liberation without joy. Such joyless liberation is emptiness, he states. Some Buddhists also claim that knowledge itself is the soul, which, like a flow of water, appears and perishes every moment, and that knowledge occurs due to the attachment of latent tendencies (vasana) that arise when it appears and perishes, and that liberation is the destruction of these vasanas. Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal, understanding this, asserts that joy is not attained in liberation when the skandhas and knowledge are destroyed. He points out their contradiction using their own principles. This idea can be found in verse 133 of Parapaksham and verse 464 of the chapter ‘Buddharai Vathil Venra Sarukkam’ in Thiruvadavur Adigal Puranam.

“Regarding this, Mahamahopadhyaya Dr. U.V. Swaminathaiyar, in his Manimegalai edition, on pages 55-56, in the section on Buddha Dharma, writes the following: In the Buddhist text ‘Samyukta Nikaya,’ when a monk named Vakkali approached Gautama Buddha, the 24th Buddha, and asked if there was such a thing as a soul, the Buddha remained silent.

“But when he again asked if there was no such thing, the Buddha remained silent then too. However, it is known from the aforementioned Samyukta Nikaya that King Prasenajit of Kosala, while traveling between Saketa and Sravasti, met a bhikkhuni named Khema, bowed to her, and clarified his doubts about the Buddha Dharma through the following questions and answers. The king asks the Buddhist nun, “Bhagavati, does Gautama Buddha exist after death?” To this, Khema replies, “O King, the teacher Buddha did not say that Gautama Buddha exists after death.” The king then asks again, “Bhagavati, but does Gautama Buddha, that is, the Tathagata, not exist after death?” The Buddhist nun replies that the teacher did not say that Gautama Buddha does not exist either. This means she states that his teacher did not say that Gautama Buddha exists after death, nor did he say that he does not exist. she replies. The king asks again, “Bhagavati, so can it be said that Tathagata, that is, Gautama Buddha, neither exists nor does not exist after death?” To this, the bhikkhuni replies, “The teacher Buddha did not say anything about this either.” Therefore, even these questions and answers do not show that Gautama Buddha emphatically stated that nirvana is a state of voidness and that there is no such thing as a soul. This is how the dialogue within their own texts is presented.

“Bhagavati is an honorific term used for bhikkhunis, female renunciants belonging to the Sangha among Buddhists. This is how that conversation unfolds.

“Therefore, if there is no conscious soul, there is no joy in liberation, and consequently no benefit. This is the summary of Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal’s argument here. This is the summary of Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal’s argument here.

“Thus, hearing those words and unable to say anything against them, Sariputta stands there. He stands saddened, with the feeling of insignificance, as the claim that the leader is in the liberation described by Buddhists has also come to naught. Sambandha Saranalayar, the beloved devotee of Pillaiyar, who is like nectar churned from the ocean of knowledge, further states: “You said that after the skandhas perished and became false, the one who leads to liberation understood righteousness and taught it, and gave instructions. How did he fully understand everything in that manner? How did he become one who understood everything even before entering liberation?

“Therefore, what you say implies that he is not one who understood everything, and this is established here.”

“Therefore, if there is no conscious soul, there is no joy in liberation, and consequently no benefit. This is the summary of Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal’s argument here.

“Thus, hearing those words and unable to say anything against them, Sariputta stands there. He stands saddened, with the feeling of insignificance, as the claim that the leader is in the liberation described by Buddhists has also come to naught. Sambandha Saranalayar, the beloved devotee of Pillaiyar, who is like nectar churned from the ocean of knowledge, further states: “You said that after the skandhas perished and became false, the one who leads to liberation understood righteousness and taught it, and gave instructions. How did he fully understand everything in that manner? How did he become one who understood everything even before entering liberation?

“Therefore, what you say implies that he is not one who understood everything, and this is established here.” Addressing Sariputta, who was sad that the definition of liberation had become void, Sambandha Saranalayar then asks the following question. Because when the five skandhas are completely destroyed, their doctrine is that there is no such thing as a soul.

“So, how did he understand everything before going into liberation? Because your argument is that objects appear and perish moment by moment. How can one fully understand objects that appear and perish moment by moment as a single entity? He asks a question in this manner. This same idea is explained in two verses, 96 and 97, in Sivagnana Siddhiyar Parapaksham. To this question, Sariputta answers Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal.

“He states that consciousness is of two types: general and specific. Among these, general consciousness is to perceive all trees in a forest as ‘trees’ generally. Specific consciousness is to differentiate and perceive all trees in that forest as ‘sandalwood,’ ‘agarwood,’ ‘vengei,’ and so on. This applies to the perception of all objects. Just as firewood, whether gathered and thrown into the fire as a heap or cut into separate pieces and thrown individually into the fire, still burns with the heat of the fire, our ancient Lord will understand, whether combined or individually differentiated, he will understand,” Sariputta replies. “Consciousness arises and goes into liberation.

“Before that, he fully understood all things.” Sambandha Saranalayar asked how your leader, as you say, created that Pitaka text after fully understanding all things. To the question of how all things were understood if knowledge is momentary, Sariputta replies in this manner. The analogy he gave was compared to the action of fire. Fire burns and consumes firewood whether it is thrown in a heap or individually.

“Similarly, consciousness understands and explains all objects both generally as a whole and specifically as differentiated. So, when he spoke, Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal replied with a counter-argument. Sariputta, you gave the action of fire as an example for the action of consciousness.

“However, the consciousness that perceives objects is not gross; it does not have a form or shape. But the fire you cited as an example for consciousness has a form, and you know this,” he counters. This is the first argument in this counter-debate, concerning place. Consciousness has no form, but fire has a form.

“Therefore, comparing a formless entity with a material entity that perceives objects and has a nature with a formless entity that perceives objects is inappropriate, says Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal, refuting the first type.

“Now, he explains why it is inappropriate in terms of time. He states that if consciousness is said to know the past and future in addition to the present, then omniscience would be somewhat appropriate.

“But your example, fire, burns the wood only in the present, not in the past or future. However, omniscience is the knowledge of all three times.

“Therefore, the fire that burns wood, which you offered as an example for consciousness that knows all three times, burns only in the present. So, this analogy is also inappropriate in terms of time, he refutes.

“Therefore, the example you gave is not appropriate.

“Thus, your statement that your leader fully understood all things has now become void. Just as your previous definition of liberation became void, this also became void. The Pitaka text authored by your primal leader with such incomplete knowledge, when he was in a state of not having attained liberation and possessed imperfect knowledge, is also a flawed text. Because a text is something spoken by an omniscient person.

“Therefore, the Pitaka text spoken by your primal leader, who had incomplete knowledge and was in a state of not having attained liberation, is a flawed text. Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal makes Sariputta accept this truth.

“Thus, the concept of God and the concept of liberation both meet with defeat; they become void.

“Therefore, Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal assures them that other things will also perish in vain, and that Saiva truths, expounded in the Vedas and Agamas, show the true path. He says that the Buddhists, unable to refute the fact that their concepts of God and liberation had become void, remained silent. Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal very appropriately explains that the truths expressed by the Buddhists, relying solely on intellect, are not truths. He naturally explains that the nature of their chosen leader, the nature of liberation (the ultimate truth he established), the nature of the leader’s comprehensive knowledge, and the nature of the Pitaka texts he spoke are not truths. Sambandha Saranalayar Swamigal aptly conveys this natural inability for them to be truths. Looking at these Buddhists who silently accepted their defeat, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman casts a compassionate glance.

“Thirugnanasambandha Peruman speaks words of grace to these Buddhists. He explains to them that Saivism is a religion associated with Shiva, and this Saiva religion encompasses all things and doctrines as its parts. He teaches them that the leader, liberation, and the texts mentioned in Saivism are the true essence. This is also how Arulnandi Sivachariyar Peruman explains in Sivagnana Siddhiyar Parapaksham, countering the arguments of the Sautrantikas. He poses counter-questions to the doctrines stated by the Buddhists and refutes them.

“Now, Arulnandi Sivachariyar Peruman explains the Siddhanta answers to these questions. What is matter? Who is the leader? What is the nature of the leader? What is the ultimate truth he established? What is the nature of liberation?

“What is the true text? All these questions are answered there. Just as a potter is needed to make pots and other vessels, this world is an effect, and therefore, an agent is needed to effect it. That agent must be an omniscient conscious being. Scriptures that declare the four ultimate purposes—dharma, artha, kama, and moksha—and are capable of bestowing knowledge and action upon souls are the Vedas and Shivagamas. These Vedas and Agamas are recited by great sages, taught by highly intelligent Brahmins and others, and have been passed down through generations.

“Therefore, there must be an omniscient being who spoke them flawlessly. One who knows how to act as commanded by those Vedas and Agamas and gives results is needed.

“Therefore, those Vedas and Shivagamas were spoken by the omniscient and all-acting Lord Shiva, and know that He alone is the primordial God. This is how the concept of God and scripture is explained in Saiva Siddhanta. He who is beginningless, without impurities, pure, superior to all things, unwavering, omniscient, possessing all actions and great compassion, is the Creator, Parameswaran alone. Through the boundless great compassion that Parameswaran, the Pasupati, has for souls, when their merits and demerits are balanced without excess or deficiency, when the balance of two karmas occurs as if pierced by a needle, He appears on this earth in the form of a Guru, bestows Shakti Nipatam upon those souls, destroys their impurities, and by casting his sacred gaze, destroys their internal instruments like the mind and external instruments like the senses, and bestows upon those souls the four types of worship—Chariya, Kriya, Yoga, and Gnana—to worship Him, and bestows them upon the mature souls. With his immensely compassionate hands, he lifts those souls from the ocean of birth that causes unbearable suffering, preventing them from falling and struggling, and places them on the shore of liberation that bestows everlasting bliss. This is the liberation described by Saiva Siddhanta.

“May you also attain the bliss of liberation by following this righteous path,” thus Saiva Siddhanta is established before the Buddhists.

“Here, Thirugnanasambandha Peruman also conveys the same. Theivasekkizhar Peruman composes the 925th verse, stating that Thirugnanasambandha Peruman declared that there is nothing but Saivism, and the Vedas, Agamas, and other countless arts understood by the wise, who spoke of endless glories, saying that there is nothing else, and when the Peruman graciously spoke to the Buddhists, whose minds were enlightened by his grace, the Buddhists understood these truths and went and bowed at the pure sacred feet of Pillaiyar, the Brahmin who was born in Sirkazhi. He states, “Saivism is the religion related to Shiva. This Saiva religion is such that all things and doctrines are encompassed within it as its parts. Thirugnanasambandha Peruman makes them understand that the leader, liberation, and the texts mentioned in Saivism are the true essence.” This is also how Arulnandi Sivachariyar Peruman explains in Sivagnana Siddhiyar Parapaksham, countering the arguments of the Sautrantikas, saying, “If so, what is matter? Who is the leader?

“What is the nature of the leader? What is the ultimate truth he established? What is the nature of liberation? What is the true text?” He asks all these questions to refute the doctrines stated by the Buddhists.

“Now, Arulnandi Sivachariyar Peruman explains the appropriate answers in Siddhanta. The Sivagamas were spoken by Thirugnanasambandha Peruman, emphasizing that Saiva religion is the only religion and that there is nothing else. And as Pillaiyar, who understood the eternal glorious Vedas, Agamas, and countless other arts that derive from them, graciously spoke to the Buddhists, his divine compassionate gaze enlightened their minds to those truths.

“Thus, those enlightened Buddhists understood these truths and went and bowed at the sacred feet of Pillaiyar, the revered Brahmin born in Sirkazhi. They accepted his guidance and bowed down to the sacred feet of Thirugnanasambandha Peruman with devotion. They truly bowed down to the ultimate truth.

“Therefore, he cast a graceful glance upon them, removed their bonds, and through initiation and instruction, Pillaiyar makes them Saivites and helps them attain salvation. Theivasekkizhar Peruman describes this in the next verse. Let’s continue to contemplate.”
