Since the gem is called ‘mani’, we can infer that other gems like ratnam are also included here. Thirugnanasambandhar’s divine hands are long, reaching down to his knees.

This physical characteristic signifies his greatness, as Sanskrit texts state that long hands reaching the knees indicate divine stature. ‘Tadakkai’ signifies mighty hands.

Here, it refers to Thirugnanasambandhar’s strength and prosperity, hands that bestow life-giving grace upon the world. The act of providing water to Mangayarkkarasi Ammaniyar and Kulachirai Nayanar. This signifies his ability to show the path to liberation to all who have come to this wedding. These are the glories of Thirugnanasambandhar’s mighty hands. They adorn his forearms with bangles, called ‘sarai’. They adorn his elbows with an ornament called ‘muzhangai pottu’.

They also adorn him with a pearl garland called ‘karamalai’. They adorn his shoulders with a pearl net, and his beautiful shoulders. As mentioned in the Thiruanthathi of Aadalur Pillaiyar, chapter forty-five: ‘the skin that is so beautiful, like gold, fitting for the embrace of the Tamil scriptures’.

Thus, the pearl net is adorned on his beautiful shoulders. Verse 1214: ‘Necklace of divine beads, a necklace of large pearls strung together, adorned with radiant brilliance.’ This verse describes the adorning of a radiant necklace of large pearls, strung in order, with a divine bead necklace, possibly Rudraksha beads, around his neck. This necklace is described as superior to a pearl necklace, with the suffix ‘divine’ (thiru), as illuminated by Sekkizhar. The divine Rudraksha necklace is something the Pillaiyar always wears. This pearl garland is strung alongside such a Rudraksha necklace. The Rudraksha beads worn on the neck are large.

Therefore, a garland of large pearls, matching the size of the Rudraksha beads, is strung with the Rudraksha necklace.

Now, Thirugnanasambandhar’s divine ears, described as ‘radiant and beautiful ears’ by Sekkizhar. It is the place where he listens to the requests of devotees who come with devotion and arise with knowledge. It is Thirugnanasambandhar’s divine ears.

Therefore, when singing of the ears, Sekkizhar describes them as ‘radiant and beautiful ears’. We should also remember here that the ears are shaped like the Pranava mantra. When the Pillaiyar began his Thirumurai, he started with ‘Thodu Udaiya Seviyan’ (He of the Holey Ears), signifying the importance of his ears in receiving divine pronouncements. Sekkizhar also points out that the Pillaiyar’s body is filled with divine wisdom.

Therefore, his ears have the quality of Shiva’s divine ears.

Now, verse 1215: ‘Resplendent forehead, adorned with divine ash, overflowing with brilliance.’ A radiant light emerged, like a pearl adorned with a crown. This adornment is placed on Thirugnanasambandhar’s divine forehead. The divine radiance of the sacred ash overflows. On this forehead, a radiant light spreads. It resembles a cool, luminous pearl, spreading its radiance. The light of the sacred ash previously shone from his forehead, and now it spreads outwards like a radiant light.

Sekkizhar, who began the divine vision from the sacred feet, concludes by stating that the divine light that bloomed at the sacred feet now shines as a radiant light spread upon the divine crown. We can witness the beauty of the divine verse. This refers to the Pillaiyar’s forehead, filled with overflowing sacred ash. When the Pillaiyar incarnated, he did not desire other adornments; he established the sacred ash on his forehead and filled it.

From that day until now, the sacred ash has continuously filled his forehead.

Thus, a beautiful crown made of pearls is added to his divine crown. ‘Thiranai’ refers to the large, curled rim below the crown. This refers to a structure resembling a crown made of many pearl garlands, twisted like a ‘pagai’ and adorned with tassels. This is called a pearl crown, and it is adorned on his divine crown, fittingly. This divine form, which rules over us, is adorned with beauty. The holy Brahmins perform the ritual. ‘He of the lotus-like chest, adorned with fragrant pollen, with long, lotus-like matted hair. He adorned himself with the divine mark, the holy garland, praised by all worlds.’ This verse describes the divine form, from the sacred feet to the divine crown, as elaborated by the divine Sekkizhar in the previous verses.

He guides us to the path of liberation, eradicates the cycle of birth, and calls to us, embodying the Guru-murti. This is Thirugnanasambandhar’s divine form. This divine form, filled with beauty, rules over us.

The Brahmins, skilled in their craft, adorned this beautiful divine form. The Pillaiyar, with a chest like a fragrant lotus, adorned himself with the divine mark, the Rudraksha garland, praised by all worlds. He took it and wore it himself. The aforementioned verses describe how Thirugnanasambandhar himself, with his divine hands, adorned himself with the Rudraksha garland, from his sacred feet to his divine crown. The divine mark garland is the Rudraksha bead, which is Shiva’s mark.

Therefore, the divine mark garland, like a woman’s thali which signifies her connection to her husband, shows that those who wear the Rudraksha garland belong to their soul’s husband, Lord Shiva. It declares that they are Shiva’s possession. All the adornments described so far were part of the wedding attire crafted by the Brahmins. Over this wedding attire, Thirugnanasambandhar himself, bowing to the Lord, adorned himself with the Rudraksha garland, the divine mark garland.

Thus, from his sacred feet to his divine crown, the divine form of Thirugnanasambandhar was revealed to us by Sekkizhar. Let us go on contemplating.

Chapter 282 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
The Great Puranam by Sekkizhar, Part 829, chapter ‘Vambara Varivandu’, Puranam of Thirugnanasambandhanayanar, verse 1217: ‘Adorning beauty with divine white ash and Panchakshara mantra, surrounded by devoted followers, he arrived at the temple. He then ascended a pearl palanquin, carried by celestial beings on a young bull, after bowing and worshipping.’ This verse states that those who chant the divine five-letter mantra and wear the divine ash, which adorns beauty, approach him, surrounded by their beloved devotees. The divine ash is the ornament that gives beauty to all ornaments. Without divine ash, other ornaments become impure, worldly things that lead to suffering. ‘As the sacred ash does not adorn the forehead...’(Thiruvasagam). It is the rule and tradition to wear the divine ash after chanting the holy name of Shiva.

As Thirugnanasambandhar, surrounded by such devotees, worshipped Shiva wholeheartedly, he ascended a pearl palanquin with the sound of trumpets. Verse 1218: ‘Conch shells sounded, everywhere auspicious flowers rained down, blessings overflowed, filling the directions, blooming across the world.’ This verse describes how, as Thirugnanasambandhar ascended the palanquin, conch shells sounded, auspicious music played, and a shower of divine celestial flowers rained down. The blessings of the meditating sages and devotees, along with Vedic chants, rose higher and higher, spreading in all directions, and the world bloomed. The phrase ‘world bloomed’ in this verse echoes the word ‘Ulagelam’ given by the Lord as the first line of this Puranam. Sekkizhar glorifies this. When the Lord of Thiru Arathurai ascended the pearl palanquin given by the Lord, he ascended with a chant.

On that day, he ascended with a chant of ‘Neetroli potri anjalithu podhu’.

Similarly, this time, as he ascended with a chant of the sacred ash, the verse concludes by stating that ‘the world bloomed’. This is the divine poetic skill of Sekkizhar. Verse 1219: ‘With flowing garlands, parasols, colorful peacock feathers, and canopies, adorned with red gold plates, like the radiant moon rising from the sea, a pearl canopy shaded him.’ Flowing garlands, tassels, canopies made of green peacock feathers, and beautiful canopies adorned with red gold plates. Like the radiant moon rising from the sea, a pearl canopy, adorned with rows of pearl strings, shaded him as Thirugnanasambandhar arrived. A large white pearl umbrella fluttered above all these decorations, providing shade over the Pillaiyar’s palanquin. Verse 1220: ‘Through the adorned streets, the wedding procession proceeded.

Pearl trumpets and symbols announced his arrival. Vedic chants proclaiming ‘The world will be saved, Gnanasambandhan has come’ echoed loudly.’ The streets adorned for the wedding procession. The wedding procession of the groom proceeds through this beautifully decorated street. The pearl trumpets and symbols, shining with light, along with the melodies, proclaimed loudly, ‘Gnanasambandhan has come for the salvation of the world,’ accompanied by Vedic chants. Verse 1221: ‘He who came to relieve the suffering of the earth, his names.’ As the symbols emerged, the divine Brahmins, who had adorned the streets for the groom’s arrival, showered blessings. Thirugnanasambandhar incarnated not for himself, but to alleviate the suffering of the world.

Therefore, he is known by many names that signify this purpose. Thirugnanasambandhar’s many names include Parasamaya Kozhari, Palaravayan, and others. The pearl symbols mentioned in the previous verse were given by the Lord. These names, proclaimed by the people during this wedding procession, are spoken by those who chant them. It is customary even today to announce the arrival of important people by chanting their names in large institutions like monasteries. This is called ‘Prithavali’.

Thus, the Pillaiyar, who is of such great stature, was being married. The auspicious sounds of blessings echoed in the mansion of Nambiyandar Nambi, a virtuous Brahmin who had the privilege of adorning him. Verse 1222: ‘The one who has attained complete wisdom, his divine hand, holding the great grace of penance, like a divine Kalpaka flower branch, adorned him with protective charms. Before the auspicious ritual, the work was done with devotion.’ This verse describes the bride, who, by her great penance, has attained the qualities of a divine Kalpaka flower branch. She was adorned with protective charms. Before the auspicious ritual, the engagement ceremonies were performed with devotion.

This bride is one who has performed great penance, and by that penance, she has received the boon of becoming the Pillaiyar’s consort. She is also one who has attained the divine state of Shiva. The Kalpaka is a good Kalpaka tree that grants liberation. This bride is like a flower branch of that divine Kalpaka. The Pillaiyar, on this auspicious wedding day, is poised to grant liberation. This implies that this bride also has a share in the liberation granted by the Pillaiyar.

Therefore, Sekkizhar describes her as ‘a divine Kalpaka flower branch, born of the grace of great penance’.

Similarly, in the following verses, Sekkizhar praises her as ‘like a coral creeper’, ‘a flame’, ‘a virtuous woman of great penance’, ‘a sprout of great penance’, ‘a lightning creeper with white clouds’, ‘a creeper with curved eyebrows’, ‘a flower branch’, ‘a parrot’, and ‘a beloved’. We can see the beauty in these praises of the mother. In the Kandapuranam, when Narada Muni informs Murugaperuman about Valli Nayaki, he says, ‘She is the mother.’ This also reminds us of that sentiment. All these preparations were made before the groom arrived at the wedding hall. Verse 1223: ‘With a red gem, adorned with golden threads, a pearl garland, a delicate coral creeper, and a divine grace, the nobleman adorned her, causing her beauty to shine.’ The bride, adorned with beautiful golden ornaments and garlands, resembling a delicate coral creeper, was decorated by the grace of the Lord, causing her beauty to shine. Like a lamp made of beautiful gold, she was adorned as if decorating beauty itself.

Verse 1224: ‘All the noble Brahmins went forth to meet him, showering flowers, perfumed powders, and nine gems. Like Brahma in the lotus, the Brahmins, along with sacred grass, poured fragrant pure water.’ The celestial beings showered divine flowers, and the fragrant southern breeze filled the air. Amidst the brightly lit toranas, the Pillaiyar, like the fruit of merit, entered the wedding pavilion. Verse 1226: ‘He arrived.’ The sound of conch shells filled the air, and a great multitude of pearl decorations shimmered. From the pearl palanquin, many flowers and fragrant golden powders were scattered over the spread carpet. Thirugnanasambandhar descended.

He came for the salvation of the three worlds. ‘Pavaadai’ means a spread carpet. It is customary to spread a carpet for elders to walk on, so they do not walk directly on the ground. This carpet is called ‘pavaadai’. It is also a form of worship. The Pillaiyar, who had descended from the pearl palanquin, now disembarked at the wedding hall. [FAILED TRANSCRIPTION]

Descending from the pearl palanquin, he arrived at the flower pavilion and then proceeded on the carpet to the wedding hall. There, auspicious women greeted him with full pots and other auspicious items. These women, holding golden pots filled with water, beautiful lamps, incense, garlands of fragrant flowers, pots of sprouted grains, and scented paste, welcomed the groom, Pillaiyar.

Here, ‘sprouted grains’ refers to grains sprouted on the seventh day before the wedding. These sprouts grew abundantly and flourished, signifying good fortune. They were held in golden pots and presented as a welcome. Having arrived at the wedding hall, the Pillaiyar was seated on a golden throne. Sekkizhar continues to describe this.

Chapter 283 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
The Great Puranam by Sekkizhar, Part 830, chapter ‘Vambara Varivandu’, Puranam of Thirugnanasambandhanayanar. Thirugnanasambandhar stood at the entrance of the wedding hall. At the entrance, under the canopy, he stood for the auspicious rituals like the ‘neeranjanam’ (water ritual) to be performed around the groom. He stood on a golden throne. Verse 1228: ‘On the golden, jewel-studded throne placed before him, the overflowing flood of wisdom rose within him, like a shining pearl ornament.

He stood, spreading his presence, having vanquished opposing schools of thought.’ On the golden, jewel-studded throne placed before him, the overflowing flood of supreme wisdom, which surpasses all, rose within him, like a shining pearl ornament. He stood, spreading his presence, having vanquished opposing schools of thought. The Pillaiyar, adorned with pearl ornaments, stood on the throne. His appearance was as if the supreme wisdom, filling him, was overflowing outwards. Wisdom is light, and thus it is customary to describe it as white. ‘Overflowing flood of wisdom’ signifies excellence in all aspects. ‘Flood’ signifies abundance. This reminds us of the first stanza, which describes the state of great wisdom that overflows.

The overflow of wisdom is here associated with the ‘Sri Panchakshara Pathigam’, signifying the completion of the decade of verses. The inner light of divine wisdom, and the outer light of the pearl ornaments, together illuminated everywhere.

Thus, the Pillaiyar stood on the throne. He, who dispelled the darkness of opposing schools of thought, and filled the world with the light of wisdom, embodied the inner meaning of his incarnation. This moment signifies the completion of the inner purpose of his incarnation. It also implies that the Pillaiyar will attain the divine union in marriage. Verse 1229: ‘The welcoming gesture, the youthful bride, the sweet auspicious chants of women, the fragrant water from the gem-studded vessel, the ritualistic circumambulation, the auspicious rituals were performed.’ The welcoming gesture, the youthful bride, the sweet auspicious chants of women, the fragrant water from the gem-studded vessel, the ritualistic circumambulation, the auspicious rituals were performed. The maidens, resembling the bride in her youth, sang sweet auspicious chants, filling the air with their blessings.

Fragrant water from a beautiful, gem-studded vessel was poured before him, and with great devotion, they performed the ritualistic circumambulation according to the rules. ‘Karakam’ refers to a small vessel with a spout. Pouring water from it without interruption and performing the circumambulation is the ritual. This is called ‘Neeranjanam’. Verse 1230: ‘Carrying auspicious items, the women entered the golden mansion, like the confluence of the Ganges and the Himalayas.’ ‘Carrying auspicious items, the women entered the golden mansion, like the confluence of the Ganges and the Himalayas. They have graced us with their presence, those who previously placed the palm leaf manuscript in the Vaigai River.’ This verse describes how, as auspicious items were carried by the Brahmin women, the pure white water, resembling the flowing waves of the Ganges, entered the golden mansion of Nambiyandar Nambi, like the confluence with the Himalayas. The Pillaiyar, who had previously placed the palm leaf manuscript in the Vaigai River to save us, entered.

Because the Pillaiyar was adorned with white pearl decorations, the white Ganga water was compared to the flowing waves of the Ganges. The waves of the Ganges flow gently and slowly, not with great force.

Therefore, it is described as the waves of the Ganges. These waves entered the mountain, called the golden mountain, just as the Pillaiyar entered the mansion called Aadhi Bhoomi. This mansion belongs to Nambiyandar Nambi. He entered the mansion, which is called Aadhi Bhoomi. He is the one who, in the past, won the river debate by placing the palm leaf manuscript in the Vaigai River, writing the hymn ‘Vaazhka Andhanar’ (May Brahmins live). In that hymn, the lines ‘Aazhka theeyathu ellam aran naamame soozhga vaiyagavum thuyar theergave’ (May all evil sink, may only the name of God surround, may the world be free from suffering) show how he saved us, future generations.

The Pillaiyar uttered commands like ‘Aazhka’ (live), ‘Soozhga’ (surround), and ‘Theerga’ (be free) using the imperative mood.

Therefore, this hymn, which bestows life not only at that time but for all future generations, is significant. Because he placed the palm leaf manuscript in the river, we are alive today, and future generations will also live. The phrase ‘to live for us’ means ‘to grant life’. The victory in the river debate and the subsequent eradication of opposing ideologies led to the establishment and growth of the Saiva faith, bringing us life. That is the significance here.

Thus, the Pillaiyar, who grants us life, entered the mansion called Aadhi Bhoomi. He is destined to grant great bliss and liberation to all who have come to the temple, which is the city of Shiva, known as Aadhi Bhoomi. One should understand this as the Lord’s grace, which was bestowed upon us by placing the palm leaf in the river in the past. ‘Aadhi Bhoomi’ also means the city of Shiva. Verse 1231: ‘Incense smoke diffused, fragrant flowers adorned the canopy, on the flower-strewn seat, with tassels, the groom, adorned with pearl necklaces, smiled. Surrounded by virtuous Brahmins, he sat there.’ This verse describes the scene as the groom, Pillaiyar, sat on the flower-strewn seat in the mansion called Aadhi Bhoomi. Incense smoke diffused, a canopy adorned with jewels shone above, maidens sang praises, and Brahmins chanted Vedic hymns.

As soon as the groom took his seat, the first ritual was performed. The next ritual will be described in the following verse. Sekkizhar continues. Verse 1232: ‘The bride’s father, a sage who received the bride, along with his virtuous wife, who performed great penance, joyfully washed the groom’s feet. They brought pure milk and water with affection.’ This verse refers to Nambiyandar Nambi, the father of the bride, who is a sage who received the bride. Sekkizhar describes him as a sage.

We saw earlier that in verse 1059, Sekkizhar referred to the groom’s father, Shivapadakirthiyayar.

Similarly, here, Nambiyandar Nambi, the bride’s father, is referred to as a sage. Nambiyandar Nambi and his virtuous wife, who have performed great penance, have attained the boon of having a daughter who is destined to become the Pillaiyar’s consort. Without such great penance, it would not be possible to have such a daughter.

Therefore, Nambiyandar Nambi’s wife also performed great penance to beget this daughter. If Nambiyandar Nambi’s wife had not performed such great penance, Nambiyandar Nambi would not have had the privilege of giving his daughter in marriage today.

Thus, Nambiyandar Nambi received such great honor. His wife performed such penance. Although they had a daughter, the right to give her in marriage belongs to the father.

Therefore, Sekkizhar first mentions Nambiyandar Nambi and then his wife. Nambiyandar Nambi and his wife, with great joy, washed the Pillaiyar’s feet. They were honored to give their daughter to the Pillaiyar, a fact that filled them with pride. This act was not merely a duty but also an expression of their right.

Therefore, they brought pure milk and water to wash the divine feet of Thirugnanasambandhar. With great joy, they washed the divine feet. They were blessed to touch, wash, and worship the divine feet, and they were filled with immense happiness. They imprinted the divine feet in their hearts. Since the Pillaiyar’s body is immaculate, washing his feet is not essential.

However, to show their detachment and devotion, they washed the Pillaiyar’s feet, as explained by the sage Sivakavi Mani Desikar. He interpreted the act as the parents of the bride treating the groom as Lord Shiva and washing his feet with cow’s milk, which is one of the wedding rituals. The Kandapuranam, in the chapter on the divine wedding, verse 39, states: ‘The celestial beings descended, accompanied by divine maidens, and washed the feet of the supreme being with milk and water.’ Similarly, in the Kandapuranam, chapter on the divine wedding of Deivanai, verse 206, it is stated: ‘Indrani, receiving the auspicious occasion, brought forth milk from a new cow and filled a vessel with it, and performed the ritual with reverence.’ In all these instances, the Lord established this ritual for the world. It signifies that in auspicious rituals, one should consider the bride as Shakti and the groom as Shiva, and both should see themselves in this manner. These are truths that reveal that the goal of auspicious rituals performed by Saivites is to attain the divine state of Shiva. These are the teachings of the Shaiva Shastras, and we see that they are perfectly embodied in the Pillaiyar.

We are about to witness how the Pillaiyar’s divine feet guided the world to liberation. Nambiyandar Nambi and his wife, in order to show the world that these divine feet are worthy of worship and lead to liberation, performed this act. The divine feet of the Pillaiyar are always in the hearts of devotees. They are worshipped with flowers by the people of this world. They are worthy of poetic composition by scholars. ‘The golden feet of the sage are divine.’ Nambiyandar Nambi later reveals this.

Now, he is showing it. Verse 1233: ‘Arriving before him, and with the merit of their past penance, Nambiyandar Nambi and the bride, with their mind fixed on the divine feet of Gnana Ponaar, poured water from the golden vessel.’ Thus, after taking pure water and cow’s milk, they arrived before the Pillaiyar. Nambiyandar Nambi, whose merit from past penance is overflowing, and his wife, poured water from the golden vessel, meditating on the divine feet of the Pillaiyar, whom they considered as Shiva with matted hair. This is the meaning of this verse.

Following this, verse 1234 states: ‘After sprinkling the pure water over their heads, they cleared the auspicious water within the house and outside. They poured it into their bellies with great joy.’ As stated in verse 1233, Nambiyandar Nambi, having performed great penance in the past, and now having the boon of giving his daughter in marriage, and anticipating the imminent attainment of bliss and liberation for himself and others, washed the Pillaiyar’s feet. By washing the Pillaiyar’s feet, the wedding ritual took place, and it also served as the worship of the Guru. As a result of this Guru worship, they attained liberation.

Thus, the merit of their past penance increased, as mentioned by Sekkizhar. ‘Kanthavar Kuzhalinar’, meaning Nambiyandar Nambi’s wife with long, fragrant hair. The fragrance is natural in the hair of virtuous women.

Therefore, Sekkizhar refers to her not by her name but as ‘Kanthavar Kuzhal’ (fragrant-haired). It is a rule to treat the groom as Shiva during wedding rituals.

Therefore, considering him as Shiva, Nambiyandar Nambi’s wife poured water from the golden vessel. It is customary for the mother of the bride to wash the groom’s feet with milk and water.

Here, not only was he the groom, but he was also being worshipped as the Guru.

Therefore, Nambiyandar Nambi’s wife poured the water from the vessel, and Nambiyandar Nambi himself performed this ritual. Verse 1234 describes how Sekkizhar states that he performed it with great affection. He sprinkled the extremely pure water on his head. This was the pure water used to wash the Gnana Ponaar’s feet.

Therefore, after sprinkling this holy water on his head, the most important part of the body, which sustains life, is the head. He first sprinkled it on his head, and then on the inside and outside of the mansion, which is the place where the body lives. As a result, the place was filled, completed, and adorned. After sprinkling the holy water inside and outside the mansion, they joyfully drank it, considering it as the source of life in their bellies. The relatives, experiencing great delight, also sprinkled it on themselves.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 284 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
The Great Puranam by Sekkizhar, Part 831, chapter ‘Vambara Varivandu’, Puranam of Thirugnanasambandhanayanar. The foot-washing ceremony performed for the groom is also considered Guru worship. This holy water is sprinkled throughout the pavilion. All the relatives cherish it with great devotion. Verse 1235: ‘The Pillaiyar, who has attained overflowing wisdom, received the flower-like hand holding the vessel of auspicious water.

He proclaimed his lineage and declared, ‘I have given my precious daughter to the Pillaiyar.’’ This verse refers to Thirugnanasambandhar as the Pillaiyar who has attained overflowing wisdom. ‘Overflowing wisdom’ here refers to divine wisdom, which has the power to dispel the inner darkness of primal ignorance.

Therefore, it is called overflowing wisdom.

Furthermore, because it has no superior light, this divine wisdom is indeed overflowing. The Pillaiyar, who has made this divine wisdom, like nectar, available to us, received the vessel of auspicious water in his lotus-like hand. Nambiyandar Nambi, holding the auspicious water in the vessel, poured it, declaring, ‘I have given my daughter.’ It is customary to pour water while giving away the daughter, signifying the ‘Kanyadhanam’ in Sanskrit. While pouring the water, Nambiyandar Nambi ...stated his lineage and family, and declared, ‘I have given my daughter, whom I cherished as a precious treasure, to the Pillaiyar.’ Thus, Sekkizhar describes Nambiyandar Nambi’s daughter as ‘Arunidhi Paavaiyar’, meaning one adorned with precious ornaments. This refers to a ‘Sallankruta Kannikadhanam’. The tradition of Krita Yuga, which was to place a young maiden, whose waist was slender like the rays of the sun, and give her hand in marriage before she was ripe, is narrated in the Thiruvilayadal Puranam.

Nambandhar Nambigal, referred to as Arunitipavaiyar, his daughter whose name is given as Stotra Purnambigai in the Tala Puranam of Tirunallur Peruman, is stated to have performed the Kanyadhanam, dedicating this maiden, this young girl, to Pillaiyar (Ganesha). ‘I have given this maiden, this young girl, whom I received, to Pillaiyar,’ thus states Nambandhar Nambigal.

Now, the thirty-sixth Tiruppadal: ‘Nattavakkanniyar Kai Gnanasambandhar Chengai Patriyudaiya Panpil Pazhuthil Narpozuthu Nanna Pettravar Udan Pirandhaar Peru.’ This refers to the act of escorting the bride to the groom and the people surrounding them, bowing and offering praise. This is from the Tiruppadal. Nambandhar Nambigal announces that he is performing the Kanyadhanam. As soon as this is announced, the auspicious moment for the wedding ceremony, Panigrahanam, arrives. This Panigraha Muhurtham, as it is called in Sanskrit, is referred to as ‘Narpozuthu, free from blemish, suitable for Gnanasambandhar to take the maiden’s hand’ by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. The ceremony of Thiru Mangalya Dharanam, tying the sacred marital thread, began later.

In earlier times, the Koda (giving away the bride) was performed by those who were accustomed to it, along with the Vedic ceremony called Velvi (fire ritual). Later came the act of holding hands, called Panigrahanam, and the adorning with garlands. That is, exchanging garlands and circumambulating the sacred fire were the initial rituals, some say. It is also said that references to wearing the Thiru Mangalyam are first found in the Matsya Purana.

However, the Thiruvilayadal Puranam, in its wedding chapter, the one hundred and eighty-fifth verse, states thus: ‘Sutru naan maraigal aarppuriyam sangam engu katra naan mugaththon velvi chadangu nool karaintha atraal utra Mangalaathi muzhuthu ulagu yandran sengkai patrina patriyilaarkke vidu arul paramayogi.’ In this, Lord Shiva, appearing as Somasundara Kadavul, during the wedding of Meenakshi Amman, and Brahma performing the Vedic ceremony. He placed the auspicious thread on Meenakshi Amman’s neck and held her hand. So goes the verse.

Similarly, in the Kanda Puranam, in the chapter on the wedding of Deivayanai Amman, the two hundred and forty-seventh Tiruppadal states: ‘Sengkmalathu iraichinthaiyin aatri angaiyin enthida aanda kai konda mangala naanai manikkazhum aarththu nangai mudikkor narunthodai suzhan.’ This verse describes how Lord Muruga tied the auspicious thread around Deivayanai Amman’s neck.

Therefore, for those who argue otherwise, the Thiruvilayadal Puranam (wedding of Meenakshi Amman) and the Kanda Puranam (wedding chapter of Deivayanai Amman) provide a beautiful and fitting answer.

Thus, now arrives the Panigraha Muhurtham. Just as we look for an auspicious time for Thiru Mangalya Dharanam, it is our custom to look for an auspicious time, a Muhurtham, for Panigrahanam as well. That moment, according to astrological texts, is a good time, a Nammumurtham, free from flaws. This is referred to as ‘Narpozuthu’ by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman. ‘Pazhuthu’ means flaw, and ‘Nalpozuthu’ means a good Muhurtham, free from defects.

Moreover, ‘Pazhuthayil Pozuthu’ means the time that causes the removal of the impurity of the souls. This signifies that in this wedding, all souls are destined to be cleansed of their impurities and attain liberation. At that auspicious time, during the Panigraha Muhurtham, having received the bride. The parents and siblings of the bride bring her into the groom’s presence. It is also customary to seat the bride on the groom’s right side. Here too, Stotra Purnambigai Amman is brought forward by her parents and siblings, surrounded by companions resembling deer, and presented before the groom, Pillaiyar.

The divine Sekkizhar Peruman mentions ‘Pettravarum Udan Pirandhaar,’ meaning parents and siblings.

Therefore, Stotra Purnambigai Amman is brought by her parents and siblings to be presented before Pillaiyar.

Thus, through this verse, we learn that Pillaiyar has siblings.

Now, the thirty-seventh Tiruppadal: ‘Ekamam Siva Meygnanam Isainthavar Valappaal Eythi.’ ‘Nagamor Panapper Alkun Natrava Kolundhu Anaarai Magamar Sodhimalka Manni Veetriruntha Vellai Megamodu Isaiyum Minnu Kodiyena Vilanga Vaithaar.’ This is the Tiruppadal. Pillaiyar is one who has attained ‘Ekamam Siva Meygnanam’ – the singular, true knowledge of Shiva. This true, unchanging, eternal knowledge is Sivagnanam. We can recall from the beginning of this Puranam the descriptions of this as ‘Perumaikkazhil Peenum Or Neriyil Varignanam’ (knowledge in a path that leads to great glory) and ‘Ennariya Sivagnanam’ (unfathomable Sivagnanam).

Thus, the benefit of the knowledge that Pillaiyar attained is now reaching its fulfillment. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman concludes this by stating, ‘Ekamam.’ ‘Siva Meygnanam Isainthavar’ (one who has attained true knowledge of Shiva) is how Pillaiyar is described here. This is the place where the state of knowledge attained by Pillaiyar is discussed. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman states this here, signifying that the fruit of that knowledge is about to be attained. Pillaiyar, who has attained that true knowledge of Shiva, has made it his very form. Pillaiyar has indeed partaken of the nectar of Sivagnanam.

The bride is seated to the right of such a Pillaiyar. That divine vision appears like a lightning streak in white clouds. It is customary for the bride to be seated on the groom’s right side until the wedding rituals are completed and the circumambulation of the fire is done.

After that, she moves to the left. The scriptures state that a woman, after observing vows and penance, obtains a suitable groom. This is what the scriptures say.

Therefore, after the fire ritual, the bride should join the groom’s left side. That is, it is the rule to seat the bride on the groom’s left side. The left side is the side meant for femininity. The stories of Uma Amman’s penance and other legends explain this concept. The fact that Amman also took her place on the left side is also part of this.

Therefore, the bride is referred to here as ‘Natrava Kolundhu Anaar’ (a tender shoot of great penance). She is seated to the right of the divine Sambandhar Peruman. How does that divine vision appear? It shines like a lightning streak in white clouds. It is natural for lightning to appear in clouds. The proverb states, ‘After lightning comes rain.’ ‘Lightning indicates the clouds, clouds indicate rain’ is the meaning.

Here, it signifies that a rain of divine knowledge is about to fall, leading to the bliss of liberation, the divine enjoyment of Shiva. This simile is used here. Our texts state that white clouds, more encompassing than dark clouds, yield great benefit. Pillaiyar is seated here like a white cloud. The whiteness of his sacred ash, the brilliance of the pearl ornaments he wears, and his radiant effulgence as a flame of knowledge – all contribute to his appearance like a white cloud. The Amman seated to his right resembles a streak of lightning, clinging to that cloud.

Now, the thirty-eighth Tiruppadal: ‘Punitha Meykolam Needu Pugaliyaar Vendhar Thammai.’ ‘Kunichilai Puruvam Men Poongombu Annaar Udaney Kooda Nanmiga Kandapozhuthil Nalla Mangalangaal Koori Manitharum Thevaraanar Kan Imaiyathu Vazhthi.’ This is the Tiruppadal. When the divine Sekkizhar Peruman saw the venerable Pillaiyar, the king of Pugali, with his pure, divine form, accompanied by the bride resembling a delicate flowering creeper with eyebrows like a bent bow, with great affection, those present there offered auspicious blessings and gazed at that divine vision without blinking. As the humans present there gazed at that divine vision without blinking, they appeared like gods. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman praises the bride of Pillaiyar here as ‘Kunichilai Puruvam Men Poongombu’ (a delicate flowering creeper with eyebrows like a bent bow). The bow’s curve indicates its usefulness; the greater the curve, the more beneficial it is.

Here, the curved state of the Amman’s eyes and eyebrows signifies her ability to bestow the benefit of liberation upon everyone through her compassionate gaze. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman implicitly conveys this. This divine vision is the first auspicious sight of the couple seated together. This is the first time that divine Sambandhar Peruman appears with his consort.

Therefore, it is a good tradition to bless such a divine vision upon seeing it. Those who witnessed this divine vision here were so captivated that they gazed without blinking and offered blessings. Those who bless the divine beings elevate themselves through that blessing. They bless the divine beings for that very purpose. ‘To bestow life upon oneself by blessing the divine, and for the celestials to bow to you, desiring to be praised,’ as stated by our Lord Manikkavachakar Peruman in the Thiruvachagam.

Therefore, those who saw and blessed Pillaiyar and his consort here attained life through their blessings. By having the opportunity to see and bless Pillaiyar and his consort in this way, they are destined to attain eternal Shiva. In ordinary worldly weddings, the blessings offered are merely formalities.

But here, the auspicious words spoken to bless Pillaiyar and his consort were genuine, not mere formalities. All those blessings are destined to culminate in eternal, unperishable divine auspiciousness.

Therefore, the divine Sekkizhar Peruman describes them as ‘good auspiciousness.’ Let us continue contemplating.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 285 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
The Periya Puranam by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, Part 832, Vambara Varivandu Sargam, ThiruGnana Sambandha Nayanar Puranam, the one thousand two hundred and thirty-ninth Tiruppadal: ‘Bhakthiyil Kuyitrum Paimpon Pavala Kaal Pandhar Naappen Chiththira Vidhanathin Keezh Sezhunthiruneelakkar Muththamizh Viragar Munbu Mudhal Marai Muraiyinodu Meyththa Namberuman Paathamevum Ullaththal Seyya.’ This is the Tiruppadal. A pandal with a base of vermilion coral, adorned with gold, supported by pillars of green gold, and a central canopy decorated with paintings. Under this canopy, the auspicious wedding rituals are taking place. The noble Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar, acting as the teacher, performs the Vedic rituals for the Pillaiyar, who is a master of the three Tamil literatures, in the presence of the divine. He performs the essential Vedic rituals according to the prescribed method, with a heart devoted to the divine feet of our Lord.

Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar is well-versed in the four Vedas, as we saw in the one thousand eight hundred and thirty-ninth Tiruppadal: ‘Gnyalamikka Naanmari Porul Vilakkiya Nalathaar.’ Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar is officiating as the Purohit, the Vedic priest, at this wedding ceremony. The term Purohit means ‘one who performs welfare in front.’ Therefore, Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar, being well-versed in the four Vedas, officiates as the Purohit and performs the wedding rituals for Pillaiyar. He performs the wedding fire ritual. It is customary to perform the wedding ritual with the groom as the central figure.

Similarly, the ritual of offering rice flakes (Porikay) is performed before the bride. These are all prescribed in the Vedas. The Vedas state that Lord Shiva alone is the Supreme Reality (Sat). With his mind contemplating the divine feet of Lord Shiva, who is described as Sat by the Vedas, Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar performs the rituals. He is very pure, an expert in the Vedas, and highly virtuous. Nevertheless, if one undertakes actions with individual consciousness, they are subject to the three Gunas and may deviate from the proper course.

Therefore, performing these rituals with individual consciousness. Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar performs them with a mind devoted to the divine feet of the Lord. As it is said, ‘True devotees who perceive the Lord’s consciousness do not succumb to karma,’ he will complete the rituals smoothly, thinking of Lord Shiva. The Tiruppadal also states, ‘Ullaththarai’ (with a devoted heart). It is also fitting to say that he performs these duties with the thought that by doing this noble work, he will attain the grace of the divine feet. We can also see that Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar is destined to attain the grace of the divine feet.

Now, the next meaning: Pillaiyar does not cherish anything other than the divine feet of the Lord.

Therefore, it is a rule that his Vedic rituals must also be performed with the same devotion. This is about. Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar performs them by remembering the divine feet of the Lord. The Śivāgamas state that when performing rituals like Pujas, one must transform their sensory organs and mind into a divine form through appropriate mantras, Nyasa, and Bhava kriyas. Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar performs these actions with the thought of dedicating himself to the task of performing Pillaiyar’s wedding rituals. Another interpretation is that although these rituals are performed with Pillaiyar as the central figure, they are done with the understanding that they ultimately reach the Lord’s feet.

Furthermore, these rituals are destined to grant the attainment of Shiva, the ultimate state, to all those present at this wedding. With the intention of bestowing eternal divine auspiciousness. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman elaborates extensively on this point, stating that Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar performs these rituals with such devotion, meditating on the divine feet of Lord Shiva. It is also mentioned that most of this commentary is based on the notes of Thiru Kayapakkam Sadashiva Chettiyar. The commentator states: ‘Now, the one thousand two hundred and fortieth Tiruppadal: ‘Maraiyoli Pongki Ongga Mangala Vazhthu Malga Niraivazhai Chengai Patra.’ ‘Neriizhai Avar Mun Anthap Poraiyani Munnool Marbar Pugazhil Van Porikai Atti Iraivarai Yetum Velai Erivilam Kolla Vendi.’ This is the Tiruppadal.

The Brahmins and relatives gathered there chanted Vedic hymns. The women of the priestly class and others proclaimed auspicious blessings. For the maiden adorned with numerous bangles to hold the hand of the groom, Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar, before her, took handfuls of faultless white rice flakes, offered them as oblations into the sacred fire, and praised the Lord. Offering white rice flakes into the sacred fire before the bride, accompanied by appropriate mantras and visualizations, and praising the Lord. This is performed for Panigrahanam. There are many rules regarding how the new rice flakes should be prepared, starting with the requirement that they be crushed by chaste women in a new, clean clay pot in a pure environment.

The rice flakes prepared according to these rules are faultless and are the best offering for the oblations. It is customary to take these rice flakes and offer them into the fire with one’s hands, not with tools.

At this time, the mantras recited convey the request for the Lord’s grace, enabling the Lord to accept this ritual and bestow its appropriate benefits. After offering the rice flakes into the fire, the groom must hold the bride’s hand and circumambulate the sacred fire seven times. This is a very important part of the wedding rituals. It is customary for the wedding rituals to conclude with this.

Therefore, before doing so, Thiru Neelanakka Nayanar supplicates the Lord by offering rice flakes into the sacred fire.

Now, the one thousand two hundred and forty-first Tiruppadal: ‘Aruppu Menmullaiyinaarththam Animmalar Kaippidiththu Angu Or Padum Udaiya Pillaiyar ThiruUllam Thannil Viruppurum Angiyaavar Vidai Uyarththavare.’ This is the Tiruppadal. The divine Pillaiyar, who is twelve years old, holding the beautiful flower-like hand of. Stotra Purnambigai Amman, reflects within his divine heart. He contemplates the Vedic fire ritual that has been performed so far and is about to undertake the circumambulation of the fire. As he holds the Devi’s hand to proceed with the circumambulation, a thought arises in his divine heart through divine grace, a clarity emerges. Pillaiyar thinks within his divine heart, ‘The fire that is pleasing is none other than Lord Shiva, who bears the bull banner.’ He reflects this within his divine heart.

The divine Sambandhar Peruman sees the fire arising in this wedding ritual as the sacred fire. However, he realizes that Shiva Himself is the fire within that fire. This thought arises in his divine heart through divine grace. The Thevaram verse states, ‘Without fire, there is no form; without the bull, there is no ascent.’ Therefore, upon seeing the fire in the wedding ritual, the thought arises in the divine heart of divine Sambandhar Peruman that Shiva Himself is the fire. This is because fire is one of the eight forms of the Lord mentioned in the scriptures. Earth, water, fire, air, ether, sun, moon, and soul are the eight forms.

We find references to these in various places in the Thirumurai, including the Thiruvachagam.

Therefore, these eight are indeed the divine forms of the Lord. Among these eight, fire is the most significant. Earth and water are considered inferior to fire. Air and ether. Although they are the first two, they are not visible to the eyes. In the sun and moon, the Lord’s form is subtle and hidden, not openly visible.

However, fire has a special characteristic: the Lord’s form resides within the fire itself. As Rudra, the embodiment of fire, the Great Rudra, the Lord manifests in the form of fire. In that Great Rudra, He is the destroyer and also the creator, bringing about regeneration.

Therefore, among these eight, fire is the superior form. However, even within this fire, the Lord remains hidden like ghee in milk.

But the places where the Lord manifests brilliantly and openly are the Guru’s form. Shivalayam, and the divine attire of the devotee.

Therefore, upon seeing the fire in this wedding ritual, the thought arises in the divine heart of divine Sambandhar Peruman that the Lord, who has the fire as His form, is none other than Him. He decides to have the darshan of Lord Shiva, who resides within the Tirupperumanam temple. Divine grace instills this clarity in his heart.

The Lord is omnipresent. Such a Lord resides in the temple of Tirupperumanam, and this thought is instilled in the divine heart of divine Sambandhar Peruman.

The Lord is everywhere.

Therefore, even in the fire of this wedding ritual, nurtured by mantras, rituals, and visualizations. Pillaiyar, thinking that the Lord is the fire, is about to go to the Tirupperumanam temple. This is because the Lord exists everywhere as inert and conscious matter. While it is true that those with true perception can see Ishwara everywhere, both as inert and conscious, the Lord shines brightly in three forms: Guru, Lingam, and Jangamam, and less so in other places.

Therefore, worshipping the Lord’s divine form within the temple is of great significance. The Sivagnana Bodham, twelfth sutra, states: ‘Although the universe is divine, worship with love.’ Even though all inert and conscious things are the form of that divine being, worship where love blossoms. We see this concept articulated in the Mahabhashyam as a command: ‘O one who has attained that non-dual Siddhanta.’ Just as milk overflows from the cow’s udder, even though the entire body is filled with milk, the Lord does not manifest Himself outwardly except through the divine form in the temple.

Therefore, it is conveyed that the love that arises there will not blossom elsewhere. Even though the Lord manifests in this sacred fire of the wedding ritual, which has been invoked through mantras, those who lack the ability to perceive Him in the fire will only see Him if invoked by the mantra’s presence. Without the mantra’s presence, He remains hidden.

However, for those with true penance or wisdom, He always appears in all places. Pillaiyar, too, was in such a state of liberated consciousness (Jeevan Mukta).

Therefore, Pillaiyar’s incarnation here was for the sake of the worldly people who lack the penance to see the Lord everywhere.

Thus, realizing that Lord Shiva Himself resides in this wedding fire, Pillaiyar decides to go to the Tirupperumanam temple where that Lord resides. This is because the Lord has manifested here due to the invocation through the sankalpa for this wedding ritual. This is because the Lord has manifested here due to the invocation through the sankalpa for this wedding ritual.

After the wedding ritual is completed, He will withdraw His presence with Udyapana (retirement) rituals. However, in the temple, the Lord resides eternally, manifesting His presence.

Therefore, Pillaiyar’s current action is to fulfill the purpose of the wedding ritual, which began with the sankalpa and invocation. This requires His presence in the eternal divine auspiciousness, allowing everyone to enter it. He understands that the appropriate place for this is not the fire of this wedding ritual, but the fire within the Tirupperumanam temple, through divine grace.

Thus, Pillaiyar, who has taken the Amman’s hand, resolves. Before completing the seven circumambulations of the fire established in that wedding ritual, he decides to have darshan of Lord Shiva, who manifests in that fire, and who resides in Tirupperumanam. Divine Sambandhar Peruman resolves this.

Let us continue contemplating.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 286 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
The Periya Puranam by the divine Sekkizhar Peruman, Part 833, Vambara Varivandu Sargam, ThiruGnana Sambandha Nayanar Puranam, the one thousand two hundred and forty-second Tiruppadal: ‘Manthira Muraiyal Uytha Eri Valamaaga Maathar Thum ThiruKaiyai Pattum Thamarai Sengaiyalar Indha Il Ozhukkam Vandhu Soozhndhathe Ival Thannodum Anthamil Shivan Thaal Serven Ennum Aathiravu Pongka.’ This is the Tiruppadal. Upon seeing the fire that arose in the wedding ritual, divine Sambandhar Peruman decided to go to the temple of the Lord located in Aachchapuramm, Tirupperumanallur. Now is the time to circumambulate the fire created by the mantra. He holds the Devi’s hand to circumambulate the fire, which has been kindled and nurtured by mantra. Pillaiyar, whose divine hands are as red as the lotus flower, holds her hand.

This fire is one created by mantra. The divine form of the Lord residing in the temple is the eternal Agni (fire). This is the implied meaning. The act of holding the Amman’s hand to circumambulate for the completion of the wedding ceremony. In this state, Pillaiyar’s divine heart exclaims, ‘Alas! This worldly life, this path of household living, has surrounded me!

With her, I will reach the divine feet of the imperishable Shiva!’ This desire grows stronger. ‘This worldly life, this path of household living, has surrounded me!’ Thus, divine Sambandhar Peruman reflects in his divine heart. The Tiruppadal states, ‘This worldly life, this path of household living, has surrounded me!’ The word ‘this’ refers to this path, which is considered lower than the path of divine knowledge. The life of divine Sambandhar Peruman is the path of divine knowledge, which transcends all else. The marriage taking place here is one of the stages of household life (Ashrama). He had attained completeness and was steadfast in his devotion to Shiva’s feet. He was born into this world.

Therefore, he was not born to marry and live a household life like others.

Thus, he reflects, ‘Alas! This household life, which deviates from the path of divine knowledge and is a lower path, has now encompassed me!’ The eleventh Tiruppadal, which is the commentary on the eighth sutra of Sivagnana Siddhiyar, states: ‘The author of Siddhiyar explains how souls attain Sivagnanam through stages. By following the paths of external religions, entering internal religions, following the paths of Smriti, and adhering to the virtues of the Ashramas as prescribed in the Vedas, and by performing arduous penances, acquiring various arts and sciences, studying the Vedas, and understanding the profound meaning of the scriptures, one attains the Saiva state. After practicing Sarikriya, Kriya, and Yoga, one attains Shiva’s feet through Gnanam.’ This is the Tiruviruttam. This Tiruviruttam explains how a soul, through a ladder-like progression, matures in its knowledge and ultimately attains the grace of Lord Shiva’s feet. This Tiruppadal explains the exquisite process through which a soul, depending on its level of maturity, progresses through external religious paths, then internal religious paths, then Smriti texts, then adhering to the Ashrama Dharma prescribed in the Vedas, then performing difficult penances, acquiring profound knowledge and sciences, studying the Vedas, and understanding the Upanishadic teachings.

By ascending this ladder through many births, the soul finally reaches the state of Siddhanta Saivam. After reaching Siddhanta Saivam, by practicing Sariyai, Kriya, and Yoga, and upon their completion, attaining Sivagnanam, the soul ultimately reaches the divine feet of Lord Shiva. This is how a soul reaches Him through a gradual process. The verse states, ‘One attains Shiva’s feet through Gnanam.’ Pillaiyar, having attained the fullness of Sivagnanam, was steadfast in his devotion to Shiva’s feet.

However, he was born into this world for its upliftment. Having been born thus for the world’s salvation, will he now regress through many stages to enter the state of household life, which is conducive to birth? If he enters household life, he will desire progeny. With progeny comes worldly attachments. The three impurities (mala, karma, maya) will surround him. It is not appropriate for such worldly entanglements to surround him.

Thus, he reflects, ‘Alas! This household life, which is lower than my path of divine knowledge and my state of Sivagnanam, has now encompassed me!’ The wedding rituals, which mark the beginning of household life, are taking place.

However, the wedding rituals are not yet complete. At the stage where he holds the Devi’s hand to circumambulate the fire, this thought arises in divine Sambandhar Peruman’s mind. Only after completing the seven circumambulations of the fire, known as Sapthapadi, will the wedding be considered complete. The wedding rituals will be completed. Even though the wedding rituals are not yet complete, since Panigrahanam has occurred, the Devi is now, in a sense, Pillaiyar’s wife.

Thus, he reflects, ‘Alas! This household life, which is lower than my path of divine knowledge and my state of Sivagnanam, has now encompassed me!’ Divine Sambandhar Peruman reflects, ‘Alas! This household life has surrounded me!’ Pillaiyar, who was initially hesitant to agree to this wedding, eventually consented due to the repeated requests of his relatives and for the sake of promoting Vedic way of life, the conduct of Brahmins, and the traditions of the priestly class in the world.

However, he realized that even after consenting to uphold the Vedic way of life, it would not end there. As mentioned earlier, it would lead to worldly entanglements. Considering this, he reflects, ‘Alas! This household life has surrounded me!’ Divine Sambandhar Peruman reflects, ‘Alas! This household life has surrounded me!’ He further contemplates, ‘With her, I will reach the divine feet of the imperishable Shiva!’ The word ‘her’ refers to Stotra Purnambigai Amman. Since the ritual of Panigrahanam, holding hands, has been performed, she has, in a sense, become his wife.

Another crucial ritual, Sapthapadi (seven steps around the fire), has not yet been completed. Although the wedding ritual is not fully complete, due to Panigrahanam, the Devi is now rightfully Pillaiyar’s.

Therefore, he reflects, ‘With her, I will reach the divine feet of Shiva!’ According to the Sivagnana Siddhiyar verse, ‘One attains Shiva’s feet through Gnanam,’ he will attain the benefit of Sivagnanam. He realizes that his purpose in this world – refuting false religions and establishing the greatness of sacred ash – has been fulfilled.

Therefore, he resolves, ‘With her, I will eternally reach the divine feet of the imperishable Lord Shiva.’ Now, the one thousand two hundred and forty-third Tiruppadal: ‘Malar Perum Kilaiyum Thondar Koottamum Malki Soozha Alagil Meygnanaththu Ellai Adaippurump Kuruppaal Angan Ulagin Emmearngum Neenga Udan Anainthu Arula Vendi Kulamana Poariviththaarththam Kovilai Nokki Vandhaar.’ This Tiruppadal states that divine Sambandhar Peruman, in this verse, refers to the Lord residing in the Tirunallur Perumanam temple as ‘one who has ordained the wedding of the clan.’ This means that the Lord, for the purpose of demonstrating the Vedic way of life of Brahmins in the world, brought them together and graciously enabled them to perform the wedding rituals suitable for that clan. Pillaiyar’s own actions are seen as nothing; everything is the Lord’s doing. This is the state of divine Sambandhar Peruman. He embraced this act of getting married as if it were the Lord’s doing. The tenth sutra of Sivagnana Bodham states: ‘He who becomes one with the divine, remaining alone, serves the Lord.’ We can understand the meanings of this. Divine Sambandhar Peruman, along with his relatives and devotees, desired to reach the boundless limit of true knowledge and merge with the Lord, free from worldly attachments, and thus proceeded towards the temple of Tirupperumanam, which is Shiva’s divine wedding abode.

Boundless true knowledge is Sivagnanam. Its limit is the fullness of divine bliss that shines upon it, the world of Shiva. Although divine Sambandhar Peruman was in a state of liberated consciousness, free from any attachments, he was born into this world by divine grace to guide it towards righteousness and salvation.

Therefore, desiring to merge with Shiva, free from all worldly ties that had gathered, and remaining steadfast in devotion to Shiva’s feet, he proceeded with his relatives and devotees towards the temple of Tirupperumanam in Aachchapuram. The one thousand two hundred and forty-fourth Tiruppadal states: ‘Shivan Amarnthu Arulum Selva ThiruPerumanaththai Eythi Thavaneri Valarkka Vandhaar Thalaippadum Saarbu Nokki Pavamaram Ennai.’ ‘Munnall Aanda Appanbu Kooda Navamalar Paatham Koottum Ennum Nal Unarvu Nannu.’ This Tiruppadal, and the six subsequent Tiruppadals that follow, describe Aachchapuram, the divine abode where Lord Shiva lovingly resides and bestows grace upon souls. The temple within that divine abode is called Tirupperumanam. It is referred to as Nallur Perumanam because it is the temple named Perumanam, located in the town of Nallur.

Thus, divine Sambandhar Peruman enters the prosperous Tirupperumanam temple where Lord Shiva lovingly resides and bestows grace upon souls. He has come to nurture the path of penance. This phrase explains the inner purpose of divine Sambandhar Peruman’s incarnation: he has come to nurture the path of penance. It is explicitly conveyed to us that marrying and living in the world was not his purpose. Pillaiyar realizes through divine grace and the Lord’s intimation that the purpose of his divine incarnation is complete, and the time to attain liberation has arrived. The divine Sekkizhar Peruman states this: ‘He came to nurture the path of penance, seeking the ultimate refuge.’ ‘Thalaippadum’ means to reach.

Therefore, divine Sambandhar Peruman, who incarnated solely to nurture the path of penance, perceives through divine grace the sign of reaching the state of liberation, which transcends worldly perception. ‘Pavamaram Ennai Munnall Aanda Appanbu Kooda Navamalar Paatham Koottum Ennum Nal Unarvu.’ A feeling arises in divine Sambandhar Peruman’s divine heart through divine grace: ‘Just as He took me under His wing in the past, He will now lead me to His newly bloomed lotus-like feet.’ This is the meaning of the phrase. The word ‘pavamaram’ appears in it. ‘Pavam’ means birth. ‘Munnall Aanda’ means ‘who ruled/graced me in the past.’ Some commentators explain this as referring to the Lord who graced him at the age of three on the banks of the Brahmateertham.

Therefore, ‘Pavamaram Ennai Munnall Aanda Appanbu’ means ‘the state of grace by which He embraced me in the past.’ ‘Kooda’ means ‘to fit’ or ‘to be suitable.’ Therefore, the thought arises in divine Sambandhar Peruman’s divine heart: ‘Just as the Lord embraced me in the past, He will now grant me that same grace and lead me to His feet.’ The phrase ‘Munnall Aanda Appanbu’ refers to the state where divine Sambandhar Peruman, in the past, was devoted to the Lord’s feet, as mentioned in the verse ‘Pantu Thiru Adimaravaapanmaiyor’ (those devoted to the Lord’s feet in the past). This state has been observed in various other instances throughout the divine Sambandhar Peruman Puranam, where it is described as ‘Ennai’ (me), indicating his unwavering devotion. You have graced me, who had forgotten Your sacred feet, with attachment, showing me the way to be born in this world. This is how the fifth verse of the Thiruthuruththi Thiruppathigam reads.

Therefore, through His own divine words, Pillaiyar has proclaimed that he was previously in a state of not forgetting the Lord’s sacred feet.

Thus, that characteristic, that state, is to be restored here again as the Lord takes him into His grace and joins him at His feet. The thought of Lord Siva arises in the mind of Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman, meaning that the Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman, who was previously in a state of not forgetting the sacred feet, will have this characteristic, which has persisted since his divine incarnation in this world and until now, removed, meaning this state will be removed, and he will see only Lord Siva henceforth.

The Lord is about to bestow His grace, so that that very state of being united with Him by constant contemplation will return. Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman enters the temple of Thiru Perumanallur. Such is the characteristic of divine bliss that the Lord’s unfading, ever-new feet are experienced anew with each experience. It is said that it joins and unites.

Therefore, unless the Lord joins, knowledge cannot unite with it. If Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman was united with those feet in the state of liberation, it was to bear the divine body and bestow grace on the people of the world, standing in a worldly state. Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman. The state that Peruman has held until now, this state, this characteristic, will be removed, and he will be adorned with the state of only ever-unfading divine experience. Peruman is about to bestow that. Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman proceeds to the temple of Thiru Perumanallur.

Let us press on with our contemplation.
Thiruchitrambalam.


Chapter 287 — ThiruGnanaSambandha Nayanar

Thiruchitrambalam.
Peruman, gifted by Devashekulār Peruman, in the Periya Puranam, volume eighty-three, chapter on the buzzing bees. The life of Thiru Gnanasambandhar Nayanar. Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman, entering the temple of Thiru Perumanallur, also known as Āchāzhpuram, experiences the thought: ‘That characteristic of having ruled me in the past will also join with the unfading feet.’ This good feeling arises in the heart of Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman. Upon its arising, he appeals to the Lord of Thiru Perumanallur, Sivālōka Thyāgar Peruman, and bestows a Thiruppathigam. Devashekulār Peruman bestows it upon us in the thousand two hundred and forty-fifth verse.

The verse is as follows: “Love, the true pathigam, Kallur Perumanam, having taken and ...removed the impurities of birth and attachment, and taking them as the essence, O Lord, the Lord of Nallūr, the Lord of Perumanam, it is time to attain the shadow of Your feet.” This is the verse. He stands before the Lord with great desire and bestows the true words of the Thiruppathigam, starting with Kallūr Perumanam. Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman, taking as the meaning of the pathigam the removal of the impurities of ego, karma, and maya, which are the causes of birth, for those who witnessed the wedding there, Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman bestowed this true pathigam. O Lord, who resides in the temple of Thiru Perumanallur! It is the time to attain the shadow of Your sacred feet.

Thus, Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman sang and bestowed. This Thiruppathigam, bestowed by Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman, is praised by Devashekhilār Peruman as “Kādal Meyppathigam”. Its meaning is: a pathigam composed with great love. Because he received the good feeling that the Lord will join the unfading feet, Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman, with overflowing desire, bestowed this pathigam. This pathigam, starting with Kallūr Perumanam, is the true pathigam. “Mey” means truth.

It means a pathigam that bestows the intended benefit by the Lord’s divine word.

Therefore, this Thiruppathigam is a pathigam that bestows the intended benefit by the Lord’s divine word.

Therefore, it is the Kādal Meyppathigam. What is the meaning of this Thiruppathigam? It is to remove all the impurities of those who have seen and worshipped Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman and to unite them with the Lord’s sacred feet.

Thus, for all who came to the wedding, it is to remove their worldly attachments and bestow the Lord’s sacred feet. Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman appealed to the Lord and sang this Thiruppathigam. All who have seen and worshipped Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman have been seen by the Lord’s merciful gaze. The meaning of this Thiruppathigam is to remove the attachments of those who have seen and worshipped.

First, the idea in the mind of Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman that he himself will join the Lord’s feet. Even though it arose, he laid the application for this pathigam with the intention of attaining the feet of Lord Siva, accompanied by his consort, relatives, and devotees.

Therefore, the intention of this Thiruppathigam is not for him to attain the Lord’s sacred feet. Because, as Devashekhilār Peruman describes the intention of this Thiruppathigam, it is to remove the impurities of birth and attachment.

However, Pillaiyar, Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman, has already been taken by Lord Siva in the cycle of birth. Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman has attained divine wisdom. He is free from attachments.

Therefore, Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman did not make this application for himself. It is to sever the worldly attachments of those who participated in the wedding. It is the meaning of this Thiruppathigam. With such a meaning in mind, Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman sang this Thiruppathigam: “O Lord, the Lord of Nallūr, the Lord of Perumanam, it is time to attain the shadow of Your feet.” “Nāthan” means Lord. Lord means one who possesses divinity. The meaning is that it is the Lord’s duty to take them into His grace by virtue of that divinity.

As the Thevaram verse states, ‘Is it not the foremost duty of the great ones to remove the sins of those who come to them?’ Addressing the Lord as “Nallūr Perumāna Nambane”, he makes this application for the pathigam. The meaning of the pathigam and the word here are “Nallūr Perumanēyambānē”, which can be seen. “Namban” means one who is trustworthy and can be attained.

Therefore, addressing Him as “Nāthanē Nallūr Mēvum Perumana Nambane”, he bestows this Thiruppathigam, saying, “It is time to attain the shadow of Your feet.” The Lord’s divine feet are sometimes called shade. The Lord’s divine feet remove the heat of worldly existence for those who have attained them.

Therefore, the Lord’s divine feet are metaphorically called shade.

Here, “Mey Nīzhal” is spoken of as the Lord’s divine feet. “Mey” means eternal. It means that which is true and indestructible. “It is time to attain such a shadow,” says Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman, singing this Thiruppathigam. “Pauruvam Idhu” means this is the appropriate time, ripened and mature. We have seen that the intention is to remove the suffering of birth and worldly attachments of all who came to witness the wedding and to unite them under the shade of our Lord’s sacred feet.

Have all the people who came to witness the wedding attained the shade of the sacred feet at the same time? Is that possible? Yes, it is possible. As the Sivagnana Siddhiyar states, ‘Everything is cultivated by us, and the seedling appears in it, the spring will pass.’ Such a thing can also happen.

Here, Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman is present as the guru of divine wisdom. It means that souls, who have attained maturity and are eligible for liberation through the gaze, grace, and divine words of the guru of divine wisdom, have gathered here to witness the wedding. Pillaiyar has, with divine intention, perceived the state of all souls with such maturity gathered there and has thus bestowed.

Thus, Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman bestows this Thiruppathigam, saying, “This is the time for all to attain liberation.” “Pauruvam” means time. As the Sivagnana Siddhiyar states, “Time, at God’s command, becomes an auxiliary cause.” According to this, the principle of time aids the command of the Lord. By the Lord’s command, the principle of time also aids souls in attaining salvation and liberation.

Therefore, Pillaiyar, understanding the divine will, and with the intention of removing the worldly attachments of all who came to witness the wedding, appealed and bestowed this Thiruppathigam. The Thiruppathigam sung thus begins with Kallūr Perumanam. The third Tirumurai, the one hundred and twenty-fifth Thiruppathigam, composed in the tune of Anthazhi Kurinji. This Thiruppathigam belongs to the sacred place of Thiru Perumanallur, also known as Āchāzhpuram. The Thiruppathigam is as follows: Thiruchitrambalam. The meaning of the ninth verse is as follows: Brahma, who resides in the cool red lotus, and Vishnu, do not know even a little of Lord Siva’s greatness.

“Now, the meaning of the tenth verse is: O Jains and Buddhists, who lack the knowledge to realize the Lord, come! Do not argue and cling to the wrong path, but come and join the righteous path of Siddhanta Saivism. Come! Join the righteous path of Siddhanta Saivism.

“Here, having commanded the Namachivaya Thiruppathigam, he made all who heard it eligible for liberation. This is the place where Pillaiyar’s consort resided.

“Hence, it is called Āchāzhpuram. It is located a short distance east of Kollidam, near Sīrkāzhi. It is also said to be a place with Āchā trees. The Lord’s name is Sivālōka Thyāgar, and the Goddess is Thiru Vennīrrumai. The sacred water is Panchāksara Theertham. There are eight sacred waters seen by sages in eight directions.

The wedding festival of Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman in Vaikāsi Mūlam and the divine forms of Thiru Gnanasambandhar Peruman with his consort are unique specialities of this place. These are the notes about the place Thiru Nallūr Perumanam.
